Adelaida's wedding will be postponed again, in order to have both weddings on the same day – what a poetic touch! Do compose a poem on their engagement, for goodness' sake, why waste time running around the room. Tonight, they'll have a visit from Belokonskaya, and by the way, she's arrived; they'll be having guests. They'll introduce him to Belokonskaya, although he's already familiar with her; they'll probably announce it aloud. They're only afraid that he might trip or break something when he enters the room as a guest, or that he might stub his toe – he's quite clumsy."

Every genuine poet is bound to be a Columbus. America existed for centuries before Columbus, but only Columbus was able to find it. The multiplication table and the concept of R-13 have existed for centuries, but only R-13 was able to discover a new El Dorado in the virgin expanse of numbers. Indeed: is there happiness wiser, cloudless, than in this marvelous world. Iron – rusts; the ancient God created the ancient man, that is, one prone to error – and thus made a mistake. The multiplication table is wiser, more absolute than the ancient God: it never – understand, never – makes a mistake. There are no happier numbers living according to the eternal, unshakeable laws of the multiplication table. No wavering, no illusions. Truth is one, and the true path is one; and this truth is two plus two, and this true path is four. And wouldn't it be absurd if these happily, perfectly multiplied twos – began to think about some freedom, that is, a clear – mistake? For me, it is an axiom that R-13 grasped the most fundamental, the most essential...

Chichikov sat in his carriage, which had been rolling along the cobblestone road for a long time, in a perfectly good humour. It was already apparent in the previous chapter what the main subject of his tastes and inclinations was, and it was no wonder that he soon became completely absorbed in it, body and soul. His hypotheses, reckonings, and considerations, wandering about on his face, were, it seemed, very pleasant, for they left behind them a trail of a satisfied smile every minute. Occupied with these, he paid no attention to how his coachman, who was pleased with the respect shown him by Mimanilov's domestics, was making some very shrewd remarks to the well-bred coach-horse, harnessed to the right-hand side. This well-bred coach-horse was cunning and showed only for appearance' sake that it was pulling the load, while the real work was being done by the sturdy little brown horse, with a golden mane, known as the Counsellor because it had been purchased from a nobleman. This horse was working from the heart, so that even their eyes betrayed the pleasure it derived from it. "Shrewd, shrewd! I'll catch you out! - said Selifan, raising himself up and lashing the lazy horse with his whip. - Know your business, you German trousers! The brown horse is a respectable one, it fulfils its duty, and I will give it a bit extra because it is a respectable one, and the Counsellor is a good horse too... Well, well! what are you whinnying for? You numbskull, listen when they speak! I, a simpleton, won't bother to teach you anything. Look where you're slouching! - Here he lashed it with his whip, adding 'Oh, savage! You cursed Bonypart!' Then he shouted at them all: 'Hey there, good fellows!' and tapped them all three with the whip, not as a punishment, but to show that he was pleased with them. Having derived this pleasure, he turned to the well-bred coach-horse again: "You think you're fooling anyone. No, behave honestly, when you want to be shown respect. That's how we were at the squire's place, good people. I'd be glad to chat with a good man; a good man is always a pleasant friend; to have a cup of tea or a snack - willingly, if he's a good man. A good man is shown respect by everyone. That's why everyone respects our squire because he, listen, fulfilled his state service, he was a collegiate counsellor..."

Occupied by them, he paid no attention to how his coachman, content with the treatment of Muenihoff's servants, made very sagacious remarks to the prancing chestnut horse harnessed to the right side. This chestnut horse was rather cunning and only pretended to be pulling, while the genuine brown and prancing piebald, named Zasedatel because he was bought from some assessor, worked with all his heart, so that even in their eyes, it was noticeable that he was enjoying the pleasure he derived from it. "Be cunning, be cunning! I'll outsmart you! — Selifan said, sitting up and lashing the idle horse with his whip. — You know your job, you German, you numbskull! The brown horse is a respectable one, he fulfills his duty, and I will gladly give him an extra measure because he is a respectable horse, and Zasedatel is a good horse as well... Ah, ah! What are you wriggling your ears for? You fool, listen when someone is speaking! I won't have the bother of teaching you, you ignorant one. Look where you're crawling! — He lashed the horse with his whip again, adding, "Oh, barbarian! Damned Bona-part you are!" Then he yelled at all of them, "Hey, you, dear people!" and struck them all three with his whip, not as a punishment, but in order to show that he was pleased with them. Having indulged in this pleasure, he again turned to the chestnut horse, "Do you think you can hide your behavior? No, live according to truth, when you want to be treated with respect. That's how the gentleman, our former master, was. I would be delighted to talk to you, if you are a good man; with a good man we are always good friends, refined companions; we can have tea or have a snack with pleasure if the person is good. Everyone shows respect to a good man. That's why everyone respects our barin, because he, you hear, fulfilled his public service, he was a councilor of the realm..."

She's got it in for me more than anything. She keeps appearing in my dreams every night: all the times she laughed at me in front of someone else. That's just how it is, brother. She goes to the wedding with me, but she's forgotten all about me, just like she forgets to change her shoes. I haven't seen her in five days, because I don't dare to go to her; she'll ask: "Why have you come?" She's embarrassed me more than enough...

No, he didn't regard her as a child! He was terrified by her new looks and her new words lately. Sometimes he thought she was holding back too much, restraining herself too much, and this frightened him. Indeed, he had tried not to think about it all these days, chasing away those heavy thoughts, but what lay hidden in her soul? This question had long been tormenting him, although he believed in her soul. And now all this had to be resolved and revealed right this very day: a terrible thought! And again – "this woman"! Why did he always think that this woman would turn up at the very last moment and tear apart his whole fate, like a rotten thread? He was so convinced of it, and this was something he was willing to swear to, although he was almost in a delirium. If he tried to forget her lately, it was only because he was afraid of her. Did he love this woman or hate her? He had never asked himself that question today; his heart was clear, he knew who he loved... It wasn't so much the meetings of the two of them that he was afraid of, not their peculiarity, not the reason for their meeting, which was unknown to him, not the permission for whatever it might be – he was afraid of Nastasya Filippovna herself. He recalled, after a few days, that in those feverish hours he often saw her eyes, her gaze, and heard her words – strange words, though some of them stuck in his memory after those feverish and dismal hours. He hardly remembered how Vera brought him lunch and he ate, or whether he slept after lunch or not; he only knew that he started to distinguish everything clearly in that evening only from the moment when Aglaya suddenly came onto the veranda and he jumped up from the sofa and went out into the room to meet her: it was a quarter to eight. The Emperor of Tang in the inner sanctum was informed of this, and he was overjoyed. He asked again, "That monk, what benefits are there in this nine-ring staff?" The Bodhisattva replied, "This staff of mine is made of copper with iron rings, and is adorned with nine sections of evergreen clematis. To hold it in one's hand dispels the sight of the dullness of bones and skin; to descend the mountain, one walks on white clouds. It can lead to Mount Tianning and roam around the Jade Pupils. Without being polluted by the slightest dust, it is a good companion to the monks who ascend to Mount Taiping."

The Emperor, upon hearing this, immediately ordered the cloak to be unfolded, and from top to bottom, he carefully examined it and found that it was indeed an excellent item. He said, "High-ranking Elder, I will not deceive you, I am now widely opening the teachings and cultivating the fields of blessings. There is a large number of monks gathered at the temple of Huaizheng, expounding the teachings. Among them, there is one with a profound virtue and merits, whose dharma name is Xuanzang. I will buy these two precious items and bestow them upon him. What is your asking price?" The Bodhisattva heard this and clasped his palms together in devotion, and with a loud voice, he invoked the Buddha's name. He then bowed and said, "Since he has virtues and merits, I am willing to give it to him without asking for money."

Having said this, he stepped back and departed. The Emperor hastily grabbed hold of him, nearly pulling him up from his seated position on the throne. "You originally said the cloak cost five thousand pieces of silver and the staff two thousand pieces," he asked, "Since you saw me wanting to buy it, why not give it to me for free? Are you suggesting that I rely on my imperial position to demand your item? This is not reasonable at all. I will pay the original price and compensate you. Please do not refuse."

The Bodhisattva rose from his seat and said, "I have a vow in mind, originally, I said I have reverence for the Three Jewels, see goodness and rejoice in it, and I am devoted to the Buddha's teachings, without asking for money, willing to give it to him. Now I see Your Majesty's virtuous deeds and preventing evil, reverence for the Buddha's teachings, and since there is a high-ranking monk with virtue and merits, who is expounding the great teachings, it should be offered to him, I will not accept any money. I am willing to leave this item behind and return."

The Emperor saw his persistent and sincere request and was greatly pleased, and immediately ordered the Grand Temple to hold a simple meal to express gratitude. The Bodhisattva, however, firmly declined and took his leave, going straight to his temple again without being mentioned further.

The emperor of the Tang on the imperial throne heard the words, and upon hearing them, he was overjoyed, and asked again, "That monk, what are the benefits of the staff of nine rings?" When it mingles with the five ancestors at the Heavenly Vow Platform, it breaks the barriers of the mortal realm. K. stopped and looked down at the floor. He was still free, he could still continue on and slip through one of the three small, dark wooden doors in front of him. It would only mean that he hadn't understood, or that he had understood but didn't care. If he were to turn around, however, he would be trapped, since he would then have admitted that he had understood, that he was indeed the one being called, and that he would follow. If the priest had called out again, K. would certainly have gone, but since everything remained silent as long as K. waited, he did turn his head a little, since he wanted to see what the priest was doing now. He stood still on the pulpit, just as he had before, but it was clear that he had noticed K's head movement. It would have been a childlike game of hide-and-seek if K. hadn't turned completely around. He did and was beckoned closer by the priest with a flick of his finger. Since everything could now be openly done, he walked – he did it out of curiosity and to cut the matter short – towards the pulpit with long, flying strides. He stopped at the first pews, but the priest thought the distance was still too great, so he stretched out his hand and pointed with his sharply pointed finger at a spot just in front of the pulpit. K. followed him in this too, he had to bend his head back far to see the priest at that spot. "You are Josef K.," the priest said and raised a hand on the railing in an indefinite movement. "Yes," K. said, thinking about how openly he had always had his name mentioned, and how it had become a burden for him lately; now people he met for the first time knew his name, how nice it was to introduce himself first and then be known. "You are accused," the priest said particularly quietly. "Yes," K. said, "I have been informed of it." "Then you are the one I'm looking for," the priest said. "I am the prison chaplain." "Ah, so," K. said. "I summoned you here," the priest said, "to speak with you." "I didn't know it," K. said. "I came here to show an Italian the cathedral." "Let's not bother with trifles," the priest said. "What's in your hand? Is it a prayer book?" "No," K. replied, "it's an album of the city's sights." "Put it down," the priest said. You, of course, reader, think that he said to himself, 'I have spent all my life enjoying all of P.'s gifts; my education, governesses, and the cure for idiocy went to Switzerland for tens of thousands; and now I'm with millions, while the noble character of P.'s son, not to blame for his father's foolish and forgetful blunders, dies from lessons. Everything that went to me, by justice should have gone to him. These enormous sums, spent on me, in essence were not mine. This was only a blind error of fortune; they were meant for P.'s son. They should have been spent on him, not on me – the offspring of P.'s fanciful and forgetful whim. If I were completely noble, delicate, just, I should have given him half of my inheritance; but since I am first of all a man of calculation and too well understand that this is not a matter of law, I won't give him half of my millions. But, at least, it would be too low and shameless (the scion forgot that he is not being prudent) of me, if I don't return to him now the tens of thousands which went to my idiocy from P.'s son. There's only one question: one's conscience and justice! For what would have been done to me, if P. hadn't taken me in and instead worried about his son?'

There was nothing to be done, Kolya, red-faced, agitated, and speaking in a quivering voice, continued reading: "But while our swift millionaire was, so to speak, basking in the Elysian fields, a quite fortuitous circumstance occurred. One morning, a visitor arrived, with a calm and stern face, with courteous, yet just and fair speech, dressed modestly and nobly, with a visible progressive tinge in his thoughts, and in two words explained the reason for his visit: he was a well-known lawyer; he had been entrusted with a case by a young man; he came in his name. This young man is none other than the son of the deceased P., although he bears a different name. The profligate P., having seduced in his youth one honest, poor girl from the lower classes, yet European in upbringing (with, of course, the participation of the baronial rights of his former serf status), and noticing the inevitable, but nearest consequence of their liaison, gave her away in marriage to one man who was already deeply in love with her, a man with a noble character and one who was employed and industrious. At first, he helped the newlyweds, but soon his help was refused by the noble character of her husband. Time passed, and P. gradually forgot about the girl and his son born to her, and then, as is known, he died without making any provision. Meanwhile, his son, who was born in a legitimate marriage, but grew up with a different surname and was completely adopted by his mother's noble husband, and despite the fact that he was completely disinherited by the deceased, was left with nothing but his meager means and a suffering, crippled mother in a remote province; he himself in the capital earned his living by teaching merchant lessons, and thus supported himself at first in the gymnasium, and later as a listener to useful lectures, with a future goal in mind. But how much would a Russian merchant pay for lessons by the guilder, especially with a sick, crippled mother, who eventually made his life in a remote province almost impossible with her own death? Now the question is: how should the heir decide justly? You, of course, think, reader, that he said to himself: 'I have spent my whole life using all P.'s wealth; tens of thousands went on my education, on governesses, and on the treatment for my idiocy in Switzerland; and now I am with millions, while the noble character of P.'s son, who is not guilty of any transgressions of his thoughtless and forgetful father, perishes from teaching. Everything that went to me should have gone to him. The huge sums spent on me were not really mine; it was only a blind error of fate; they belonged to P.'s son. They should have been used on him, not on me – the product of the fanciful whimsy of the thoughtless and forgetful P. If I were truly noble, delicate, and just, I should have given him half of my inheritance; but as I am a calculating person and understand perfectly well that this is not a matter of law, I will not give him half of my millions. But it would be too low and shameless (the heir forgot that it is not very reasonable) for me not to return now those tens of thousands that went to my idiocy from P.'s son. There is only one thing – my conscience and justice! For what would have happened to me if P. had not taken me in for upbringing, and instead had looked after his son?'"

There was nothing to be done, Kolya, red and flushed, excited, with an agitated voice, continued reading: "But as the prompt millionaire was, so to speak, in his empyrean, a completely external circumstance occurred. One fine morning a visitor appeared before him, with a calm and stern face, with polite but worthy and just speech, dressed modestly and nobly, with a visible progressive hue in thought, and in a few words explained the reason for his visit: he was a well-known attorney; he had been entrusted with a case by a young man; he came on his behalf. This young man was nothing more or less than the son of the late P., although he bore another name. The amorous P., having seduced in his youth a decent, poor, but European-educated maid from the ranks of serfs (though, naturally, with a touch of baronial privilege, having passed the estate of serfdom), and having noted the inevitable but immediate consequence of his connection, quickly married her off to one trading and even serving man with a noble character, who had already long loved this girl. Initially he helped the newlyweds, but soon he was refused assistance by the noble character of her husband. Some time passed, and P. gradually forgot both the girl and his son by her, and later, as is known, died without making any dispositions. Meanwhile, his son, born already in a legitimate marriage but grown up under another surname and completely adopted by the noble character of his mother's husband, who, however, had long since died, remained completely on his own means and with a sick, suffering, legless mother in one of the distant provinces; while he himself, in the capital, earned his living by teaching merchant's lessons daily, and used the money to support himself first in a gymnasium, and then as a listener to useful lectures, with a future goal in mind. But how much would a Russian merchant pay for lessons for a ruble, and to boot with a sick, legless mother who, in the end, did not ease his situation at all with her death in a distant province? Now the question arises: how should the heir have judged in fairness? You, of course, reader, think that he would have said to himself, "I have used all of P.'s benefits throughout my life; I went to Switzerland with tens of thousands for my education, for governesses, and for curing my idiocy; and now I have millions, while the noble character of P.'s son, who was not guilty of any fault of his thoughtless and forgetful father, dies from teaching. Everything that went into me should have gone into him in fairness. These enormous sums, which were spent on me, were, in essence, not mine. It was just a blind fortune's error; they should have followed P.'s son. They should have been used on him, not on me – a product of a fanciful whim of a thoughtless and forgetful P. If I were entirely noble, delicate, fair, I should have given him half of my inheritance; but as I am first and foremost a practical person and very well understand that it is not a legal matter, I won't give him half of my millions. But, by all that's holy, it would be too low and shameful (the heir forgot that he was not being practical) for me not to return now those tens of thousands that went into my idiocy from P. to his son. That is one thing and only one – conscience and fairness! For what would have happened to me if P. had not taken me in for education and instead taken care of his son?'"

"Disciple, I'm just bowing to him, why not you just bow to him too, and stand by the side, laughing away. What's the reason for that?" The Monkey King said, "You don't know, this one's got his head in his pocket and his tail outside, he deserves a beating, but I only spared him because he shows respect to the Buddha, and he let him off. If he had received my respects, would he still dare to take it? Since I was a kid, I've never been a fan of bowing to people, not even when I met the Jade Emperor or the Supreme Lord Laojun, I'd just nod in acknowledgement and that was enough."

Tripitaka said, "Not a good child! Don't talk nonsense! Get up quickly, don't miss the road!" Only then did the master get up and start preparing to leave for the West.

"Disciple, you see me kneel down, you also wouldn't bow to him once, and yet you're standing there grinning. What's the reason for that?" The Monkey King said, "You wouldn't know, someone with a concealed head and a visible tail, I should have given him a good beating just for his sake, but since the Bodhisattva has shown him mercy, he still dares to accept my old Sun's bow? Old Sun has been a good fellow since childhood and never knew what it means to bow to others, not even to the Jade Emperor or the Most High Jade Purity, I just nod and smile at them and that's it." Tripitaka said, "Not a proper child! Don't talk nonsense! Get up quickly, we mustn't miss our journey." That master only stood up and started packing to head west.

"Disciple, I'm about to kowtow to him, and you're right here beside me, just laughing and finding it amusing, what's the reasoning behind this?" The Monkey King said, "You wouldn't understand, since he's a menace who's prone to hiding his true intentions and revealing his tail, I should thrash him to teach him a lesson, just so I could spare his face for the Bodhisattva's sake. Now, he has it too good for his own good, and he still dares to receive my homage? I, the old Sun Wukong, have been a good man since I was young and didn't know the meaning of bowing down to anyone, even if I were to meet the Jade Emperor or the Great Emperor of the Heavens, I would only bow my head slightly in respect. "The Master of the Law said, "You are not a true disciple! Stop talking nonsense! Get up quickly, don't waste time and ruin our journey!" That old master finally stood up, gathered his belongings, and set off towards the west."

"Disciple, I'm about to kneel down; you also just bow down to him and stand by the side, just watch him laugh, what's the principle? Monkey said, 'How would you know? Since he's hiding his head and showing his tail, I should thrash him; only because I'm considerate of the Bodhisattva's face, I let him get away. Would he dare accept an old Monkey's bow? From my childhood days, I've never known to bow to people; even if I see the Jade Emperor or the Great Immortal, I would just say 'yes' and that's enough.' The Tang Monk said, 'Not a filial son! Don't talk nonsense! Get up quickly, don't waste time on the road!' The master just got up and put away his belongings before leaving for the West."

"Ah, young disciple, I'm going down on my knees to pay respects, and you, why don't you go pay your respects as well, and stand beside me, laughing it off, what's the reason for that?" The Monkey said, "You wouldn't know, seeing as he's such a 'hide the head and show the tail' type, I should've given him a good scolding just to see the Bodhisattva's face, but I spared him, and now he still dares to accept my venerable Master Sun's prostration? From a young age, I've always been a good fellow and never knew how to kowtow to anyone, even if it was to the Jade Emperor or the Supreme Patriarch, I'd just give a humble nod and that would suffice." The Tang Monk said, "Not a filial son! Don't speak nonsense! Get up quickly, we mustn't miss our journey!" The Master only just stood up and busied himself preparing to set off westward.

The next day, the Emperor Zhen set the morning court, gathered his ministers and generals, and wrote an imperial decree for the mission, using the auspicious seal. The chief astronomer presented a report, saying, "Today is a propitious day for humans, fitting for embarking on a long journey." The Tang Emperor was overjoyed.

He also received a memorial from the Director of the Imperial Household, stating that his younger brother, the Master of the Law, was waiting outside the palace gates to receive an imperial edict. The Emperor immediately summoned the Master of the Law to the upper throne and said, "Brother, today is an auspicious day for travel. Here is a passport for safe passage. I also have a purple-gold bowl to present to you for use along the way. Please select two reliable attendants and a silver-hoofed horse for your long journey. You can now depart."

Xuanzang was overjoyed and humbly thanked the Emperor, accepted the gifts, and showed no sign of hesitation. The Emperor, surrounded by many officials, escorted Xuanzang to the border. As they approached the border, they saw a monk from the Hongfu Temple and his disciples waiting with Xuanzang's winter and summer clothing.

The Emperor ordered the officials to collect Xuanzang's luggage and mount his horse. Then he bade them bring wine and wine cups. The Emperor raised his cup and asked, "Brother, what is your Buddhist name?" Xuanzang replied, "I am but a humble monk, I dare not claim a title."

The Emperor said, "At that time, the Buddha spoke of a collection of three Sutras in the West. Would you, brother, like to take one of the Sutras as your title? How about being called 'Three Sutras'?" Xuanzang thanked the Emperor, accepted the wine, and said, "Your Majesty, drinking wine is the first precept of monks. As a layman, I am not skilled in drinking wine."

The Emperor said, "This occasion is different from all others. This is plain wine, and I invite you to drink only one cup to fulfill my parting gift. The Three Sutras will not be refused." Just as Xuanzang was about to drink, the Emperor bent down and took a pinch of dust from his fingers and dropped it into the wine.

The next morning, the Emperor set the throne, gathered officials from the literary and military bureaus, and composed an imperial edict for sending a Buddhist pilgrim on a journey. The Director of the Bureau of Astrology submitted a memorial saying, "Today is a day auspicious for the Bodhi star, favorable for embarking on a long journey." The Crown Prince was overjoyed. As the Grand Minister of the Privy Affairs Bureau announced, "His Highness the Buddhist Master is waiting at the gate." The Emperor immediately dispatched a messenger to the Treasure Hall to proclaim, "His Highness, today is a propitious day for departure. This is a document granting passage through the various passes. I have another alms bowl, made of purple gold, to send with you on your journey. Furthermore, choose two escorts for the long journey and a silver-studded horse, and give them to support your travel. Set off now." Xuanzang was overjoyed, thanked the Emperor, accepted the gifts, and had no intention of tarrying. The Emperor mounted his carriage and, accompanied by many officials, escorted him to the frontier pass. As they reached the pass, he saw that the monks from the Hongfu Temple, along with their disciples, were all waiting there to hand over Xuanzang's winter and summer garments. The Emperor ordered the officials to gather up his luggage and horse before having them pour wine from a ceremonial vessel. The Emperor raised his cup and asked, "Your Highness, what is your monastic name?" Xuanzang replied, "As a monk, I dare not assume a name." The Emperor said, "When the Buddha said that the scriptures in the Western Heaven were the Tripitaka, why not use the Tripitaka as your name?" Xuanzang thanked the Emperor, accepted the wine cup, and said, "Your Majesty, wine is the first prohibition for monks. As a layman, I do not know how to drink." The Emperor said, "Today's circumstances are different from any other. This is plain wine, only drink this one cup to fulfill my intention of sending you off." The Tripitaka hesitated but did not refuse. As he held the cup in his hand, he saw the Emperor bend his head and pick up a small amount of dust from the floor with his finger and flick it into the wine.

The next morning, the Emperor Taizong held court and assembled the high officials, wrote an imperial decree for the expedition, and affixed his imperial seal. The official in charge of astrology presented a memorial saying, "Today is an auspicious day for humans, suitable for embarking on a long journey." The Emperor Taizong was overjoyed. The Grand Master of Ceremonies presented a memorial saying, "The Emperor's younger brother, a Buddhist master, has come to the gate, awaiting orders." Immediately, the Emperor summoned the Buddhist master to the imperial throne, saying, "Today is an auspicious day for the journey. Here is the pass decree. I also have a purple-gold bowl to present to you as you journey on. I have selected two more attendants for the long journey, and a silver saddled horse to aid your footsteps. You can now depart." Xuanzang was overjoyed, thanked the Emperor, and took the gifts without any hesitation. The Emperor Taizong boarded his imperial carriage, accompanied by many officials, and escorted Xuanzang to the border, where they saw the monk from the Temple of Great Fortune and his disciples waiting with Xuanzang's winter and summer clothing at the border. The Emperor Taizong instructed them to tidy up Xuanzang's baggage and horses, then had officials pour wine. Emperor Taizong lifted his cup and asked, "What is your honorary name?" Xuanzang replied, "I am a humble monk, unworthy to have an honorable name." The Emperor Taizong said, "At that time, the Bodhisattva said that the western heaven has the three canons. You may take your name from them, what name would you like to choose?" Xuanzang thanked the Emperor again, took the imperial wine, and said, "Your Majesty, wine is the first prohibition for monks, and I, as a layperson, do not know how to drink wine." The Emperor Taizong said, "This journey today is different from other occasions. This is plain wine, and I just want to give it to you as a farewell gift. Just drink this one cup to signify my good wishes." Xuanzang could not refuse, took the wine, and just as he was about to drink, the Emperor Taizong bent his head, picked up a pinch of dust with his finger, and flicked it into the wine.

The next morning, the emperor held court, gathered his civil and military officials, wrote the imperial decree of pilgrimage, and affixed the imperial seal. The celestial offices submitted, "Today is an auspicious day with a heavenly star that is auspicious for a long journey." The king was overjoyed. He then received a memorial from the Chamberlain stating, "The imperial younger brother is waiting for an audience outside the gate." He immediately summoned the Chamberlain to ascend to the imperial throne, saying, "Imperial younger brother, today is an auspicious day for departure. This is the decree for passing through. I have also given you a purple-gold bowl, to use as an alms bowl during your travels. In addition, I have selected two attendants to accompany you, and given you a horse with a silver bridle, to help you on your distant journey." Xuanzang was greatly pleased, and immediately expressed his gratitude, took the gifts, and without any hesitation, set off. The king led his imperial carriage, accompanied by many officials, and escorted him to the border, where they saw the monks of the Hongfu Temple, together with their disciples, waiting at the border with all of Xuanzang's winter and summer clothing. The king ordered the officials to gather up his luggage and horses, then told them to serve him wine. The emperor raised his cup and asked, "What is the honorific title you are known by, imperial younger brother?" Xuanzang replied, "As a monk, I am not bold enough to take a title." The emperor said, "At that time, the Buddha said that there are three Sutras in the West. Can you identify the Sutras, and take that as your title, and be called 'Sutra Master'?" Xuanzang expressed his gratitude, accepted the imperial wine, and said, "Your Majesty, wine is the first of the Eight Precepts of monks. As a monk, I am not skilled at drinking wine." The emperor said, "This occasion is different from other times. This is plain wine, only drink this one cup, in order to consummate my intention of bidding you farewell." The Tripitaka hesitated no more, accepted the wine, and just as he was about to drink, the emperor bowed his head, and with his imperial fingers, picked up a clump of dust and patted it into the wine.

The next morning, the Emperor Gaozong convened court, gathered civil and military officials, and wrote a document for his pilgrimage. He affixed his imperial seal, allowing free passage. The Astronomical Observatory reported, "Today is a propitious day for human affairs, suitable for long journeys." The Emperor's face lit up with joy. The Chamberlain then reported, "His Imperial Brother, the Grand Preceptor, is waiting at the gate for an audience." The Emperor then ordered, "His Imperial Brother, today is a propitious day for departure. This is the passage permit. I have another gift, a purple-glazed bowl, which you can use for alms-giving on your journey. Choose two attendants and one horse with silver-bell harness, to serve as companions for your long journey." Xuanzang was overjoyed and expressed his gratitude, accepting the gifts, and had no intention of lingering. The Emperor ordered his carriage and, accompanied by many officials, escorted Xuanzang to the pass. There he saw the monks of the Temple of Great Fortune and his disciples waiting outside the pass, each holding a bundle of winter and summer clothing. The Emperor saw this and ordered his attendants to tidy the luggage and horses. He then had his officials hold a vessel and pour wine. Emperor Gaozong raised the cup and asked, "Your Imperial Brother, what is your honorific title?" Xuanzang replied, "I am a humble monk, not worthy of a title." Emperor Gaozong said, "As the Bodhisattva once said, the Western Heaven has the Three Baskets of Scripture. Your Imperial Brother may take the scriptures and assume the title of Three Baskets. How does that sound?" Xuanzang expressed his gratitude and accepted the cup of wine, saying, "Your Majesty, wine is the first prohibition of monks. As a layman, I do not know how to drink wine." Emperor Gaozong said, "This is not like other occasions. This is plain wine, and I wish to bid you farewell with it. Just drink this one cup." The Three Baskets did not dare refuse. After accepting the wine, he was about to take a sip when Emperor Gaozong leaned forward, picked up a pinch of dust with his imperial finger, and flicked it into the wine.

The Bodhisattva led the multitudes into the hall and after paying respects to the Jade Emperor, he met with the Old Lord and the Queen Mother, and they all sat down. He then asked, "How was the Peony Feast?" The Jade Emperor replied, "Every year we hold the feast, and there is great joy and jubilation. However, this year, the mischievous monkey caused trouble, and it was a pretentious invitation." The Bodhisattva asked, "Where did the mischievous monkey come from?" The Jade Emperor replied, "The mischievous monkey was born from the stone egg of Flower Fruit Mountain in the Ao Lai Kingdom of the Eastern Victory Land. When he was born, he possessed the power to shoot golden light, piercing the Heavenly Treasury. At first, no one paid much attention to him, but later, he cultivated himself and subdued dragons and tigers. He even took his own life away. The Dragon King and the King of the Underworld reported this to me. I wanted to capture him, but Long Geng star spoke up and said, 'In the three realms, anyone with nine orifices can become a immortal.' I thus dispatched wise officials to enlighten him and promoted him to the Upper Realm, appointing him the Official in Charge of the Royal Steeds and the Stable Master. He, however, looked down on his office and revolted against the heavenly palace. I then ordered Li Tianwang and Nezha the Prince to persuade him to surrender. I also issued a decree to calm him down, and promoted him to the Upper Realm, appointing him the Great Sage Equal to Heaven. However, he did not abide by the law, and as he had no income, he took the large peaches from the old trees and ate them all. When the time for the feast arrived, I did not invite him, but he designed to deceive the Barefoot Immortal, disguising himself to attend the feast, and he stole all the heavenly delicacies and heavenly wine. He even stole the Old Lord's elixir and a great deal of heavenly wine, taking it away to enjoy with the monkeys on his mountain. I am thus troubled by this, and therefore mobilized ten million heavenly troops and a heavenly net to capture him. But one day passed, and I do not know the outcome of the battle."

The Bodhisattva led the multitude inside, and, upon greeting the Jade Emperor, they all took their seats. Then they asked, "What was the occasion of the Peach Banquet this year?" The Jade Emperor replied, "Every year, we hold the banquet in celebration, but this year, the mischievous Monkey Spirit created chaos, making the invitation mere formalities." The Bodhisattva asked, "Where did the Monkey Spirit originate?" The Jade Emperor said, "The Monkey Spirit was born from the rocks of Flower Fruit Mountain in the Beidi Prefecture of the Eastern Golden Island. When he was first born, he emitted golden light from his eyes and shot it into the Imperial Authority. Initially, I didn't pay much attention to him. He subsequently refined his form, subdued dragons and tigers, and ruthlessly killed his enemies. Thereupon, the Dragon King and the King of the Underworld reported him to me. I sought to capture him. Longgan the Star interceded and said, 'Throughout the Three Worlds, anyone with nine orifices can become a transcendent.' I then bestow upon him enlightened knowledge, promoted him to the Upper Realm, and appointed him as the official in charge of the Stables. The official was dissatisfied with his position and rebelled against the Heavenly Court. I then ordered Li the Heavenly King and Nezha the Prince to capture him, and even sent an edict to reassure and promote him, promoting him to the Upper Realm and bestowing upon him the title of 'Peerless Great Sage.' However, he was given no stipend. He, with nothing to do, wandered to the East and strayed to the West. I was afraid that he might cause more trouble, so I ordered him to manage the Peach Banquet Garden. He, however, refused to follow the law and recklessly ate all the big peaches from the old trees. By the time the banquet was set up, he was no longer employed, and he wasn't invited. He then devised a plan to deceive the Ancestral Immortal, and in disguise, he attended the banquet, stealing all the immortals' delicacies and liquor. He even stole some of the Old Master's elixir and a certain amount of imperial liquor, taking it to share with the monkeys on the mountain. My heart was troubled by this, so I sent a force of ten million heavenly soldiers and used the Heavenly Net and the Earthly Net to subdue him. To this day, I've yet to see any results, and I do not know whether I've succeeded or not."

Buddha invited the multitude to enter, and, upon arriving, he performed ceremonial rites with the Jade Emperor, after which he met with Laojun and Wangmu, and they all sat down. He then asked, "What about the Peaches of Immortality banquet?" The Jade Emperor replied, "Each year I host a banquet in celebration, filled with joy and festivity. This year, however, the mischievous monkey caused a commotion, and it was a futile invitation indeed." 

Buddha asked, "Where did the mischievous monkey come from?" The Jade Emperor replied, "The mischievous monkey originated from the Flawless Mountain on the Eastern Ocean's Proudness Country, and was born from a rock egg. At the time of its birth, it emitted golden light and shot upwards, piercing the Heaven of Effulgence. Initially, I did not take it seriously, but it later became refined and conquered dragons and tigers, and even self-exterminated its own register. The Dragon King and King of the Underworld then reported to me. I wanted to apprehend it, but Long Geng Star interceded, saying, 'In the Three Realms, any being with nine apertures may become a transcendent.' I then granted it education and promoted it to the heavens, appointing it the Marquis of the Stables and the Protégé of the Heavenly Steeds. It, however, grew tired of its humble position and rebelled against the heavenly court. I then dispatched Li Tian Wang and Nezha, the Prince, to pacify it, and issued a decree to soothe and appease it, promoting it to the heavens and appointing it the 'Great Sage Equalling Heaven.' Although it held a high position, it had no stipend. As a result, it had no occupation and indulged in carefree wandering. I was again concerned that it might cause more trouble, so I appointed it to manage the Peach Garden. But it did not follow the law and ate all the large peaches from the old trees. When the banquet was finally set, I did not invite him as he had no stipend. He then devised a plan to deceive the Barefooted Immortal, disguising himself as his appearance and eating all the divine delicacies and divine wine. He even stole Laojun's elixir and a substantial amount of imperial wine to take back to his troop of monkeys to enjoy themselves. My heart was filled with frustration, and I ordered ten million heavenly soldiers and the Heavenly Nets and the Earthly Nets to apprehend it. But on this day, I have seen no return on my efforts and do not know the outcome."

The Bodhisattva led the assembly in, after paying homage to the Jade Emperor.  They sat down, then asked, "How was the Peaches banquet?" The Jade Emperor replied, "Every year, I would hold it, and all the gods would be joyful.  This year, the mischievous Monkey King caused trouble and made the invitation utterly futile." The Bodhisattva asked, "Where did the Monkey King originate from?" The Jade Emperor replied, "The Monkey King was born in the Flower Fruit Mountain of the Brazen Capital in the Eastern Florescent Land.  When he was born, a golden light shot out of his eyes, striking the Heavenly Juvenal.  He did not receive much notice at first, but gradually, he refined himself, tamed dragons and tigers, and reduced his name from a mortal to a saint.  Then, the Dragon King and the King of Hell reported to me.  I wanted to capture him, but the Long Geng Star was summoned and stated, 'In the three realms, any one with nine orifices can attain immortality.'  I therefore granted him instruction, allowed him to ascend to heaven, and appointed him as the Grand Marshal of the Stable of Horses and the Ward of the Heavenly Steeds.  He hated the honor because it was too lowly, and turned against the Heavenly Palace.  I then dispatched Li the Heavenly King and Nezha the Prince to capture him, but instead, I dispatched a summons to pacify him, and let him ascend to heaven.  I gave him the title of the Great Sage Equal to Heaven, but he had no income.  He had nothing to do, so he wandered east and west.  I then feared that some new trouble might arise, so I ordered him to take charge of the Peaches Garden.  He disobeyed the law and secretly ate all the old peaches, the most valuable of the trees.  At the time of the gathering, since he was an official without an income, I did not invite him.  He then devised a plan to deceive the barefoot Daoist, stole all the delicacies and wine of the immortals, and also stole the old immortal's elixir and a great deal of imperial wine.  He went and enjoyed himself with his fellow monkeys on his mountain.  I was troubled by this and therefore ordered the dispatch of ten million heavenly soldiers and the heavenly net to capture him.  But today, we have not seen any results, and do not know whether he was captured or not."

The Bodhisattva brought all the guests into the hall, and, after paying his respects to the Jade Emperor, sat down with the Old Master and the Mother Wang.  He then asked, "What about the Grand Peaches Banquet this year?" The Jade Emperor replied, "We always hold the banquet annually, and it's always filled with joy and festivity. But this year, a mischievous monkey caused trouble, making the invitation empty and hollow." The Bodhisattva inquired, "Where did the mischievous monkey come from?" The Jade Emperor replied, "The mischievous monkey was born from an egg on Flower Fruit Mountain in the Flower Fruit Mountain country of the Eastern Victory Island. When it was first born, it emitted golden light, shooting towards the astronomical mansion. At first, we didn't pay much attention to it. As it grew stronger, it became powerful and could tame dragons and subdue tigers. But then it claimed to be self-deified and erased its name from the official register. The Dragon King and the King of the Underworld reported this to me. I wanted to capture it, but the Long Geng star advised me that 'in the three realms, any being with nine apertures can become a immortal.' I then summoned him and instructed him to ascend to the heavenly realm, and appointed him as an official overseeing the divine horses. But he was dissatisfied with the official position and rebelled against the heavenly court. I then ordered the Li Tian Wang and the Great Sage Nezha to pacify him and summon him to the heavenly realm, and I issued a decree to pacify and comfort him. I promoted him to the position of 'Heavenly Great Sage.' Although he was an official, he had no stipend. He was idle and roamed freely, and I was afraid of him causing trouble again, so I entrusted him with the management of the Grand Peaches Garden. He didn't follow the rules, and ate all the big peaches from the old trees. When the banquet was set, he was not invited, but he devised a plan to deceive the Immortal with No Feet, and snuck into the banquet by changing his appearance. He stole all the divine delicacies and divine wine, and even stole the Old Master's elixir and a large quantity of divine wine, and took them to share with the other monkeys on his mountain. I am troubled by this, and that's why I sent a million heavenly soldiers and a net of heaven and earth to subdue him. I haven't received any news for a day, and I don't know who won or lost."

While the attendants were busy with their duties, the gentleman went into the common hall. What kind of common halls these are, every passerby knows very well: the same walls, painted with oil paint, darkened at the top by pipe smoke and besmeared with the backs of various travelers, and especially with the backs of local merchants, who, on their trading days, came here to drink their usual pair of teas; the same blackened ceiling; the same smoke-stained chandelier with numerous glass drops that would rattle and jingle every time the servant would run over the worn-out linoleum, briskly waving a tray, upon which there sat as great an expanse of tea cups as there were birds on a seaside shore; the same paintings on the entire wall, painted with oil paints – in short, all that which is everywhere; the only difference being that on one painting there was a nymph with breasts as enormous as the reader would probably never have seen them. A similar play of nature occurs on various historical paintings, brought to us from unknown times, unknown sources, and by unknown artists, sometimes even by our noblemen, art lovers, who purchased them in Italy on the advice of their couriers. The gentleman removed his cap and unwound his woollen ribbon, which a married man would have made himself, with instruction, to tie on his neck, and a bachelor, I suppose, would not know how to tie it, God only knows, I never wore one myself. Having unwound his ribbon, the gentleman ordered his dinner to be brought. Meanwhile, different common dishes served in inns, such as sour soup with a pie, conserved for passing travelers for several weeks, brains with peas, sausages with cabbage, a fried pottach, a pickled cucumber, and an eternal sweet pie, always ready for service; meanwhile, all these dishes were brought, both hot and cold, he ordered the servant, or the boy, to tell any nonsense – who had managed the inn before and who now, and how much profit it made, and was the owner a great scoundrel or not; to which the servant, as usual, replied, 'Oh, a great one, sir, a scoundrel.' As in enlightened Europe and in enlightened Russia, there are now many respectable people who, without any special occasion, cannot eat in an inn without talking to the servant, and sometimes even amusing themselves by jesting with him. However, the guest was not asking questions for nothing; he asked, with extraordinary accuracy, who was the governor of the city, who was the chairman of the board, who was the prosecutor – in short, he did not miss any notable official; but asked, even more accurately, about all the notable landowners: how many peasants each one had, how far they lived from the city, what character they had, and how often they visited the city; he inquired carefully about the state of the region: had there been any epidemic diseases in their province – fever, deadly agues, smallpox, or the like, and all this with such accuracy, which showed more than simple curiosity. In his reception, the gentleman had something dignified and blew his nose with extraordinary loudness. It is unknown how he did it, but only his nose sounded like a trumpet. This, in my opinion, quite harmless dignity, however, earned him a great deal of respect from the inn servant, so that every time he heard this sound, the servant would shake his hair, straighten up, bow more respectfully, and, bending his head down, ask, 'Is anything needed?' After dinner, the gentleman drank a cup of coffee and sat on a couch, putting a pillow behind his back, which, in Russian inns, is stuffed with something extremely similar to brick and cobblestones instead of elastic wool. At this point, he began to yawn and ordered himself to be taken to his room, where, lying down, he fell asleep for two hours. Having rested, he wrote down on a piece of paper, at the request of the inn servant, his rank, name, and surname, for the purpose of informing the authorities. On the paper, the servant, descending from the stairs, read the following: 'Councilor of State Pavel Ivanovich Chichikov, landowner, for his needs.' While the servant was still examining the note, Pavel Ivanovich Chichikov himself went to take a look at the city, which seemed to have pleased him, since he found that the city did not lag behind other provincial cities: the yellow paint on the stone buildings stood out brightly, and the grey on the wooden ones quietly darkened. The houses were one, two, and one and a half storeys high, with an eternal mansard, very beautiful, in the opinion of the gubernatorial architects. In some places, these houses seemed to be lost among the broad, like a field, streets and endless wooden fences; in other places, they clustered together, and there was more movement and life. One could see almost washed-off signs with crests and boots, sometimes with blue breeches and the signature of some Arshavsky tailor; where a shop with hats, fur caps, and the inscription: 'The Foreigner Vasily Fyodorov'; where a billiard was drawn with two players in frock coats, which we wear to the theatre, entering the stage in the last act; the players were shown with aimed cues, slightly bent hands and crouched legs, just having jumped into the air. Under all this was written: 'And that's the place.' In some places, tables were simply standing on the street, with nuts, soap, and cakes that looked like soap; where a tavern with a thick fish drawn and a fork stuck into it. Most of all, one could notice faded double-headed eagles, which are now replaced by a brief inscription: 'Drunken House.' The pavement was bad everywhere. He glanced into the city park, which consisted of thin trees, poorly standing with props at the bottom, in the shape of triangles, very beautifully painted with green oil paint. However, although these trees were not higher than a reed, they were described in the newspapers in the description of illumination, that 'our city was decorated, thanks to the civil governor's care, with a garden consisting of shadowy, broad-leaved trees, providing shade on a hot day,' and that at the same time 'it was very touching to see the citizens' hearts tremble with an abundance of gratitude and pour out streams of tears in gratitude to the gentleman governor.' Having asked the town crier in detail where one could go closer to the cathedral, to the official offices, to the governor, he went to take a look at the river, which ran through the middle of the city, tore off the posted notice from a stake, so that, having come home, he could read it carefully, looked carefully at the passing woman of not very good appearance, who was followed by a boy in a military uniform, with a bundle in his hand, and, looking around again, as if to remember the place well, went straight home to his room, supported by the inn servant on the stairs. Having eaten his tea, he sat down at the table, ordered a candle to be brought, pulled the notice from his pocket, brought it close to the candle and began to read, squinting a bit with his right eye. However, there was nothing remarkable about the notice: a drama by Mr. Kotschubey was being performed, in which Mr. Poplyavin played Rolya, Kory – Miss Zhyalova, and the other actors were even less remarkable; however, he read all of them, even reaching the price of the parterre, and learned that the notice had been printed in the gubernatorial government's printing office, then turned it over to the other side: to see if there was anything there, but, not finding anything, he wiped his eyes, folded it neatly, and put it in his box, where he was accustomed to put everything that came his way. The day, perhaps, was concluded with a portion of cold beef, a bottle of sour sauce, and a strong sleep until the night's coiled whirlwind, as they express in some places of the vast Russian state.

While the servants were attending to their duties, the gentleman went into the common room. Everyone who travels knows these common rooms well: the walls, painted with oil paint, have soot on them from the stove pipes and are speckled below with the backsides of various travelers, particularly local merchants who came here on trading days to drink their usual couple of cups of tea; the sooted ceiling; the smoky chandelier with numerous glass drops that clinked and clattered every time the orderly ran by, brandishing his tray with a flourish as he bore all the same abundance of tea cups as the sea has seagulls; the paintings on the walls, painted with oil paints; in a word, it's all the same everywhere; only one painting depicted a nymph with breasts as big as any reader might have never seen. Such a whimsy of nature is not unknown on historical paintings, imported from who-knows-when and from who-knows-where to Russia, sometimes even by our nobles, art lovers, who bought them in Italy on the advice of the carriers. The gentleman doffed his hat and unwound the woolen scarf with multicolored fringes, which wives make for their husbands, teaching them how to wrap up properly, while unmarried men – well, I wouldn't know, I've never worn such a scarf – when he finished unwinding the scarf, he ordered his meal to be brought. While he was being served various usual dishes found in inns – beet soup with a layered pie, carefully kept for travelers for several weeks, brains with peas, sausages with cabbage, fried patty, salted cucumber, and the eternal sweet pastry – all of which were served hot and cold, he ordered his orderly, or the inn servant, to tell him all the chatter about who used to run the inn and who now does, and whether they make a profit, and whether the innkeeper is a sly one. To which the orderly, as usual, replied, "Oh, yes, sir, a big cheat." Just as in enlightened Europe, so too in enlightened Russia, there are many respectable people who cannot eat at an inn without talking to the innkeeper, and sometimes even making fun of him. However, the traveler wasn't asking idle questions; with great precision, he inquired about the governor, the head of the court, the prosecutor – in a word, he didn't miss a single notable official – and with even greater precision, and almost with participation, he inquired about all the notable landowners: how many serfs each has, how far they live from the city, what kind of characters they are, and how often they come to the city; he inquired carefully about the condition of the region: were there any epidemic fevers, deadly agues, smallpox, or anything similar; and all this in such detail and with such precision that it showed more than mere curiosity. In his mannerisms, the gentleman had something dignified and he cleared his throat with great noise; I don't know how he did it, but his nose resounded like a trumpet. This, in my opinion, completely innocent dignity earned him a great deal of respect from the innkeeper's servant, so that every time he heard this sound, he would ruffle his hair, straighten up respectfully, and, bending his head down from above, ask if anything was needed? After lunch, the gentleman drank a cup of coffee and sat down on the divan, placing a pillow behind him, which in Russian inns is stuffed with something extremely similar to brick and cobblestone instead of elastic thread. Then he began to yawn and ordered the innkeeper's servant to take him to his room, where, lying down, he fell asleep for two hours. After resting, he wrote on a scrap of paper, at the innkeeper's request, his rank, name, and surname for communication with the authorities. As the innkeeper was going down the stairs, reading the note, which was scrawled in the following words: "Kollegial Councilor Pavel Ivanovich Chichikov, landowner, for his own convenience." When the innkeeper was still examining the note, Pavel Ivanovich Chichikov himself went out to see the city, which seemed to him to be just like other provincial cities: the yellow paint stood out on the stone houses, and the gray on the wooden ones was subdued; the houses were one, two, or one-and-a-half stories high, with a perpetual mezzanine, very pretty, in the opinion of the city architects. Sometimes these houses seemed to be hidden in the broad, like a field, streets and endless wooden fences; sometimes they were crowded together, and it was noticeable that there was more movement of people and animation there. There were almost washed-off signboards with boot tops and loafers, somewhere with blue breeches and the inscription of some Arshavsky's tailor; somewhere there was a store with hats, caps, and the inscription: "Foreigner Vasiliy Fyodorov"; somewhere there was a billiard table with two players in opera coats, as they wear on our stages when they enter the stage in the final act. The players were depicted with aimed cues, slightly bent hands, and slanted legs, just as they had made a sudden splash in the air. Under it all was written: "And this is the establishment." Sometimes tables stood simply on the street, with walnuts, soap, and prunes that looked like soap; somewhere there was an eating house with a painted thick fish and a fork stuck into it. Most of all, however, you could notice the dark double-headed eagles, which are now replaced by a concise inscription: "Public House." The road was everywhere wretched. He looked into the city park, which consisted of thin trees that had taken root poorly, with props at the bottom in the shape of triangles, very beautifully painted with green oil paint. However, these little trees were no taller than reeds; but it was said in the newspapers in the description of the illumination that "our city was decorated, thanks to the civic administrator, with a park consisting of shady, broad-branched trees, providing shade on a hot day," and that, at the same time, "it was very touching to see the citizens' hearts tremble with gratitude and pour forth streams of tears as a sign of appreciation for the patronage of the governor." After inquiring carefully of the beadle where he could go closer, if needed, to the cathedral, to the official places, to the governor, he went to take a look at the river flowing through the middle of the city, tore off the posted notice attached to the post, so that, having arrived home, he could read it thoroughly, looked intently at the woman of not-so-beautiful appearance walking along the wooden sidewalk, followed by a boy in a military livery, with a package in his hand, and, glancing around again as if to remember the place well, he went straight home to his room, accompanied by the innkeeper's servant. After having tea, he sat down at the table, ordered a candle to be brought, took out the notice from his pocket, held it to the candle, and began to read, narrowing his right eye slightly. However, there was nothing remarkable in the notice: a drama by Mr. Kozebo, in which Mr. Poplyevin played the role of Rollo, Cora was played by Miss Zhyabolova, and the other characters were even less notable; yet he read all of them, even reached the price of the parterre, and learned that the notice was printed at the governor's chancellery; then he turned it over to the other side: maybe there's something there too; but finding nothing, he rubbed his eyes, folded it neatly, and put it in his box, where he had a habit of putting everything that came his way. The day, it seems, was closed with a serving of cold meat, a bottle of sour soups, and a strong sleep throughout the evening, as they say in other parts of the vast Russian state.

As the servants bustled about, the master made his way to the general hall. One knows what these halls are like, since they can be found in any inn: the same walls painted with oil-based paint, which had darkened with the smoke of pipes at the top and were stained with the backsides of all sorts of travelers, and particularly those of native merchants, as these would often visit here on market days to drink a couple of cups of tea; the same soot-stained ceiling; the same candlelit chandelier, adorned with a multitude of glass ornaments that would clink and clatter every time the footman scurried along the creaking floorboards, carrying a tray with as many tea cups as there were seagulls on a beach; the same oil paintings on the wall, painted with oil-based paint – in short, everything was the same as everywhere else; the only difference being that one of the paintings depicted a nymph with such enormous breasts that a reader, for certain, had never seen anything like it. It is a trick of nature, by the way, that occurs in various historical paintings, which, at some unknown time, from an unknown place, and by unknown hands, had been brought to Russia, and occasionally even by our nobles, who had bought them in Italy at the advice of their couriers.

The master removed his hat and unwound the woolen, rainbow-colored tress that his wife had prepared for him, giving him instructions on how to wear it properly, or rather, how not to get himself entangled in it. It is not clear to me who does this for bachelors, but I, for one, have never worn anything like this. After unwinding the tress, the master ordered his dinner to be brought. While this was being served, he was offered various dishes common to inns, such as stew with a layered pie, which had been kept for travelers over several weeks; brains with peas; sausages with cabbage; fried pottage; pickled cucumbers; and the ever-present sweet layered pastry. Everything was served both hot and cold, and the master ordered the footman, or more accurately, the servant, to regale him with all manner of gossip – about who used to run the inn and who now did, and how much profit it brought, and whether their master was a great scoundrel or not. The servant, as was his habit, replied, "Oh, a big one, sir, a great scoundrel." Just as in enlightened Europe, so too in enlightened Russia there are a great many respectable people who cannot dine at an inn without talking to the servant, and sometimes even making merry at his expense. However, the traveler did not ask all empty questions; he asked with the utmost precision about the governor, the chairman of the board, the prosecutor – in short, he did not miss any of the important officials; but he asked with even greater precision, if not with a certain air of superiority, about all the significant landowners: how many serfs each of them owned, how far from the city they lived, what sort of character they had, and how often they came to the city. He asked about the state of the province: had there been any epidemics in their province – cholera, deadly fevers, smallpox, or the like – and all this with such detail and precision that it seemed more than mere curiosity. In his mannerisms, the master had something dignified, and he blew his nose with great force. It is not clear how he did it, but only that his nose sounded like a trumpet. This quite innocent trait, I believe, earned him great respect from the inn servant, so that every time he heard this sound, the servant would shake his head, straighten up respectfully, and, bending his head as far back as he could, ask, "Is there anything you need?" After dinner, the master sipped a cup of coffee and sat on the couch, propping himself up with a pillow, which in Russian inns they fill with something very similar to brick and cobblestone. At this point, he began to yawn and ordered himself to be taken to his room, where, lying down, he fell asleep for two hours. After resting, he wrote on a scrap of paper, at the request of the inn servant, his rank, name, and surname, to be reported to the proper authorities. On the piece of paper, the servant, going down the stairs, read the following: "Pavel Ivanovich Chichikov, landowner, according to his own needs." While the servant was still examining the note, Pavel Ivanovich Chichikov himself went out to take a look at the city, which seemed to please him, since he found that it was not inferior to other gubernatorial cities: the yellow paint on the stone buildings was very striking, and the gray on the wooden houses was discreetly subdued. The houses were of one, two, or one and a half stories, with a permanently annexed mezzanine, which was very pretty, according to the opinion of the gubernatorial architects. In some places, these houses seemed to be lost among the broad, like a field, streets and endless wooden fences; in other places, they clustered together, and it was clear there was more movement and bustle. One would occasionally catch sight of water-worn signs with boots and wooden clogs, sometimes with blue trousers and a sign reading "Arshavsky, tailor"; where a shop selling caps, greatcoats, and a sign reading "Foreigner Vasily Fyodorov"; where a billiards game was painted with two players in tailcoats, which we wear at the theater in the final act on stage; the players were depicted with shotguns cocked, their hands slightly raised, and their legs bent at an angle, just having made a jump. Under it all was written: "And that's the establishment." In some places, simply on the street, tables were set out with nuts, soap, and pastries that looked like soap; where a tavern was painted with a thick fish and a fork stuck into it. More often than not, one could see dark double-headed eagles, which had long since been replaced with a laconic inscription: "Pity Inn." The pavement was bad everywhere. He looked into the city park, which consisted of thin trees that had taken root poorly, propped up at the bottom with triangles, which were very attractively painted with green oil-based paint. However, though these trees were no higher than a stalk of wheat, they had been described in the papers as a "shade that had adorned the city, thanks to the care of the civil governor, consisting of shady, broad-branched trees that provided a coolness on a hot day," and that it was very moving to behold how the hearts of the citizens trembled with gratitude and shed tears of appreciation to the lord governor. Having asked the city crier in detail where one could go closer to the cathedral, to the presence, to the governor, he set out to take a look at the river flowing through the city, pulled off the notice stuck to a post as he walked, in order to read it thoroughly when he got home, looked intently at the woman of poor appearance walking along the wooden sidewalk, followed by a boy in a military livery, carrying a bundle under his arm, and, taking a second glance at everything as if to commit it to memory, went straight to his room, accompanied on the stairs by the inn servant. Having eaten his tea, he sat down at the table, ordered a candle to be brought, pulled out the notice from his pocket, held it up to the candle, and began to read, half-closing his right eye. However, there was nothing remarkable in the notice: there was a drama by Mr. Kozebue, in which Mr. Poplyavin played the part of Rollo, Zhyablova played the part of Core, and the other actors were no more remarkable; however, he read them all, even getting to the price of the parterre, and found out that the notice had been printed in the typographer's office of the gubernatorial administration, then turned it over to see if there was anything on the other side, but finding nothing, he rubbed his eyes, neatly folded it up, and put it in his small box, where he usually kept everything that came his way. It seemed to him that the day was ended with a portion of cold beef, a bottle of sour soup, and a sound sleep through the entire night, as they say in some parts of the great Russian state.

The waiters bustled about; the gentleman meanwhile made his way into the common room. Everyone who has ever passed through this land knows what these common rooms look like: the same walls, painted with oil paint, discolored by the smoke of the stoves and marked by the backsides of various travelers, and especially those of more savage and unrefined merchants, who came in on market days to drink their regular two cups of tea; the same blackened ceiling; the same chandelier, smoked to a dark gray, with a multitude of suspended glass globes that would rattle and clatter every time the servant ran past on his wobbly clogs, briskly carrying a tray loaded with as many teacups as there are birds on a seaside shore; the same paintings covering the entire wall, painted in oil; in short, everything was just as it was everywhere, with the only difference that on one of the paintings a nymph had been depicted with breasts of such enormous size that the reader could hardly ever have seen any such. Nature, one must note, plays tricks of this sort on many historical paintings, which have been imported from God knows where, by God knows who, to Russia, and sometimes even by our nobles, who are connoisseurs and have bought them in Italy on the advice of their guides.

The gentleman removed his cap and unraveled the woolen clout with colorful fringe that his wife had knitted for him, armed with useful instructions on how to tie it properly, and for bachelors, I don't know who does it, God knows, I've never worn such a clout. Unraveling the clout, the gentleman ordered to bring him his meal. Up to this point, the waiter had been bringing him all the usual dishes found in inns, such as, say, stew with a layered pie, carefully set aside for travelers over the course of several weeks, mashed brains with peas, sausages with cabbage, fried potted meat, salted cucumber, and the ever-present sweet pastry, always at the ready; all this was brought to him either warmed up or cold, and he ordered the waiter, or rather the servant, to regale him with idle chatter – about who used to run the inn and who ran it now, and how much income it made, and if the owner of the inn was a big rogue. After his meal, the gentleman sipped a cup of coffee and sat on the divan, placing a pillow behind his back, which in Russian inns is stuffed with something very much like brick and cobblestone instead of elastic wool. He began to yawn and ordered the servant to take him to his room, where he lay down and fell asleep for two hours. After resting, he wrote on a scrap of paper, at the request of the innkeeper's servant, his title, name, and surname for notification to the authorities. Most of all, however, it was noticeable that the two-headed state eagles had been soot-stained, which are now replaced by a laconic inscription: 'Drinking establishment.' The pavement was everywhere quite rough. He glanced into the city park, which consisted of thin trees that had become sickly and had supports at the bottom in the shape of triangles, very nicely painted with green oil paint. However, although these trees were no higher than a reed, they had been described in the newspaper as part of the illumination, as 'our city was decorated, thanks to the care of the civic administrator, with a park of shady, spreading trees that provided shade on a hot day', and that it was 'very charming to see the hearts of the citizens beating with gratitude and spouting streams of tears in gratitude to our ruler'. Having asked the town crier for directions on where to go closer to the cathedral, to the city institutions, to the governor, he went to look at the river running through the middle of the town, tore off an advertisement stuck to a post, in order to read it properly when he got home, took a good look at the woman with a not-very-pleasant face walking along the wooden sidewalk, followed by a boy in a military livery with a package under his arm, and having taken a second look around, as if to memorize the location of the place, he went home directly to his room, escorted lightly up the stairs by the innkeeper's servant. After having tea, he sat at the table, ordered to bring him a candle, pulled out the advertisement from his pocket, held it up to the candle and began to read, squinting slightly with his right eye. The day, it seems, was concluded with a portion of cold beef, a bottle of sour soup, and a sound sleep right through the entire creaking of the linings, as people in certain parts of the vast Russian state are wont to express.

While the servants were busy and fiddling around, the master went into the main hall. What these common halls are like, every traveler knows very well: the same walls painted with linseed oil paint, darkened up top by pipe smoke and scrawled with the backsides of passing travelers, even more native-looking and more so by the merchant class, since merchants came here on trading days and drank their customary pair of cups of tea; the same charred ceiling; the same soot-covered chandelier with numerous glass drops that would jump and jingle every time the servant would run past on worn-out linoleum, brandishing a tray with a mountain of teacups like birds on a seashore; the same paintings on the wall, painted with linseed oil, all the way around, – in short, everything was the same as everywhere; the only difference was that one of the paintings depicted a nymph with breasts as large as any reader would never have seen.
