The master took off his hat and unwound the woolen, multicolored headscarf his wife had made for him by hand, which he wore around his neck, providing him with suitable instructions on how to wrap it, and which, presumably, I couldn't tell you who would make for bachelors, God knows, I've never worn such headscarves. Unwinding the headscarf, the master ordered the servant to bring him a meal. While he was being served the usual dishes found in inns, such as: beet soup with a layered pie, saved for travelers for several weeks, brains with peas, sausages with cabbage, fried pult, salted cucumber, and a forever ready sweet pie, he ordered the servant, or the boy, to tell him all sorts of nonsense – who used to run the inn before and who now, and whether they brought in a lot of income, and whether their owner was a big cheat. To which the servant, as usual, replied: "Oh, big one, sir, a swindler." Just like in enlightened Europe and in enlightened Russia, there are now a lot of respectable people who can't eat at an inn without talking to the servant, and sometimes even making a witty remark at their expense. However, the traveler was not asking pointless questions; he asked with extreme accuracy who the governor of the city was, who the chairman of the court was, who the prosecutor was – in short, he didn't miss a single high-ranking official; but he asked even more accurately, if not with any particular enthusiasm, about all the significant landowners: how many peasants each one had, how far they lived from the city, what kind of character they were, and how often they came to the city; he asked carefully about the condition of the region: had there been any widespread diseases – fevers, deadly agues, smallpox, and the like, and all of it in such detail and with such accuracy that it showed more than just simple curiosity. In his mannerisms, the master had something dignified and smacked his nose extremely loudly. It's unknown how he did it, but only his nose rang out like a trumpet. This, in my opinion, completely harmless dignity had, however, earned him a lot of respect from the inn servant, so that every time he heard this sound, the servant would shake his hair, straighten up more respectfully, and, bowing his head from the top, ask: "Do you need anything?" After dinner, the master drank a cup of coffee and sat on the divan, placing a pillow behind his back, which, in Russian inns, is filled with something very similar to brick and cobblestones. Then he began to yawn and ordered to have himself taken to his room, where, lying down, he fell asleep for two hours. Having rested, he wrote on a piece of paper, at the inn servant's request, his rank, name, and surname for reporting to the authorities. When the servant, going down the stairs, read the note aloud, saying: "Count P. I. Chichikov, landowner, by necessity," the servant was still unfolding the note when Count Pavel Ivanovich Chichikov went out to see the city, which seemed to have pleased him, as he found that the city in no way lagged behind other gubernatorial cities: the yellow paint on the stone houses was striking, and the grey on the wooden ones was modestly dark. The houses were one, two, and a half stories high, with a permanent mezzanine, very beautiful, in the opinion of the city architects. Sometimes these houses seemed lost amidst the broad, like a field, streets and endless wooden fences; sometimes they crowded together, and here one could see more movement of the people and liveliness. There were almost washed-out billboards with boots and umbrellas, sometimes with blue trousers and the inscription of some Arshavsky tailor; where a store with caps, boots, and the inscription: "Foreigner Vasiliy Fedorov"; where a billiard table was depicted with two players in frock coats, which we wear to the theater, entering the stage in the last act; the players were shown with aimed cues, hands slightly thrown back, and crooked legs, just about to make a leap. Under it was written: "And this is the establishment." In some places, tables were simply standing on the street with nuts, soap, and pastries that looked like soap; where a tavern with a depicted fat fish and a skewer stuck into it. Most of all, one could see the dark double-headed state eagles, which are now replaced by a concise inscription: "Drinking hall." The road was in a sorry state everywhere. He looked into the city garden, which consisted of thin trees, poorly taking root, with supports at the bottom in the shape of triangles, very beautifully painted with green linseed oil paint. However, although these saplings were not higher than a reed, it was said in the newspapers in the description of the illumination that "our city was adorned, thanks to the care of the civil governor, with a garden consisting of shaded, broad-leaved trees, providing shade on a hot day," and that at this "it was very touching to see the hearts of the citizens tremble with gratitude and pour streams of tears in gratitude to the lord of the city." After asking the beadle in detail where one could go closer, if necessary, to the cathedral, to the respectable places, to the governor, he went to look at the river, flowing through the middle of the city, tore off the glued-on advertisement on a post, so that, having arrived home, he could read it carefully, took a close look at the passing along the wooden sidewalk woman of poor appearance, who was followed by a boy in a military greatcoat with a bundle in his hand, and, glancing around one more time, as if to remember the place well, went home straight to his room, accompanied by the inn servant who slightly supported him on the stairs. After having his tea, he sat down at the table, ordered the servant to bring him a candle, took the advertisement from his pocket, brought it closer to the candle, and began to read, narrowing his right eye slightly. However, there was nothing remarkable in the advertisement: a drama by Mr. Kozebub was being given, in which Rola was playing Mr. Popovlev, Kor was Zheblov, the other characters were less notable; however, he read them all, even got to the price of the parterre and found out that the advertisement was printed in the typography of the gubernatorial government, then he turned it over to the other side: perhaps there was something on the other side as well, but not finding anything, he rubbed his eyes, folded it neatly, and put it in his trunk, where he had the habit of storing everything that came his way. It seems the day was concluded with a portion of cold beef, a bottle of sour broths, and a strong sleep until the morning, as they say in other parts of the great Russian state.

The words of kindness still linger in my ears, but how long must I wait to see the Heavenly Sea? Monkey King Sun Wukong pressed his forehead and flew straight to Flower Fruit Mountain. He walked along the road, and suddenly he heard the cries of a crane and the wails of monkeys. The crane's cry pierced the sky, and the monkeys' wails were so pitiful and heart-wrenching. Immediately he opened his mouth and called out, "My sons, I'm here too!"

A multitude of monkeys, big and small, leaped out from the cliff below, among the grasses and trees. They encircled Monkey King, knocking their heads and saying, "Great King, be at ease! Why have you been away for so long? We've been stuck here, eagerly waiting for your return! Lately, we've been tormented by a devil who's trying to occupy our Water Curtain Cave. We're willing to risk death and forget our lives to fight him. This devil has even stolen our fire, caught many of our descendants, and made us lose sleep day and night, guarding our territory. We're lucky that you've come! If you don't come back next year, we'll all belong to others!"

Monkey King heard the words and his heart filled with anger. "What kind of devil is this, that dares to act so shamefully?" he said. "You tell me more details, and I'll go and exact revenge." The monkeys bowed their heads and said, "We beg Great King to inform you that this devil calls himself the Master of the Devil World and resides in the direction of the North."

Monkey King asked, "How many miles is it from here to his place?" The monkeys replied, "He comes in clouds and goes in mist. Sometimes it's windy, sometimes it's rainy, sometimes it's thunderous, sometimes it's electrifying. We don't know how many miles it is." Monkey King said, "Since it's like that, don't be afraid. Just play and have fun, and I'll go find him for you."

Monkey's reminders still linger in my ears, when will the time come to see the East Sea? Monkey pressed his head against the cloud, went straight to Flower Fruit Mountain. As he walked, he suddenly heard the cry of a crane and the wail of a monkey. The cry of the crane soared high up to the Heavens, and the wail of the monkey was full of sorrow and anguish. Monkey immediately opened his mouth and called out, "My children, I have come too!" Beneath the precipice, on the stone steps, among the flowers and grass, among the trees, monkeys big and small jumped out in the thousands and the millions, gathering around Monkey King, knocking their heads on the ground and saying, "Great King, don't worry! Why have you been away for so long? You've been away from us for such a long time, leaving us in such great anxiety! Recently, a monster has been bullying us here, trying to take over our Water Curtain Cave. We're willing to die in order to fight against him. This time, he took away our fire and caught many of my nephews, making us sleepless through the day and the night, guarding the household. Thank the heavens, Great King has come! If the Great King doesn't come back next year, we monkeys will all belong to him!"

Monkey listened and his heart filled with great anger, saying, "What kind of monster is he, daring to behave like this? You tell me the details, and I'll go and take revenge." The monkeys all knocked their heads on the ground, "Report to Great King, the monster calls himself the Supreme Demon King, and lives at the north below." Monkey said, "How many miles is it to his place?" The monkeys said, "When he came, it was cloudy, and when he left, it was foggy, sometimes windy, sometimes rainy, sometimes with thunder and lightning, and we don't know how many miles it is." Monkey said, "Since it's like this, don't be afraid, you monkeys just play around, and I'll go look for him and come back."

The parting words still linger in my ears, when suddenly I see the dawn of the East Sea. Monkey King pressed his palm against the cloud, then straight away went to Flower Fruit Mountain, searching for a path as he went. Just as he was listening carefully, the cries of a crane and a monkey reached him, and the cries of the crane and the wails of the monkey pierced the clouds and soared to the heavens. Monkey King suddenly opened his mouth and shouted, "The youngsters, I'm here too!" 

At the foot of the cliff, at the stone steps, amidst the flowers and grasses, and among the trees, the monkeys of all sizes, big and small, leaped out, with the Monkey King in the center, their faces covered in their hands, and exclaimed, "Great King, please be calm! Why have you been away for so long? We've all been watching for you with longing like people parched with thirst! Recently, this wicked demon has been exploiting and oppressing us here, trying to seize our Water Curtain Grotto. We had to sacrifice our lives to resist him. He took away our hearth, caught many of my younger brothers, and forced us to stay up all night, guarding our property. It's fortunate that the Great King has come! If the Great King doesn't come again next year, we'll all belong to this stranger!" Monkey King heard the words and his heart seethed with anger, saying, "What kind of demon is this, that dared to act so outrageously? You tell me more about it in detail, and I'll go look for him to take revenge." The monkeys bowed their heads and said, "We dare report to the Great King that this demon calls himself the Demon King of the World, and resides at the Northern Regions." Monkey King asked, "How many miles is it from here to his place?" The monkeys replied, "He comes in clouds and goes in fog, or with the wind, or with rain, or with thunder and lightning, we don't know how many miles it is." Monkey King said, "It's like that, don't worry, just play around and enjoy yourselves, and I'll go find him and come back!"

The words of parting are still ringing in my ears, yet I hope to see the great sea in the twinkling of an eye.  Monkey King pressed down on the cloud, heading straight for Flower Fruit Mountain. Taking a path as he went, he suddenly heard the call of a crane and the cries of apes, the sound of the crane's call piercing through to the heavens, the apes' cries full of sorrow and pain. Underneath the rocky outcroppings, among the grasses and among the trees, numerous monkeys, big and small, leapt out in the thousands and tens of thousands, surrounded Monkey King in the middle, kowtowing and calling out, "Great King, please be calm! Monkey King heard this and his heart filled with anger, saying, "What kind of devil would dare to be so lawless? You tell me in detail, and I'll go look for him and exact revenge." The monkeys kowtowed, "Please tell the Great King, that fellow claims to be the King of Devils, and resides in the Northeast."

Monkey King asked, "How many stages of the journey is it to his place?" The monkeys replied, "He comes when the cloud is present and goes when the fog is present, or it's windy, rainy, or thunderous or with lightning, and we don't know how many stages there are." Monkey King said, "Since it's like that, don't be afraid, just keep playing around, and wait for me to go find him and come back."

The words of good counsel still linger in my ears, when shall I see him suddenly at the East Sea. Monkey King pressed on his head the clouds, and headed straight for Flower Fruit Mountain. Walking along the path, he suddenly heard the cry of a crane and the sorrowful shriek of a monkey, the cry of the crane resounded to the Han-dynasty heavens, the shriek of the monkey was so pitiful and moved him so much. When entering, he almost stumbled because there was a step behind the door. "One doesn't take much notice of the public," he said. "One takes no notice at all," said the court usher. "Just look at the waiting room." It was a long corridor from which unworked wooden doors led to the individual sections of the top floor. Although there was no direct influx of light, it was not entirely dark because some sections had instead of uniform board walls mere, but extending to the ceiling wooden grilles, through which some light penetrated and through which one could see individual officials sitting at tables or standing at the grilles, observing the people on the corridor through the gaps. There were, probably because it was Sunday, only a few people on the corridor. They made a very modest impression. In almost regular intervals from one another they sat on the two rows of long wooden benches that were installed to either side of the corridor. All were slovenly dressed, although most, judging by their facial expression, posture, beard fashion, and many, barely ascertainable, small details, belonged to the higher classes. As there were no coat racks, they had put their hats, probably following the example of one another, under the bench. When the one sitting nearest the door spotted K. and the court usher, they rose to greet, and since those behind saw them do so, they also felt they had to greet, so that all stood up as the two passed by. They stood never fully upright, their backs bent, their knees bent, they stood like beggars on the street. K. waited for the court usher, who was walking a bit behind him, and said, "How humiliated they must be." "Yes," said the court usher, "they are all accused, all the ones you see here are accused." "Really," said K. "Then they are my colleagues." And he turned to the next one, a big, slender, almost grey-haired man. "What are you waiting for?" K. asked politely. The unexpected address, however, left the man bewildered, and this looked all the more awkward since it was clearly a well-traveled person who, elsewhere, no doubt, knew how to keep himself in hand, and would not easily relinquish the superiority he had acquired over many. Here, however, he did not know how to answer a simple question and looked at the others as if they were obligated to help him, and as if no one could ask him for an answer if that help were lacking. Then the court usher stepped forward and said, to calm and encourage the man, "The gentleman here is only asking what you're waiting for. Do answer." The man, probably known to the court usher, seemed calmer, "I'm waiting—" began, but then stalled. Apparently, he had chosen this beginning in order to precisely answer the question, but now he couldn't find the continuation. Some of the waiting people had moved closer and stood around the group, and the court usher said to them, "Step aside, step aside, let the corridor clear." They moved back a bit, but not to their earlier seats. In the meantime, the questioned man had collected himself and answered, even with a small smile, "I made some motions for evidence in my case a month ago and I'm waiting for them to be processed." "You seem to be making a great effort," said K. "Yes," said the man, "it's my case, after all." "Not everyone thinks like you," said K., "I, for example, am also accused, but I, as true as I want to become blessed, neither made a motion for evidence nor undertook anything of the kind. Do you think it's necessary?" "I don't know exactly," said the man again in complete uncertainty; he probably thought K. was joking with him, and so would have liked to repeat his earlier answer out of fear of making some new mistake, but at K.'s impatient glance he only said, "As for me, I made motions for evidence." "You don't believe that I'm accused?" asked K. "Oh please, certainly," said the man, and took a step to the side, but in his answer there was not faith but fear. "You don't believe me?" asked K. and, unconsciously prompted by the humble nature of the man, grasped him by the arm as if he wanted to force him to believe. But he didn't want to cause him pain, had only grasped him lightly, yet the man screamed as if K. had not taken hold of him with two fingers but with a scorching tongs. This silly screaming made K. utterly fed up; if one didn't believe him that he was accused, so much the better; perhaps they even thought him a judge. And K. grasped him firmly now as a farewell, pushed him back onto the bench, and continued on his way. "Most of the accused are so sensitive," said the court usher. Behind them, almost all the waiting people were now gathering around the man who had stopped screaming, and seemed to be questioning him about the incident in detail. Just then, a guard came up to K., who was mostly recognizable by a saber he wore, the scabbard of which, at least in color, was of aluminum. K. was amazed and even reached out to touch it with his hand. The guard, who had come due to the screaming, asked about the incident. The court usher tried to calm the man with a few words, but the guard explained that he needed to look into it himself, saluted, and went on, his very hasty but very short, probably due to gout, strides.

— A non-Christian faith, to start with!— Prince spoke again with extreme agitation and excessive vehemence, — it's a non-Christian faith first and foremost, and in the second place, the Roman Catholic faith is even worse than atheism, that's my opinion! Yes, that's my opinion! Atheism only preaches nothingness, while Catholicism goes further: it preaches a distorted Christ, one who has been slandered and blasphemed, an opposite Christ! It preaches anti-Christ, I swear to you, I assure you! It's my personal and long-held conviction, and it's tormented me... The Roman Catholic faith believes that the church cannot stand on earth without universal state power, and it cries out: "Non possumus!"[31]. In my view, Roman Catholicism is not a faith, but rather the resolute continuation of the Western Roman Empire, and in it everything is subordinated to this thought, starting from faith. The Pope has seized the land, the earthly throne, and taken up the sword; since then everything has continued like this, with the addition of lies, cunning, deceit, fanaticism, superstition, crime, and the people's most holy, true, simple, and ardent feelings, they have traded everything for money, for lowly earthly power. Atheism started from them first and foremost: could they believe in themselves? It's taken root from their disgust towards them; it's the fruit of their lies and spiritual weakness! Atheism! He whistled a tune, jumped into the air, took out his Dragon Seeing Eye, and looked around, but there was no sign of the horse anywhere. He descended back to the mountain and reported to his master, "Master, I'm afraid the demon has eaten our horse, and I've looked around but can't see it." The Tang Monk said, "My disciple, how could that demon have such a big mouth that it could swallow our big horse whole, including the saddle and bridle? Maybe it was startled and fled into a valley. Take a closer look again." 

The Monkey King said, "You don't know my abilities. My eyes are accustomed to seeing over a thousand li of auspicious and inauspicious signs. Just like how I can see a cicada spreading its wings a thousand li away, I shouldn't be unable to see that big horse!" The Tang Monk said, "If it really has eaten it, how can we proceed? Oh, woe is us! With the numerous rivers and mountains in front of us, how can we possibly go on?" As he spoke, his tears fell like rain. The Monkey King saw him crying and couldn't bear it any longer, bursting into a loud cry. "Master, please don't be such a crybaby! Sit down! Sit down! I'll go find that scoundrel and get my horse back for you!" The Tang Monk just grasped his hand and said, "My disciple, where are you off to?"

As he was speaking, two big, black eyes appeared in the peephole of the door and looked at the two guests for a moment before disappearing; but the door didn't open. The uncle and K. exchanged a look, confirming to each other that they had both seen the eyes. "A new maid, who's afraid of strangers," said the uncle, and he knocked on the door again. The eyes reappeared, and this time one could almost feel sorry for them, perhaps it was just a deception caused by the strong gas flame, which was burning just above their heads, producing little light. "Open up," called the uncle and pounded on the door with his fist, "we're friends of the lawyer!" "The lawyer is ill," was whispered to them from behind.

In a doorway at the other end of the corridor stood a gentleman in a dressing gown and announced this news in an extremely quiet voice. The uncle, who was already angry due to the long wait, turned around with a jerk, called out: "Ill? You say he's ill?" and took a few menacing steps towards the gentleman, as if the illness was the gentleman. "The door has been opened," said the gentleman, pointing to the lawyer's door, straightened up his dressing gown, and disappeared. The door had indeed been opened, and a young girl, K. recognized the dark, slightly puffed-up eyes, was standing in a long, white apron in the entrance hall, holding a candle. "Open it earlier next time," said the uncle, instead of a greeting, as the girl made a small curtsy. "Come on, Josef," said the uncle to K., who moved slowly in front of the girl. "The lawyer is ill," said the girl, as the uncle, without stopping, hurried towards a door. K. was still staring at the girl, while she had already turned around to shut the door again, she had a doll-like, rounded face, not just her pale cheeks and chin were rounded, but her temples and the edges of her eyebrows as well.

"Josef!" the uncle called out again, and he asked the girl: "Is it his heart condition?" "I think so," said the girl, who had found the time to move the candle forward and open the bedroom door. In a corner of the room, where the candlelight hadn't yet reached, a face with a long beard rose up from the bed. "Leni, who's there?" asked the lawyer, blinded by the candle and unable to recognize the guests. "It's Albert, your old friend," said the uncle. "Ah, Albert," said the lawyer and lay back on the pillows as if this visit didn't require any pretenses. "Is it really that bad?" asked the uncle and sat down on the bedside. "I don't believe it," said the lawyer quietly, "it's just another attack of my heart condition, and it'll pass just like the previous ones." "Possible," said the lawyer softly, "but it's worse than it's ever been. I'm struggling to breathe, I'm not sleeping at all, and I'm losing strength every day." "So," said the uncle and pressed his panama hat tightly onto his knee. "That's bad news. Do you have the right care, by the way? It's also so gloomy here, so dark. It's been a long time since I was last here, it seemed friendlier then. Even your little Fräulein here doesn't seem very cheerful, or maybe she's just pretending." The girl was still standing near the door with the candle; as much as her uncertain glance let appear, she looked more at K. than at the uncle, even when the uncle was speaking to her. K. leaned against a nearby armchair, which he had moved closer to the girl. "When one is as ill as I am," said the lawyer, "one needs to rest. It's not depressing for me." After a short pause, he added: "And Leni takes good care of me, she's a good girl." But the uncle couldn't be convinced, he was clearly biased against the nurse, and even though he didn't say anything to the sick man, he followed the nurse with stern looks as she went to the bedside, put the candle on the nightstand, leaned over the sick man and whispered to him as she tidied up the pillows. He almost forgot to consider the sick man; he stood up, paced back and forth behind the nurse, and K. wouldn't have been surprised if he had grabbed her by the back of her dress and pulled her away from the bed. K. watched everything calmly; the lawyer's illness wasn't even entirely unwelcome to him, he couldn't counter the uncle's enthusiasm for his case, and the distraction it was now experiencing without his involvement was welcome to him. "Fräulein, please, let us be alone for a bit," said the uncle, perhaps just to insult the nurse, "I have a personal matter to discuss with my friend." The nurse, who was still leaning over the sick man and smoothing the bed sheet, just turned her head and said very calmly: "You see, the gentleman is ill, he can't discuss any matters." 

This stark contrast to the uncle's speech, which was choked with rage and then overflowing with words, made her words seem mocking to a disinterested observer; the uncle, however, reacted naturally like someone being stabbed: "You wretched creature," he growled in his initial stammering rage, K. was startled, even though he had expected something like this, and he walked towards the uncle with the intention of covering the uncle's mouth with both hands. Fortunately, the sick man got up from his bed, the uncle's face darkened as if he had swallowed something disgusting, and said then calmly: "We still have our sanity; if what I'm asking for weren't possible, I wouldn't ask for it. Please, leave now!" The nurse stood up straight, facing the uncle, and stroked the lawyer's hand with one hand, K. thought he could see. "You can tell me anything in front of Leni," said the lawyer, no doubt with a pressing request. "It's not my business," said the uncle, "it's not my secret." And he turned around, as if he had decided not to engage in any negotiations anymore, but was still giving the nurse a little time to think. "Whose business is it, then?" asked the lawyer, his voice fading, and laid back on the pillow again. "My nephew's," said the uncle, "I've brought him along." And he introduced him: "This is Josef K., my nephew." "Oh," said the lawyer more lively, and stretched out his hand to K., "forgive me, I didn't even notice you. Come, Leni," said the lawyer to the nurse, "get out." "You can go," said the lawyer to the nurse, who didn't even turn around as she quickly left the room.

"Dear Uncle," said K., "the commotion is quite pointless, it's on your side and it would be on mine as well. We don't win cases with commotion; let my practical experience count for something, just like yours, even if it surprises me, and even now I very much appreciate it. Since you say that the family would also be affected by the trial – which I don't fully understand, but it's beside the point – I'll follow you in everything. But I don't think a stay in the countryside would be beneficial, as that would mean flight and feelings of guilt. Furthermore, I'm being pursued more here, but I can also tackle the matter more myself."

"That's right," said the uncle in a tone, as if they were finally drawing closer to each other, "I only made the proposal because, if you stay here, I saw that the matter was in danger of being compromised by your indifference and I thought it better for me to work for you instead. But if you want to tackle it with all your might, it's of course much better." "In that, we're in agreement," said K. "And do you have a proposal as to what I should do first?" "I have to think about the matter for myself," said the uncle, "you have to consider that I've been living on the land for nearly twenty years without interruption, and in that sense, my intuition has waned. Various important connections with personalities who might be more familiar with the situation here have loosened up on their own. I'm a bit isolated on the land, you know. It's only apparent when occasions like this arise. Partly I didn't expect your situation, even though I somehow sensed something of the sort from Erna's letter, and today I almost knew it with certainty when I saw you. But that's beside the point; the most important thing is not to lose any time." 

While he was speaking, he was standing on the tips of his toes and waving at an automobile; now, as he was yelling the address to the driver, he led K. behind him into the car. "We're going to see Attorney Huld," he said, "he was my schoolmate. You must know his name, don't you? Not? That's strange. He has a significant reputation as a defender and poverty lawyer. But I have particularly great trust in him as a person." "Whatever you do is fine with me," said K., though the uncle's hasty and urgent manner in handling the matter caused him unease. It wasn't very pleasant to be driven to an attorney as an accused person. "I didn't know," he said, "that one could engage an attorney in a case like this." "But of course," said the uncle, "that's only natural. Why not? And now tell me, so I'm well informed about the matter, everything that has happened so far." K. began to tell right away, without leaving out anything, his complete openness being the only protest he allowed himself against the uncle's view that the trial was a great shame. He mentioned Fräulein Bürstner's name only once, and casually, but that didn't detract from his openness, since Fräulein Bürstner was not connected with the case in any way. While he was speaking, he looked out the window and observed how they were approaching that very suburb where the courtrooms were located; he pointed this out to the uncle, who didn't find it especially noteworthy. The car stopped in front of a dark house. The uncle rang the doorbell immediately on the ground floor at the first door; while they were waiting, he smiled with his big teeth and whispered, "Eight o'clock, an unusual time for visits. Huld won't mind, though." In the peephole of the door appeared two big, black eyes, looked at the two visitors for a bit, and then disappeared; the door, however, did not open. The uncle and K. confirmed to each other that they had seen the two eyes. "A new maid who's afraid of strangers," said the uncle, and he knocked again. The eyes reappeared, one could almost call them sad, perhaps it was just an illusion, caused by the gas flame burning above their heads, which was zinging strongly but gave little light. "Open up!" cried the uncle, and he struck the door with his fist, "it's friends of the attorney!" "The attorney is ill," whispered something behind them. In a door at the other end of the short hallway stood a man in a dressing gown, and with extremely soft voice he made this announcement. The uncle, who was already annoyed due to the long wait, turned around abruptly, exclaimed, "Ill? You say he's ill?" and walked almost menacingly towards the man, as if the man were the sickness. "We've been let in," said the man, pointing to the attorney's door, pulled his dressing gown together, and disappeared. The door was indeed open, and a young woman – K. recognized the dark, slightly puffy eyes again – was standing in the entryway in a long, white apron, holding a candle in her hand. "Don't you open the door earlier!" said the uncle instead of a greeting, while the woman made a small bow. "Come, Josef," said he to K., who was moving slowly past the woman. "The attorney is ill," said the woman, as the uncle hurried on towards a door. K. was still staring at the woman, while she had already turned around to block the door again, she had a doll-like rounded face; not only her pale cheeks and the chin were rounded, but also her temples and the edges of her forehead. "Josef!" called the uncle again, and he asked the woman, "Is it his heart condition?" "I think so," said the woman, who had found time to move forward with the candle and open the door to the room. In a corner of the room, where the candlelight hadn't yet penetrated, a face with a long beard rose up from the bed. "Leni, who's visiting?" asked the attorney, blinded by the candle, and he didn't recognize his guests. "It's your old friend Albert," said the uncle. "Ah, Albert," said the attorney and lay back on the pillows, as if he needed to make no pretense before these visitors. "Is it really that bad?" asked the uncle and sat down on the bedside bench. "I don't believe it. It's just an attack of your heart condition and will pass, just like the previous ones." "Possible," said the attorney softly, "but it's worse than it's ever been. I'm short of breath, don't sleep and lose strength every day." "So," said the uncle and pressed his panama hat tightly onto his knee with his large hand. "That's bad news. Do you have the proper care? It's also sad here, so dark. It's been a long time since I last came here, then it seemed friendlier too. Your little Fräulein here doesn't seem to be very cheerful, or is she just pretending." The woman was still standing with the candle near the door; as far as one could tell from her vague gaze, she seemed to look more at K. than at the uncle, even when he was speaking to her now. K. leaned against an armchair that he had pushed close to the woman. "When someone is as sick as I am," said the attorney, "one needs to have peace. I'm not sad." After a small pause, he added, "And Leni takes good care of me, she's obedient." But the uncle couldn't be convinced; he was clearly biased against the caregiver, and even though he said nothing to the sick man, he followed the caregiver with stern glances as she went over to the bed, placed the candle on the nightstand, bent over the sick man, and whispered to him while adjusting the pillows. He almost forgot to take the sick man's condition into account, stood up, walked behind the caregiver, and K. wouldn't have been surprised if he had grabbed her by the skirt and pulled her away from the bed. K. watched everything calmly, even the attorney's illness was not altogether unpleasant to him, he couldn't help but feel some annoyance with the uncle's eagerness for his cause, and he was glad to accept the distraction that this eagerness now received without his intervention. 

Then the uncle said, perhaps just with the intention of insulting the caregiver, "Please, ma'am, let us have a bit of time to ourselves, I have a personal matter to discuss with my friend." The caregiver, who was still bent over the bed and was smoothing the sheet against the wall, only turned her head and said very calmly, which was strikingly different from the uncle's furious and then overflowing speeches: "You see, the gentleman is so sick, he can't discuss matters." She had probably just repeated the uncle's words out of politeness; nevertheless, they could be taken as mocking by someone uninvolved, but the uncle was certainly provoked to the core, and he exclaimed in a gurgling frenzy, "You wretched woman!" – K. was startled, even though he had been expecting something similar, and he hurried towards the uncle with the intention of clapping his hands over his mouth. Fortunately, the sick man got up from behind the woman, the uncle made a dark face as if he had swallowed something disgusting, and then said calmly, "We haven't lost our minds; if what I'm asking for weren't possible, I wouldn't be asking for it. Please, leave now!" The caregiver stood straight up beside the bed, facing the uncle, and with one hand stroked the attorney's hand, as K. thought he could see; "You can tell Leni everything," said the attorney, undoubtedly in a tone of urgent entreaty. "It doesn't concern me," said the uncle, "it's not my secret." And he turned around as if he had no intention of engaging in any negotiations, but still wanted to give some consideration. "Who is it concerning, then?" asked the attorney in a dying tone and lay back on the pillows. "My nephew," said the uncle, "I brought him with me." And he introduced: "Procurator Josef K." "Oh," said the attorney more lively and stretched out his hand to K., "forgive me, I didn't notice you. Go, Leni," said he to the caregiver, who didn't even turn around.

A monster heard these words, and repeatedly replied in a humble tone, returned the treasure staff, and had Nuwa seize him to go see Guanyin. He knelt his head down, and said: "Sage, forgive my transgressions, let me narrate my story. I am not a demon or a fiend, I am a Junior Guardian of the Folding Screen of the Divine Halls. Only because I accidentally broke the glass vase at the Peach Blossom Meeting, the Jade Emperor struck me eight hundred times, demoted me down to the world below, and made me this way; again instructed me to endure seven days, with a flying sword piercing me under my armpits, over a hundred times, thus this agony. Alas, with hunger and cold unbearable, I spent two, three days, ventured out of the waves to seek an ordinary person to eat. I never thought today I would, unknowingly, collide with the Great Compassionate Bodhisattva." 

The Bodhisattva said: "You committed a sin in heaven, having been demoted down, and now, in such a way, suffering from your injuries, this is exactly a case of sin compounded by sin. I now take the Bodhisattva's decree and seek out the Buddhist scripture person. Why don't you enter my door, take refuge in the good karma, follow that scripture person as a disciple, to pay respects to the Buddha in the West and seek scriptures? I will instruct the flying sword not to pierce you. At that time, when the task is accomplished, sin will be forgiven, and your original duty will be restored. How do you feel in your heart?"

Upon hearing the creature's words, it repeatedly answered "yes" and "yes", returned the treasure wand, and let Wuzi take it to see Guanyin. Prostrating with its head bowed, it spoke: "Bodhisattva, forgive my sins and allow me to recount my story. I am not a demonic creature, I am the folds-curtain general of the Palace of the Divine Umbrella, serving the Imperial Retinue. It was only because, at the insect- peach gathering, I inadvertently shattered a glass cup, that the Jade Emperor struck me eight hundred times, exiling me to the mortal realm, transforming me into this wretched form. Then, every seven days, I would send my flying sword to pierce me at my armpit over a hundred times, hence this constant anguish. Unable to bear the pangs of hunger and cold, in two or three days, I emerged from the waves to seek out a passerby to eat from. Unbeknownst to me, I collided with the Great Compassionate Bodhisattva today." 

The Bodhisattva said: "You committed a crime in the heavens, and upon being exiled, you now have sustained these injuries, this is truly 'sin upon sin.' I shall carry out the Buddha's will, and go to the east to find a sutra master. Why not join my teaching and take refuge in good karma, accompanying the sutra master as a disciple, and prostrate before the Buddha in the West to request the sutras? I shall instruct the flying sword not to pierce you. When the mission is accomplished, you shall be pardoned of your crimes, and restored to your original position. What is your wish?"

The monster heard the words, repeatedly assenting, took back the staff, and had Nuwa lead it to see the Bodhisattva. It kowtowed, saying: "Bodhisattva, forgive my offense, and let me explain. I am not a wicked fiend, but the Bat Roll Great General of the Spirit Palace's imperial carriage. It was only because I accidentally broke the glass vase at the Heavenspear Gathering that the Jade Emperor struck me eight hundred times, demoting me to the lower realm and transforming me into this shape; and that the jade god brings me the flying sword to pierce my side every seven days, thus causing me this anguish. Alas, I was starving and chilled, and in the past two days, I emerged from the waves to find a pedestrian to eat with. But who could have known that today, without knowing it, I would collide with the Great Compassionate Bodhisattva." The Bodhisattva said: "You committed a crime in the heavens, and after being demoted, you behave in this way, thus committing a greater sin. I have received the Buddha's decree. I shall go east to fetch the Buddhist scriptures. Why don't you come into my door and renounce your evil deeds, become a disciple of the one who fetches scriptures, and go to the West to offer incense and scriptures to the Buddha? I shall teach you to avoid the flying sword. When the task is accomplished, your sin will be expiated, and your original position will be restored, and what will be your state of mind?"

The monster spoke, repeatedly nodding and then grasped the divine sceptre, sending wood gourd back to see Guanyin. He knelt on the ground, expressing his contrition: "Bodhisattva, forgive my transgressions, let me recount my tale. I am not a fiend, I am the Vanguard of the Imperial Relay of the Palace of Numinous Trinity. It was at the gathering of cicadas that I inadvertently shattered a glass cup, and the Jade Emperor had me beaten eight hundred times and cast down to the mortal realm, transforming me into this wretched state. Furthermore, the Jade Emperor instructed me to endure the blade of the Flying Sword once every seven days, striking me a hundred times or so, causing this distress. Unable to bear the pangs of hunger and cold, I resorted to the depths of the waves to find a traveler to feed upon, only to unwittingly collide with the compassionate Bodhisattva today. "The Bodhisattva said, "You have committed a crime in heaven and have now, after being demoted, incurred this suffering – it is truly a case of sin upon sin. I have accepted the Buddhist edict and will search for the scripture-keeper. Why not convert to my teachings, become a disciple of the scripture-keeper, and together ascend to the Western Heaven to pay homage to the Buddha and seek scripture? I will instruct the Flying Sword not to pierce you. When we achieve our goal, your guilt will be absolved and your original position will be restored. How would you feel then?"

The monster spoke, repeatedly nodding its head in assent, and taking back the staff, led by Ta to see Guanyin. It bowed its head and kowtowed, saying, "Bodhisattva, forgive my transgressions, I beg you to listen. I am not a demonic being, but the Dragon Veil General of the Heavenly Palace's carriage. It was only because I accidentally smashed a glass vase at the Peach Blossom Meeting that the Jade Emperor punished me with 800 blows, demoting me to the mortal realm and transforming me into this state. I am also subject to having the heavenly sword thrust into my side every seven days, causing me such suffering. With no choice but to endure the hardships of hunger and cold, I ventured out over the waves to beg for food from a passerby, not knowing I would accidentally run into the Great Compassionate Bodhisattva today." 

The Bodhisattva said, "You committed a sin in heaven, and after being demoted, you now take on this suffering body, adding sin to sin. I will go to receive the Buddha's edict, and go to the East to seek out the scriptures. Why don't you take refuge in the path of goodness, become a disciple of the scripture seekers, and together go to West Heaven to pay homage to the Buddha and seek the scriptures? I will teach you the art of deflecting the heavenly sword, and when the mission is accomplished, you will be free of sin, restored to your former position. What will you say to this?"

— You didn't understand me, — she said, — I didn't come to you to quarrel, though I don't love you. I came to you with a human word. Inviting you, I already knew what I would say to you and I won't retract my words even if you don't understand me at all. It would be worse for you than for me. I wanted to answer your letters, and I wanted to answer you personally because it seemed more convenient to me. Listen to my answer to all your letters: for the first time I felt sorry for Prince Lev Nikolaevich on the very day we met, and when I later found out about everything that happened at your party. I felt sorry for him because he is such an innocent person and, due to his innocence, he believed he could be happy with a woman of my character. What I was afraid of for him happened: you couldn't love him, you tormented him and abandoned him. You couldn't love him because you're vain... no, I'm wrong, because you're self-absorbed, even more so: you're self-absorbed to the point of madness, and your letters to me are proof. You couldn't love him, such an innocent one, and maybe you even looked down on him and laughed at him, you could only love your own shame and your constant thought that you've been dishonored and that you've been insulted. If you had less shame or none at all, you'd be even unhappier... (Aglaya said these words with satisfaction, words that had rushed out but were already long prepared and thought out, still thought out even in her sleep when this meeting was not yet imagined; she watched with a venomous gaze the distorted face of Nastasya Filippovna as she spoke; the color of which Aglaya had not let fade even after she started speaking).

Do you remember, — she continued, — then he wrote me a letter; he says you know about this letter and even read it? This letter helped me understand everything and I did understand it correctly; he himself recently confirmed this, that is, everything I'm telling you now, word for word. After the letter, I started waiting. I guessed that you would come here because it's impossible for you to stay in the provinces; you're still too young and handsome for the provinces... However, that's not my phrase, — she added, her face having turned red with rage, and from that moment, the redness didn't fade from her face until the end of her speech. — When I saw Prince Lev Nikolaevich again, I felt such pain and offense for him. Don't laugh; if you laugh, you're unworthy of understanding this.

— You didn't understand, she said, — I didn't come here to quarrel with you, though I don't love you. I... I came here with a human voice. I had decided what I would tell you and I wouldn't budge, even if you didn't understand me at all. That would only be worse for you, not for me. I wanted to answer your letters personally because it seemed more convenient to me, and I implore you to listen to my answer to all your letters: it was only when I met Prince Lev Nikolayevich and found out what had happened on your evening party that I began to feel sorry for him for the first time. I felt sorry for him because he's such a simple-minded person and in his simplicity believed he could be happy... with a woman... of my character. What I was afraid of came true: you couldn't love him, you tormented him, and left him. You couldn't love him because you're vain... no, I was mistaken, because you're vain to the point of madness, and your letters to me are proof of it. You, a simple person like that, couldn't love him, and perhaps you even secretly despised and laughed at him, and could only love your shame and the continuous thought that you'd been shamed and insulted. If you had less shame or none at all, you would be even more wretched... (Aglaya enjoyed saying out loud these words that had been bursting to be said, but had been long prepared and thought out; she had thought them out even in her sleep, when the present meeting hadn't seemed possible; she watched with a venomous gaze how the distorted face of Nastasya Filipovna reacted to her words; she had that look prepared for her, not quite with the intention of affecting her, but with the intention of completely exposing her).

Do you remember, she continued, — then he wrote me a letter; he says you know about that letter and even read it? From that letter I understood everything, and I understood correctly; he recently confirmed this to me himself, that is, everything I'm saying to you now, word for word. After the letter, I waited. I guessed that you would come here because it's impossible for you to be without St. Petersburg: you're still too young and too beautiful for the provinces... However, that's not my words, she added, her face turning a horrible shade of red and staying that way until the end of her speech. — When I saw him again, I felt extremely sorry and offended for him. Don't laugh; if you start laughing, you're not worthy of understanding it.

— You didn't understand, she said, — I didn't come here... to quarrel, although I don't love you. I... I came to you... with human speech. Calling you, I had already decided what I would say to you and wouldn't back down from it, even if you don't understand me at all. It would be worse for you, not for me. I wanted to answer your letter to me and answer in person because it seemed more convenient to me. Listen to my response to all your letters: I felt sorry for Prince Lev Nikolayevich for the first time on the very day I met him, and when I later learned everything that happened at your party. I pitied him because he's such a simple soul and because of his simplicity believed he could be happy... with a woman... of such a character. What I was afraid for him happened: you couldn't love him, you tormented him, and abandoned him. You couldn't love him because you're too proud... no, I was wrong, because you're vain... no, that's not it: you're self-absorbed to the point of madness, as your letters to me prove. You couldn't love him, such a simple person, and even, maybe, secretly despised and laughed at him; you could only love your own shame and your continuous thought that you've been dishonored and that you've been insulted. If you had less shame or none at all, you'd be even more unhappy... (Aglaia said these words, which had long been prepared and thought out, with great satisfaction, as if they had burst out too quickly, but were still well-considered; she watched with a venomous gaze how they affected Nastasya Filippovna's distorted face, contorted by agitation). You remember, she continued, — then he wrote to me; he says you know about this letter and even read it? Based on this letter, I understood everything, and correctly understood it; he recently confirmed it himself, that is, everything I'm saying to you now, word for word. After the letter, I started waiting. I guessed that you would come here because you couldn't stay without St. Petersburg: you're still too young and too handsome for the provinces... But that's not my words, she added, horribly blushing, and from this moment on, the flush didn't leave her face until the end of her speech. — When I saw Prince again, I felt a deep, piercing pain and shame for him. Don't laugh; if you laugh, you won't deserve to understand this...

— You didn't understand, — she said, — I didn't come here... to argue with you, although I don't love you. I... I came here... with human words. I had already decided what I would tell you, and I won't retreat from my decision, even if you don't understand a thing. It would be worse for you, not for me. I wanted to answer you in person about what you wrote to me, because it seemed easier that way. Listen to my response to all your letters: I felt sorry for Prince Lev Nikolayevich for the first time on the very day I met him and when I found out everything that had happened at your soiree. I pitied him because he is such a simple-minded person, and because of his simplicity, he believed he could be happy... with a woman... of my character. What I was afraid of, happened: you couldn't love him, you tormented him, and left him. You couldn't love him because you're too vain... no, I made a mistake, it's not that: you're arrogant to the point of... madness, and your letters to me serve as proof of that. You couldn't love him, such a simple soul, and even, perhaps, secretly despised and mocked him; you could only love your own shame and the constant thought that you were shamed and insulted. If you had less shame or had none at all, you'd be even unhappier... (Aglaia spoke out these words, which had rushed out too quickly but had been long prepared and thought out, and were thought out even when she was sleeping, and at the sight of Nastasya Filippovna's distorted face, twisted with agitation, she watched with a venomous gaze, noting the effect of her words). You remember, — she continued, — then he wrote me a letter; he says you know about that letter and have even read it? Based on that letter, I understood everything correctly; he recently confirmed it himself, which means what I'm telling you now, word for word. After that letter, I started waiting. I guessed that you would come here, because it's impossible for you to be without Petersburg: you're still too young and attractive for the provinces... However, that's not my words, — she added, turning a dreadful shade of red, and this flush didn't leave her face until the very end of her speech. — When I saw the prince again, it became very painful and humiliating for me. Don't laugh; if you laugh, you're unworthy of understanding this...

You look at this Monkey King, who, having parted the waters, went back to Iron Board Bridgehead, leapt up with a flourish. Just then, he saw four old monkeys, leading the rest of the monkeys, waiting by the bridge's edge. On seeing Monkey King jump out of the water, not a single drop on his body, shining gold, and walking up to the bridge, the monkeys were all taken aback and knelt down, exclaiming in unison: "Great King, you are resplendent! Great King, you are resplendent!" Monkey King's face beamed with joy as he ascended to the throne, placed his iron staff in the center. Those monkeys, not knowing what to do, all came to grab the treasure, but like a cicada bumping into an iron tree, they could not even budge it. One after another, they bit their fingers and stuck out their tongues, saying: "Grandpa! This is heavy! How did you manage to bring it here?" Monkey King approached, extended his hand, and gave a big wave, chuckling and said: "Each thing has its owner. This treasure has been sealed within the Ocean of Treasures for several thousand or hundreds of years, and only now, with the current year's light, has it been set free. The Dragon King took it for a black iron slab, and called it the Bottom Jewel of Heaven River. They all couldn't carry it, so I went there personally to fetch it. At the time, it was over two yards long and thick as a fist. When I gave it a wave, it was smaller; I gave it another wave, it was smaller still; I gave it another wave, and it was even smaller still. I looked up at the sky and saw the words 'One-million, three-thousand, five-hundred jin', "Just stand back, I'll give it another transformation for you to see." He flipped the treasure in the palm of his hand, calling out, "Smaller! Smaller! Smaller!" Instantly, it shrunk down to a needle, similar to an embroidered flower needle, which could be stuck into the ear and hidden. The monkeys were shocked and called out in unison: "Great King! Come out and play some more!" The Monkey King actually took it out of his ear, placed it on the palm of his hand, and called out: "Larger! Larger! Larger!" And it grew back to its original size of two yards in length and thickness. He played with it happily, jumped onto the bridge, stepped out of the cave, grasped the treasure in his hand, used a celestial-like divine power, bent his waist, and called out: "Long!" And it grew to be ten thousand feet tall, its head as high as Mount Tai, its waist as steep as a precipice, its eyes as swift as lightning, its mouth as big as a cauldron, and its teeth as sharp as a spear. The iron staff in his hand reached up to the 33 heavens and down to the 18 hells, striking fear into the hearts of tigers, panthers, wolves, and all manner of monsters and spirits in the mountains and the 72 grottos of the demons. The spirits and demons all trembled, prostrated, and offered their respects, and fled in terror, their souls scattered. In an instant, he reabsorbed the divine image, transformed the treasure back into an embroidered flower needle, and hid it in his ear, returning to the cave. The various demon kings from each grotto came to pay their respects.

You see that monkey king, who parted the water, and went back to Iron Board Bridgehead, climbed up, and saw four old monkeys leading the other monkeys: all were waiting on the bridge.  Suddenly he jumped out of the water, and his body was completely dry, shining with gold, walked up to the bridge.  The monkeys all knelt down in unison, and said, "Oh, great king, so magnificent! Oh, great king, so magnificent!" The Monkey King beamed with joy, ascended the throne, and erected his iron staff in the center.  Those monkeys didn't know what was good or bad, and all came to take the treasure, but it was as if they were hitting an iron tree with a cicada, and not a bit of it could be moved.  One by one, they all bit their fingers and stretched out their tongues, and said, "Grandfather! How can this be so heavy?"  The Monkey King came closer, unfolded his hand, and seized it with a "thwack", then looked at the crowd with a smile and said, "Each thing belongs to its owner. This treasure has been stored in the Ocean of Jewels for thousands and ten thousand years, and can only be revealed this year. The Dragon King took it for a piece of black iron, and called it the Heaven River's bottom treasure.  Each of them couldn't lift it, so I went and fetched it for them personally. This treasure is two yards long and as thick as a fist; I hit it with my hand, and it was smaller; I made it smaller and smaller, and smaller still; I looked up at the heavenly light, and there was a line of words that read: 'The Wish-Granting Iron Staff, 15,375 catties.'  You all move back, I will change it a bit and let you take a look." He flipped that treasure back and forth in his hand and said, "Smaller! Smaller! Smaller!"  Instantly, it shrunk to the size of a embroidery needle and could be hidden inside one's ear.  The monkeys were startled, and cried, "Great king! Can you bring it out to play with us!"  The Monkey King indeed took it out of his ear and placed it in the palm of his hand and said, "Larger! Larger! Larger!"  It immediately grew back to two yards in length and thickness.  He played around and then leapt onto the bridge, came out of the cave, grasped the treasure in his hand, made a heavenly image and an earth image of divine power, bent his waist, and shouted, "Long!"  He became as tall as ten thousand zhang, his head like Mount Tai, his waist like a steep ridge, his eyes like lightning, and his mouth like a blood bowl, his teeth like a halberd; his staff, which reached up to the 33 heavens and down to the 18th layer of the underworld, shook with a great tremor, and all the tigers, leopards, wolves, and other fiends and spirits in the mountains and the seventy-two caves trembled in fear, kowtowing and paying homage, their spirits scattered and fled in terror.  Instantly, he ceased the divine image, and the treasure changed back into a needle, which he hid in his ear, and returned to his cave.  The various spirits of the other caves were so frightened that they came to congratulate him.

You look at that monkey king, who parted the waters and walked back towards the Iron Bridge Head, went up and climbed down, where he saw four old monkeys, leading the crowd of monkeys, all waiting by the bridge.  Just then he leaped out of the water, not a single drop of water clinging to his body, shining with gold, and walked up the bridge.  The monkeys were startled and all knelt down, exclaiming, "Great King, so resplendent! So resplendent!"  Monkey King beamed with joy, raised his seat of dignity, and planted his iron staff in the middle.  Those monkeys didn't know what they were doing, and came to grab the treasure, but they couldn't budge it at all, like trying to gnaw on an iron tree, not an inch could be moved.  One after another, they bit their fingers and stuck out their tongues, saying, "Grandpa! Grandpa! This is so heavy, what on earth did you bring it here for!"  Monkey King stepped forward, spread out his hands, and gave a mighty swing, lifting it up, and laughing to the crowd, "This treasure has been at the bottom of the sea for tens of thousands of years. I don't know when it was illuminated this year. The Dragon King only took it for a piece of black iron and called it the Treasure of the Heavenly River's Gods. He had to have someone go and take it, and each of them could not budge it. I came to take it for him, and it is over two yards long and as thick as a tub. I gave it a swing with one hand and it seemed too big, I made it a bit smaller, it was too small, I made it a bit smaller still, and it was too small, then I looked up to the light, and there was a row of words, 'The One-thousand-and-thirty-five-hundred- weight Wish-granting Iron Whip'. You all move back, and let me show you some more tricks." He flipped the treasure in his hand, calling out, "Small! Small! Small!" Instantly, it turned into a needle-like object with embroidered flowers, small enough to be hidden inside an ear.  The monkeys were shocked and shouted, "Great King! Come out and show us some more!"  The Monkey King actually retrieved it from his ear and put it on his palm, calling out, "Big! Big! Big!"  Instantly, it turned back to its original size, two yards long and thick.  He was pleased to a great extent and leaped onto the bridge, walked out of the cave and grasped the treasure tightly in his hand, and made a miraculous illusion,  bending to one side and saying "length!" it suddenly grew to a height of ten thousand yards, its head towering like Mount Tai, its waist as steep as a mountain ridge, its eyes flashing like lightning, its mouth as wide as a cauldron, its teeth as sharp as a sword; the iron staff in his hand reached the 33 Heavens and the 18 Underworlds, causing the tigers, leopards, wolves and worms of the mountain, and the seventy-two Devil Kings of the caves, all to quake with fear,  and their souls scattering and their spirits flying.  In the blink of an eye, he ended the miraculous illusion, changed the treasure back into a needle with embroidered flowers and hid it in his ear, and returned to his cave.  The various Devil Kings of the various caves all came to congratulate him.

You look at that Monkey King, cross the river, come back to the Iron Board Bridge, and up he goes. When you see four old monkeys leading the monkeys, all waiting on the bridge. Suddenly, the Monkey King jumps out of the water, completely dry, shining golden, and walks up the bridge. The monkeys are all startled, one by one, kneel down and say: "Great King, so resplendent, so resplendent!" The Monkey King is smiling with a benevolent air, sits on a precious throne, and stands his iron staff in the middle. Those monkeys do not know what is good or bad and come to take that treasure, but it is like a cicada hitting an iron tree, they cannot move it a hair's breadth. Each of them bites their fingers and sticks out their tongues and say: "Grandpa, this is so heavy, how did you manage to bring it here?" The Monkey King comes closer, extends his hand, and gives it a flick, and with a laugh, says: "Each thing has its owner. This treasure has been kept in the Sea of Wutong for thousands of years and has been sealed to shine this year. The Dragon King thought it was a piece of black iron and called it the Immortal Treasure of the Heaven River's Bottom. Each of them could not carry it, so I went to take it for him. When I got it, it was over two yards long and thick; I gave it a flick, and it seemed smaller; I made it smaller, it seemed even smaller; I made it smaller again, and it seemed smaller still. Suddenly I looked up to the sky and there was a line of characters saying: 'One-infinity Five-hundred Three-thousand Gold Encircling Rod, 15,300 jin.' You all stand back, I will make it change size again for you." He tosses that treasure in the air, calls out: "Small, small, small!" Instantly, it becomes a needle embroidered with flowers, like a needle that can be inserted in the ear. The monkeys are amazed and shout: "Great King, bring it out and play with it!" The Monkey King really puts it in his ear and takes it out, puts it on his palm, and calls out: "Big, big, big!" Instantly, it becomes two yards long and thick. He plays with it with joy, jumps up the bridge, comes out of the cave, and holds the treasure in his hand, uses his divine power to become a heaven-and-earth image, bends his waist, calls out "Long!" and it becomes high as ten thousand feet, as high as Mount Tai, as steep as a ridge, as flashing as lightning, as deep as a blood basin, as sharp as a sword's blade. The rod in his hand, the upper part touches the thirtieth heaven, and the lower part reaches the eighteenth netherworld, causing some tigers, leopards, wolves, and insects, as well as the seven-twelve caves' demon kings, to be frightened into prostrating themselves and making salutations, their souls scattered and fleeing. In an instant, he puts away the divine image, puts the treasure back into a needle embroidered with flowers, and hides it in his ear and returns to the cave. The demon kings of the various caves are frightened and come to congratulate him.

Suddenly, he leaps out of the water, without a single drop on his body, shining gold, and walks up onto the bridge. The monkeys are startled and, all at once, kneel down, saying: "Great King, good and wonderful! Good and wonderful!" The Monkey King, with a face full of springtime joy, sits on a treasure throne, puts the Iron Staff upright in the middle. Those monkeys, not knowing good from bad, all try to take the treasure, but, just like a cicada trying to shake an iron tree, they cannot even budge it by an inch. Each one bites their fingers and sticks their tongues out, saying: "Oh, grandpa! It's this heavy! How did you manage to bring it here?" The Monkey King steps forward, opens his hand, and, with a single grasp, takes hold of it, then looks at the monkeys with a smile and says: "Each thing has its owner. This treasure, placed in the Ocean's Treasure Repository, has been there for thousands and hundreds of years, but it shines brightly this year. The Dragon King takes it for a piece of black iron and calls it the Heaven River's Sacred Treasure. He doesn't know how to lift it, so he asks me to get it for him. This treasure is over two yards long, as thick as a fist; I grasp it with one hand, and it seems too big; I make it a bit smaller, and it is smaller; I make it smaller still, and it is smaller still; I look up to the sky and see a line of words saying: 'The Wish-Fulfilling Golden Binding Rope, ten thousand, three thousand, five hundred catties.' You all stand back and wait for me to make it change shape again." He holds that treasure, flips it in his hand, and says: "Small! Small! Small!" Instantly, it becomes a needle-like thing, similar to an embroidered flower needle, which can be hidden in the ear. The monkeys are terrified and call out: "Great King! Let's have it out and play some more!" The Monkey King, indeed, brings it out from his ear, places it in the palm of his hand and says: "Big! Big! Big!" And, in an instant, it becomes two yards long and thick, as before. He was having so much fun that he jumped onto the bridge, walked out of the cave, grasped the treasure in his hand, and displayed a divine skill like a heaven and earth so divine, bending his waist, calling out "Long!" And, in an instant, it grows high as tens of thousands of yards, its head as high as Mount Tai, its waist as steep as a mountain, its eyes as quick as lightning, its mouth as big as a tub, and its teeth as sharp as swords and spears; the rod in his hand reaches the thirty-three heavens and goes down to the eighteen layers of the underworld, and the tigers, leopards, wolves, and vermin in the mountains and the crowds of strange creatures in the seventy-two caves all tremble and prostrate themselves in worship, their courage scattered and their souls flying. He, in an instant, retracts the divine image, and the treasure becomes a needle-like thing again, which he hides in his ear, then returns to his palace. And, in a flurry, the various cave spirits all come to congratulate.

— No, Constant wasn't there then; he was traveling with a letter... to Empress Josephine then; but instead of him, two ordinaries, a few Polish lancers... well, that was the entire entourage, of course, minus the generals and marshals, whom Napoleon brought along to survey the area, troop dispositions, and confer... Mostly Dau was with him, as I now recall: a huge, full, phlegmatic man in glasses, with a strange gaze. He consulted with him most often. Napoleon valued his thoughts. I remember they were conferring for several days; Dau came in the morning and evening, often even arguing; eventually Napoleon seemed to be agreeing. They were alone in the cabinet, and I was nearly invisible to them. Suddenly Napoleon's glance falls on me by chance, a strange thought flashes in his eyes. "Child!" he says suddenly, "how do you think: if I were to accept Orthodoxy and liberate your slaves, would the Russians follow me?" — "Never!" I shouted in indignation. Napoleon was taken aback. "In the eyes of this child, blinded by patriotism, I have read the opinion of the entire Russian people," he said. "Enough, Dau! It's all fantasies! Present me with your other plan."

In these gates, which were dark enough already, it was extremely dark at this moment: a thunderous cloud had rolled in and swallowed the evening light, and just as the prince was approaching the house, the cloud suddenly burst open and poured down. At the same time as he hastily moved forward after a brief pause, he found himself at the very beginning of the gates, right at the entrance under the gate from the street. And suddenly he saw, in the depths of the gates, in semidarkness, at the entrance to the staircase, one person. The person seemed to be waiting for something, but quickly flashed by and disappeared. The prince was unable to clearly see this person and, of course, could not possibly say for sure who he was. Moreover, many people were going through here; there was an inn, and people continuously passed through and ran through the corridors and back. But he suddenly felt an absolute and inescapable conviction that he had recognized this person and that this person was definitely Rostanevich. A moment later the prince dashed up the staircase after him. His heart stopped. "It will all be resolved now!" - he muttered to himself with a strange conviction.

Just as they were drinking, the Monkey King paused his cup and asked, "What's the rank of this 'prefect of horse stables' of mine?" Everyone replied, "This is just its official name." He asked again, "What's the rank of this official?" They said, "It has no rank, no gradation." The Monkey King said, "No rank, it must be at the highest degree." Everyone said, "Not high, not high, it's simply called 'not yet in the official rolls'." The Monkey King asked, "What's called 'not yet in the official rolls'?" They said, "Inferior, it's a low-ranking official. This sort of official, after taking office, is so diligent in caring for horses, feeding them till they're fat. But if the horses are merely a bit thin, they're censured; if they're greatly emaciated, they're penalized, with a fine and punishment added." The Monkey King heard this and, without a moment's notice, his face flushed with anger. He gritted his teeth and shouted, "How you have belittled me! In Flower Fruit Mountain, I am the king, the ancestor, and how have you hoodwinked me into taking on the task of caring for horses? Those who care for horses are nothing but lowly youngsters, not fit for me. I won't do it! I won't do it!" With a loud crash, he pushed over the official table, took the precious treasure from his ear, and, whipping the ribbon out in one go, at once made for the Imperial Stables, right out the South Heavenly Gate. The Heavenly Officials, knowing he had received his heavenly mandate and that he was a prefect of horse stables, didn't dare intervene and let him go out the heavenly gate.

Just as they were all drinking and enjoying themselves, the Monkey King suddenly stopped his cup and asked, "I've got this 'bìmǎ wēn' title, what does it mean?" Everyone replied, "That's just its official name, that's all." He then asked, "Is this title a rank?" The others said, "It has no rank." The Monkey King said, "No rank, I suppose it's the most supreme of all." The others said, "No, it's not the greatest, it's called 'unpromoted'." The Monkey King asked, "How is it called 'unpromoted'?" The others said, "It's a lowly rank. An official like that is at the very bottom, only fit to attend to the horses. After the magistrate assumes office, he's so busy tending to the horses that they get fat, but if the horses even look a bit thin, he'll be reprimanded; if they suffer any real damage, he'll be punished and have to make amends." 

The Monkey King heard this and his heart burned with rage. He ground his teeth in anger and said, "How contemptuous of me! I, the King of the Peach Garden, having the prestige of a monarch, how could I be fooled into coming here to feed horses? To feed horses is the lowest, most menial task, not something befitting me! I won't do it! I won't do it! I'll be off!" With a loud thud, he knocked over the official desk, took out the treasure from his ear, and, flicking his sleeves, a coarse-rimmed bowl appeared. Uncoiling the whip, he rode straight out of the Imperial Stable and straight through the South Heavenly Gate. The heavenly officials knew he had been granted the celestial enrollment and was a bìmǎ wēn, so they dared not stop him and let him leave.

The lowest judges, including my acquaintances, don't have the right to acquit definitively; this right belongs only to the highest court, which is, of course, entirely inaccessible to us. As for what it's like there, we don't know and don't want to know. The great right to release from accusation rests with our judges, but they do have the right to release from accusation. That is, if you're acquitted in this way, you're only released from the accusation, not acquitted in the true sense. They can't grant the latter; only the highest court can do that, and that's something we can never reach."

— I'm saying, gentlemen, that those famines were indeed frequent at the time. Although I know little history, I've heard about them. It seems it had to be so. When I found myself in the Swiss mountains, I was amazed at the ruins of old knightly castles built on the mountain slopes, on steep cliffs, and at least half a verst straight up (that's several versts along winding paths). A castle, they say, is a whole mountain of stones. The work was terrible, impossible! And, of course, all these poor vassals managed to do it. On top of that, they had to pay all those taxes and maintain the clergy. How could they feed themselves and cultivate the land? There must have been hardly enough of them, and they probably died off terribly from hunger, and, literally, may not have had anything to eat.
