Someone must have denounced Josef K., for without his having committed any crime, he was arrested one morning. The housekeeper of Frau Grubach, his landlady, who always brought him his breakfast at eight o'clock in the morning, failed to appear this time. This had never happened before. K. waited a little while, looked from his pillow at the old woman who lived opposite and observed him with an unusual curiosity, but then, at the same time feeling uneasy and hungry, he rang. The knocking came immediately, and a man he had never seen before entered the room. He was slender but well-built, and he wore a black suit that was designed to be practical, with various pockets, compartments, and fasteners, so that its purpose remained unclear. "Who are you?" asked K., and sat up halfway in bed. But the man disregarded the question as if one was supposed to accept his appearance without question, and merely said, "You rang?" "Anna should bring me my breakfast," said K., and attempted at first silently to determine the stranger's identity through attention and contemplation. However, the man did not let him study him for long, but turned towards the door, which he slightly opened to say to someone who was apparently standing just behind it, "He wants Anna to bring him his breakfast." A small laugh from the adjacent room followed, which did not sound like it came from only one person. Although the stranger could have learned nothing from this that he didn't already know, he now told K. in a tone of a report, "It's impossible." "That would be new," said K., sprang out of bed, and quickly put on his trousers. "I want to see who is in the other room and how Frau Grubach will be responsible for this disturbance towards me." It occurred to him that he shouldn't have said this out loud and that he was thereby acknowledging the stranger's supervision, but it didn't seem important to him at the moment. Nevertheless, the stranger took it that way, for he said, "Don't you want to stay here?" "I don't want to stay here, nor be spoken to by you as long as you don't introduce yourself," said K. "It was kindly meant," said the stranger, and opened the door voluntarily. As K. slowly entered the other room, which he had entered more slowly than he wanted, he saw that it almost looked exactly like it had the evening before. The room was cluttered with furniture, carpets, china, and photographs, and one couldn't notice that it was perhaps a bit more crowded today. There was no other notable change, apart from the presence of a man sitting by the open window with a book, who now looked up at him. "You should have stayed in your room! Didn't Franz tell you so?" said the man by the window, and K. looked from the stranger to the one who had been named Franz, who was standing in the doorway, and then back again. Looking out the open window, one could see the old woman, who had gotten up to the window next to him and was watching everything with an almost archaic curiosity. "I want to see Frau Grubach," said K., and made a motion as if he was freeing himself from the two men standing far away from him, and wanted to leave. "No," said the man by the window, threw his book onto a little table, and stood up. "You can't leave; you are under arrest." "It looks that way," said K., and then asked, "Why, then?" "We are not authorized to tell you," said the other. "Go to your room and wait. The proceedings have been initiated, and you will be informed of everything in due time." The man seemed to be going beyond his orders when he spoke in a friendly tone, "I am going beyond my orders if I say this to you, but I hope that no one else will hear it except Franz, and he is friendly to you, in spite of all the formalities. If you continue to be lucky with the choice of your guards, as you have been with the selection of your guardians, you can be optimistic." K. wanted to sit down, but now he saw that there was no place to sit in the entire room, except for the armchair by the window. "You will see that everything is true," said Franz, and at the same time he and the other man approached K. The latter towered over K. significantly and frequently tapped him on the shoulder. Both inspected K.'s night shirt and told him that he would now have to put on a much worse shirt, that they would keep his shirt and the rest of his clothing, and if his case turned out well, they would return them to him. "It's better that you give them to us rather than to the storage room," they said, "because in the storage room, there are often missing items, and besides, they sell everything after a certain time, regardless of whether the relevant procedure is finished or not. And how long do such procedures take, especially in recent times! You would then receive the proceeds from the storage room, but this is already relatively low, since the sale price is determined not by the price offer, but by the bribe, and the proceeds from such sales are reduced, as a rule, when passed from hand to hand and from year to year." K. hardly paid attention to their words; he did not value the right to control his belongings, which he may still have had, highly; it was much more important to him to get clarity about his situation, but he was unable to think in the presence of these people; every time he looked up at the second guard – they could only be guards – his belly would touch him almost affectionately, but looking up at him, he saw a dry, bony face with a strong, laterally twisted nose, which spoke to the other guard. Who were these people? What were they talking about? To which authority did they belong? K. lived in a state governed by law, everywhere there was peace, all laws remained in force, who dared to raid his apartment? He was always inclined to take things as lightly as possible, not to worry about the future until the worst came to pass, not to take precautions even when everything was threatened. Here, however, it seemed that this was not the right approach; one could indeed see the whole thing as a joke, as a crude joke that his colleagues at the bank had arranged for him on some unknown reason, perhaps because today was his thirtieth birthday, it was certainly possible that he just had to laugh in the face of the guards somehow and they would laugh with him, maybe they were just hirelings from the street corner, they didn't look very different – yet he had decided from the first glance at the guard Franz that he would not give up any advantage he might have over these people. In that it would later be said that he didn't understand the joke, K. saw a minimal danger; however, he remembered – without it being his usual habit to learn from experience – a few cases in which he had acted carelessly, with awareness, without any sense of the possible consequences, and had been punished by the outcome. It should not happen again, at least not this time; if it was a comedy, he wanted to participate.

He was prone to take everything lightly, not to believe the worst until it happened, and not to take any precautions for the future, even when everything threatened; here, however, he didn't think that was right; one could see the whole thing as a joke, as a coarse joke, that his colleagues in the bank might have organized for him for unknown reasons, perhaps because today was his thirtieth birthday, it was certainly possible, perhaps he just needed to laugh at the guards in some way, and they would laugh along; perhaps they were the type of porters one might find at the street corner, they looked like that, but still, he was resolute from the first glance of the guard Franz not to give up any advantage he might have over these people; in that no one would later say he didn't understand the joke, K. saw a very small danger, but he remembered – without it being his habit to learn from experiences – a few, insignificant cases in which he had behaved carelessly, in contrast to his friends, with full awareness, without feeling the least concern for the possible consequences, and had been punished by the outcome; it should not happen again, at least not this time; if it was a comedy, he wanted to participate.

Someone must have slandered Josef K., for without having done anything wrong, he was arrested one morning. The cook of Mrs. Grubach, his landlady, who brought him breakfast every day at eight o'clock in the morning, did not come this time. This had never happened before. K. waited for a little while, looked from his pillow at the old woman who lived opposite and who observed him with an unusual curiosity, then, both bemused and hungry, he rang the bell. It rang immediately, and a man he had never seen in this apartment before entered. He was slender and yet sturdy, he wore a close-fitting black suit, similar to traveling suits, which was equipped with various folds, pockets, buckles, buttons, and a belt, and as a result, it seemed particularly practical without it being clear what its purpose was. "Who are you?" asked K. and sat up half in bed. The man, however, ignored the question as if one was expected to accept his presence, and said only: "Did you ring the bell?" "Anna should bring me my breakfast," said K. and first tried to figure out who the man was by paying attention and thinking, but he did not keep his gaze for long and turned towards the door, which he opened slightly in order to tell someone who was apparently standing just behind it: "He wants Anna to bring him his breakfast." A small laugh from the next room followed, it was not clear whether it was not several people who participated in it. Although the strange man could not have learned anything from this that he did not already know, he nonetheless said to K. in a tone of a report: "It's impossible." "That would be something new," said K., jumped out of bed, and quickly put on his pants. "I want to see who is in the next room and how Mrs. Grubach will answer for the disturbance she's causing me." He was aware at once that he should not have said this out loud and that he thereby acknowledged the man's right to supervision, but it didn't seem important to him now. The man, however, took it that way, because he said: "Don't you want to stay here?" "I won't stay here, nor will I be spoken to by you as long as you don't introduce yourself," said K. "It was meant kindly," said the man and opened the door voluntarily. In the next room, into which K. entered more slowly than he had intended, it looked almost exactly the same as it had the evening before. It was Mrs. Grubach's living room, perhaps there was a little more room in this room, which was cluttered with furniture, blankets, china, and photographs, one didn't notice this right away, even less so since the main change in the presence of a man sat by the open window with a book, from which he now looked up. "You should have stayed in your room! Didn't Franz tell you that?" "Yes, what do you want?" said K. and looked from the new acquaintance to the one called Franz, who was standing in the doorway, and then back. Through the open window, one could see the old woman again, who had stepped up to the window opposite K.'s with truly grey-haired curiosity in order to see everything further. "I want to see Mrs. Grubach –" said K., made a movement as if he were freeing himself from the two men, who were standing far away from him, and wanted to go on. "No," said the man by the window, threw the book onto a small table, and stood up. "You can't leave, you're arrested." "It looks that way," said K. "And why?" he asked then. "We're not authorized to tell you that," said the other two. "Go to your room and wait. The procedure has been initiated, and you will learn everything in due time." I'm going beyond my instructions, if I'm speaking to you in a friendly manner," said the man. "But I hope it's not overheard by anyone else but Franz, and he is friendly towards you, too, against all regulations. If you continue to have as much luck as you did with your wardens, then you can be hopeful." K. wanted to sit down, but then he saw that there were no seats available in the whole room, except for the armchair by the window. "You will see that it's all true," said Franz and walked over to K. with the other man. Especially the latter towered over K. noticeably and kept knocking on his shoulder. Both examined K.'s nightshirt and said that he would have to put on a much worse shirt now, but that they would take care of his other clothes and, if his case turned out well, return them to him. "It's better for you to hand over your belongings to us rather than to the depot," they said, "because in the depot there are often pilfering, and besides, all items are sold after a certain time, without regard for whether the respective case is finished or not. And how long do such cases last, especially these days! You will, however, get the proceeds from the depot, but the proceeds are small, because at the sale, it is not the price offered that decides, but the amount of bribery, and they are usually reduced as they are passed from hand to hand and from year to year." K. paid little attention to these speeches; he didn't think highly of the right to dispose of his belongings, which he might still have; more important was for him to get clarity about his situation; but in the presence of these people, he couldn't even think straight, every time he looked up, he caught the belly of the second guard, who was essentially hitting him up in a friendly manner, but his gaze met a face that was quite unsuited to this stout body, a dry, bony face with a strong nose that was slightly tilted to the side, which nodded at the other guard as it gazed over K. What kind of people were these? What were they talking about? To which authority did they belong? K. lived in a country governed by the rule of law, there was peace everywhere, all laws stood firmly in place, who dared to arrest him in his own home? He was accustomed to taking things as lightly as possible, only believing the worst at the moment it happened, taking no precautions for the future, even when everything seemed threatened. But here it seemed not right, one could view the whole thing as a joke, as a coarse joke that his colleagues at the bank had organized for him, perhaps because today was his thirtieth birthday, it was possible, he might have only needed to laugh in the face of the guards in some way, and they would laugh along with him, perhaps they were messengers from the street corner, they didn't look unlike them – nonetheless, from the first sight of the guard Franz, K. had made up his mind not to give up even the smallest advantage he might have over these people. In that people would later say he hadn't understood the joke, K. saw a slight risk; but he remembered – without it having been his habit to learn from experience – some insignificant cases, in which he, unlike his friends, had acted recklessly, with awareness, without the slightest feeling for the possible consequences, and been punished by the outcome. It should not happen again, at least not this time; if it was a comedy, he wanted to play along.

Someone must have slandered Josef K., for without having done anything wrong, he was arrested one morning. The housekeeper of Mrs. Grubach, his landlady, who brought him breakfast every day at eight o'clock, failed to appear this time. That had never happened before. K. waited a little while, saw from his pillow the old woman who lived opposite and was watching him with an uncommon curiosity, then, feeling both befuddled and hungry, he rang. Immediately there was a knock at the door, and a man he had never seen before in this apartment entered. He was slender and yet well-built, wore a close-fitting black coat, which, like travel coats, was adorned with folds, pockets, buckles, buttons, and a belt, and thus appeared, without anyone quite understanding its purpose, to be particularly practical. "Who are you?" K. asked and sat up in bed. But the man disregarded the question, as if it were something that had to be endured, and merely said, "You rang?" "Anna is supposed to bring me breakfast," said K., and, initially, in silence, by paying attention and thinking, he attempted to determine who the man really was. But this man did not put up with K.'s gaze for long and turned to the door, which he slightly opened to tell someone, apparently standing just behind the door, "He wants Anna to bring him his breakfast." A small laugh from the next room followed, it was unclear whether more than one person was involved. Although the stranger could not have gained any knowledge that he did not already possess, he now spoke to K. in a tone of a report: "It's impossible." "That would be new," said K., leapt out of bed, and quickly put on his trousers. "I want to see who is in the next room and how Mrs. Grubach will account for this disturbance in front of me." It immediately occurred to him that he should not have spoken out loud and that he had, as it were, acknowledged the other man's supervision, but it did not seem important to him now. The other man, however, interpreted it that way, because he said, "Would you rather stay here?" "I want neither to stay here nor to be addressed by you until you introduce yourself." "It was meant kindly," said the other man, and now opened the door freely. In the next room, into which K. entered more slowly than he had wanted to, it looked almost exactly the same as the evening before. It was Mrs. Grubach's living room, perhaps the room was a little more spacious today than usual, you could not tell, all the less so since the main change was the presence of a man who sat with a book at the open window and now looked up from it. "You should have stayed in your room! Did Franz not tell you so?" "What do you want?" said K. and looked at the new acquaintance, then at the man named Franz, who stood in the doorway, and then back. From the open window, one could see the old woman again, who had approached the adjacent window with genuinely grey-haired curiosity in order to watch everything further. "I want to speak to Mrs. Grubach –" said K., made a movement as if to break free from the two men, who, however, were far away, and wanted to go on. "No," said the man at the window, tossed the book onto a small table, and stood up. "You may not leave, you are under arrest." "It appears so," said K. "And why?" he asked then. "We are not ordered to tell you," said the other man. "Go into your room and wait. The proceedings have been initiated, and you will learn everything in due time. I'm going beyond my assignment by speaking to you in this friendly manner. But I hope that no one else but Franz hears it, and he is friendly towards you in any case, contrary to all regulations. If you continue to be as fortunate as in the selection of your guards, you can be optimistic." K. wanted to sit down, but now he saw that there was no place to sit in the whole room, except for the armchair at the window. "You will see, it's all true," said Franz, and at the same time walked with the other man towards him. The latter towered over K. significantly and kept hitting him on the shoulder. Both men checked K.'s nightshirt and said that he would now have to put on a much worse shirt, that they would keep his current shirt and the rest of his clothing, and if his case turned out well, they would return it to him. "It's better for you to hand the items over to us than to the depot," they said, "because in the depot, theft occurs frequently, and besides, they sell off all items after a certain time, regardless of whether the case has been concluded or not. And how long do such cases drag on, especially in recent times! You would get the proceeds from the depot, however, but the proceeds are initially low, because the selling price is decided not by the offer, but by the bribe, and the proceeds are reduced in any case when they are passed from hand to hand and from year to year." K. paid little attention to their words; he did not rate the right to manage his belongings, which he might still possess, high; more important to him was to gain clarity about his situation. But he could not even think in the presence of these people; he kept looking up, and then he saw the bony face of the second guard, which was not suitable for his stout body, with its strong, sidelong twisted nose, and the other guard looked at him and nodded to him. What kind of people were these? What were they talking about? To which authority did they belong? K. lived in a state ruled by law, peace reigned everywhere, all laws were in effect, who dared to break into his apartment? He was prone to taking things as easy as possible, believing the worst only when it happened, making no provision for the future, even when everything threatened. Here, however, it seemed to him not quite right, one could perhaps regard the whole thing as a joke, a crude joke that his colleagues in the bank had organized for him out of unknown reasons, perhaps because today was his thirtieth birthday, it was certainly possible, he only needed to laugh at the guards in some way, and they would laugh along, perhaps they were street men from the corner, they didn't look unlike them – still, he was now, since the first glance at the guard Franz, determined not to give up the slightest advantage he might have against these people. In that people might later say that he had not understood the joke, K. saw a relatively small danger; but he recalled – without it having been his habit to learn from experience – a few, seemingly insignificant cases in which he had behaved carelessly, without being conscious of the possible consequences, and had been punished by the outcome. It should not happen again, at least not this time; even if it was a comedy, he wanted to play his part.

— Ah, morality! I'm just a boy, I know it myself, — Ganya interrupted warmly, — and just that conversation with you is proof of it. I, a prince, am not going into this darkness out of calculation — I would have erred, probably, for the very reason that I'm still not strong-headed enough in my character and youth. I'm going in out of passion, out of impulse, because I have a substantial goal. You think I'd get seventy-five thousand and then right away buy a carriage. No, I'd still be wearing the shabby old coat of a third-year student and would have thrown in the towel on all my club acquaintances. We have so few people with backbone, even though they're all us moneylenders, and I want to be one of them. The main thing is to see this through to the end — that's the challenge! Petya Ivanych was a 17-year-old street kid who used to sell small trinkets with his little scissors and started from scratch; now he has sixty thousand, but what a feat he had to go through! I'll be like that; I'll somehow endure the feat and start from scratch with the capital; in fifteen years they'll say: 'That's Ivolgin, the Jewish king.' You say I'm not an original man. Note this to yourself, dear prince: there's nothing more insulting to a person of our time and our tribe than to be told they're not original, lack backbone, don't have any special talents, and are just an ordinary person. You've even not even given me the credit of being a good rascal, and you know, I wanted to eat you up for that yesterday. Epanchin's even hurt me more than you, who thinks (without any doubt, without any enticement, in all sincerity, take note of this) that I'm capable of selling his wife! That's been annoying me for a long time, and I want the money. Know this, when I've made some money, I'll be an original person to the highest degree. Money's so terrible because it even gives talents. And it will keep giving them until the end of time. You'll say it's all childish or poetic nonsense — well, that's all the more fun for me, and that's the way it will be done. I'll see it through and endure. Rira bien qui rira le dernier! 1 Why is Epanchin hurting me out of spite? Never! It's simply because I'm so insignificant. Oh, well, that's enough; time to go. Kolya's already shown his nose twice: he's inviting you to dinner. And I'm off. I'll sometimes drop by your place. You'll be welcome; we'll practically be family. Just don't betray me. I think we'll be either friends or enemies. And how do you think, prince, if I had kissed your hand yesterday (as sincerely as I wanted to), would I have become your enemy later on for it?

"Ah, morality! What I'm still a child, I know that myself, — Ganya interrupted hotly, — and you only had to have this conversation with me to prove it. I, a prince, did not come to this darkness for calculation, — he continued, wounded in his own self-esteem as a young man, — if I had calculated, I probably would have made a mistake, both in terms of head and character. I came from passion, from inclination, because I have a fundamental goal. You think I'll get seventy-five thousand and buy a carriage right away? No, I'd then start wearing a worn-out, third-hand coat and I'd give up all my social connections. We have few people who can stand the test, although they're all usurers, but I want to stand the test. The main thing is to see it through to the end — that's the task! Petya Pechkov at seventeen slept on the street, traded with scissors and began with a copper coin; now he has sixty thousand, but only after such gymnastics! I'll jump over all that gymnastics and start right from the capital; in fifteen years they'll say, 'There's Ivogin, the king of Judea.' You're telling me I'm not an original person. Notice this to yourself, dear prince, that there's nothing more insulting to a person of our time and breed than to say he's not original, that he's weak-willed, lacks special talents, and is an ordinary person. You didn't even consider me a decent rascal, and I wanted to eat you for that yesterday. You've offended me more than Epanchin, who considers me (and without any discussion, without any temptation, in simple sincerity, notice this) capable of selling his wife! This has been pissing me off for a long time, and I want money. When I earn money, you'll know — I'll be an original person in the highest degree. Money is just what's most contemptible and loathsome because they even give talents. And they'll give them until the end of the world. You'll say this is all childish or, perhaps, poetry — well, it'll be all the more enjoyable for me, and the business will still be done. I'll see it through and stand by it. He who laughs last laughs best!1 I'm not angry with Epanchin because of malice; no, it's just because I'm too insignificant. Well, so what... But however, let's finish, and it's time. Kolya has already showed you out twice; it's him inviting you to dinner. And I'm leaving. I'll sometimes drop by to see you. You'll have a good time with us; now you'll be welcomed into our family as kin. Just watch yourself, don't betray us. I think we'll either be friends or enemies. And how do you think, prince, if I had kissed your hand yesterday (as I genuinely wanted to), would I become your enemy for that later on?"

— Ah, morality! You know I'm just a kid, I'm a kid myself, — Ganya broke in heatedly — and just because of this conversation you started with me, for instance. The Jade Emperor summoned the ministers of both civil and military, and inquired, "How many years was this mischievous monkey born and what age was he in when he was born? Yet he has become so profound?"  Before the Jade Emperor finished speaking, there was a sudden flash of sight from the ranks, and it was the Thousand Li Eye and the Ears of the Wind, who exclaimed, "This monkey was born from heaven three hundred years ago, and it was a stone monkey at the time. We did not take it seriously, and we did not know where he was cultivating and rising to sainthood, controlling dragons and taming tigers, eradicating his auspicious record as well."

The Jade Emperor spoke, "Which divine general brought him to the mortal realm to subdue him?"  Before the Jade Emperor finished speaking, the Great White Luminous Star appeared in the ranks, bowing to report, "In the three realms of heaven, any being with nine apertures can cultivate sainthood. Yet this monkey is a body created by heaven and earth, born from the womb of the sun and moon; he can soar to the heavens and tread on the earth; he feeds on dew and eats sunshine. Since he has now cultivated the Way of the Immortals, he possesses the ability to control dragons and tame tigers. What is he different from others? I humbly request Your Majesty to consider the benevolent kindness of birth and transformation, and issue a royal edict, summoning him up to court, assigning him a minor or major official position, and recording his name in the heavenly register, placing him under constraint in this place. If he complies with heaven's decree, there will be future rewards; if he violates heaven's decree, I beg to capture him."

The Jade Emperor heard these words and was greatly delighted, saying, "In accordance with your proposal." He ordered the officer in charge of documents to draft an edict, and ordered the Great White Luminous Star to issue a summons to bring him in.

The Great Emperor spoke before the assembly of literary and martial immortals: "This malicious ape, how many years old is it, in which dynasty was it born, yet it possesses such profound Dao? His words had not yet fully ceased when the thousand-mile eye and wind-attentive ear of the class suddenly flashed forth and said: 'This ape is a heavenly-generated stone ape from three hundred years ago. At the time, we did not take it seriously, not knowing it had been cultivating the Dao in some unknown place, has subdued dragons and tigers, and has eradicated its own mortal record.' 

The Jade Emperor said, 'Which divine general is responsible for bringing it down to the world and taming it?' His words had not yet ceased when the Star of Great Brightness suddenly flashed forth and bowed to announce: 'In the Three Realms, all who possess the Nine Apertures may cultivate the Dao. But this ape is the body nurtured by the heaven and earth, the body begotten by the day and moon, it goes on top of the sky and treads on the ground, feeds on dew and dines on the sun's radiance; now that it has cultivated the Dao of the Immortals and possesses the ability to subdue dragons and tigers, how is it different from mortals? Your Majesty, I beg you to take into consideration the benevolent grace of life and death, issue an imperial decree to invite it to the palace, grant it a small or a great official position, and fix its name in the records. If it follows heaven's command, later we will again promote it; if it does not follow heaven's command, then it will be seized and captured. This way, we will avoid mobilizing a great army, and we will also be appeased by its cultivation of the Dao.'

The Jade Emperor listened with great joy and said: 'I agree with what you have proposed.' He then instructed the Music Rhapsody Star Official to draft an edict, and ordered the Great Bright Star to invite the ape.

The Great One of the Heavenly Realm summoned the scholars of virtue and martial prowess and asked, "This monkey is how many years old? Which generation did it belong to? Yet, it has already reached this level of cultivation." He had not yet finished speaking when the Star of Thousand Miles Vision and the Ears of the Favorable Wind suddenly flashed into the assembly and said, "This monkey is one born by the heavens through the stone monkey technique three hundred years ago. At the time, no one took it seriously and did not know where it cultivated its way to immortality and subdued dragons and tigers, and its name was even erased from the registers."

The Jade Emperor then asked, "Which of the gods collected it in the mortal realm?" He had not yet finished speaking when the Great White Star Long Gan appeared and bowed his head to report, saying, "Your Majesty, within the three realms, all beings with nine orifices can cultivate immortality. But this monkey was a body created by the heavens and earth, conceived by the sun and the moon, and with the breath of heaven and earth nourished it to maturity. It stands on the clouds and traverses the heavens, feasts on dew and drinks the rays of the sun; now that it has reached the level of a perfected immortal, its ability to subdue dragons and tigers is nothing out of the ordinary. I, your humble subject, dare submit a recommendation to Your Majesty: consider the benevolent compassion of creating life, and send down a decree to summon it to the heavenly realm, appoint it to a noble official position, and allow it to be listed in the official records. Should it heed the heavenly mandate, later on, it will be rewarded. Should it disobey the heavenly mandate, capture it immediately." The Jade Emperor was very pleased and said, "I will follow your suggestion." He then instructed the Star Official of the Literary Arts to draft an edict and ordered the Great White Star to summon the monkey.

The Great Sage summoned the crowd of scholars, warriors, and deities to ask, "This mischievous monkey is how many years old, of what generation was he born, yet he has such incredible power?" Before he finished speaking, the Immortal with the Eye That Sees a Thousand Li and the Ear that Listens to the Wind suddenly appeared in the middle of the gathering, saying, "This monkey was born by a heavenly miracle three hundred years ago. At the time, we did not think much of him. Now it's not known where he was cultivating his spirit in the past few years, but he has certainly become a deity by now, taming dragons and tigers, and has such great accomplishment."

The Jade Emperor spoke, "What road god summoned him from the mortal realm?" He hadn't finished speaking when the Star of Great White, Long Biao, bowed to offer an explanation, saying, "Your Majesty, in the three realms of the heavens, those with nine apertures can cultivate the path of immortality. But this monkey is a being nurtured by the heavens and the earth, born of a lunar conception. He has achieved the peak of power, treading upon the heavens and the earth, feeding on dew and eating sunshine. Now that he has achieved the Way of the Immortals, having the power to tame dragons and tigers, what makes him different from others? I beg Your Majesty to consider the benevolence of granting him the imperial favor. Send a decree calling him to the palace, grant him a high official position, and have him register his name in the ledgers. If he obeys heaven's decree, wait for him to achieve even greater accomplishments and reward him further. If he violates heaven's decree, seize him and punish him in this lifetime." The Jade Emperor was very pleased with this proposal, saying, "Let's do as you have suggested." He then ordered the Text-Weaver Star to compose a decree, and the Star of Great White to bring the monkey to the palace.

The Grand Emperor summoned the renowned literati, military officers, and immortals, asking, "This mischievous monkey, how many years was it born and in which generation did it appear, yet it already possesses extraordinary abilities?" No sooner had he spoken than a thousand-mile gaze and an ear that hears from afar in the ranks sprang out and said, "This monkey is a heavenly birthed stone monkey, born three hundred years ago. At the time, it was not deemed extraordinary, nor did one know that it was cultivating its powers in some corner of the world to become an immortal, subdue dragons and tigers, and outshine all beings."

The Jade Emperor spoke, "What celestial marshal was it that brought it under control?" He had barely spoken when the Long Hanging Star (Venus) appeared before him, bowing its head to report, "Among the three realms of the divine, any being with nine apertures (heavenly bodies) can cultivate to become an immortal. Alas, this monkey is a product of heaven and earth, and its body was nurtured by the sun and the moon. Its behavior is as if it has mounted the heavens and trodden the earth; it consumes dew and feeds on the colors of the clouds. Having now achieved the Way of Immortality and having the ability to subdue dragons and tigers, how can it differ from others? I, your servant, humbly submit a proposal to Your Majesty: please think on the benevolence of creation and transmission, issue a royal decree to call it to the imperial court, and grant it an official position and a place on the records, with bounds to this world, that if it accepts the will of Heaven, it may be rewarded later; but if it disobeys Heaven's will, seize it at once. In this way, there will be no expenditure of the nation's labor, and it will be beneficial to the cultivation of the Dao." The Jade Emperor was pleased with his words and said, "Following your proposal." He then commanded the official in charge of decree-making (a minor star) to draft a decree, and ordered the Venus (Long Hanging Star) to issue an imperial edict to call it to the imperial court.

When this official notice arrived in the Haizhou region, one man named Chen with the given name Lü (lit. Glorious Orb) immediately returned home to inform his mother, Mrs. Zhang, saying, "The imperial court has published the yellow notice, calling for talented scholars to take part in the examination. My son intends to travel to take the examination. If he succeeds in gaining an official position, he will bring glory to our family and make his parents' names renowned. This is my son's ambition. I have come to inform you, Mother." Mrs. Zhang replied, "A child of a scholar should 'study when young and take action when strong.' It is only natural that you would participate in the examination. However, when traveling, you must be cautious. Once you've gained an official position, hurry back home." Lü thereupon instructed his house servant to pack his luggage, then bid farewell to his mother and hurried off. Upon arriving in Chang'an, he coincidentally found himself at the site of the grand examination, whereupon he entered the examination hall. After completing the examination and writing three essays, the emperor himself personally granted Lü a position as the first rank, allowing him to ride horseback through the city streets for three days. Unbeknownst to him, during this time he passed in front of the mansion of the prime minister, Yin Kaidong, and saw the prime minister's daughter, named Mianju, who had never been married. At the time, Mianju was seated in a brightly decorated tower, throwing and catching embroidered balls to find a groom. As it happened, Chen Lü was walking underneath the tower and was seen by Mianju, who was impressed by his distinguished character and recognized him as the newly-promoted first rank. Delighted, she threw down an embroidered ball which coincidentally landed on Chen's black hat. Upon hearing a sound of harps and flutes, several maidservants descended the tower, tied Lü's horse's bridle, and escorted him into the prime minister's mansion for his marriage. The prime minister and his wife promptly emerged from the main hall, summoned the officials, and arranged for a ceremony to pair the young woman with Chen Lü. After the couple paid their respects to heaven and earth, they exchanged greetings, and then paid their respects to the prime minister and his wife. The prime minister then instructed his staff to prepare a feast, and the two of them spent the night drinking.

When the imperial proclamation reached the Huizhou region, there was one person surnamed Chen, named Lu, with the style name Guirui. As soon as he saw the proclamation, he immediately returned home, telling his mother, Zhang, "The imperial court has issued the yellow edict, proclaiming the opening of the province's examination, and I wish to go and take the exam. If I succeed in obtaining a position, I will bring glory to the family and raise our fame, thereby fulfilling my son's ambition. I especially come to inform you of my decision to leave." Zhang replied, "As a scholar, one should 'learn at a young age and take action when strong.' You should go to take the examination. Be careful on the road and return home early if you succeed." Guirui ordered the household servants to pack his luggage, bid his farewell to his mother, and hastened his journey forward. 

Upon arriving in Chang'an, he coincidentally encountered the day of the grand examination, and Guirui entered the examination grounds. After passing the examination and completing the imperial court's test, he was awarded the top honor by the emperor himself. Riding his horse through the streets for three days, he was unexpectedly riding past the residence of the Grand Secretary, Yin Kaishan, when he saw the Grand Secretary's daughter, a woman named Wen Jiao, who was also known as Mándāng Jiao. Unmarried and residing within the household, she had built a high tower, from which she was throwing paper balls to search for a son-in-law. Chen Guirui happened to be passing beneath the tower when Miss Jiao saw that Guirui was an exceptional individual and recognized him as the new year's top scorers, she was extremely delighted, and threw a paper ball which hit Guirui's black hat. 

A sudden burst of elegant music from a string instrument and zither filled the air, and ten or so maidservants descended from the tower and tied up Guirui's horse, and escorted the exam candidate into the Grand Secretary's mansion for the purpose of their marriage. The Grand Secretary and his wife immediately came out, invited guests to witness the ceremony, and arranged for Miss Jiao to marry Guirui. After they performed the rituals of paying respect to the heavens and earth, the couple exchanged bows with each other and then with their parents-in-law. The Grand Secretary ordered the preparations for a banquet, and they feasted into the night.

As this list arrived at the prefecture of Haizhou, there was a man by the name of Chen, surname Chen and given name Ci, nickname Ming Rui. The moment he saw this list, he immediately rushed back home and told his mother, Mrs. Zhang, "The imperial decree has issued the golden list, decreeing the opening of the province, seeking out capable men to take the civil service examination. My son intends to go forward and take part in it. Should he secure a post or half a post, to bring glory to the family, to make his name known, to bestow on his wife and children official patronage, to adorn the family gates, this is the son's heart's desire. I therefore come to inform you before I depart." Mrs. Zhang said, "My son, a scholar, a reader from a young age and a traveler from a mature age, exactly the way it should be. Go ahead and take the examination, but be careful on the way. If you succeed, be sure to return home early." Ming Rui then instructed the servant to pack his luggage and bid his mother farewell before setting off in haste. Upon arriving at Chang'an, he happened to arrive just as the imperial examination was underway, so he went inside. Having finished the first round of the examination and the three tiers of the imperial court examination, the Tang Emperor personally bestowed on him the top grade of the list, so he spent three days riding on horseback to celebrate. It just so happened that while he was strolling past the gate of Prime Minister Yin Kai Shanshan's residence, he saw the prime minister's daughter, named Weng Jiao, also known as Man Tang Jiao, unmarried and young, preparing to throw the embroidered balls to choose a groom in a high-rise tower. By coincidence, Chen Ming Rui was walking by below the tower, and upon seeing him, the young lady's eyes lit up at his remarkable talents and her heart was filled with great joy. She tossed down an embroidered ball that just so happened to hit Ming Rui's black silk hat. Suddenly, the sound of fine zither music and pipes filled the air, ten or more maidservants descended the stairs and lassoed Ming Rui's horse's head, escorting the successful candidate into the prime minister's manor to wed. The prime minister and his wife promptly stepped out of the hall and summoned the attendants to prepare the betrothal rites, and the prime minister assigned the young woman to be the bride of Ming Rui. After completing the ceremonial bow to heaven and earth, Ming Rui and his bride exchanged bows, and then paid respects to her parents. The prime minister instructed his servants to prepare a feast, and they spent a whole night drinking together.

When this decree reached the Haizhou area, there was a man by the surname Chen and the given name Lelei, with the courtesy name Guangru. Upon seeing this decree, he immediately went home to tell his mother, Lady Zhang, "The imperial court has posted the yellow list, decreeing the opening of the province to seek out talented individuals, and I, your son, intend to proceed to take the exam. If I can secure a position or half a title, it will bring honor to our kin and raise our family's name, and make a dazzling reputation. I am particularly reporting this to you, Mother, before I leave." Lady Zhang replied, "As a scholar's child, I should follow the path of 'learning from youth and acting from vigor.' This is the proper thing for you to do. When you go to take the exams, you must be cautious on the road, and if you get a position, be sure to return soon." Guangru thereupon ordered the servant to pack his luggage, and, after bidding farewell to his mother, he set off early on his journey. When he arrived in Chang'an, it was the day of the great selection, and Guangru proceeded to enter the competition area. After completing the selection and submitting his three essays, he was awarded the position of first rank by the imperial secretary's own handwriting. He was showered with felicitations as he rode through the streets for three days. Just then, he happened to pass by the entrance of the family home of Prime Minister Yin Kaishan, where there lived a daughter of the prime minister's, named Wenxia, also known as Man Tangxia. She was a maiden who had never been married, standing high atop a decorated tower, tossing and throwing embroidered balls in search of a husband. It just so happened that Guangru passed by beneath the tower, and upon seeing him, the young lady was delighted with his refined features and knew that he was the newly promoted top-ranking scholar, her heart overflowing with joy. She therefore tossed the embroidered ball downwards, hitting Guangru right on his black hat. Just as he heard the sound of a group of pipa and zither music, a group of maidservants came down from the tower and caught Guangru's horse's head, and escorted the top-ranking scholar into the prime minister's mansion for a wedding. The prime minister and his wife immediately appeared on the hall, summoned the attendants to announce the ceremonial rituals, and married off their daughter to Guangru. They performed the sacrifices to Heaven and Earth, and the husband and wife exchanged the ritual bows, then also performed the rituals to their in-laws. The prime minister ordered a banquet to be arranged, and they celebrated through the night.

On arriving at the prefectural office, Chen Chen, styled Gongyang, saw the imperial decree and immediately returned home. He told his mother, Zhang: "The throne has issued the yellow list, decreed the opening of the province, and selected virtuous talents. My son wishes to go ahead and take the examinations. If he succeeds in securing an official position, half a post, he will bring honor to his family, spread his family's reputation, and illuminate the gate, which is my son's ambition. I specially come to inform my mother of this decision to depart." Zhang said, "My son is a scholar, the saying 'learn while young, move forward while strong' is suitable for him. Go to the examinations, and on the road, be careful. If he gets an official position, return early." Gongyang instructed the household servant to pack his luggage and bid farewell to his mother before proceeding on his journey. When he arrived in Chang'an, the grand selection was in full swing, and Gongyang entered the examination hall. After completing the selection, he went on to compose three essays, and the Tang Emperor, with his imperial brush, personally bestowed on him the title of Number One Scholar, whereupon he spent three days riding on horseback through the streets in triumph. It just so happened that while he was riding, he passed by the main gate of the Minister's residence, and the Minister, Yin Kai Shan's daughter, named Wen Jiao, also known as Man Tang Jiao, a virgin of marriageable age, stood on the balcony of a decorated pavilion, scattering embroidered balls to find a son-in-law. Chen Gongyang was just passing by beneath the balcony when Wen Jiao saw his exceptional talent, recognized that he was the newly-minted Number One Scholar, and felt inwardly delighted. She cast an embroidered ball that just happened to hit Gongyang's hat. Suddenly, the sound of a zither and flutes could be heard, and ten or so maid servants descended the stairs, took hold of Gongyang's horse bridle, and led him into the Minister's mansion to marry him off. The Minister and his wife immediately came out of the hall, summoned the attendants to pay their respects, and married Gongyang to Wen Jiao. After paying their respects to heaven and earth, the couple exchanged their respects, and then paid their respects to the bride's parents and mother-in-law. The Minister instructed the arrangements for a banquet, whereupon they spent the night drinking.

After passing three years, the patriarch once again sat on the throne, and his discourse was delivered to the assembly. He spoke of karmic cases and analyzed external appearances. Suddenly he asked, "Where is the Monkey?" The Monkey approached, kneeling down, and said, "Your disciple is here." The patriarch said, "You have been practicing what kind of method?" The Monkey replied, "Your disciple has recently developed a clear understanding of the dharma nature, and my root has also gradually stabilized." The patriarch said, "Although you have understood the dharma nature and grasped the root, you are still beware of the 'three calamities that bring harm'." The Monkey heard this and pondered for a long time, saying, "The words of my master are misguided. I have often heard it said that to cultivate the great dharma is to be as long-lived as heaven, and that when the Yang and Yin are in harmony, all illnesses will disappear. Why, then, are there three calamities that bring harm?" The patriarch said, "This is an extraordinary dharma. It means to snatch the creative power of heaven and earth, to penetrate the subtle essence of the sun and the moon. Even if one achieves a divine body and attains long life, it is still inevitable that after five hundred years, heaven will unleash a calamity upon you in the form of a thunderbolt, and you must see your true nature and mind beforehand to avoid it. If you avoid it, you will be as long-lived as heaven; if you cannot avoid it, you will meet your end. After another five hundred years, heaven will unleash a fire calamity upon you. This is not a natural fire nor a mundane fire; it is called the 'Yin fire.' It will burn from the Dan Tian, through the gates of the thousand chambers, dissolving the five viscera and the four limbs, reducing all one's meritorious deeds to nothing. After another five hundred years, heaven will unleash a wind calamity upon you. This is not the wind of the east, south, west, or north, nor is it the gentle wind of the dawn or the cool wind of the willows and the cedars. It is called the 'Ghost Wind.' It will blow into your skull, pass through the gates of the hundred passages, and disintegrate your bones and flesh. This is why one must avoid it."

The Monkey heard this and felt his bones tremble with fear. He bowed his head in respect, saying, "Great Master, you have shown me the method to avoid the three calamities. I dare not forget your kindness." The patriarch said, "This is not difficult, but you are different from others, so it is not easily transmitted." The Monkey said, "I, too, am a living being with a round head and flat feet, with nine orifices and four limbs, five viscera and six passages. How am I different from others?" The patriarch said, "Although you look like a human, you are missing a cheek." The Monkey had a cleft palate and a pointed chin. The Monkey reached out and felt his face, laughing and saying, "The master has miscalculated! I may be missing a cheek, but I have more of this spongy cheek, which can also be made to fit over my face." The patriarch said, "Very well, you want to learn how to transform? There are the heavenly stems, with their thirty-six transformations, and the earthly branches, with their seventy-two transformations." The Monkey said, "I am willing to put in the effort and learn just one earthly transformation." The patriarch said, "If you are willing, come closer and I will impart the secret phrase to you." And with that, the patriarch leaned over and whispered something in the Monkey's ear, without revealing the contents of the secret phrase. The Monkey was quick to understand and memorized the phrase. He then practiced and cultivated himself, mastering all seventy-two earthly transformations.

It had been three years since the Old Master had ascended to his throne again and preached to the multitude, using parables and discussing the external form. Suddenly, he asked, "Where is the Awakened Monkey?" The Awakened Monkey came forward, kneeling down, and said, "I am your disciple." The Old Master asked, "What kind of doctrine have you been practicing lately?" The Awakened Monkey replied, "I have recently made progress in my understanding of the true nature and have also solidified my foundation." The Old Master said, "If you have achieved understanding of the true nature and mastered the source, why do you still worry about the three calamities and their misfortunes?" The Awakened Monkey pondered this for a long time and said, "Master's words are incorrect. I have always heard that the Way is elevated and virtuous, coequal with Heaven, and when the yin and yang have reached harmony, no sickness arises. So how can there be these three calamities and their misfortunes?" The Old Master said, "This is an extraordinary Way: it involves taking away Heaven and Earth's creative power and invading the subtle mechanisms of the sun and moon. After attaining enlightenment, it is difficult for ghosts and spirits to abide. Although you may maintain your youth and long life, after five hundred years, a thunder calamity will come and you must use your insight and wisdom to avoid it in advance. If you can avoid it, your life will be as long as Heaven's, but if you fail to avoid it, your life will come to an end. After another five hundred years, a fire calamity will descend and burn you. This fire is neither divine fire nor ordinary fire, and it is called '陰火' or 'dark fire'. It will arise from your 'mingmen' meridian, pass through the 'hudun' palace, burn the five viscera to ashes, and reduce your limbs to withered bones, rendering all your thousand-year efforts futile. After another five hundred years, a wind calamity will come and blow you away. This wind is neither an eastern, southern, western, or northern wind, nor a gentle breeze, nor a gentle wind from flowers and willows, and it is called '赑風' or 'bare wind'. It will blow into your crown, pass through the dantian, pierce the nine apertures, dissolve your bones and flesh, and finally cause your body to disintegrate. Therefore, you must avoid them all." When the Awakened Monkey heard this, his bones were chilled with fear, and he bowed his head, paying his respects, saying, "I implore you, Grand Old Man, to be compassionate and teach me the method to avoid the three calamities." The Old Master said, "This is not difficult, but since you are different from others, I have not been able to teach you." The Awakened Monkey said, "I too am round-headed and stand on the ground with square feet, just like other people. I have nine apertures, four limbs, five viscera, and six bowels, how am I any different from others?" The Old Master said, "Although you look like other people, you are less cheeky." Indeed, the monkey had a concave face and a pointed nose. The Awakened Monkey chuckled and said, "Master hasn't quite counted you correctly! Although I may be less cheeky, I have an additional pouch in my cheek, which is more than what others have, and I can still narrowly escape, I suppose." The Old Master said, "That doesn't matter, but you still want to learn the usual methods? There are ninety-six stellar permutations, seventy-two earth prison transformations. You want to learn the seventy-two earth prison transformations, right?" The Awakened Monkey said, "I'm willing to explore and learn, let me learn one earth prison transformation." The Old Master said, "If you are this willing, come forward and I will teach you the incantation." The Old Master whispered some mysterious words into his ear, and the Awakened Monkey quickly absorbed and practiced them, finally mastering the seventy-two earth prison transformations.

Not long after, the Patriarch once again occupied his seat, and the assembly listened as he explained the principles of the doctrine. Using an analogy, he was discussing the process of cultivating the "flesh skin" outside the body. Just then, he inquired: "Where is the Monkey?"

The Monkey stepped forward and knelt down, saying: "I am your disciple."

The Patriarch asked: "You have been cultivating the Way, what has your spiritual practice been?"

The Monkey replied: "My spiritual nature has become clear, and my roots have grown deep."

The Patriarch said: "If your spiritual nature is clear, and you've mastered your roots, you've already obtained the divine body. However, you must beware of the three calamities."

The Monkey listened attentively and pondered for a long time before responding: "Father's words are mistaken. I often hear it said that a sage is lofty and venerable, and his lifespan equals the heavens; his yin and yang are harmonious, and all illnesses are eradicated. How could there be three calamities?"

The Patriarch replied: "This is a superior and rare type of cultivation. It involves stealing the creative power of heaven and earth, and violating the subtle essence of the sun and moon. Even though you may attain immortality, after five hundred years, the heavenly forces will bring down a calamity to strike you, requiring you to see your true nature and cultivate your wisdom to avoid it in advance. If you can avoid it, your lifespan will equal that of the heavens; if not, you will die at that time. Five hundred years later, a fire calamity will come to ravage you. This is not ordinary fire, nor is it mundane fire; it's called the 'dark fire.' It will rise up from the 'fountainhead' below your navel, pass through the palace of the Muddy Pellet, reduce your five organs to ashes, and rot your four limbs, rendering all your hard work in the past thousand years an illusion. Another five hundred years will pass, and the wind calamity will blow. This is not the wind from the east, south, west, or north, nor is it the wind of the grain-harvesting or the frost's chill; it's called the 'Descending Wind.' It will blow into your brain cavity, pass through your elixir field, and pierce your nine orifices, dissolving your bones and muscles, so that your body will be disintegrated. Therefore, you must avoid all three calamities."

The Monkey listened and his very bones were chilled to the marrow. He bowed his head in respect, saying: "Great-grandfather has compassionately imparted the method to avoid the calamities; I shall not forget this great debt."

The Patriarch said: "This is no difficult matter. It's just that you are different from others, so you cannot be taught."

The Monkey said: "I too, have a round head reaching to the heavens, feet that are square, capable of standing on the earth, and possess the nine orifices, four limbs, five organs, and six viscera, just like ordinary people. How am I any different?"

The Patriarch replied: "Although you appear human, you have fewer facial whiskers."

In fact, the Monkey had a small chin and a pointed mouth. The Monkey reached out to feel his face, laughing and saying: "Father has made a mistake! Although I may have fewer whiskers, I have this special pouch; it's quite useful, don't you think?"

The Patriarch said: "Fine, you want to learn from ordinary people? There are 36 heavenly stars, which correspond to 36 different transformations, and 72 terrestrial stars, corresponding to 72 different transformations."

The Monkey said: "I would like to deeply understand, let me learn one type of terrestrial star transformation."

The Patriarch said: "Since you're so eager, come forward and I'll teach you the oral formula."

He whispered into the Monkey's ear, but the Monkey didn't know what wise method he spoke. At that moment, the Monkey had suddenly understood all the mysteries and was able to cultivate the 72 terrestrial star transformations; he spent a long time practicing and refining himself, and eventually mastered all of them.

Three years had passed, the Patriarch ascended to the throne again and preached to the assembly. His teaching focused on subtle affairs, analyzing the external appearance and inner reality. Suddenly, he asked, "Where is the Monkey King?" The Monkey King approached, bowing down: "Your disciple is here." The Patriarch asked, "What has your disciple been cultivating?" The Monkey King replied, "My recent practice has gained a deeper understanding of the Buddha-nature, and my root is gradually solidified." The Patriarch said, "If you have attained the Buddha-nature and grasped the root, yet still have the Buddha-body divine energy (qi), then why do you need to guard against 'Three Calamities'?" The Monkey King listened and pondered for a long time before saying, "Your words are wrong, venerable master. I often heard that a Great Sage cultivates virtue that matches the heavens and lives forever, and that water and fire are harmonized, resulting in no illness. Why would there be 'Three Calamities'?" The Patriarch said, "This is an extraordinary path: stealing heaven and earth's creative power, invading the celestial mechanism of the sun and moon. After becoming a dan, the gods and spirits find it difficult to bear. Although one maintains a youthful appearance and longevity, after five hundred years, a thunder disaster will be sent from heaven, and you must see your true nature and illuminate your mind beforehand to avoid it. If you can avoid it, you will live in harmony with heaven, but if not, you will die. Five hundred years later, a fire disaster will be sent, which is neither divine fire nor ordinary fire, called 'Dark Fire'. From the spring well (jīn qióng shuǐ) at the base of the spine, it will rise up and pierce the mud palace, reducing the five viscera to ash, and making the four limbs rotten. Another five hundred years later, a disaster of 'chaotic wind' (fàn fēng) will blow. This is not the wind of the eight directions, nor is it the gentle breeze of the golden sun or the fragrant wind of flowers and trees, but is called 'chaotic wind'. From the fontanelle (wú dé róu) at the top of the head, it will blow into the six cavities, passing through the nine orifices, and dissipate the bones and flesh. Thus, it's necessary to avoid all three calamities." The Monkey King listened, and his bones felt cold with fright, prostrating himself in reverence and bowing down, saying, "The Venerable Lord shows pity, transmitting the method to avoid the Three Calamities. I will never forget your benevolence." The Patriarch said, "This is no difficult matter; the reason you cannot receive the transmission is that you are unlike others." The Monkey King said, "I also have a head that reaches the sky and feet that cover the earth, just like ordinary people, with nine apertures and four limbs, five viscera and six cavities, what makes me different from them?" The Patriarch said, "Although you are similar to people, you have fewer facial whiskers." The Monkey King stretched out his hand to feel, laughed and said, "Venerable Master, you've under-estimated! I may have fewer whiskers, but I have this forehead bag (qī tóu xiū dài), and it's enough to allow me to transform." The Patriarch said, "Very well, then you should learn the general transformations, of which there are thirty-six types, or the specific talismans, of which there are seventy-two types." The Monkey King said, "I wish to delve deeper and study one type of transformation, let's say, a specific talisman." The Patriarch said, "Since you're willing to do so, come forward and I'll transmit the secret manual to you." So the Patriarch whispered in his ear, saying something wondrous, and at the time, the Monkey King was enlightened to all aspects and mastered the hundred transformations. The Monkey King then studied and practiced the secret, mastering all seventy-two transformations.

But after three years had passed, the Venerable Master returned to his throne and taught the scriptures. His lecture was about analogies and cases, and he discussed the essence of one's external form. Suddenly he asked, "Where is the Monkey?" The Monkey drew near and bowed: "Your disciple is here." The Venerable Master said, "What practices have you been cultivating these days?" The Monkey replied, "Your disciple has recently achieved a relatively thorough understanding of the true nature, and his roots have become relatively firm." The Venerable Master said, "Since you have attained the true nature and understood the roots, you have already achieved enlightenment, yet you still need to be mindful of the 'three calamities that bring harm'." The Monkey listened and pondered for a long time before saying, "Your words are wrong, Master. I have often heard that one who cultivates the Way is endowed with great virtue and lives as long as heaven and earth, and when water and fire have been harmonized, there is no illness, so how can there be three calamities that bring harm?" The Venerable Master said, "This is an extraordinary doctrine: by seizing the creative power of heaven and earth and intruding upon the subtle mechanism of the sun and moon, one can attain the state of enlightenment. However, after one has transformed and perfected oneself, even the spirits will find it difficult to bear. Although one's appearance remains youthful and one's life is prolonged, after five hundred years, heaven will send a thunderstorm to strike you, and you must be able to see your true nature and wise heart beforehand and avoid it in time. He then leaned in close and whispered some profound teachings, but I do not know what they were. This Monkey King became enlightened in an instant and, at that time, learned the incantation and practiced it, thus mastering all seventy-two transformations.

The room was larger and higher than mine, better furnished, and lighter; it had a closet, a dresser, a couch, and my bed, a large and broad one, covered with a green silk quilt. But in that room I noticed a terrible animal, some kind of monster. It looked like a scorpion, but not a scorpion, and even much more frightening; and, as if it was just that there aren't such animals in nature, and that it appeared on purpose, and that this is what the mystery is about. I looked at it very closely: it was brown and armored, a crawling creature four finger-widths long, two fingers thick at the head, getting thinner towards the tail, so that the tip of the tail was not thicker than one-tenth of a finger-width. Two legs, one on each side, two finger-widths long, came out from the body at an angle of forty-five degrees from the head; so that the whole animal looked, when seen from above, like a sickle. I didn't look at its head, but saw two antennae, not long, like two strong needles, also brown. Two antennae at the end of the tail and two at the end of each leg, so eight in total. The animal was running very fast across the room, thumping with its legs and tail, and when it ran, the body and legs wiggled like snakes, at an incredible speed, despite the armor, and it was very disgusting to watch. I was terribly afraid it would sting me; I was told it was poisonous, but I was mainly tormented by who had brought it into my room, and what they wanted to do with it, and what the mystery is about. It was hiding under the dresser, under the closet, crawling into the corners. I sat on a stool with my legs tucked under me. It quickly crossed the room at an angle and disappeared near my stool. I looked around in fear, but since I had my legs tucked under me, I was hoping that it wouldn't crawl onto the stool. Suddenly I heard a rustling noise behind me, almost at my head, and turned to see the monster crawling up the wall and already level with my head and even touching my hair with its tail, which was twisting and wriggling with incredible speed. I jumped up, and the animal disappeared. I was afraid to lie down on the bed, in case it crawled under the pillow. My mother and one of her acquaintances came into the room, and they started catching the creature, but they were calmer than I was, and even weren't afraid. But they didn't understand anything. Suddenly the creature slithered out again; this time it was moving very quietly and as if with some special intention, slowly wriggling, which was even more disgusting, across the room to the doors. At that point, my mother opened the door and called Norma, our big, black, shaggy terrier; she's been dead for five years. She rushed into the room and pinned the creature to the ground. The creature stopped, but was still wriggling and tapping the floor with the ends of its legs and tail. Animals don't feel supernatural fear, or so I think; but at this moment, it seemed to me that there was something quite extraordinary, almost mystical, in the fear of Norma, as if she too sensed, like me, that there was something fateful and mysterious about the creature. She slowly backed away from the creature, quietly and carefully slithering towards her; it seemed to her as if it might suddenly leap and sting her. But, despite her fear, Norma looked ferociously, though her whole body was shaking. Suddenly she slowly bared her dreadful teeth, opened her huge, red mouth, adjusted, hooked, decided, and suddenly grabbed the creature in her jaws. It must have been quite a struggle for the creature to wriggle free, so Norma caught it again, mid-air, and twice swallowed it whole with her whole mouth, just like eating. The exoskeleton crackled on her teeth; the creature's tail and legs, which were protruding from her mouth, wriggled with an awful speed. Suddenly Norma let out a piteous wail; the creature had managed to sting her tongue. With a cry and a scream, she opened her mouth in pain, and I saw the mangled creature still wriggling inside her mouth, spewing out from its crushed body onto her tongue a lot of white juice, similar to the juice of a crushed black cockroach... At that moment, I woke up, and the prince came in.

It was a very rainy, stormy morning when K. came to the office, already full of troubles about the day ahead of him, at seven o'clock in order to finish at least some work before the visit would take him away from it. He was very tired because he had spent half the night studying an Italian grammar to prepare a bit; the window, which he had often sat at lately, lured him more than the desk, but he resisted and sat down to work. Unfortunately, the servant just then entered and announced that the Director had sent him to inquire if the Procurator was there yet; was he here, then he should be so kind as to go over to the reception room, since the gentleman from Italy was already there. "I'm coming," said K., stuffed a small dictionary into his pocket, took an album of the city's sights, which he had prepared for the visitor, under his arm, and went through the office of the Deputy Director into the directors' room. He was pleased that he had come to the office so early and could be available, which was probably not seriously expected of anyone. The Deputy Director's office was, of course, just as empty as in the depth of night; probably the servant should also have called him into the reception room, but it had been unsuccessful. As K. entered the reception room, the two gentlemen stood up from the deep armchairs. The Director smiled pleasantly, clearly he was very pleased about K's arrival, and immediately made the introductions; the Italian shook K's hand firmly and, smiling, called someone a "dawn riser." K. did not quite understand whom he meant; it was also a strange word, the meaning of which K. only slowly comprehended. He answered with some flat sentences, which the Italian laughed at again, while he several times stroked his grayish-blue, bushy moustache with a nervous hand. This moustache was, apparently, scented; one was almost tempted to approach and sniff it. When they had all sat down and a small, introductory conversation began, K. noticed with great discomfort that he only understood the Italian in snippets. When he spoke quietly, he understood him almost completely, but these were rare exceptions; mostly, his words poured out of his mouth, he shook his head as if out of pleasure at this. In such speeches, however, he entangled himself regularly in some dialect that had nothing Italian about it anymore, but which the Director not only understood but also spoke, which K. could have anticipated, since the Italian came from southern Italy, where the Director had also spent several years. In any case, K. recognized that the possibility of communicating with the Italian was largely taken away from him, for his French was only barely understandable as well; also, the moustache hid the lip movements, whose sight might have helped with understanding. K. began to foresee many annoyances, but for the time being, he gave up trying to understand the Italian – in the presence of the Director, who understood him so easily, it would have been unnecessary effort – and limited himself to grumblingly observing how he rested deeply yet lightly in the armchair, how he often tugged at his short, sharply cut jacket, and how he once tried to convey something with raised arms and loose, swinging hands that K. did not understand, although he kept his eyes fixed on the hands. Finally, as K., who was otherwise unoccupied, only mechanically followed the flow of conversation with his gaze, made aware of his earlier fatigue, he caught himself in his alarm, fortunately just in time, in the moment when he had been about to get up, turn around, and leave. In the end, the Italian looked at the clock and sprang up. After he had bid the Director farewell, he pressed himself against K., so tightly that K. had to push his armchair back in order to move. The Director, who certainly recognized the distress in which K. found himself facing the Italian, intervened in the conversation, cleverly and delicately, so that it seemed as if he was only giving a few suggestions, while in reality he made everything that the Italian, tirelessly speaking into his face, presented, instantly clear to K. K. learned from him that the Italian had to attend to some matters, that he unfortunately only had a little time, that he by no means intended to rush through all the sights, but rather – although this was only possible if K. agreed, and the decision lay in his hands – had decided to visit only the cathedral, and this in detail. He was extremely pleased to be able to make this visit with a scholar and amiable man – that was K., who was engaged in nothing but ignoring the Italian and quickly taking in the Director's words – and he asked him, if the hour suited him, to meet him in the cathedral in two hours, around ten o'clock. He himself hoped to be there at this time, if not earlier. K. answered in a suitable manner, the Italian first shook the Director's hand, then K.'s, then the Director's again, and left, with both of them following, but still half-turned towards them, still talking, to the door. K. then stayed a little while with the Director, who looked particularly pale today. He thought he had to apologize somehow to K. and said – they stood close together in secret – that he had originally intended to go with the Italian himself, but then – he gave no specific reason – had decided to send K. instead. If the Italian did not understand him at the start, he should not be taken aback by it; understanding would come quickly enough, and even if he understood nothing at all, it was not so bad, since it was not so important for the Italian to be understood. Besides, K's Italian was surprisingly good, and he would certainly make a good impression. With that, K. was dismissed. The time still available to him he spent writing out rare vocabulary that he would need to guide him in the cathedral from his dictionary. It was an extremely tiresome work, servants brought the mail, officials came with various requests and stood at the door, since they saw K. busy, but did not budge before he had listened to them, the Deputy Director did not miss the opportunity to disturb K., came often in, took the dictionary from his hand, and apparently completely senselessly leafed through it; even parties appeared, when the door opened, in the semidarkness of the ante-room and hesitantly bowed – they wanted to draw attention to themselves, but were not sure if they were seen –; everything moved around K. as if he were the center, while he himself compiled the words he needed, then looked them up in the dictionary, then wrote them out, then practiced their pronunciation and finally tried to learn them by heart. His earlier good memory, however, seemed to have completely deserted him; sometimes he became so angry with the Italian, who was causing him this effort, that he buried the dictionary under the papers with the intention of not preparing himself anymore, but then he realized that he could not stand before the works of art in the cathedral with the Italian in silence, and with greater rage, he pulled the dictionary out again.

K replied with some corresponding words, the Italian first pressed the director's hand, then K's, then the director's again, and went out, followed by both, with his back only half-turned, still talking, to the door. The time that was left to him was spent on writing down rare vocabulary that he would need for the tour at the cathedral from the dictionary. His earlier good memory seemed to have completely deserted him; he became so angry with the Italian, who was causing him this exertion, that he buried the dictionary under papers with the firm intention of not preparing himself anymore, but then saw that he could not stand before the works of art at the cathedral silent and mute, and he pulled the dictionary out again with even greater anger.
