It seemed, therefore, that one had to calm down, look at the situation calmly, and wait. But, alas, serenity did not last for ten minutes. The first blow to calmness was dealt by the news that had come during mother's absence. It happened while Elizabeth Prokofyevna was on her trip to Stone Island on the very same morning after the prince had arrived the previous day at one o'clock instead of ten. The sisters, in response to their mother's inquisitive questions, told her everything in great detail, first of all that it seemed that nothing had happened, that the prince had arrived, that Aglaya had stayed away from him for half an hour, then came out and as soon as she did, immediately offered the prince a game of chess. That the prince did not know how to play chess at all, and that Aglaya had won right away. She had become very merry and had scolded the prince terribly for his lack of skill, laughed at him horribly, so that it was a pity to look at him. Then she suggested playing cards, cards, but this time the opposite happened: the prince turned out to be such a great card player as... as a professor; he played masterfully; it was Aglaya who was cheating and switching cards and stealing from his eyes, and yet he left her in the game every time; five times in a row. Aglaya got extremely angry and went completely wild; she told the prince such insults and cruel words that he had stopped laughing and had even paled when she finally said to him that 'her foot would not be in this room while he was sitting there, and that it was simply indecent of him to come to them, especially at night, at one o'clock, after everything that had happened'. Then she slammed the door shut and left. The prince went out like he was attending a funeral, despite all their consolations. Suddenly, twenty-five minutes later, after the prince had left, Aglaya ran out onto the veranda and with such haste that she didn't even wipe her eyes, and her eyes were tear-stained; she ran out because Kolya had come and brought a hedgehog. They all looked at the hedgehog; Kolya explained to them that it wasn't his, but that he was now taking it with his friend, another classmate, Kostya Lebedev, who had remained outside and was ashamed to come in because he had a hatchet; that they had bought the hedgehog and the hatchet from a passerby peasant; the hedgehog was sold to them for fifty kopecks, and they had even managed to convince the peasant to sell them the hatchet because it was convenient and it was a very good hatchet. But then Aglaya started pestering Kolya to sell the hedgehog to her immediately, treating him very kindly and even calling him 'dear'. Kolya resisted for a long time, but eventually gave in and called Kostya Lebedev, who did indeed come in with the hatchet and looked very flustered. But then it turned out that the hedgehog didn't belong to them at all, but to some third boy, Petrov, who had given them both money to buy 'The History' by Schloesser from some fourth boy who, being in need of money, had sold it for a profit; that they had gone to buy 'The History' by Schloesser, but couldn't resist buying the hedgehog instead; therefore, the hedgehog and the hatchet belonged to that third boy whom they were now carrying instead of 'The History' by Schloesser. But Aglaya kept pestering Kolya so much that they finally agreed to sell the hedgehog to her. As soon as Aglaya got the hedgehog, she immediately, with Kolya's help, put it in a wicker basket, covered it with a handkerchief, and started asking Kolya to take it to the prince immediately, without stopping anywhere, as a token of her deep respect. Kolya agreed with joy and gave his word that he would deliver it, but then started pestering her: 'What does the hedgehog and a gift like it mean?' Aglaya replied that it was none of his business. He replied that he was convinced there was an allegory involved. Aglaya got annoyed and snapped at him, saying he was a child, and nothing more. Kolya immediately retorted that if he didn't respect her as a woman and, in addition, his own convictions, then he would have immediately shown her that he knew how to answer such an insult. In the end, however, Kolya did go off to deliver the hedgehog with great enthusiasm, with Kostya Lebedev running after him; Aglaya, seeing that Kolya was swinging the basket a bit too freely, screamed at him from the veranda: 'Please, Kolya, don't drop it, darling!' - almost as if she hadn't just been scolding him. Kolya stopped and, equally composed, shouted back at her with great willingness: 'No, I won't drop it, Aglaya Ivanovna. Be completely calm!' - and then ran off again in great haste. It seemed, therefore, that one had to calm down, be calm and wait. But, alas, the tranquility did not last for ten minutes. K. stared at the warder. Did he get school-teaching from a person perhaps younger than himself here? For his openness, he was punished with a reprimand? And he was not told the reason for his arrest or who was behind it? He became agitated, walked up and down, and, with no one stopping him, pushed back his cuffs, felt his chest, smoothed his hair, passed by the three men, said, "It is pointless," upon which they turned to him and looked at him kindly, but seriously, and finally stopped before the warder's desk again. "The prosecutor Hasterer is my good friend," he said, "can I telephone him?" "Certainly," said the warder, "but I do not know what it could mean, unless you had a private matter to discuss with him." "What meaning?" K. cried out, more startled than irritated. "Who are you? You're looking for meaning and leading the most nonsensical thing there is? Is it not too ridiculous? They overpowered me first, and now they sit or stand here, and I'm to lecture here on the high school before you. What sense is there in telephoning a prosecutor if I'm supposed to be arrested?" "Alright, I won't telephone," said K., and went to the window. Over there, the society was at the window, and only now, because K. stepped up to the window, were they slightly disturbed in their calm observation. The old men wanted to get up, but the man behind them calmed them down. "Over there are such spectators," K. shouted loudly to the warder and pointed with his index finger outside. "Away from there," he then shouted across. The three took a few steps back immediately, the two old men even behind the man who shielded them with his broad body and, from his mouth movements, appeared to be saying something inaudible at a distance. However, they did not disappear entirely, but seemed to be waiting for the moment they could approach the window unnoticed again. "Pushy, thoughtless people!" said K., as he turned back into the room. The warder possibly agreed with him, as K. thought he could see from a side glance. But it was equally possible that he had not heard him at all, since he had his hand pressed on the table and seemed to compare the length of his fingers. The two guards sat on a suitcase covered with a decorative cloth and rubbed their knees. The three young people had their hands on their hips and looked around aimlessly. It was quiet like in some forgotten office. "Well, gentlemen," K. shouted, as if he was carrying the weight of all of them on his shoulders, "I conclude from your appearance that my affair is over. I think it would be best to stop thinking about the justification or lack thereof of your actions and to give the matter a conciliatory conclusion through a handshake. If you agree with me, then—“ and he approached the warder's desk and extended his hand. The warder looked up, chewed on his lips, and looked at K.'s outstretched hand; K. still believed that the warder would shake it. But the warder stood up, took a hard, round hat from Fräulein Bürstner's bed, and set it on carefully with both hands, like one does when trying on a new hat. "How easy everything seems to you!" he said to K. "We should give the matter a conciliatory conclusion, you meant? No, no, that won't do. On the other hand, I don't mean to say you should despair. No, why should you? You're just arrested, that's all. That's what I had to tell you, did tell you, and saw how you took it. That's all for today, and we can part, although only provisionally. You'll probably want to go to the bank now?" "To the bank?" K. asked, "I thought I was arrested." K. asked with a certain stubbornness, for although his handshake had not been accepted, he felt, especially since the warder had stood up, increasingly independent of all these people. He was playing with them. He had the intention of following them if they were to leave, up to the front door and offer them his arrest. That's why he repeated himself: "How can I go to the bank when I'm under arrest?" "Ah," said the warder, who was already by the door, "you misunderstood me. You are arrested, of course, but that shouldn't stop you from fulfilling your profession. You shouldn't be hindered in your usual way of life." "Then being under arrest isn't very bad," said K. and went closer to the warder. "I never meant otherwise," said the warder. "It seems, however, that the notification of the arrest was not very necessary," said K. and came even closer. The others had also come closer. They were all now gathered in a small space by the door. "It was my duty," said the warder. "A foolish duty," said K. relentlessly. "Maybe," replied the warder, "but we want to avoid wasting time on such words. I had assumed you wanted to go to the bank. Since you're paying close attention to every word, I'll add: I'm not compelling you to go to the bank, I just assumed you wanted to. And to make it easier for you and to make your arrival at the bank as unobtrusive as possible, I've kept these three gentlemen, your colleagues, here at your disposal." "What?" cried K. and looked at the three in astonishment. These uncharacteristic, pale, young people, whom he had always just remembered from photographs as a group, were actually officials from his bank, not colleagues, that was too much to say and showed a gap in the warder's omniscience, but they were indeed subordinate officials from the bank. How had K. overlooked them? How had he, to let himself be taken in by the warder and the guards, not noticed these three? The stiff, hand-waving Rabensteiner, the blonde Kullich with his deep-set eyes, and Kaminer with his inexcusable, smile caused by a chronic muscle spasm. "Good morning!" said K. after a while and extended his hand to the correctly bowing gentlemen. "I didn't recognize you. Now we'll get to work, won't we?" The gentlemen nodded laughing and enthusiastically, as if they had been waiting for it all along, only when K. missed his hat, which had been left in his room, they all ran after it in a row, which suggested a certain embarrassment. K. stood still and watched them through the two open doors, the last one being the indifferent Rabensteiner, who had only set a elegant pace. Kaminer handed him the hat, and K. had to explicitly say that Kaminer's smile was not intended, yes that he didn't even intend to smile. In the anteroom, Frau Grubach, who did not look very guilty, opened the door to the whole company, and K. saw, as often before, down on her apron, which cut unnecessarily deeply into her powerful body. Below, K. decided to take an automobile to avoid increasing the already half-hour delay unnecessarily. Kaminer ran to the corner to fetch the car, the other two tried to distract K., as suddenly Kullich pointed to the opposite front door, where just the big man with the blonde goatee appeared and, for a moment, looked embarrassed about showing himself in his full size, stepped back against the wall and leaned against it. The old men were probably still on the stairs. K. was annoyed with Kullich for pointing out the man he himself had seen earlier and was even expecting. "Don't look!" he shouted out without noticing how awkward such a remark is when addressed to independent men. It was not even necessary to explain, for the automobile had just arrived, they got in and drove off. At that moment, K. remembered that he hadn't even noticed the warder and the guards leave, the warder had hidden the guards and now the guards had hidden the warder. Not a lot of mental agility was required for that, and K. decided to be more observant in this regard. However, he still turned unvoluntarily and leaned over the back of the car to possibly see the warder and the guards again. But he turned back and leaned comfortably into the corner of the car without even trying to look for anyone. Although it didn't seem like he would have needed encouragement at that moment, but now the gentlemen seemed tired, Rabensteiner looked to the right from the car, Kullich to the left, and only Kaminer stood with his grin ready to make a joke, unfortunately, humanity forbade it.

The monkey king sprang forward, jumping to the edge of the steep gorge, and with a flick of his wrist, displayed his extraordinary ability to stir up the ocean. He churned the water in the gorge to a state of utter clarity, making it seem like a tributary of the Yellow River overflowing with turbulent waves. The malevolent dragon was settled deep within the gorge, reclining peacefully, and in his heart, he thought, "This is indeed the combination of an advantageous omen and calamity. I had narrowly escaped death by escaping heaven's decree, and within a year, I've been fated to live by chance, and yet I've encountered this kind of fiend! He's come to harm me!"

As he grew more and more agitated, unable to endure his humiliation, he clenched his teeth and leapt out, cursing, "Where have you come from, you odious fiend? You dare to deceive me like this!" The monk replied, "Don't bother asking where I come from; all you need to do is return my horse, and I'll spare your life." The dragon said, "Your horse is inside my belly; how can I possibly regurgitate it? If I don't return it to you, what shall I do?" The monk retorted, "Don't even think about it! I'll just strike you dead to make up for the value of my horse's life!" The two of them clashed in a fierce battle at the foot of the cliff. The battle raged for only a few exchanges, but the smaller dragon was utterly no match for the monk. The monk brandished his rod and, with a swift motion, transformed into a water snake and slipped into the reeds.

Master Xuanzang lavished praise, saying, "He is a genuine heavenly being!" Bajian said, "What ability do you possess that you dare to lavish such praise? This is just a coincidence. Come on! Hurry up and peel the tiger, cook some meat, and get it ready to treat us too!" He grasped a fork with one hand and dragged the tiger with the other, leading the way. Master Xuanzang led the horse, following closely behind, journeying up the mountain slope, and suddenly they came upon a mountain village. In front of the gate, it was: towering ancient trees and meandering wild vines; desolate wind and dust, and extraordinary scenery. A single path was filled with the fragrance of wildflowers, and several stalks of green bamboo leaned against the side. The grass gate, lattice fences, and courtyard were worthy of being depicted and painted; stone slabs, whitewashed walls, were truly delightful and rare. Autumn foliage withered and deserted, the weather was crisp and lofty. Yellow leaves fell along the path, and white clouds floated above the peaks. In the dense forest, birds sang loudly, while outside the village gate, small dogs howled softly. Bajian arrived at the gate, threw down the dead tiger, and called out, "Where are you all?" Only then did a few household servants emerge, with grotesque and ugly appearances, came forward to drag and pull the tiger inside. Bajian instructed, "Hurry up and peel the skin, prepare it to be served later." Then he turned to welcome Master Xuanzang to come in. After meeting each other, Master Xuanzang again bowed to thank Bajian for his kindness and pity, saying, "You are a kind and merciful person, saving my life." Bajian said, "We are fellow villagers, why trouble yourself to thank me?" After drinking tea, an old woman led a young wife to bow to Master Xuanzang. Bajian said, "This is my mother and the mountain wife." Master Xuanzang said, "Please, your elder, please take a seat, I offer my respects." The old woman said, "Long-distance guest, you please take care of yourselves, don't trouble yourself to bow." Bajian said, "Mother, he is a person sent by the Tang Emperor to go to the West to seek scriptures. He was just at the mountain pass and met my child, and my child invited him to come home to rest his horse, and I will send him off tomorrow." The old woman heard and was extremely delighted, saying, "Good! Good! Good! I'll invite him, no need for such trouble, just in time for your father's anniversary tomorrow, I'll ask him to do some good deeds, recite scriptures, and send him off the next day." This Liu Bajian, despite being a tiger-killer and a guardian of the mountain, he still has filial piety in his heart, and upon hearing his mother's words, he wanted to prepare incense paper to retain Master Xuanzang.

The venerable monk Songshan said, "No need to praise him excessively, he is truly a god of the mountain!" Boding asked, "What abilities does he have, to be so lavishly praised? This is the blessing of the elder. Come, let's hurry up and prepare some food, and make arrangements for him as well." With one hand holding a fork and the other dragging a tiger, he led the way. The venerable monk followed closely behind, and as they walked along the mountain slope, they suddenly came upon a mountain estate. Before the entrance, truly, there stood towering ancient trees, and wild vines entwined across the path. The dusty air was cool, and the scenery was unlike anything else. A wildflower-scented path beckoned, and the tall, slender bamboo seemed to lean against each other in tender dependence. The grass hut, the rammed-earth walls, and the stone pavement were worthy of being sketched and painted; the stone bridge, the white-tiled walls, truly, it was a haven of peace and a rare beauty. The autumn wind was melancholic, the air was crisp and high. Yellow leaves lay scattered along the path, while white clouds drifted lazily above the ridges. In the dense forest, birds made their noise, while outside the gate, a small dog barked loudly. Boding arrived at the entrance, threw the dead tiger down, and called out, "Where are you young ones?" Four or five servants came out, all with grotesque and ugly features. They rushed forward, pulling and tugging to drag the tiger away. Boding gave orders, saying, "Hurry up and skin it, and make preparations for our guest." Then he turned back to greet the venerable monk as he entered the house. They greeted each other, and the venerable monk again thanked Boding for his kindness and mercy in saving his life. Boding said, "As fellow countrymen, there's no need for gratitude." They sat down and finished their tea. An old lady, accompanied by a young woman, came forward to pay their respects to the venerable monk. Boding said, "This is my mother and the mistress of the mountain." The venerable monk said, "Please, have your honored elder sit, and I shall pay my respects." The old lady said, "The venerable elder is a distant guest, please take care of yourselves, there's no need to kowtow." Boding said, "Mother, he is a Tang prince's emissary, sent to the West to seek the Buddha's scriptures. He was just on the mountain pass when he met my son, who, as a native of a neighboring country, invited him home to rest his horse. Tomorrow we will send him on his way." The old lady heard this and was overjoyed, saying, "Excellent! Excellent! Excellent! Since he is here, we can't just let him go without doing something good for him. It just so happens that tomorrow is my husband's anniversary of death, let the venerable elder do some good deeds, recite some scriptures, and send him off the next day." Although Liu Boding was a tiger slayer and a mountain's preserver, a brave and powerful figure, he still had a filial heart. When his mother spoke, he immediately wanted to prepare incense paper to keep the venerable monk.

"Your virtues are beyond description," said Tripitaka, "You are truly a mountain god!" Bajiao said, "What remarkable abilities do you have, deserving of such praise? It's the blessings of the venerable one that has led you here. Come! Let's get to it quickly, we'll skin the tiger, cook some meat, and have it ready for you." He grasped a pitchfork with one hand and dragged the tiger with the other, leading the way. Tripitaka led his horse behind, and they continued on, passing over a hillside when they suddenly came upon a village house. In front of the entrance were towering ancient trees, overgrown vines winding about. The roads were blanketed in a cold, faded dust, and the rock formations possessed a majestic air. Wildflowers swayed, releasing their fragrance, while towering bamboo stalks leaned against the sides of the lane. The thatched roof, the fence, and the courtyards were suited for being painted or drawn; the stone bridge and white plastered walls seemed like a truly delightful and unusual sight. The autumn scenery was melancholic, the air was crisp and lonely. Yellow leaves lay scattered along the paths, while white clouds drifted up on the mountain peaks. Birds chirped within the grove, and dogs barked outside the village gate. Bajiao arrived at the entrance, and threw the tiger down, calling out, "Where are the young ones?" A few houseboys then emerged, each one peculiar in appearance and wicked in demeanor, who came forward and dragged the tiger into the house. Bajiao instructed, "Let's get the skin off it and prepare for our guest." He turned around and welcomed Tripitaka into the house. The two met, and Tripitaka again expressed his gratitude for Bajiao's kindness and compassion in saving his life, Bajiao said, "As a fellow townsman, there's no need for gratitude." They sat down, and after drinking tea, an elderly woman, accompanied by a young wife, came forward to greet Tripitaka. Bajiao said, "This is my mother and the wife of the mountain master." Tripitaka said, "I request that the elder lady take her seat, I pay my respects." The elderly woman said, "The venerable one has traveled far, let us look after you, there's no need for such courtesy." Bajiao said, "Mother, he is an envoy of the Tang King, sent to the Western Heavens to seek the Buddhist scriptures. Yesterday, he encountered my child on the mountain top, and he kindly invited him to come home to rest his horse, and to send him off on his journey the next day." Upon hearing this, the elderly woman was overjoyed, saying, "Good! Good! Good! Please do have him stay, it would be just in time for Father's anniversary, let the venerable one stay and recite scriptures for us, and we'll send him off the next day." This Bajiao, though he is a tiger slayer and a mountain's guardian, the 'Heavenly Protector', still has filial thoughts, and upon hearing his mother's words, began to prepare incense sticks and to hold back Tripitaka.

The Master of the Scriptures highly praised him, saying, "You are truly a fierce tiger demon!"  Bi Qin said, "What special ability do you possess to deserve such great praise? This is just the old master's good fortune. Go, go! Hurry up and remove the tiger's hide, cook some meat, and prepare a meal for me too!" He grasped a pitchfork in one hand and led a tiger by the leg with the other, leading the way. The Master of the Scriptures led his horse, following closely behind, passing over the mountain slope, then suddenly a mountain inn came into view. The entrance was truly magnificent: towering ancient trees and overgrown vines carpeted the road. The mountain wind and dust were cool, and the air was filled with the sights and sounds of the precipitous mountain. Wildflowers filled the air with their fragrance, while the green silvery bamboo leaned against each other. The grass gate, the latticework fence, and the courtyard were worthy of brush and paint. The stone pavement, the white earth walls, and the edifice itself were truly delightful, truly rare. The autumn scenery was melancholic and serene, the atmosphere was lofty and isolated. The path on the side was littered with yellow leaves, and white clouds floated on the mountain peak. Within the sparse forest, the mountain birds made a cacophonous din, while at the entrance of the manor, a group of small dogs barked melodiously. Bi Qin came to the entrance, threw the tiger to the ground, and shouted, "Where are the young servants?" Only four or five houseboys with bizarre appearances and evil looks emerged, and pulled and dragged the tiger inside. Bi Qin instructed, "Hurry up and remove the hide, and make arrangements to receive our guests." Returning to welcome the Master of the Scriptures inside, the two saw each other and exchanged bows. The Master of the Scriptures again thanked Bi Qin's great kindness and mercy, saying, "A fellow countryman should not feel obligated to express gratitude." After tea, an elderly woman led a young woman in to greet the Master of the Scriptures. Bi Qin said, "This is my mother, the mountain wife." The Master of the Scriptures said, "Please have her seat upstairs, I, a humble monk, shall pay my respects." The elderly woman said, "A traveling old monk, please take care of yourselves, there is no need to show respect." Bi Qin said, "Mother, he is a messenger from the Tang Emperor, sent to the West to seek the scriptures from the Buddha. Just now, he was on the mountain pass and the child from our village invited him to come home to rest his horse. Tomorrow we will send him on his way." The elderly woman heard this and was overjoyed, saying, "Excellent! Excellent! Excellent! Just as it happens that tomorrow is my husband's commemoration, I hope you, old master, can do some good deeds, recite scriptures, and take him on the road the next day." This Liu Bi Qin, although a fierce tiger-slayer and a great guardian of the mountain, he still had a filial heart, and upon hearing his mother's words, immediately wanted to prepare incense and paper to keep the Master of the Scriptures.

"This one's exploits are beyond praise," said Tripitaka. "He's truly a divine being!" 
Pu-jin said, "What has he done to deserve such praise? This is just the older master's good fortune. Come along, come along! Go ahead and get the meat ready, and we'll treat him too." Holding a fork in one hand and leading the tiger with the other, Pu-jin led the way forward. Tripitaka led the horse, following behind, and as they continued their journey up the mountain slope, they suddenly caught sight of a village. The door in front was under a towering ancient tree, with a wild vine-covered path leading up to it. The air was cool and quiet, the scenery strange and wondrous. A winding path was fragrant with wildflowers, and the tops of the bamboo groves were lush and green. The thatched cottage gate, the wicker fence, and the garden walls all looked like something out of a painting. The stone bridge, the white-clay walls, and the rolling hills all brought joy and delight. Autumn leaves rustled in the breeze, and high up on the mountain the clouds drifted lazily by. In the woods, birds chirped and trilled, and outside the gate, a tiny dog yapped and barked. Pu-jin reached the gate and tossed the dead tiger down, shouting, "Where are the boys?" As the four or five young men who came out were all misshapen and ugly-looking, they pulled and dragged the tiger towards the house. Pu-jin ordered, "Hurry up and get the skin off, we'll arrange something for him to eat." Then he turned and invited Tripitaka inside. The two of them greeted each other, and Tripitaka bowed to thank Pu-jin for his great kindness in saving his life. Pu-jin said, "What's the point of thanking me? We're countrymen after all." After tea was served, an old woman led a young woman to offer their respects to Tripitaka. Pu-jin said, "This is my mother and my mountain wife." Tripitaka said, "Please, esteemed madam, may I beg a seat, and I'll pay my respects." The old woman said, "A distant guest such as you, we ask you to take care of yourselves. There's no need to pay respects." Pu-jin said, "Mother, he's a emissary from the Tang king who has come to the West to seek out the Buddha's scriptures. Just now he was at the mountain peak and met our young son. The young man, being a native of the same land, invited him home to rest his horse, and tomorrow we'll send him on his way." The old woman heard this and was extremely happy, saying, "Good! Good! Good! If we hadn't invited him, we wouldn't have been able to use this occasion to have the old master perform some good deeds, reciting scriptures and sending him off the next day. This Liu Pu-jin, although he's a tiger-slayer and a mighty Taibao who keeps the mountain in awe, he does have a filial heart. As soon as he heard his mother's words, he wanted to prepare some incense paper and ask Tripitaka to stay awhile.

The Monkey King said, "According to what you say, he is a filial gentleman, so he is bound to have good fortune. I also hope you can show me the way to his abode, so I can pay him a visit." The woodsman said, "It's not far, not far. This mountain is called the Pinnacle Peak. In the mountain, there is a cave called the Sloping Moon Three Stars Cave. Inside the cave lives a sage, called the Venerable Patriarch of Bodhi. His disciples number by the hundreds, and there are now over thirty or forty of them still practicing with him under his tutelage. You go down that small path, walk south for about seven or eight li, and you will reach his place." The Monkey King grasped the woodsman's hand and said, "You come with me. If I gain any good fortune, I will never forget your kindness in guiding me." The woodsman said, "You, sir, are quite unsophisticated. I just told you this, and you still don't get it? If I go with you, wouldn't I be abandoning my business? Who will support my old mother? I need to chop firewood, you go on, go on."

The Monkey King said, "According to what you say, he's a virtuous son, and good things are bound to follow. I'm also hoping you can take me to that celestial residence to visit him." The woodcutter said, "Not far, not far. This mountain is called the Pine Crag Hill. There's a cave called the Crescent Moon Three Stars Cave in the mountain. Inside the cave, there's a celestial being called Master Bodhidharma, the Ancestor. His disciples are countless, and there are still three or four dozen disciples studying under him now. You just follow that small path to the south, walking about seven or eight li, and you'll be right at his doorstep." The Monkey King grasped the woodcutter's hand and said, "Brother, come with me. If we get a good thing out of it, I'll never forget your kindness in guiding me." The woodcutter said, "You, a man of the world, can't even understand me. I just told you that a while ago, and you still don't get it? If I go with you, won't I be letting my business go to ruin? Who will take care of my old mother? I have to chop firewood. You go on your own, go on your own."

The Monkey King said, "As you say, this must be a paragon of filial piety. I daresay he will be well rewarded for it. But do tell me where I can find his abode, so that I may pay my respects." The woodcutter said, "Not far, not far. This mountain is called the Spirit Platform Hills. There is a cave called the Slanting Moon Three Star Cave in the mountain. Within that cave there is a god who calls himself the Patriarch of Bodhi Mind. His disciples are innumerable; I see there are still thirty or forty of them still practicing there with him now. You follow the small path to the south, walk about seven or eight li, and you'll reach his home." The Monkey King seized the woodcutter by the wrist and said, "Good fellow, let's go together. If we get something good out of it, I won't forget your kindness in guiding us." The woodcutter said, "You, a man of the world, still don't get it. I just told you a while ago and you still didn't understand. If we went with you, wouldn't we be neglecting my business? Who would take care of my old mother? I have firewood to chop, you go on, you go on."

The Monkey King said, "According to what you say, he is a filial gentleman. There will surely be benefits for him in the future. But I would also like you to point out the location of the immortal's dwelling place, so that I can pay a visit too." The woodsman said, "Not far, not far. This mountain is called Lingtai Fangcun Mountain. Inside the mountain is a cave called Suan Yue Three Star Grotto. In that grotto lives an immortal named Xushu Tici Old Master. The Old Master has countless disciples, and today there are over thirty or forty of them who are studying under him with him. You follow the small path to the south for seven or eight li, and you will reach his place." The Monkey King grabbed the woodsman with his hand and said, "Come along with me, old fellow. If we get any benefits, I will never forget the kindness you have shown me." The woodsman said, "You are a man of the human world, and you don't understand the circumstances. Just now I explained it to you, but you still don't understand. If I went with you, wouldn't I be neglecting my own business? Who would take care of my old mother? I have to chop wood to make a living. Go on your own, go on your own."

The Monkey King said, "As you describe it, he is indeed a virtuous son, and good things will surely come his way in the future. But may I ask you to direct me to the abode of the Immortal? I'd like to pay him a visit as well." The woodsman said, "Not far, not far. This mountain is called the Ling Tai Fenshu Mountain. In the mountain there is a cave called the Slightly Moon Three Stars Cave. Inside that cave lives an Immortal, named Master Shoupu. He has a multitude of disciples, and I estimate that there are three or four dozen of them still under his instruction at present. If you follow the small path to the south, walking for seven or eight li, you will reach his place." The Monkey King grasped the woodsman's hand and said, "Old fellow, let us go together! If we get good things, I shall never forget your kindness in pointing the way." The woodsman said, "You are a coarse fellow, unperceptive of situations. I just told you this earlier, and you don't seem to understand. If I go with you, I'd surely ruin my livelihood. Who would care for my aged mother? I need to cut wood, you go by yourself, go by yourself."

Twenty-seventh? That's good by some calculation. Farewell, you seem to have a lot of business, while I need to get dressed and go; take your portrait. Give my regards to poor Nina Alexandrovna. Goodbye, dear prince; come often, and I'll go on purpose to old woman Belokonskaya to talk about you. And listen, dear: I believe that God brought you precisely for me from Switzerland to St. Petersburg. Perhaps you have other matters, but most importantly for me. God precisely calculated that. Goodbye, my dears. Alexandra, come to me, my friend.

—is it the twenty-seventh? It's good, as per some arrangement. Farewell, it seems you have many appointments, and I have to dress and go; take your portrait. Pass on my regards to poor Nina Alexandrovna. Farewell, dear prince. Do come by more often, and I'll make a point to visit the old lady Belokonskaya to speak about you. And listen, darling: I firmly believe that you were brought to St. Petersburg from Switzerland specifically for me. Maybe you have other matters, but for me, it's the most important. God arranged it that way. Farewell, dears. Alexandra, come see me, my friend.

Alexandrovna. Until we meet again, Prince, dear fellow! Come over often, and I'll go out of my way to the old woman Belokonskaya to tell her about you. — Twenty-seventh? That's good by some account. Farewell, you have, it seems, a lot of appointments, and I need to get dressed and leave; take your portrait. Give my regards to poor Nina Alexandrovna. Until we meet again, Prince, dear fellow! Come more often, and I'll deliberately visit the old woman Belokon'ski for news of you. And listen, dear: I believe that it was God who brought you to St. Petersburg from Switzerland for me. Maybe you have other affairs, but what's most important to me. "It's not the life in prison that I disagree with," said the prince, "I once heard a story from a man who spent twelve years in prison. He was one of my professor's patients, and I met him when I was studying. He had fits, was sometimes agitated, cried, and even tried to kill himself. His life in prison was very sad, I assure you, but by no means inexpensive. And the only things he was familiar with were a spider and a tree that had grown under the window... But I'll tell you about another person I met last year. The strange thing about this case, and it's a very rare occurrence, is that this person was a condemned man, sentenced to death by firing squad for a political crime. Twenty minutes after the death sentence was read, a reprieve was announced and a different sentence was issued; however, in the twenty-minute interval between the two verdicts, he lived under the incontestable conviction that he would die in a few minutes. I felt a shiver when I listened to him recounting his memories and I had to ask him again and again. He remembered everything with an extraordinary clarity and said he would never forget a single moment of those minutes.

About twenty paces from the scaffold, where the crowd and soldiers stood, three posts had been dug in. The first three prisoners were led to the posts, tied up, dressed in the death clothes (long white kaftans), and blindfolded with white caps so that the rifles wouldn't be visible; then a team of several soldiers formed up in front of each post. My acquaintance stood eighth in line, so he would have to go to the posts third in line. A priest walked around everyone with a cross. It looked like he had five minutes to live, no more. He said that these five minutes seemed like an endless term, an enormous wealth to him; he thought he would live countless lives in those five minutes, that he didn't even need to think about the last moment, so he made different arrangements: he calculated the time to say goodbye to his companions, put two minutes aside for that, then another two minutes to think about himself for the last time, and finally, to take one last look around. He remembered very well what he did and exactly how he calculated. He was twenty-seven years old, healthy and strong when he died; when saying goodbye to his companions, he remembered that he had asked one of them a rather odd question and was even very interested in the answer. Then, when the two minutes he had counted to think to himself had passed, he knew in advance what he would think about: he wanted to imagine as quickly and vividly as possible how it would be - that he now exists and lives, but in three minutes he will no longer be anything or anyone. He thought about all this in those two minutes, trying to solve it. There was a church nearby, and the top of the cathedral with its gilded roof sparkled in the bright sunlight. He remembered that he stared intently at this roof and the rays shining from it; he couldn't tear himself away from the rays; they seemed to him to be his new nature, that he would somehow merge with them in three minutes. The uncertainty and repulsion from this new thing that was about to happen were terrible; but he says that nothing was heavier for him at that time than the unceasing thought: 'What if I didn't die? What if I could turn life back? What an eternity! And it would all be mine! I would then turn every minute into a century, I wouldn't lose a thing, I would count every minute, and wouldn't waste a single thing!' He said that this thought finally turned into such a rage that he wanted to be shot sooner."

— As for life in prison, one can't help but disagree, the Prince said. — I heard a story from a man who spent twelve years in prison; he was one of my professor's patients and was being treated by him. He had seizures, was often distressed, cried, and even tried to kill himself. His life in prison was very sorrowful, I assure you, but certainly not cheap. All he knew, of course, were a spider and a sapling that had grown under the window... But I'll tell you a different story, one from last year, about a man I met. There was one rather strange circumstance, a circumstance that, I must say, is extremely rare. This man was hanged along with others and sentenced to death by firing squad for a political crime. Twenty minutes after the sentence was read, a pardon was read and a lesser punishment was imposed; however, within the interval between the two sentences, twenty minutes, or at least a quarter of an hour, he lived with the incontestable conviction that he would die within minutes. I found it very fascinating to listen to him when he occasionally recalled his past experiences, and I kept asking him again and again. He remembered everything with an extraordinary clarity and said that he would never forget a single moment from those minutes. Just twenty paces away from the scaffold where the people and soldiers were standing were three posts stuck in the ground, as there were several prisoners. Three of the first were led to the posts, tied them up, put the black executioner's robes on them, and covered their eyes with white masks so that the guns wouldn't be visible; then a team of several soldiers was stationed in front of each post. My acquaintance was eighth in line, so he would be led to the posts in the third wave. The priest walked around all of them with a cross. It seemed that he still had five minutes left to live, not a minute more. He said that these five minutes seemed like an endless period, a vast wealth to him; he thought that in those five minutes he would live through so many lives that he shouldn't even think about the last moment, so he made different arrangements: he counted the time to bid farewell to his comrades, gave two minutes for that, then another two minutes to think about himself one last time, and finally two minutes to glance around one last time. He remembered very well what he did exactly and made those three decisions exactly as he had planned. He was twenty-seven years old, healthy and strong, when bidding farewell to his comrades, he remembered asking one of them an offhand question and even showed a strong interest in the answer. Then, when he bid farewell to his comrades, those two minutes he had counted on thinking about himself came, and he knew in advance what he would think: he wanted to imagine as quickly and vividly as possible that he now exists and lives, and within three minutes he would be something or someone else; who and where? He thought about this in those two minutes, trying to solve it all. The church was not far away, and the top of the church's dome, with its golden roof, glittered brightly in the sunlight. He remembered staring intensely at the roof and the rays streaming from it; he couldn't tear himself away from the rays; it seemed to him that these rays were his new nature, that he would somehow merge with them in three minutes... The uncertainty and the aversion to this new existence, which was about to overtake him, were terrible; but he says that nothing was harder for him in that time than the ceaseless thought: 'What if I weren't to die? What if I could turn back time? What an eternity! And it would all be mine! I would then count each minute as an age, lose nothing, count every minute carefully, and waste nothing!' He said that this thought finally boiled over into such anger that he even longed for them to shoot him quickly.

"I must admit," said the Prince, "that I don't entirely agree with you about life in prison. I once heard a story from a man who had spent twelve years behind bars; he was a patient of my professor and was being treated. He suffered from fits, would become agitated, cry, and even tried to kill himself. His life in prison was very sorrowful, but, of course, not at all inexpensive. All the company he had was a spider and a sapling that had grown up under the window... But I'll tell you a story from my last year's meeting with someone else. There was one unusual circumstance, and what was strange was precisely that such a case is very rare. This person was put up on the scaffold with others, and a death sentence by firing squad was read to him for a political crime. Twenty minutes later, a pardon was read and a different sentence was announced, but in the interval between the two sentences, this man lived under the unquestionable conviction that he would die in a few minutes. I was extremely interested when he sometimes reminisced about his past experiences and I would ask him again and again. He remembered everything with remarkable clarity and said that he would never forget those minutes. There were three stakes, about twenty paces from the scaffold, where the prisoners had been tied up. The first three were led to the stakes, tied up, put into white robes, and white caps were placed over their eyes so the rifles wouldn't be visible; then a squad of several soldiers formed up in front of each stake. My acquaintance was eighth in line, so he would go to the stakes third. A priest passed by all of them with a cross. It seemed that there were only five minutes left to live, no more. He said that these five minutes seemed to him to be an endless period, a vast fortune; it seemed to him that he would live a hundred lives in those five minutes, that it was too early to think about the last moment, and that's why he made various arrangements: he calculated the time to bid farewell to his fellow prisoners, which he allocated two minutes for, then he allocated two more minutes to think about himself one last time, and then he allocated time to look around once more. He remembered very well that he made these three arrangements and calculated them precisely. He died at twenty-seven, healthy and strong; bidding farewell to his fellow prisoners, he remembered that he had asked one of them a rather odd question and was very interested in the answer. Then, when he had bid farewell to his fellow prisoners, the two minutes he had allocated to think about himself arrived; he knew in advance what he would think about: he wanted to imagine as vividly and quickly as possible how it was: he is and lives now, and in three minutes he will be nothing, some person or some thing - who, where? He thought about this for two minutes to resolve it! A church was nearby, and the top of the tower with its gilded roof sparkled in the sunlight. He remembered that he looked at the roof and the rays emanating from it with all his might; he couldn't tear himself away from the rays; it seemed to him that these rays were his new nature, that he would merge with them somehow in three minutes... The uncertainty and aversion to this new thing, which would soon come, were terrible; but he said that there was nothing harder for him in that time than the constant thought: 'What if I weren't to die! What if I could turn back my life - what a boundlessness! And all this would be mine! I would then make every minute into an eternity, lose nothing, count every minute, and waste nothing!' He said that this thought eventually drove him to such anger that he wanted to be shot sooner."

As soon as he finished greeting him - after inviting him to sit down in the armchair, which he had no time to do - he asked K. for a brief conversation in private. "It is necessary," he said, struggling to swallow, "it is necessary for my peace of mind." K. immediately dismissed the servant from the room with the instruction not to admit anyone. "What did I hear, Josef?" the uncle cried out as soon as they were alone, sat on the table, and stuffed various papers under himself without looking up, in order to sit more comfortably. K. was silent, he knew what was coming, but, suddenly relaxed from the exertion of the work, as he was, he gave himself over to a pleasant lassitude at first and gazed out of the window at the opposite side of the street, from which only a small, triangular section was visible from his seat, a piece of empty wall between two shop facades.

"You're looking out of the window!" the uncle exclaimed with raised arms, "For goodness' sake, Josef, answer me! Is it true, can it be true?" "Dear Uncle," said K. and shook himself out of his distraction, "I don't know what you want from me." "Josef," said the uncle warningly, "you've always spoken the truth as far as I know. Should I take your last words as a bad sign?" "I guess I know what you want," said K. obediently, "you've probably heard about my trial." "So it is," replied the uncle, slowly nodding, "I've heard about your trial." "From whom?" K. asked. "Erna wrote to me," said the uncle, "she doesn't have any contact with you, you don't pay much attention to her, despite that, she found out. I received the letter today and came here right away, and it's for no other reason, but it seems like a good enough reason. I can read you the part of the letter that concerns you."

He pulled out the letter from his wallet. "Here it is." It reads: "Josef, I haven't seen you for a long time; I was at the bank last week, but Josef was so busy that I wasn't allowed in; I waited almost an hour, but then I had to go home because I had a piano lesson; I would have liked to speak with him, perhaps an opportunity will arise soon. On my name day he sent me a big box of chocolate, it was very kind and thoughtful. I had forgotten to tell you about it at the time, it's only now, when you asked me, that I remembered. Chocolate, by the way, disappears immediately in the pension as soon as one becomes aware of it, and it's gone. But what concerns Josef, I wanted to tell you. As I mentioned, I wasn't allowed to see him at the bank because he was in a discussion with a gentleman. After waiting for a while, I asked a servant if the discussion would take long, he said it probably would, since it probably concerned the trial against the prokurist. I asked what kind of trial it was, if he wasn't mistaken, he said he wasn't, it was a serious trial, but he didn't know any more. He himself would like to help the prokurist because he is a good and just gentleman, but he didn't know how to start, and he only wishes that influential gentlemen would take him under their wing. This will certainly happen, and it will ultimately have a good ending, but for now it's not looking good, as he could gather from the prokurist's mood. I didn't give much importance to these stories, I also tried to calm down the simple servant, forbade him from speaking about it to others, and thought the whole thing to be nonsense. Still, it might be a good idea if, dear Father, on your next visit you looked into the matter further, it will be easy for you to get to the bottom of things, and if it really needs to be done, through your great and influential connections. But if it doesn't need to be done, which is probably the most likely, then it will at least give your daughter a chance to hug you soon, which would delight her." - "A good child," said the uncle, after finishing reading, and wiped away some tears from his eyes. K. nodded, he had completely forgotten about Erna due to various distractions in the past, even her birthday had slipped his mind, and the story about the chocolate was obviously made up only to protect him in front of Uncle and Aunt. It was very touching, and with the theater tickets he would regularly send her from now on, he was certainly not doing enough to repay her, but he didn't feel suitable for visits to the pension and conversations with a small eighteen-year-old high school student.

"And what do you say now?" the uncle asked, having forgotten his haste and agitation in the face of the letter and now reading it again. "Yes, Uncle," said K., "it's true." "True?" the uncle cried out.

K. sat in the armchair, having forgotten his distraction, and looked through the letter once more, his eyes scanning the sentences, then put it on the table. "Tell me, Josef," the uncle said gently, as if to himself, "did Erna know about the bank?" "No," said K. "And that business with the chocolate, is it true?" "No," said K. again. "And the prokurist, did she tell you about that?" "No," said K. once more. The uncle thought for a moment and then said, "I see, I see. Well, Josef, I'll say this to you: it seems to me that there's a lot that Erna doesn't tell you."

As K. passed the corridor that separated his office from the main staircase on one of the next evenings – he was almost the last one to go home, only two servants were still working in the small glow of a lamp in the expedition – he heard sighs coming from behind a door that he had always suspected to be a storage room, without ever having seen it himself. He stopped in amazement and listened again to see if he wasn't mistaken – it was quiet for a bit, then the sighs came back. – At first, he wanted to call one of the servants, maybe a witness was needed, but then a desire for inquiring overcame him so unbridled that he almost ripped the door open. As he had rightly suspected, it was a storage room. Useless, old print sorts, overturned empty earthen ink bottles lay behind the threshold. But in the room itself, three men were hunched over in the low space. A candle fixed to a shelf gave them light. "What are you doing here?" K. asked, excitement overpowering him, but not loudly. The one man who apparently dominated the others and who caught the others' gaze first was dressed in a sort of dark leather clothing that left his neck down to his chest and his entire arms bare. He did not answer. But the other two cried out: "Sir! We are to be flogged because you complained about us to the investigator!" And only now did K. realize that it was indeed Franz and Willem, the guards, and that the third man held a whip to flog them. "Now," said K. and stared at them, "I did not complain, I only said how things had gone in my apartment. And you haven't behaved blamelessly either." "Herr," said Willem, while Franz, behind him, seemed to secure himself, "if you knew how poorly we are paid, you would judge us more leniently. I have a family to feed, and Franz here wanted to marry; we try to get rich, as one can, not through work alone, but through whatever means available. Even the most diligent work does not achieve this. Your fine clothes have tempted me, of course it is forbidden for the guards to act like this, but it's a tradition that the clothes belong to the guards, it has always been so; it's understandable, what do such things mean to one who is unfortunate enough to be arrested? But if one brings it up in public, then punishment must follow." "What you are saying, I didn't know," said K., "I didn't request their punishment at all; I was concerned with a principle." "Franz," Willem turned to the other guard, "didn't I tell you, sir didn't demand our punishment? Now you hear that he didn't even know we would be punished." "Don't be swayed by such talk," said the third man to K., "they've become a bit feeble-minded through fear of the flogging. What this one, for example," he pointed to Willem, "tells about his possible career is simply laughable. Look at how fat he is – the first flogging blows will probably get lost in his fat. – Do you know how he got so fat? He has the habit of eating the breakfasts of the arrested. Didn't he also eat your breakfast? Well, I said so. But a man with a belly like that can never and will never become a flogger, it's out of the question." "There are also such floggers," Willem claimed, who was just unfastening his belt. "No," said the flogger, and struck him with the whip across the neck so that he jerked, "you're not to listen, you're to undress." "I would reward you well if you let them go," said K., and without looking at the flogger again – such deals are best conducted with lowered eyes – he pulled out his wallet. "You want to report me to the authorities as well and get flogged?" said the flogger, "and now, through me, too? No, no!" "Be sensible," said K., "if I had wanted them punished, I wouldn't want to buy them off now. I could simply close the door here, see and hear nothing more, and go home. But I'm not doing that; I'm genuinely interested in freeing them; I wouldn't have mentioned their names if I had suspected they were to be punished or could be punished. I don't consider them guilty, the organization is guilty, the high officials are guilty." "That's right!" cried the guards, and immediately got a lash across their already bare backs. "If you had under your rod a high judge," said K., and pushed the rod down, which was rising again, "I wouldn't stop you from striking; on the contrary, I'd give you more money to strike for the good cause." "What you're saying sounds convincing," said the flogger, "but I won't be bribed. I've been appointed to flog, so I'll flog." The guard Franz, who had been somewhat reserved until now, waiting for a favorable outcome of K.'s intervention, now stepped out, naked but for his pants, to the door, leaned on K.'s arm and whispered: "If you can't get us released, try at least to free me. Willem is older than I, in every way less sensitive, and he's had a light flogging a few years ago; but I, I'm not yet discredited and was led astray by Willem in good and bad alike. My poor bride is waiting for me below by the bank, I'm so ashamed." He dried his face, which was completely drenched with tears, with K.'s coat. "I won't wait any longer," said the flogger, grasped the rod with both hands, and struck Franz, while Willem cowered in a corner, watching secretly, without making a move to turn his head. Then the scream that Franz let out was unbroken and unaltered; it seemed to come from a tortured instrument rather than a human being; the entire corridor echoed with it, the whole house must have heard it. "Don't scream," cried K., unable to hold back, and while he gazed intently in the direction from which the servants were coming, he pushed Franz, not hard, but hard enough so that the dazed man fell to the ground and frantically felt around with his hands; but the blows found him on the ground as well; as he writhed under them, the point of the rod rose and fell regularly. And already, in the distance, a servant appeared, and a few steps behind him, a second one. K. quickly slammed the door shut, moved to one of the windows, and opened it. The screaming had completely stopped. To keep the servants from approaching, he called out: "It's me!" "Good evening, Procurator!" it was replied from outside. "Is something the matter?" "No, no," K. answered, "it's just a dog barking in the yard." When the servants didn't stir, he added: "You can stay at your work." To avoid talking to the servants, he leaned out of the window. When he looked out into the corridor again after a bit, they were already gone. K. now stayed by the window, did not dare to go into the storage room, and didn't want to go home either. It was a small square courtyard that he looked down into; offices were housed all around it; all the windows were already dark, only the upper ones caught a reflection of the moon. K. strained his eyes to penetrate into the darkness of a courtyard corner where some carts were jammed together. It tormented him that he hadn't managed to prevent the flogging, but it wasn't his fault that he hadn't succeeded; if Franz hadn't screamed – it must have hurt badly, but in a crucial moment one must be able to control oneself – he would have certainly found another way to persuade the flogger. If the entire lowest administrative echelon was rascals, why should the flogger, who had the most inhumane position, have been an exception? K. had also observed how the flogger's eyes had gleamed at the sight of the banknote; he had clearly only made the flogging serious in order to raise the bribe amount a bit. And K. would not have spared any money; it really mattered to him to free the guards; if he had already started to combat this corruption, so...
