A Heavenly Saint from Fruitful Mountain, came to visit me this morning, claiming to be my neighbor, and later requested a certain kind of armor, refusing the steel trident as too small, and the painted halberd as too light. He then took a piece of Heavenly River- decreeed treasure iron, took it out with his own hands, and discarded some techniques. Now he is sitting in the palace, asking for some kind of suit of armor. I have none, that's why the drums are beaten and the bells are rung, calling for your wise presence. Perhaps you brothers have some armor you can lend him, and send him on his way." Ao Qin heard the words and was greatly enraged, saying: "My brothers, mobilize the troops and apprehend him at once!" The Old Dragon said: "Don't say apprehend! That piece of iron, just gripping it is death, just striking it is doom, getting hit a few times will be wounded, rubbing against it a few times will injure one's tendons!" West Sea Dragon King Ao Jun said: "The elder brother shouldn't take action against him; just lend him a suit of armor and send him on his way, then report it to the heavenly court, and heaven itself will deal with him." North Sea Dragon King Ao Shun said: "That's right. I have a pair of lotus silk step-walk shoes here." West Sea Dragon King Ao Jun said: "I have a set of golden-scale armor here." South Sea Dragon King Ao Qin said: "I have a purple-gold phoenix crown here." The Old Dragon was overjoyed, and led him into the crystal palace to meet the Heavenly Saint, and offered it to him. The Heavenly Saint put on the crown, the golden-scale armor, and the lotus silk step-walk shoes, and struck the Wish-fulfilling Staff with ease, and with it, he went out the door, saying: "A commotion! A commotion!" The four Dragon Kings were greatly displeased, and on one side they consulted and decided not to mention it in the imperial report.

Back when we were young, the beat of drums and the chime of bells would indeed stir up the Three Sea Dragon Kings. Before long, they all came together, and Ao Qin said, "Brother, is there some pressing matter that requires the beating of the drums and the striking of the bells?" The Old Dragon replied, "It's not worth mentioning, brother. There's a sage from the Peach Blossom Mountain who came to see me early in the day, and then asked me for a weapon. I presented him with a steel trident, but he thought it was too small, and I offered him a painted halberd, but he thought it was too light. He then produced a block of Iron from the Bottom of the Heaven River and took out some divination numbers. Now that he's sitting in the palace, he's asking for something to wear. Since I don't have any armor, I beat the drums and strike the bells, and asked you, brother, to come. Do you happen to have some armor that you could give him and send him off?" Ao Qin heard this and flew into a rage, saying, "My brothers, let's mobilize our troops and apprehend him!" The Old Dragon said, "Don't talk about apprehending him! That block of iron is bound to kill him with just a scratch, wound him with just a touch, or bruise him with just a tap, and wound his tendons with just a rub!" Ao Xu, the Western Sea Dragon King, said, "Brother, do not act rashly; why don't we just assemble some armor for him and send him off, then submit a petition to heaven and let heaven itself decide." Ao Shun, the Northern Sea Dragon King, said, "That makes sense." The Old Dragon was delighted, and brought him to the Crystal Palace for an introduction, presenting the items he had obtained. Monkey, donning the golden crown, the golden armor, and the cloud-slip shoes, brandished his easy-to-wield rod and sent him off on his way. He paraded in front of the assembled dragons, shouting, "Hue and cry! Hue and cry!" The four Dragon Kings were very displeased, and on the side began to deliberate on how to submit a petition to heaven.

In olden times, when the drums sounded and the bells rang out, it indeed disturbed the three Dragon Kings of the Ocean, who arrived shortly, all gathering outside. Ao Qin said: "Big Brother, what's the hurry, to beat the drums and ring the bells?" The Old Dragon replied: "Esteemed Brother, it's not a good thing to say! A Saint Man from the Heavenly Peach Mountain came to recognize me as a neighbor early this morning, and later requested a piece of armor. He thought a steel fork was too small and a painted halberd too light. He took out a piece of divine iron from the Heavenly River's bed, and wasted some techniques. Now he's sitting in the palace, and yet he's asking for some more armor. My place has none, so I struck the drums and beat the bells to call you. Do you brothers have any armor to give him? Give him a set and send him out the door at once." Ao Qin heard this and flew into a rage, saying: "My brothers, get the troops ready, let's take him on!" The Old Dragon said: "Don't say that. That piece of iron is so hard it's liable to kill, so cold it's liable to wound; just brush against it and it's like peeling skin, scratch it and it's like breaking bones!" Ao Jun of the Western Ocean said: "My dear Second Brother, don't stir him up; just make up a set of armor for him and send him off, then inform the heavens, and the heavens will take care of him." Ao Shun of the Northern Ocean said: "That's right." Ao Qin of the Southern Ocean said: "I have a pair of lotus-silk cloud shoes." Ao Jun of the Western Ocean said: "I have a golden-armor set with locks." Ao Qin of the Southern Ocean said: "I have a purple-gold phoenix crown." The Old Dragon was overjoyed, led him into the crystal palace and presented it to him. After Monkey King donned the crown, the armor, and the cloud shoes, and wielded his Ruyi Staff, he marched out and struck the drums, shouting "Hurry up! Hurry up!" The Four Dragon Kings of the Ocean were all displeased and whispered among themselves, deciding to draft a memorial to submit to the heavens.

In the past, when the drums beat and the bells rang, the three Dragon Kings of the Sea were indeed roused, and soon came to meet at the outside of the hall. Ao Qin said, "Big brother, what's the urgent matter, beating the drums and clanging the bells?" The Old Dragon said, "Dear brother, it's not a good thing to say. There's a Saint from Mount Guangfeng who came to me early in the morning to acknowledge me as his neighbor. Later, he requested an armament from me, but I offered him the steel trident, thinking it too small, and the painted halberd, thinking it too light. He took out a block of Heavenly River Heavenly Iron for himself, and was about to give me some measures. Now that he is seated in the palace, he wants something else to don. I have nothing, so I struck the drums and clanged the bells to summon you, dear brother. Do you have some armament to lend him, and send him out? That would be best." Ao Qin heard this and his countenance changed to great anger, saying, "My brothers, prepare to attack him!" The Old Dragon said, "Don't say that! That piece of iron, once it's grasped, is sure to be fatal; once it's bumped, it's sure to be fatal; once it's hit and scratched, the skin will break and the tendons will be injured!" The Dragon King of the West, Aojun, said, "Brother, you mustn't harm him. We'll just lend him an armament and send him out, and then report to heaven, and heaven will take care of him itself." The Dragon King of the North, Ao Shun, said, "That's right." The Dragon King of the South, Ao Qin, said, "I have a pair of lotus silk cloud-soles here." The Dragon King of the West, Aojun, said, "I have a golden scaled corselet on me." The Old Dragon was overjoyed and led him into the crystal palace to see him, and then presented it to him. Monkey King donned the golden crown, the golden corselet, and the cloud-soles, and wielded his heavenly rod, and went out, shouting to the assembled dragons, "Hush! Hush!" The four Dragon Kings were not pleased, and they started to confer on how to write a memorial to be submitted to heaven.

Long ago, when the drums and bells resounded, as expected, the three sea dragons were startled, and soon arrived. All of them met outside and Ao Qin said, "Elder brother, is there some urgent business that has caused the drums to beat and the bells to ring?" The eldest dragon said, "Honorable younger brother, it's not good to talk about it! There's some numinous being from the Peach Flower Mountain who came to recognize me as his neighbor in the morning, and later asked for a weapon, deeming steel hooks too small and painted halberds too light. He then took out a block of sacred iron from the Heavenly River bottom and put it in his hand, losing some ancient knowledge. Now, sitting in the palace, he's asking for some more armor. My place has none, that's why I've rung the drums and beaten the bells, summoning honorable younger brother to come. You brothers, do you have some armor that you can give him, and send him off?"

Ao Qin heard this and became enraged, saying, "My brothers, we should set up our troops and give him a good lesson!" The eldest dragon said, "No need to take action. That block of iron is tough, and if you grab onto it a bit, you'll die, and if you hit it a bit, you'll be mortally wounded. Your skin will be broken and your sinews injured." Ao Ruan from the Western Sea said, "Brother, don't do anything to him. Let's just prepare a suit of armor for him and send him off. We'll report the situation to the heavenly court, and let Heaven itself decide his fate." Ao Shun from the Northern Sea said, "That makes sense." The eldest dragon was overjoyed and invited him to enter the Crystal Palace to meet him. The six-armed figure accepted the golden armor, golden crown, and cloud-step shoes, and then wore them, making his movements swift and agile. He took the "cosmic rod" in hand and departed, saying, "Ruckus! Ruckus!" The four sea dragons were greatly displeased and began to discuss how to report the matter to the heavenly court.

The next day, the Dragon King's messenger, Cloud Boy, Thunder God, Lightning Mother, and Lightning Child ascended to the nine heavens above the Chang'an city. As it was near the auspicious hour, he ordered the clouds to be dispersed; at noon, he unleashed thunder; at midnight, he sent down rain, which stopped at three feet and forty points, and so he waited for an hour before releasing more rain, adding just three inches and eight points to the total. After the rain had stopped, he dispersed his troops, then descended from the clouds and transformed back into a resplendent, refined scholar, and entered the street outside the Western Gate. Chancing upon the diviner Yuan Shou Cheng's shop, he burst in without a word, breaking his sign, brush, inkwell, and all the other objects in the shop. The gentleman sat on his chair, completely unfazed. The Dragon King then flung open the door and shouted and scolded: "You wicked sorcerer who recklessly speak good or bad fortune, you knave who bewitches people's minds! Your divination isn't reliable, your words are absurd! You said that the hour and point at which the rain would fall were utterly mismatched, and yet you sat there unblinking, arrogant as ever. Why don't you get out of here before I report you for a capital offense!" Yuan Shou Cheng still looked completely unfazed and laughed up at the ceiling with a cold, scornful smile: "I'm not afraid, I'm not afraid. I have no capital offense to fear, only that you, sir, may have one! You may deceive others, but not me. I recognize you; you're not that refined scholar but the Dragon King of the Jing River, who has disobeyed the Heavenly Emperor's decree and altered the hour and cancelled the point total, committing a transgression of heaven. On the steps of the Drunken Dragon Platform, you may well be in danger of losing your head. Why do you still scold me?" Upon hearing this, the Dragon King's heart skipped a beat with shock and terror, his bones froze with fear, and he hastily dropped the door panel and prostrated himself, bowing before the gentleman and saying: "Gentle sir, please forgive me. I merely spoke in jest, and didn't know that I had committed a serious transgression. What shall I do now? Please, sir, have mercy on me and save me!"

The next day, Wind God, Thunder God, Cloud Boy, and Lightning Mother appeared, stretching all the way to the sky above Chang'an City. He waited till the morning hour to spread clouds, the noon hour to produce thunder, the night hour to bring rain, and the late hour to stop the rain, yet it only rained to the depth of three feet and forty points. He changed the hour by one time block, surpassing by three and a half points, and then the rain subsided. After releasing the great army, he pressed down the clouds once more and transformed into a handsome scholar dressed in white. He entered through the West Gate's great street, and then crashed into Yuan Shou Cheng's divination stall. Unhesitatingly, he smashed the sign, brush, ink slab, and other things all at once. The Mr. sittting on the chair did not budge.

The dragon king then flipped open the door and roared and scolded, saying, "You trifling fellow who talks about good fortune and misfortune at random, and deceives people's minds recklessly! Your divination is useless, and your words are madly and groundlessly absurd! You said that today's rain hour and number of points did not tally at all, yet you're boldly sitting upright; hadn't you better be off already and spare your life?" Yuan Shou Cheng still courageously did not show a hint of fear, looked up to the sky with a cold laugh and said, "I'm not afraid! I'm not afraid! I don't have a death sentence, only you have a death sentence, ha! You can deceive others, but you can't deceive me. I know you; you are not a scholar, but the Dragon King of Jing River. You broke the heavenly edict, changed the hour, surpassed the points, and offended the heavenly laws. You might be beheaded on the Dragon Scales Platform, yet you're here cursing me?" The dragon king having heard, felt his heart filled with terror, his bones trembling with fear, hastily dropped the door plank, adjusted his clothes, and fell to his knees, saying, "The Master, please forgive me. I was joking earlier; who would have known that what I spoke in jest became true and, in the end, I indeed offended the heavenly laws; what can I do? I beg you to spare my life!"

The next day, he summoned the wind god, the thunder god, the cloud boy, and the lightning mother to Long'an City in the ninth heaven above. He waited till nine o'clock to disperse the clouds, at noon to unleash thunder, at twelve o'clock to bring rain, and at five o'clock to stop the rain, yet only garnered three inches and forty points of water, changed his timing by a quarter of a day, and his precipitation by three inches and eight points, and then unleashed the multitude of troops back into their camps. He then calmed the clouds and transformed into a refined gentleman in white robes, arriving at the Western Gate Inner Street, and then burst into Master Yuan Shoucheng's divination shop. He didn't even give anyone time to speak, and smashed Master Yuan's signboard, brushes, and inkstone, all at once. The gentleman sat calmly in his chair, unmoved. The dragon king then started beating on the door and scolding, "You vicious deceiver, responsible for spreading rumors of blessings and calamities, and causing trouble for the masses! Your divination skills are useless and your words are full of lies! You said that the time of rain would be so and so, but it didn't match at all. You sit there calmly, feeling bold, get out of here before I sentence you to death!" Shoucheng still dared not show the slightest sign of fear, and laughed out loud with his face up towards the sky, saying, "I'm not afraid, I'm not afraid! I'm not afraid of the death sentence, I'm only afraid that you might meet with a capital punishment! Others might try to fool me, but they can't fool me. I know who you are, you're not a refined gentleman, but the dragon king of the Jing River. You disobeyed the heavenly decree, changed the timing and reduced the precipitation, breaking the heavenly law. You're probably doomed to suffer a beheading at the dragon-skin scaffold, and yet you're scolding me?" The dragon king heard this and was shocked, his heart trembling with fear, his bones chilled, and in a rush, he abandoned the door and quickly prostrated himself, kneeling down and begging, "Mr. Shoucheng, please pardon me. I was just speaking carelessly, I didn't know that my words would turn out to be true, and I truly disobeyed the heavenly law, what can I do? I beg you to spare my life!"

The next day, he dispatched the Wind God, the Thunder God, the Cloud Boy, and the Electric Mother straight up to the nine heavens above Chang'an. When he reached the hour of the Snake, he would spread clouds, at the hour of the Ox he would unleash thunder, at the hour of the Goat he would rain, and at the hour of the Horse, the rain would stop. But the rainfall would amount to only 3.4 inches, so he lengthened the hour by one more hour, thereby shortening the rainfall to 0.32 inches. After the rain, he ordered the generals of the multitude to withdraw. He returned the clouds to their place, transformed himself into a handsome scholar in white robes, and went to the west gate street. He ran into Yuan Shou Cheng's divination shop, entered without a word, and smashed all of his placard, brushes, inkwell, and other items in one go. The Mr. seated on the chair didn't flinch. The Dragon King then raised the doorboard and shouted and scolded, "This perverse person who speaks of blessings and misfortunes, this foolish person who deceives the minds of the multitude! Your divination didn't work, and your words were wildly off the mark! You said that the time and numbers for the rain today didn't match, and yet you still sit calmly, taking advantage of the situation to save your life!" Yuan Shou Cheng still didn't flinch, coldly laughing upwards towards the sky with a relaxed expression, "I'm not afraid! I'm not afraid! I'm not guilty of a capital offense, I'm only afraid you might be in big trouble! It's not that you deceive others easily, but I also know you're not a scholar, but the Dragon King of the Jing River. You disobeyed the edict of the Jade Emperor, altered the time and shortened the numbers, and committed a heavenly transgression. It's likely that you'll meet a beheading at the Dragon-Slayer's Platform. Why are you scolding me?" The Dragon King, having heard this, was startled and terrified, his hair stood on end, hastily dropped the doorboard, composed himself, and knelt down, saying, "Don't be angry, Mr. sir. I was just joking. Who would have known that it would come to pass and that I would have actually disobeyed the heavenly decree, causing a heavenly transgression? What can I do? I beg you, sir, to spare my life!"

On the following day, the Heaven Spreader, the Thunder Official, the Cloud Boy, the Electric Mother, and the Rain God ascended to the nine heavens above Chang'an City. At xi (around 11 am), he spread clouds, at wu (around 11 am), he sounded thunder, at wei (around 5 pm), he produced rain, but only a mere three feet and forty inches, and then, having prolonged it by a whole watch, he only gained a mere three inches and a half. After the rain let up, he released his attendants and returned to where he had come from. Then he changed back into the clothes of a cultivated scholar and went into the street in the west gate. He suddenly stormed into Yuan Shoucheng's divination shop, grabbed his signboard, brushes, inkstone, and other items, and smashed them all. The scholar sat calmly in his chair, unflinching. The Dragon King then yanked open the door and cursed and scolded him: "This arrogant person who speaks of fortunes and misfortunes, this reckless commoner who dupes the crowd! Your divination is useless, your words are absurd! You said the time when the rain would fall was entirely off, and yet you just sit here coolly, you had better get out, spare me the trouble of killing you!" Shoucheng remained defiant, still unperturbed, and gazed up at the sky with a cold smile: "I'm not afraid! I'm not afraid! I don't have a death sentence, but you do! You won't be able to fool anyone else, but you can't fool me either. I know who you are: you are not a scholar, but the Dragon King of the Jing River. You disobeyed the imperial edict, prolonged the time, reduced the rainfall, and broke the heavenly code. You'll likely be beheaded at the Dragon Scaling Platform. Why are you still cursing me?" The Dragon King, upon hearing this, was filled with trepidation, and his skin crawled with fear. He hastily dropped the door panel, smoothed out his clothes, and bowed, kneeling down before the scholar, and said: "Sir, don't hold it against me. I spoke idly, and who would have thought it would actually come true, and I did indeed break the heavenly code. What can I do? I beg you to pardon me!"

— This is just how it is, Prince, — Rogozhin said gloomily, scowling. — Just like Zalyezhev used to say. Then, I was running across Nevsky in my father's worn-out boots and in my stockings, and she comes out of the shop, gets into her carriage. That's when I felt a burn inside. I run into Zalyezhev; the fellow looks like a shop assistant from a barber's, and he's got a monocle in his eye. Back then, when I was still a kid and wore my family's broken-down boots and woolen stockings, we were nothing alike. He says, 'No, you're not him; that's the Princess,' — 'Her name is Nastasya Filipovna Barashkova,' he says, 'and she lives with Tozky, but Tozky has been unable to free himself from her, for he is now a man of fifty-five years and wants to marry the most beautiful woman in Petersburg.' He whispers to me that I can see Nastasya Filipovna in the theater today, in the ballet, in her box, in the loge, she'll be sitting there. 'Go to the ballet,' my parents say, 'one slap and she'll kill you!' But I slipped out quietly for an hour and saw Nastasya Filipovna again; I didn't sleep all that night. The next day, the old man gave me two five-per-cent coupons for five thousand each; 'Go, sell them,' he says, 'and bring me seven thousand five hundred to the Andreyevs' office, pay them off, and hand the remaining nine hundred back to me without going anywhere; I'll be waiting for you.' I sold the tickets, took the money, but I didn't go to the Andreyevs' office; instead, I went to the English shop and bought a pair of earrings, each containing almost a diamond the size of an almond, and was left with four hundred rubles; I told my name, and they believed me. With the earrings, I went to Zalyezhev; let's go, brother, to Nastasya Filipovna. We left. I have no idea what was under my feet, what was before me, what was beside me at that time, and I don't remember. We went straight into her box, and she came out to meet us. I didn't introduce myself then as myself, but Zalyezhev said, 'From Parfen, from Rogozhin, as a souvenir of our meeting yesterday; permit us to offer it to you.' She opened it, looked, smiled, and said, 'Thank your friend, Mr. Rogozhin, for his kind attention' — she bowed and left. Why didn't I die then and there! If I did go, it was because I thought, 'I'll never come back alive, anyway!' But what was most embarrassing for me was that this scoundrel Zalyezhev took all the credit for himself. I'm short, and I'm dressed like a sycophant, and I stand there silently, gazing at her, feeling ashamed, and he, well-dressed, made-up, ruddy, with a striped cravat, falls apart, he talks a lot, and I guess she must have taken him for me! 'Don't even think about it,' I say to him as we leave, 'you understand?' He laughs, 'And what about giving an account to Semen Parfenyevich?' I wanted to throw myself into the water then and go home without stopping, but I thought, 'What's the difference, anyway?' — and like a cursed wretch, I went back home.

— That's exactly how it is, said Rogauchin, gloomily and frowning, — just like Zalezhin used to say. Then I, your highness, was crossing the Neva on horseback, wearing my father's dilapidated caftan, and she steps out of the shop, gets into her carriage. I was seared by that. I run into Zalezhin, he wasn't exactly my equal, he walked like a barber's lackey, with a monocle in his eye, and we, my parents, used to be in worn-out boots and greasy shoes; he says, "This is not you, this is Princess; her name's Nastasya Fyodorovna Barashkova, and she lives with Tozky, and Tozky, being completely besotted, is now over fifty-five and wants to marry the most beautiful woman in St. Petersburg." He whispered to me then that you might see Nastasya Fyodorovna in the Bolshoi Theatre today, in the ballet, in her own box, in the loge; she'll be sitting there. "Go to the theatre with us, father," they said. "One little pleasure, and I'll die." I, however, quietly slipped away for an hour, and I saw Nastasya Fyodorovna again; I didn't sleep the whole night through. In the morning, the deceased gives me two five-per-cent bonds, each for five thousand, saying, "Sell them, they say, and bring me seven thousand five hundred to the Ananjevs' office, pay, and hand over the remaining nine thousand, without setting foot out; I'll be waiting for you." I sold the bonds, took the money, but didn't go to the Ananjevs' office, but instead went, not looking around, to the English shop and chose a pair of earrings, each with a briolette almost as small as an almond; I left a debt of four hundred rubles, gave my name, and they believed me. With the earrings, I went to Zalezhin: let's go, brother, to Nastasya Fyodorovna. We set off. I don't know and don't remember what was under my feet, in front of me, and beside me; we went straight to her box. She came out to meet us. I didn't introduce myself, that it was me; Zalezhin said, "From Parten, your highness, this is Rogauchin, a gift in memory of our meeting yesterday; kindly accept." She opened it, looked, smiled: "Thank your friend, Mr. Rogauchin, for his kind attention," she said, bowed and left. Well, that's why I'm still alive now! If I had gone, it would have been better if I hadn't returned alive! What hurt me most was that this scoundrel Zalezhin took everything for himself. I'm short of stature, I'm dressed like a fop, I'm standing there, silent, gazing at her, and it's embarrassing; he, on the other hand, is dressed in the latest fashion, with powder, curls, and a striped cravat, he's all a-flutter, a-flutter, and she probably took him instead of me! "You won't even think of being at my place now, do you understand?" he says, laughing. "And how are you going to account to Semen Parfenovich for this?" I thought about drowning myself, not going home, but thought, "What's the point, anyway?" and, like a scoundrel, I went home again.

— That's it, just as it is, Rostanev muttered, his face dark and scowling, — exactly what Zalëzhëv said then. I was then crossing Nevsky Prospect in the same old caftan my father used to wear, and she comes out of the shop, gets into her carriage. That set my blood on fire at the time. I run into Zalëzhëv, that swaggering poseur, wearing a monocle and dressed like a hairdresser's assistant, and we were once quite different, you know, in worn-out boots and a worn-out coat. 'It's not you,' he says, 'that's the countess, her name is Nastasya Fëdorovna, the Barashkova, and she lives with Tozsky, and Tozsky's stuck to her for dear life, being already over fifty-five and wanting to marry the most beautiful woman in St. Petersburg.' He whispered to me that I could see Nastasya Fëdorovna in the theatre today, at the ballet, in the imperial box, in the loge. Why don't you go and take in the ballet at our place? — it's one way to get rid of me! I snuck out for an hour, and I saw Nastasya Fëdorovna again, and I didn't sleep that whole night. The old fellow gave me two five-percentage theatre tickets, each for five thousand, saying, Go, sell them, take seven thousand five hundred to the Andreyevs' office, pay it off, and keep the rest, without going anywhere, I'll be waiting for you. I sold the tickets, took the money, and didn't go to the Andreyevs' office, but went instead to the English shop and bought two pairs of earrings with diamonds, one diamond in each, almost like cherries, and owed 400 rubles, and I gave my name, and they believed me. With the earrings, I went to Zalëzhëv: all right, come on, brother, let's go to Nastasya Fëdorovna. We went. I have no idea what was under my feet, what was in front of me, what was beside me — nothing. We went straight into the room, and she came out to us. I didn't introduce myself then as being the one I was; Zalëzhëv says, 'From Parfen, the Count Rostanev, for your memories of our meeting yesterday; would you be so kind as to accept it?' She took it, glanced at it, smiled, 'Thank your friend, Count Rostanev, for his friendly gesture,' — she bowed and left. Why, I didn't die on the spot right then! If I had gone, it was because I thought: 'I won't be alive to return!' And what hurt me the most was that this bounder Zalëzhëv had taken it all for himself. I'm short, dressed like a servant, standing there in silence, ogling her, feeling ashamed, and he's in the latest fashion, painted, powdered, with a striped tie, laughing and winking, and probably she took him for me! 'You can't even think I'm here now,' I said to him as we were leaving, 'do you understand?' He laughs: 'How are you going to account to Semën Parfënich for this?' I wanted to drown myself right then, without going home, but I thought, 'What's the point anyway?' — and, wretched as I am, I went back home.

— That's just the way it is, Prince, — said Rogozhin gloomily, scowling, — just what Zaleshov said back then. I was running across the Nevsky in my father's old caftan, and she comes out of the shop, gets into her carriage, and that's when I got burned up. I ran into Zaleshov, and he's not my match, walks like a barber's assistant, has a monocle in his eye, and we used to be different, back when we were wearing muddy boots and standing at the cookstove. He says: "Not you, that's not you, that's a countess," and her name is Nastasya Filippovna, surname Barashkova, and she lives with Tozsky, and Tozsky's got no way to get free of her now, as she's got five and fifty years and he wants to marry the loveliest woman in Petersburg. He told me that I could see Nastasya Filippovna at the opera today, in the ballet, in her own box, in the dress circle. My father said, "Just try going to the ballet," and I'd have killed one of us! But I, however, managed to slip away for an hour in secret and saw Nastasya Filippovna again; I didn't sleep that whole night. Next morning, the deceased gives me two five percent bills for five thousand rubles each, and says, "Just go, I mean, sell them, and bring me seven thousand five hundred to the Andreyevs' office, pay it in, and give the rest of the ten thousand, not stepping foot out, to me, and I'll be waiting for you." I sold the tickets, took the money, and didn't go to the Andreyevs' office, but instead went to the English store and chose a pair of pendants, each with a diamond almost like an almond, and I owed them four hundred rubles; I gave them my name, and they believed me. With the pendants I went to Zaleshov: come on, brother, let's go to Nastasya Filippovna. We set off. I don't know or remember what was under my feet, in front of me, or to the sides of me; we went straight into the box. She came out to meet us herself. I didn't introduce myself, that it was me, the very one, and Zaleshov says, "From Parfen, from Rogozhin, as a gift in memory of our meeting yesterday; will you kindly accept?" She opened it, looked, smiled: "Thank your friend Mr. Rogozhin for his kind attention," she said, and took her leave, and went away. And that's why I'm still alive today! If I had gone at all, it was because I thought, "I won't be coming back alive, anyway!" But what hurt me the most was that this scoundrel Zaleshov had taken everything onto himself. I'm short, dressed like a lackey, standing, silent, staring at her, and I'm ashamed, but he's all done up in the style, in powder, and perfumed, with a striped cravat, so stylish, so flippant, and I'm sure she took him for me! "Now, I said, as we left, you won't even dare think about me, do you understand?" He's laughing: "And how are you going to account for yourself to Semen Parfenych?" I was really wanting to jump into the water, not coming home, but I thought, "Anyway, it's all the same," and like a wretch, I went back home.

— That's how it is, — said Rogozhin with a sullen expression, — just what Zalyezhev was talking about. At that time, Your Highness, I was crossing the Nevsky Prospekt in my father's caftan, and she stepped out of the shop and got into a carriage. It all left a burn on me. I run into Zalyezhev, the fellow, and he's not at all like me, walks like a barber's lackey, and has a lorgnette in his eye, while we used to wear muddy boots and stockings with big patches. This, he says, isn't you, it's Princess, and her name is Nastasya Filipovna, surname Barashkova, and she lives with Tozky, and Tozky can't now part with her, having reached the ripe age of fifty-five, and he wants to marry the most beautiful woman in all Petersburg. He whispered to me that you might see Nastasya Filipovna today at the Bolshoi Theatre, in the ballet, in her own loge, in the private box, that she'll be sitting in. Our father says, try to get to the ballet, he'll kill you! But I, however, quietly slipped out for an hour and saw Nastasya Filipovna again; I didn't sleep that whole night. Next morning, the deceased hands me two five percent bonds, each for five thousand roubles, says, sell them, collect seven thousand five hundred from the Andreys in their office, pay it in, and bring me the remaining change from ten thousand, don't go anywhere, I'll be waiting for you. I sold the bonds, took the money, but instead of going to the Andreys' office, I went to the English shop, chose a pair of diamond studs, almost like grains of grit, and owed them four hundred roubles; said my name and they believed me. With the studs I went to Zalyezhev, all right, all right, let's go, brother, to Nastasya Filipovna's. We set out. I don't remember, I don't know what was under my feet, in front of me, on the sides – we walked straight to her box, and she came out to meet us herself. I didn't say I was the one and the same, but Zalyezhev says, "From Partenka, to Rostanev, as a token of our meeting yesterday; with your permission, please accept it." She unfolded it, looked at it, smiled: "Thank your friend, Mr. Rostanev, for his kind attention," – bowed and left. I almost died on the spot then. I only went because I thought: "What's the point, I won't come back alive anyway!" But the most humiliating thing was that this fiend Zalyezhev had taken everything for himself. I'm small in stature, dressed like a lackey, stand there, dumbfounded, staring at her, feeling ashamed, and he's all the rage, in powder and curl, reddened, with a striped cravat – he's bursting with laughter, making a show of himself, and I bet she's taken him instead of me! "What's this, I said, when we came out, you mustn't think about this now, understand?" He's laughing: "And what about your account to Semen Parfenych then?" I wanted to drown myself right then, without going home, but I thought: "It's all the same anyway," and like a scoundrel, I went back home.

He twirled his staff and unsheathed his sword, dashing forward together, as the Executioner struck wildly with all his might, hacking back and forth, tap-tap-tapping a score of blows or more. The Monkey King stood motionless in the center, seemingly oblivious. The Executioner sneered at him, saying, "Good monk, you're certainly hard-headed!" The Monkey King smiled and said, "You've just begun to see how good I am! You're also getting tired, so I'll just take out my needle and thread and show you what I can do." The Executioner retorted, "You're a doctor of acupuncture and moxibustion, transforming into a physician. We have no ailments, so why do you talk about sticking needles?" The Monkey King reached into his ear and pulled out a silk-covered needle, but as the wind caught it, it turned out to be a thick iron rod, about the size of a bowl, which he wielded in his hand, saying, "Don't run! Let me try out my hand with this one!" The Executioner was frightened into scattering and running off in all directions, but the Monkey King seized him and chased after him, eventually killing one by one. He stripped them of their clothes and belongings, laughing as he exclaimed, "My master, you're free to go! The Executioner has been handled." 

The Tang Monk scolded, "You've caused a lot of trouble! Even though he was a disciple of the Cutting-Off-All-Laws Sect, he shouldn't have been sentenced to death. You might have dissuaded him and sent him away; how could you kill them all? You've caused people's lives unnecessarily. This is something a monk should avoid, lest he accidentally kill an ant or a fly. As a Buddhist, you should cultivate compassion and loving-kindness. Why don't you distinguish between right and wrong? You struck them dead without showing any mercy or compassion! If we were in the wilderness, there was no one to investigate; but if we enter a city, what if someone accidentally bumped into you? You'd be aggressive and beating people up with a staff, I'd be put in a predicament. How can I talk my way out of this?" The Monkey King retorted, "If I didn't kill them, they would have killed you instead." The Tang Monk scolded, "As a monk, I dare not be aggressive. Even if I die, it's just my body; you, on the other hand, killed six people, and this is no small matter. If this gets reported to the authorities, even the Buddha himself couldn't exonerate me." The Monkey King said, "I'm not going to hide anything from my master: five hundred years ago, when I was the king of Flower Fruit Mountain and renowned as a terror, I must have killed many people. If it were to be reported to the authorities, it might have earned me some praise." The Tang Monk exclaimed, "You've always been reckless in the world, inflicting harm on people, deceiving the heavens, and defying the law. Now that you're a monk, if you continue to be aggressive and cause harm, you'll be unable to reach the Western Heavens and become a monk. This is terrible, simply terrible!" The Monkey King was enraged and, as the Tang Monk lectured him, his anger boiled over, and he said, "If you say I can't become a monk and won't be able to reach the Western Heavens, then I'll just go back! I'm leaving!" The Tang Monk didn't even respond, and the Monkey King then somersaulted into thin air, shouting, "I'm off!" The Tang Monk quickly looked up, but the Monkey King had already vanished, leaving behind only the sound of his cry as he flew off eastwards. The Tang Monk was left alone, shaking his head and lamenting his fate, saying, "This rascal! This fool of a disciple! He doesn't take any of my teachings to heart! I just scold him a few times, and he vanishes into thin air and returns to his home. Fine, fine, fine! I'm probably not destined to take disciples or enter the clergy. Now I'll never be able to find him; I'll call out to him, but he won't answer. Where can I find him? How can I call him back?"

He twirled his gun and brandished his sword, rushing forward, and the sworn disciple gave him a flurry of hits, "bang, bang, bang," striking him about seventy or eighty times. The Monkey King stood still in the middle, as if he knew nothing. The sworn disciple said, "Good monk! You truly have a hard head!" The Monkey King laughed and said, "Don't you think I'm just barely holding out? You and your gang must be tired, why don't I take out a needle to play around with you?" The sworn disciple said, "This monk must be a licentiate in needle therapy who has become a master of acupuncture. We don't have any ailments to say anything about your needle therapy!" The Monkey King reached into his ear and pulled out a silk embroidery needle, which turned out to be an iron rod, as thick as a bowl, and said, "Don't move! Let me try out my skill with a hit!" The sworn disciple was startled and fled, but the Monkey King chased after him, and after catching up to the others, one by one, he struck them dead. After stripping them of their clothes and seizing their money bags, he laughed and headed off, saying, "Master, please proceed. That bandit has been dealt with by the Old Monkey." The Tang Monk said, "You've done a good deed, but this time you've got yourself into trouble! Although he was a ferocious ruffian, it wouldn't be fitting to put him to death; if he had been taken to the authorities, he wouldn't have deserved the death penalty. You, with your talent, should have only chased him off, not killed him. Now, you've ended up harming someone unnecessarily. As a Buddhist monk, I'd rather sweep the street and avoid harming even a tiny insect; I'd rather cherish the silk covering on a candle flame. Why didn't you distinguish between right and wrong, and kill them all off at once? There's not a shred of compassion or benevolence in you! If I were in a remote mountain area and no one was around to monitor us, it wouldn't be a problem. But if we were in a city and someone bumped into you, and you struck him down in anger, I, a beggar like myself, wouldn't know how to defend myself!" The Monkey King said, "If I hadn't killed them, they would have killed you!" The Tang Monk said, "I, as a Buddhist monk, would never dare to engage in violence. I'd rather die myself than harm others. You, however, killed six of them, and now this will be a problem if it gets reported to the authorities, even if your father were the emperor, you wouldn't be able to talk your way out of it." The Monkey King said, "I'm not kidding Master, in the past, when I was the king of the Peach Flower Mountain, I don't know how many people I killed. If you were to report this to the authorities, it would just be a few warrants to sign!" The Tang Monk said, "It's because you had no discipline and have been roaming the world, offending heaven and deceiving the emperor that you've come to face this predicament. Now that you've taken the tonsure, if you continue to be as violent as before, always harming living beings, you'll never be able to reach the Western Heaven, and you won't be able to become a monk! What a shame! What a shame!" The Monkey King, unable to contain his anger, shot back at the Tang Monk, "You're lecturing me like this, yet saying I can't become a monk and can't reach the Western Heaven? Don't lecture me like that; I'm going!" The Tang Monk hadn't even finished speaking when the Monkey King suddenly vanished in an instant, shouting "Old Monkey is off!" The Tang Monk lifted his head to look around, but he was nowhere to be seen. All he could hear was the sound of the Monkey King's shouting as he disappeared into the east. The Tang Monk was left standing there, alone and helpless, shaking his head in dismay, "This fiend! He just can't listen to reason! I just lectured him a bit, and he's suddenly gone off! That's it! That's it! That's it! It seems I shouldn't have taken him on as a disciple; I shouldn't have brought trouble to myself. Now, I have no idea where to find him, and if I call out to him, he won't respond. What a shame! What a shame!"

He danced his whip and brandished his sword, rushing forward in a flurry. A Xiyou xianzun chopped at him wildly, hacking down 70 or 80 times. The Buddha was standing still in the middle, feigning ignorance. The bandit said, "Good monk! You really have a hard head!" The Xiyou xianzun smiled and said, "It's nothing! You're all tired, and it's time for me to take out my needle and play around." The bandit said, "This monk is a licenced acupuncturist who has turned into a doctor. We have no ailment to treat, what are you talking about needles?" The Xiyou xianzun pulled out a colorful needle from his ear and flapped it in the wind, revealing an iron rod a bowl's diameter thick. He said, "Don't run away! Let old Xiyou try his hand at one swing." He scared off the six bandits, who scattered and fled. Xiyou caught up to them and chased them down, killing each one. After stripping them of their clothes and confiscating their valuables, he laughed and approached the Buddha, saying, "Master, please go. The bandit has been captured by old Xiyou."

The Buddha said, "You've really caused trouble this time! Although he was a delinquent who had cut off his kinship, if he was brought to the authorities, he wouldn't deserve death. Even if you have the means to handle the situation, you should have chased him away, why did you kill them all? This is completely unnecessary taking of human life, how can you be a monk? Monastics have to sweep away evil deeds as carefully as they would sweep away ants and moths. How could you be so uncompassionate and merciless? Even in the mountains, no one would inspect us, but in the city, if someone bumps into you, and you resort to violence, using your staff to hurt people, I would be a silent witness, and I don't know how I could escape retribution."

The Xiyou said, "Father, if I didn't kill them, they would have killed you instead." The Buddha said, "As a monk, I would rather die than resort to violence. I would die alone, but you've killed six people, how can I explain this? If this were to be reported to the authorities, even if my father were the emperor, he wouldn't be able to speak on my behalf."

The Xiyou said, "I'm telling you the truth, father. Five hundred years ago, when I ruled over Flower Fruit Mountain and was known as a strange figure, I killed countless people. If you say this would get me in trouble, I'd just get a commendation for reporting the wrongdoing."

The Buddha said, "It's because you've been unaccountable and violent in the world, deceiving Heaven and deceiving the officials, that you've suffered this calamity. Now that you've entered the monastery, if you continue to be violent and kill people, you won't be able to reach the Western Heaven or be a monk. How despicable! How despicable!" The monkey, who could not bear the scolding, began to burn with anger. He thought to himself, "Since father is criticizing me like this, saying I'm not worthy to be a monk, and can't go to the Western Heaven, why should I waste any more of his words? I'll just leave now." The Buddha hadn't even responded yet, when the monkey gave a loud "I'm off!" and jumped into the distance, disappearing from sight as he headed east. The Buddha was left standing alone, shaking his head and sighing, lamenting and grumbling to himself, saying, "That rascal! How could he not take a lesson! I just criticized him a bit, and he just vanished into thin air, fleeing back to his lair! Well, I'm probably destined not to take on disciples, it seems. Now I can't find him anywhere, and even if I call him, he won't answer."

He wielded the gun and danced the sword, and with a burst of rage, he hacked wildly, "dapon-dapon-panpan," striking seven or eight dozen times. The monkey stood in the middle, pretending not to know. The thief exclaimed, "Good monk! Your head is really hard!" The monkey laughed and said, "You can just take a look at me, alright! You've had enough, but I'm just getting started. Why don't you let me pull out a needle and play around a bit?" The thief said, "You're just a monk who has turned into a doctor of acupuncture. We have no ailments to be treated, so why are you talking nonsense about needles?" The monkey stretched out his hand to pull out a needle from his ear and, as it fluttered in the wind, it turned out to be an iron club, as thick as a bowl, and he said, "Don't run! Let Old Monkey try his hand at beating you!" This frightened the six thieves to scatter and flee, but he chased them down and caught up, killing them one by one. He undressed them, took their belongings, and walked off, humming to himself, saying, "Master, the thief has been dealt with by Old Monkey." The master said, "You've caused a great calamity! Although he was a disciple of the Divergent Path and a formidable figure, if we had taken him to the authorities, he wouldn't have deserved the death penalty. Why did you kill them all? You have no compassion, no benevolence! Monks are supposed to show kindness, even to the most insignificant creatures. You didn't distinguish between right and wrong and killed them all. If we had stayed in the mountains, nobody would have reported us, but if we go to the city, and someone happens to bump into you, and you use your staff to attack them, I'll be implicated and can't escape." The monkey said, "If I didn't kill them, they would have killed you." The master said, "As a monk, I would rather die than resort to violence. If I die, it's just my own fault, but you've killed six people, how can we explain that? If this gets reported to the authorities, even if my father were the ruler, it would be hard to justify." The monkey said, "I won't conceal the truth from you, Master. Five hundred years ago, when I was the king of Flower Fruit Mountain and the most unusual figure, I killed countless people. If I had to take this case to court, I'd be justified in presenting evidence." The master said, "You've never managed or controlled your own affairs, and you've bullied and deceived people in the world. That's why you've been punished with the karma of five hundred years ago. Now that you've become a monk, if you still resort to violence and cause harm to living beings, you won't be able to go to the Western Heavens and won't be able to become a monk. That's terrible, that's terrible!" The monkey, not able to endure the master's scolding, grew angrier and angrier, and without waiting for the master to finish speaking, he leapt up and shouted, "I'm off!" and with a loud "Old Monkey has gone!" he vanished from sight, disappearing in the east. The master looked up, startled, but by the time he did, the monkey had already left, and all that was left was the sound of his departure. The master shook his head, sighing and complaining, saying, "This rogue! He wouldn't listen to advice and teaching! The moment I scold him, he just disappears, and I'm left all alone. I should have never taken him on as a disciple. I wish I could find him, but where can I find him? I wish I could call for him, but he won't respond. He's gone!"

He brandished his spear and swung his sword, and they rushed forward in a wave, with the Straw Sand Monk hacking wildly, hitting seventy or eighty times. The Monkey King stood still in the middle, pretending not to know. The outlaw shouted, "Good monk! Your head is indeed hard!" The Monkey King chuckled and said, "You're just making do, that's all! You're getting tired, and you're supposed to pull out a needle to fiddle with. That monk is a medical doctor who specializes in acupuncture. We have no ailments, what's the point of talking about acupuncture?" The Monkey King reached into his ear and pulled out a decorative needle, which, upon a gust of wind, transformed into a rod of iron, thick as a bowl handle. He held it in his hand and said, "Don't run! Let the Old Monkey try his hand at it!" The six outlaws were startled and scattered in all directions, only to be pursued and caught, each one killed. They stripped them of their clothes and stole their belongings, then laughed and sang as they departed, "Master, please proceed; the outlaws have been dealt with by the Old Monkey." The Master said, "You've caused trouble again! They may be evil scholars, but they shouldn't be put to death. Even if you have means, you should just frighten them off. Why did you kill them all? You have no compassion or kindness! If we're in the wilderness, no one checks up on us, but if we're in the city, and someone suddenly offends you, you'll attack them, wielding a staff and injuring people. I'm a guest, how can I escape?" The Monkey King replied, "If I didn't kill them, they would kill you instead." The Master said, "As a monk, I dare not harm anyone. If I were to die, it would only be my own body, but you killed six people, how can that be justified? If this matter were reported to the authorities, even if your father were the official, it wouldn't be believable." The Monkey King said, "Don't hide the truth from me, old master, I was the one who ruled over Flower Fruit Mountain five hundred years ago, and I don't know how many people I killed then. If it's reported to the authorities, it would even be something to write about." The Master said, "You're an irresponsible brute, recklessly harming people in the world and deceiving heaven. That's why you've encountered the difficulties of five hundred years ago. Now that you've taken the tonsure, if you continue to harm people, you won't be able to go to the West, or become a monk. What a terrible, terrible thing!" The monkey was impatient and couldn't bear it, and seeing the Master's repetitive scolding, he snapped with rage. He said, "You've accused me of not being qualified to become a monk, and of not being able to go to the West. I'll just go back!" The Master didn't even answer, and the Monkey King suddenly leaped into the air, shouting, "I'm off!" The Master looked up to see him disappear, only hearing a loud thud, and he went back east. He left the Master alone, sighing and lamenting, saying, "This scoundrel! He just wouldn't listen to teaching! I scold him a few times, and he just vanishes into thin air and disappears. What's the point? The point is that I must have brought misfortune upon myself by taking on a disciple. Now I want to find him, but there's no place to find him; I want to call him, but he doesn't answer. I'm done!"

— All of it! The entire pack of it! Listen, gentlemen! — declared Nastasya Filippovna, placing the pack next to Gleb. — And he didn't go, he endured! So he has even more pride than a thirst for money. Good, he'll snap out of it! Maybe he would have cut him, perhaps... Look, he's coming to himself already. The general, Ivan Petrovich, Darya Alekseyevna, Katerina, Pasha, Rostov, listen! This pack is for Ganya. I give it to him in full ownership, as a reward... well, for whatever it is! Tell him. Let him lie there beside it... Rostov, go! Farewell, Prince, I've seen a man for the first time! Farewell, Afanasy Ivanovich, thank you!

-- Everything of his! The whole package of his! Listen, gentlemen! -- declared Nastasya Filipovna, putting the package next to Ganya. -- And he hasn't gone, he held out! So it means he's got even more self-love than greed for money. Never mind, he'll come to his senses! Or maybe he'd have cut himself, I dare say... Look, he's even starting to come to himself now. The general, Ivan Petrovich, Darya Alekseyevna, Katya, Pasha, Rostov, listen! That's Ganya's package. I'm handing it all over to him as a gift, in reward... well, whatever! Tell him. Let it just lie there next to him... Rostov, go! Goodbye, Prince, the first time I've seen a man like that! Goodbye, Afanasy Ivanovich, thank you!

— All of it! The whole pack! Listen, gentlemen! — declared Nastasya Filipovna, putting the pack next to Ganya. — And not gone, then he endured! So much more pride than thirst for money. Well, he'll recover! Perhaps he would have cut himself... Look, he's even coming to his senses now. The general, Ivan Petrovich, Darya Alekseyevna, Katya, Pasha, Rostanev, heard? This is Ganya's pack. I give it to him as a free gift, as a reward... or for anything else, really! Tell him. Let it lie there near him... Rostanev, go! — All of it, the whole pack of it! Listen, gentlemen! — declared Nastasya Filipovna, placing the pack beside Gania. — And he didn't go, endured! So he's got more pride than a thirst for money. Oh well, he'll come to himself! Maybe he'd even have stabbed him... Look, and he's coming around. General, Ivan Petrovich, Darya Alexeievna, Katya, Pasha, Rostov, did you hear? It's Gania's pack. I'm giving it to him, in full ownership, as a reward... or for whatever. Tell him. Let it lie there near him... Rostov, off you go! Farewell, Prince, for the first time I've seen a human being! — The whole thing, the whole package, I'm telling you! Listen, gentlemen! Nastasya Filipovna declared, placing the package near Gan. — But he hasn't gone off, has he? Then it's more about his pride than the desire for money! No matter, he'll get over it! Maybe he'd have killed him, who knows... Look, he's coming to. General, Ivan Petrovich, Darya Alekseyevna, Katerina, Pasha, Rostov, did you hear? It's Ganin's package. I'm giving it to him as a gift, as a reward, whatever you call it! Tell him. Let it lie there next to him... Rostov, go! Farewell, Prince, the first time I've seen a human being! Farewell, Afanasy Ivanovich, thank you!

As soon as Rui returned home, he paid a visit to his mother-in-law, Zhang Shi. Zhang Shi said, "Congratulations to my son, and also coming back after getting married." Rui said, "The son owes his good fortune to his mother's blessings, and it was a great honor to be ranked first in the exams, with the emperor graciously granting him a tour of the city, passing in front of the minister Yin's mansion, where he met him by chance, and he was invited to take his daughter as a daughter-in-law. The emperor then appointed the son as the Prefect of Jiangzhou, and now he came to take his mother and leave for his post." Zhang Shi was overjoyed and busied herself preparing their journey. A few days into their trip, they arrived at a fruit store run by Liu Er'er, where Zhang Shi suddenly fell ill, and said to Rui, "I don't feel well, and let's stay here for two more days to rest before leaving." Rui obeyed. The next morning, Rui saw a vendor selling a gold-colored carp in front of the store, and he bought it with a string of coins, intending to cook it for his mother to eat. Just as the carp glared at him with its beady eyes, Rui was astonished and said, "They say that fish with beady eyes are no ordinary things!" He then asked the fisherman, "Where did this fish come from?" The fisherman replied, "It was caught fifteen li away from the official Yin's residence, in the Hong River." Rui immediately took the fish back to the Hong River and released it back into the water. When he returned to the store and told his mother about this, Zhang Shi said, "Releasing the fish is a good deed, and I'm very happy." Rui said, "We've been here for three days, the deadline is pressing, and the son wants to set out tomorrow, but how is your health?"

Bao Liu returned home, accompanied his wife to pay his respects to his mother, Madame Zhang. Madame Zhang said, "Hurray, my son, and you're back with a bride. " Bao Liu replied, "I'm fortunate to have my mother's blessings and to have passed the civil exam. I've been granted the privilege of a ceremonial procession, which passed right in front of the Prime Minister Yin's gate. Just as we were tossing the embroidered balls, the Prime Minister invited my future daughter-in-law to be my bride on the spot. The imperial court has appointed me as the Governor of Jiangzhou, and now I've come to take you to the province." Madame Zhang was overjoyed and began to prepare for the journey. A few days later, they stopped at the Wanghuazhai shop run by Liu Er'er. Madame Zhang suddenly fell ill and told Bao Liu, "I don't feel well. I'll rest here in the shop for two days before continuing our journey." Bao Liu obeyed. The next morning, he saw a man carrying a gold-colored carp to sell outside the shop and immediately bought it with a hundred coins, intending to cook it for his mother to eat. But the carp gazed at Bao Liu with an unwavering stare, and Bao Liu was astonished and exclaimed, "They say that fish and snakes have a piercing stare, so it's not an ordinary thing!" So he asked the fisherman, "Where did you catch this fish?" The fisherman replied, "It was caught from the River Hong, fifteen li away from the prefecture." Bao Liu immediately returned the fish to the river and let it go. He told his mother about this and said, "I've released the fish back into the river." Madame Zhang said, "Releasing the fish is a good deed, and I'm very happy. " Bao Liu said, "We've stayed here for three days already. Our journey to the province is urgent, and I was thinking of leaving tomorrow, but I don't know how you're feeling."

Gong'r returned home, accompanied by his wife to pay their respects to his mother, Zhang Shi. Zhang Shi said, "Congratulations, my son, and also welcome back with your new bride." Gong'r said, "I owe my good fortune to Mother's blessings and owe my passing the examination as a top scholar to her protection. I was granted a ceremonial procession through the streets, which passed right by the entrance to the house of the Chief Minister, Yin. At the time, I met the Chief Minister and was invited to take his daughter as my wife. I was appointed as the governor of Jiangzhou, and now I have come to take Mother to join me at my post." Zhang Shi was overjoyed, and busied herself with preparing their departure. 

After a few days, they arrived at the Liu Er'er's house at the Flower Market and dismounted. However, Zhang Shi's body suddenly fell ill, and she said to Gong'r, "I'm not feeling well, let's stay at this inn for a couple more days before continuing our journey." Gong'r obeyed her orders. The next morning, as he went out, he saw a man standing outside the shop, hawking a golden fish. Gong'r immediately bought the fish with a string of coins, intending to cook it for his mother to eat. "Well, my soul," Sobakievich said, "if I were to do it myself, I'd tell you straight out that I wouldn't eat such filth. I'll have a frog covered in sugar, I won't take it in my mouth, and neither will I take oysters – I know what oysters are like. Take a lamb," he said, addressing Chichikov, "it's a lamb's side with some porridge! That's not the kind of fricassee they make on the barons' tables out of lamb, which lies on the market for four days! It's the Germans and the French who thought that up – I'd hang them for it! They invented a diet, to cure hunger with it! They imagine that their German liquid nature is what will sweeten the Russian stomach. No, that's not it, that's all just a lot of nonsense – just talk about the Enlightenment, Enlightenment, but this is a load of rubbish! He shook his head indignantly. "They'd rather say something else, but there's only one thing I won't say at the table. I'm not like that. If there's pork on the table, bring on the whole pig! If there's lamb, bring the whole lamb, if there's a goose, bring the whole goose! It's better I eat two dishes, but I'll eat to the measure that my soul demands. Sobakievich proved it by his actions: he overturned half the lamb's side onto his plate and ate everything, chewed it up, sucked the marrow out of every bone."

"Oh, my soul," said Sobakevich, "if I were doing it myself, but I'll be frank with you, I wouldn't stoop to eating such rubbish. Even if you smother a frog in sugar, I wouldn't take it in my mouth, and I wouldn't touch the oysters either; I know what oysters are like. Take the mutton, continued Sobakevich, addressing Chichikov, mutton with porridge! That's not those mutton fricassee concoctions they make in the butchers' shops from mutton that rots on the market for four days! This is all a product of those German and French doctors' fancy, I'd hang them for this! They've invented diets and are treating people to starvation! What, with their liquid German nature, do they think they can sweet-talk the Russian stomach? No, this isn't it, this is all nonsense, it's all... — Here Sobakevich even shook his head in anger. They go on and on about 'enlightenment, enlightenment,' but this 'enlightenment' of theirs is nothing but a load of rubbish. I'd say something else, but there's no polite word to say at the table. I'm not that kind. When there's pork on the table, give me all the pork, when there's mutton, bring the whole mutton, when there's a goose, bring the whole goose! It's better for me to eat two dishes in moderation, just as my soul demands. Sobakevich confirmed this with action: he upturned the other half of the mutton chop onto his plate, ate everything, gnawed on the bones, sucked the marrow out of them to the last bit."

The prince took off his tin cross, and Parfen his gold one, and they exchanged them. Parfen was silent. The prince, with a heavy look of astonishment, noticed that his namesake brother's previous incredulity, his former bitter and almost mocking smile, still lingered on his face, at least occasionally greatly visible. After a moment of silence, Rogozhin finally grasped the prince's hand and stood for a time as if not daring to do anything; finally, he suddenly pulled him along, speaking in a barely audible voice: "Come." They passed over the landing of the first floor and rang at the door opposite the one from which they had come. They were let in soon. An elderly woman, bent and dressed in black, with a handkerchief bound around her head, bowed low to Rogozhin in silence; he asked her something briefly, and not waiting for an answer, led the prince further through the rooms. Again they went through dark, cold, and austere rooms, furnished with old furniture in white, spotless covers. Not saying a word, Rogozhin straightaway led the prince into a small room, like a sitting room, divided by a polished partition of red wood, with two doors on either side, behind which, probably, was the bedroom. In the corner of the sitting room, by the stove, in armchairs, sat an old woman, still not looking very old, even with a rather healthy, pleasant, and round face, but already completely gray and (one could infer from the first glance) completely infantile. Both of them, it was clear, had been silent all the time. The first old woman, seeing Rogozhin and the prince, smiled at them and several times graciously inclined her head in a sign of pleasure.

— Parfen, I am not your enemy, and I mean to interfere with you in nothing. This I repeat just as I declared and have always declared, once, almost at the same moment. When your wedding was taking place in Moscow, you know I did not hinder you. At first she flung herself at me almost under the veil, begging me to "rescue" her from you. I am repeating her very words to you. Then she ran away from me too, and you again found her and led her to the altar, and now, they say, she has run away from you again. Is this true? I was told by Lebedev, that's why I came here. And about your reconciliation, I only learned it yesterday in the carriage for the first time from one of your former friends, from Zalozhev if you want to know. I was traveling here intending to: I wanted to finally persuade her to go abroad for her health; she is very distressed in body and soul, and, in my opinion, greatly in need of care. I didn't want to accompany her abroad myself, but had planned everything to arrange for her without me. I speak the truth to you. If it's an absolute truth that you two have reconciled again, then I won't even show myself to her, and I'll never come to see you again. You know yourself that I'm not deceiving you, because I've always been frank with you. I've never concealed my thoughts about this from you and have always said that her being with you is her certain doom. Your doom too... perhaps even more so than hers. If you two were to part again, I would be very pleased; but I don't intend to interfere with you or cause you any trouble. Be at ease and don't suspect me. And you know yourself: have I ever been your true rival, even when she ran away to me? You are laughing now; I know what you're smiling at. Yes, we lived differently, in different cities, and you certainly know that. I even explained to you before that I "don't love her with love, but out of pity." I think I define it precisely. You said you understood these words then, did you? did you really understand? Look at you, full of hatred! I came to comfort you because you are dear to me. I very much love you, Parfen. Now I will leave and never come back. Farewell.

— Parfen, I am not your enemy and have no intention of interfering with you in anything. I repeat this just as I did before, and once more, in nearly the same moment. When your wedding was taking place in Moscow, you know I didn't interfere with you. The first time it was she herself who ran to me, almost under the veil, asking me to "rescue" her from you. I am repeating her own words to you. Then she ran away from me too, and you managed to track her down and bring her to the altar, and now it is said she's run away from you again. Is this true? That's what Lopukhin told me, and that's why I came here. As for the rumor that the two of you have made up again, I only found out about it yesterday on the train for the first time from one of your old acquaintances, Zalezhin, if you'd like to know. I was coming here with the intention of trying to convince her to go abroad for her health; she is very distraught in body and soul, and especially in mind, and I think she needs great care. I didn't plan to accompany her abroad myself, but I had everything else organized for her without me. I'm telling you the truth. If it is true that the two of you have made up again, then I won't appear before her, and I won't come to you again either. You yourself know that I don't deceive you, because I have always been honest with you. I never hid my thoughts about this from you and always said that you would inevitably ruin her; you might even be more of a destroyer than she is. If the two of you were to split up again, I would be very pleased, but I don't intend to meddle in your affairs or to upset them. So be calm and don't suspect me. And you know as well as I do: was I ever your true rival, even when she ran to me? You've smiled; I know what you're smiling at. Yes, we lived apart, in different cities, and you must remember this. You said you understood my words back then; is that true? did you understand them? Just look at how you're scowling at me! I came to calm you down because you are dear to me. I very much love you, Parfen. And now I'll leave and never come back. Goodbye.

I dare not deceive Minister Xü, as from childhood I have mastered the art of calculating the fate, knowing that the emperor will not die. Just as he finished speaking, a great outcry resounded from inside the coffin, "Murder! Murder!," startling the officials and generals, making their faces turn pale like autumn's yellow locust tree leaves and their waists thin like spring's tender willow branches. The heir apparent's legs were weak, unable to hold his staff in the mourning ceremony; the prime minister's spirit fled, how could he wear the ceremonial cap and follow the rites of filial piety? The imperial consorts stumbled and fell, the maidens tilted to one side. When the imperial consorts stumbled and fell, they tumbled like a fierce gust of wind knocking over a fallen magnolia; the maidens tilted to one side, looking as if a sudden downpour had knocked over a delicate orchid. The ministers cowered in fear, their bones turned soft and their muscles numb. They trembled with fear, looking vacant and witless. The imperial palace was turned into a shattered dragon pavilion and the mourning dais resembled a collapsed temple. At that moment, the palace ladies ran away with speed, none dared to come close to the spirit and the coffin. Fortunately, it was thanks to the integrity of Minister Xú Mào Gōng, the righteousness of Prime Minister Wèi Zhēng, the courage of General Qín Jīng, and the bravery of Ěr Dédé, who rushed forward to support the coffin, saying, "Your Majesty, what is there for you to worry about, tell us, don't create a ghost and frighten the Imperial Family." Prime Minister Wèi Zēng said, "This is not creating a ghost, it's Your Majesty returning to life. Fetch the tools quickly!" They opened the coffin lid, and true enough, there sat the Taizong sitting inside, still shouting "Murder! Who saved me!" Minister Xú Mào Gōng et al. came forward to lift him up, saying "Your Majesty, don't be afraid, we officials are here to protect you." The Crown Prince finally opened his eyes and said, "Just now, I was in a terrible plight, escaping the calamities of the underworld and then met with a disaster on the water." The officials said, "Your Majesty, be at ease, what disaster could there be on the water?"

Not to conceal from Mr. Xu, since childhood, I have studied the art of divination, and I am most certain that the emperor will not die. As I was speaking, only to hear the coffin give voice to cries from within, "You've doomed me! You've doomed me!" The officials present were terrified, and the empress and concubines were beside themselves with fear. One by one, their faces turned as pale as autumnal silk, and their waists as slender as willow branches in the spring.

The crown prince's legs were as weak as if he might collapse in grief, and the chief minister's soul had fled his body; he dared not put on his ceremonial hat to follow the rites of mourning. The concubines stumbled, their beauty like delicate flowers blown down by a gust of wind; the maidservants leaned drunkenly, like blossoms battered by a sudden downpour.

All the officials were quaking with fear, their bones soft and their sinews weak. They were abject, overcome with anxiety, staring blankly into space. The Hall of the White Tiger seemed to be on the verge of collapse, and the Mourning Tower was like a ruined temple about to crumble. By now the palace attendants had all fled in panic, and no one dared to approach the coffin to pay their respects.

It was thanks to the integrity of Xu Mougong, the bravery of Wei Zhongxian, the courage of Qin Jiong, the boldness of Jingde, who stepped forward to support the coffin, saying, "Your Majesty, you have nothing to worry about. Tell us, and we will spare no effort to make sure you're safe. Don't frighten the imperial family."

Wei Zhi said, "This isn't a ghost. It's Your Majesty who has come back to life. Bring out the sacred instruments!" As the coffin lid was opened, to their amazement, the emperor was indeed sitting inside, still crying out, "You've killed me! Who saved me?" Mougong and the others rushed forward to help him up, saying, "Your Majesty, don't be afraid. We are all here to protect you." The crown prince only then opened his eyes and said, "I just barely escaped the calamity in the underworld, only to meet another disaster on the water. I thought I was doomed."

The officials replied, "Your Majesty, calm your fears. What water disaster is there?"

"Do not keep it from Mr. Xǔ," I shall explain, "as a subordinate from a young age mastered the art of divination and estimated the calculation to be most clear, I dare to claim that the Emperor will not die." Just as we spoke, a voice came from within the coffin, wailing loudly, "Have you come to kill me? Have you come to kill me?" and the officials, with their hearts in disarray and their souls terrified, paled as autumn yellow locust trees and their waists slumped as tender willow twigs in spring.

The heir apparent's feet were unsteady, it was difficult for him to support his funeral candelabrum, let alone follow the proper funeral rites; the Chancellor's soul had taken flight, how could he wear a ceremonial hat and follow the ritual? The attendants stumbled, and the naiad maidens slumped at an angle; the attendants stumbled, just as a gust of wind blew down a defeated paulownia; the naiad maidens slumped at an angle, looking like a sudden downpour had knocked over a delicate peony. The officials cowered in fear, their bones soft and their sinews limp. They trembled and quaked, lost in daze.

The white Tiger Hall seemed to be a broken bridge, the funeral platform like a collapsed temple. At this time, the palace ladies scurried off in an instant; who dared to approach the spirit tablet to support the coffin. Luckily, there was the honest Xu Mǎogōng, the fervent Weǐ Zhēngxiàng, the bold Qin Qióngróng, and the resolute Jìngdé, who rushed forward to support the coffin, saying, "Your Majesty has no cause to worry, tell us what troubles you, do not play a ghostly trick, frightening the royal family."

Weǐ Zhēng said, "This is not playing a ghostly trick, but rather the Emperor's return to life. Quickly fetch the tools!" We opened the coffin lid and indeed found Emperor Taizong sitting inside, still wailing, "You killed me! Who rescued me?" Mǎogōng et al rushed forward to lift him up and said, "Your Majesty, do not be afraid, we officials are here to guard you."
