One day, the Patriarch and his many disciples were frolicking in the courtyard of Three Star Cave, enjoying the evening scene. The Patriarch said, "Monkey, has the matter been accomplished?" Monkey replied, "Thanks to my venerable Father's blessings, I have achieved a complete success and can now lift up the Nine Heavens." The Patriarch said, "Let me try lifting up myself and see." Monkey displayed his abilities, and with a sudden jerk, jumped up six or seven paces, leapt into the air, walked on a cloud for a period of time, and then fell back down within three miles. He landed in front of the Patriarch and crossed his hands, saying, "Father, this is the way of flying and soaring." The Patriarch smiled and said, "This does not count as flying and soaring, it only counts as climbing clouds. In ancient times, it was said, 'During the morning the gods would visit the North Sea, and in the evening they would visit the Cangwu.' You take half a day to go no farther than three miles, so even climbing clouds is not something you can do."

Monkey asked, "How does the saying go, 'During the morning the gods would visit the North Sea, and in the evening they would visit the Cangwu'?" The Patriarch replied, "As for those who can fly through the clouds, they would set out from the North Sea at daybreak, tour the East Sea, the West Sea, and the South Sea, and then turn around to visit the Cangwu. Cangwu is actually an old way of speaking for the Lingling area of the North Sea. Only after touring all four seas, can one be said to have truly flown through the clouds."

Monkey exclaimed, "That is indeed difficult! That is indeed difficult!" The Patriarch said, "The world has no impossible tasks, only those who lack the heart to do it." Hearing these words, Monkey bowed his head and said, "Father, 'One must thoroughly cultivate one's character,' so let us put aside compassion, and I shall accept this flying technique from you. I will never forget your kindness."

The Patriarch said, "All the immortals who fly through clouds fall down, but you only manage to jump up with a single jerk. I've never seen anyone like you before. I shall just impart this technique to you, the 'corkscrew cloud somersault'." Monkey kowtowed and begged, and the Patriarch gave him a secret oral transmission, saying, "This cloud, grasp the secret, recite the sacred name, clench your fists tightly, and shake your body. Then, somersaulting in mid-air, you can travel tens of thousands of miles!" The crowd heard this and burst out laughing, "Monkey's talents are amazing! If you master this technique, you can send official documents, deliver orders, and look for food anywhere!" The Patriarch and disciples all returned to their respective caves, each returning in a daze.

That night, Monkey began to practice and exercise his technique, mastering the corkscrew cloud somersault. From then on, he was unencumbered and carefree, and had a life of infinite joy.

One day, the Patriarch and his disciples were playing at the West Pagoda. The Patriarch said, "Monkey, have you mastered your accomplishments?" The Monkey said, "Thanks to the benevolence of my Master, I have made great progress and am already capable of floating and rising into the air." The Patriarch said, "Try lifting me up and see." The Monkey put his powers to work, threw himself up, and then tumbled backward, jumping away six or seven yards, before landing on a cloud and remaining there for a while. He then returned in the space of a meal, but could only make it back a few miles and fell in front of the Patriarch. He spread his arms and said, "Master, this is what it means to float and rise into the air." The Patriarch smiled and said, "This isn't floating and rising into the air; it's just crawling onto a cloud. As the saying goes, 'In the morning he strolls by the North Sea, and in the evening, he goes to the dark woods.' You've only managed to climb up a bit, and it's far from being able to float and rise into the air." The Monkey asked, "What's meant by 'morning stroll by the North Sea'?" The Patriarch said, "Those who can float and rise into the air start from the North Sea at dawn, visit the East Sea, West Sea, and South Sea, and then return to the dark woods. Dark woods, however, is actually a phrase from the language of Zeroingland in the North Sea. Only when you've visited all the seas and regions outside of the four seas in one day can you be said to have floated and risen into the air." The Monkey said, "That's a difficult task indeed, a difficult task indeed!" The Patriarch said, "There are no difficult tasks in the world, only people with no determination." The Monkey heard these words, bowed down, and kowtowed, and said, "Master, 'as a person, one must be thorough;' I'll give up my great compassion and have you impart to me this art of floating and rising into the air once and for all, so I won't forget your kindness." The Patriarch said, "All the immortals who can float and rise into the air do so by jumping and rebounding. But you, when you first went, only managed to jump up by taking a few tugs. I will only pass on to you the '.Cloud-Whirlwind' method based on your own strength." The Monkey bowed and begged for it, so the Patriarch imparted a password to him. He said, "This cloud, grasp the password; recite the true words, make a tight fist, shake your body, and jump up – in one Cloud-Whirlwind, you'll be able to cover ten million eight thousand li of distance!" When the crowd heard this, they all burst out laughing and said, "Monkey is so clever! If he learns this method, he can sell his labor, deliver documents, or carry messages; he'll never go hungry anywhere!" The Master and his disciples returned to their mountain dwellings. On this very night, the Monkey used his divine energy to practice and mastered the Cloud-Whirlwind method. From then on, he was free and unrestrained, and lived a long and carefree life in this beautiful world.

One day, the Patriarch and the multitude of his disciples were playing in the evening at the Three Star Grotto. The Patriarch said, "Monkey, have you accomplished your tasks?" Monkey replied, "Thanks to my venerable Father's blessings, I have completed my endeavors and can now ascend to heaven with a single leap." The Patriarch said, "You try flying and leaping for me to see." Monkey practiced his arts, and suddenly leaping into the air, he tugged his queue and jumped six or seven paces, leaving the ground for the space of a meal, and floated away with the clouds before returning to within three miles of his former position, where he landed before the Patriarch, clasped his hands and said, "Father, this is what flying and leaping among the clouds is like." The Patriarch smiled and said, "This is not flying and leaping, but only climbing clouds. Anciently it was said, 'The immortals sail the northern sea in the morning and roam in the woods of the south in the evening.' You can't reach even three miles in half a day; that's just climbing clouds, not really flying and leaping." Monkey said, "What is 'sailing the northern sea in the morning and roaming in the south in the evening'?" The Patriarch replied, "As for those who fly through the clouds, they start from the northern sea at daybreak, travel through the eastern sea, the western sea, and the southern sea, then turn back to the woods of the south. The phrase 'sailing the northern sea in the morning and roaming in the south in the evening' actually refers to the southern woods, and it's a phrase used in the dialect of the north of the Li kingdom. It means having toured all the seas outside of the Four Seas in one day, and this is what flying and leaping is all about." Monkey said, "This is hard indeed; it's indeed hard!" The Patriarch said, "In the world, there's no task that can't be accomplished; only fear lies in a lack of heart." Monkey heard these words, bowed his head in reverence and worship, and asked, "Father, 'one must be all-inclusive as a person,' so I'll use my great compassion to beg of you, pass on the method of flying and leaping to me, and I will not forget your kindness." The Patriarch said, "All the immortals fly and leap by striking their feet on the ground. You just sprang up with a tug of your clothes when I saw you. I will now teach you the 'somersault cloud' with the momentum you've got." Monkey bowed and implored, the Patriarch then transmitted a secret incantation to him, saying, "Grasp this cloud, recite the true words, contract your fist tightly, and give your body a shake. Then jump up, and with one somersault, you'll traverse a distance of ten million, eight thousand li!" When the multitude heard this, they all burst out laughing and said, "Monkey's gotten enlightened! If he can master this art, he can use it to deliver messages, send reports, and make deliveries, and everywhere he'll find food to eat!" The Patriarch and his disciples then returned to their caves, one by one. On that very night, Monkey practiced his spiritual powers and cultivated the technique of the somersault cloud. From then on, he was unencumbered and carefree, passing his days in idyllic leisure, enjoying the beauty of a long life.

One day, the Patriarch and the numerous disciples were leisurely strolling in front of the Trifling Star Cave at dusk. The Patriarch said, "Monkey, has your business been accomplished?" Monkey said, "Thanks to my master's great mercy, your disciple's accomplishments are complete, and I am now able to levitate and fly up to the clouds." The Patriarch said, "Let me see you try flying up." Monkey performed a feat, suddenly raised his body, and sprang a few feet into the air, leaving the ground for about the time it takes to eat a meal, before dropping back down within a few miles, landing in front of the Patriarch. He clasped his hands and said, "Master, that's how one levitates and flies." The Patriarch laughed and said, "This doesn't count as levitating; it's just climbing the clouds. It is said: 'The gods roam the North Sea in the morning and go to the Cangwu region in the evening.' A feat like yours, barely reaching three miles up, wouldn't even count as climbing clouds!" Monkey said, "How do you interpret 'roaming the North Sea in the morning and going to the Cangwu region in the evening'?" One day, the Patriarch and his disciples were playing at dusk in front of the Three Stars Cave. The Patriarch said, "Monkey, have you completed your tasks?" Monkey said, "Thanks to the benevolence of the Patriarch, the disciple has fulfilled his duties and can now effortlessly ascend to heaven." The Patriarch said, "Try to fly up and show me." Monkey displayed his skill, stood up straight, pulled a handful of hair, jumped a distance of five or six zhangs, stepped on a cloud, and went to look for a meal's worth of time, but only returned to a spot within three li. Monkey said, "This is difficult; this is indeed difficult!" The Patriarch said, "There is nothing difficult in the world, only that one has to have a heart to accomplish it." The first ring at the lawyer's door was, as usual, futile. "Leni could be more nimble," K thought. Finally, two eyes appeared in the peephole of the lawyer's door, but they were not Leni's eyes. Someone opened the door, pushed against it briefly, called back into the apartment, "He's here!" and only then opened it fully. K had pushed against the door because he already heard the key being hastily turned in the lock of the other door behind him. As the door finally opened in front of him, he rushed into the waiting room and saw Leni, who the warning shout from the door-opener was meant for, running away in a white apron through the hallway that ran between the rooms. He looked after her for a moment and then turned to the door-opener. It was a small, thin man with a full beard, holding a candle in his hand. "Are you employed here?" K asked. "No," the man replied, "I'm a stranger here, the lawyer is my representative, I'm here regarding a legal matter." "Without a coat?" K asked, nodding towards the man's inadequate attire. "Ah, forgive me," the man said and lit himself up with the candle, as if he had never noticed his condition before. "Leni is your mistress?" K asked shortly, with a slight smile. He had spread his legs slightly, had his hands, in which he held his hat, behind him wrapped. Just by owning a sturdy overcoat, he felt very superior to the thin man. "Good God," the man said, raising one hand in frightened defense in front of his face, "no, no, what do you think?" "You seem plausible," K said with a smile, "still – come." He waved to him with his hat and let him go ahead of him. "What's your name, then?" K asked as they walked. "Block, Kaufmann Block," the little man replied, turning to K when introducing himself, but K did not let him stop. "Is that your real name?" K asked. "Of course it is," was the answer, "why would you doubt it?" "I thought you might have reason to conceal your name," K said. He felt as free as one usually does when speaking with lower people in a foreign land, keeping everything that concerned him to himself, talking neutrally about the other person's interests, thereby raising himself above them, but also being able to let them go as he pleased.

When K stopped in front of the door to the lawyer's office, he opened it and called back to Kaufmann, who had gone along obediently: "Not so quickly! Light here!" K thought Leni might be hiding in here, and he had Kaufmann search all the nooks and crannies, but the room was empty. In front of the judge's picture, K grabbed Kaufmann by the suspenders and held him back. "Do you know him?" K asked, pointing upwards with his finger. Kaufmann raised the candle, blinked up, and said, "It's a judge." "A high-ranking judge?" K asked and stood to the side of Kaufmann to observe the impression the picture made on him. Kaufmann looked up in admiration. "It's a high-ranking judge," he said. "You don't have much insight," K said. "He's the lowest of the lower investigating judges." I must confess: reality snared me on its hook these past six months and sometimes captivated me so much that I forgot about my verdict, or rather did not want to think about it and even took steps to counteract it. By the way, let's talk about the situation at the time. When I fell ill eight months ago, I severed all ties and abandoned my former comrades. As I was a rather taciturn person to begin with, they easily forgot about me, of course they would have done so without this circumstance. The atmosphere at home, that is, within the family, was also isolated. Five months ago I locked myself indoors and completely separated myself from the rest of the family's quarters. They all treated me with deference, and no one dared to enter my room except for the set hour when they would come in to tidy it and bring me my meals. My mother trembled before my commands and even dared not scold me in front of me, when I sometimes decided to let her in. She constantly scolded the children to keep them quiet and not disturb me; I often complained about their crying, and they probably love me now! 'Faithful Kolya', whom I called him, I also, I think, tormented quite a bit. Lately, it was he who tormented me: this was all natural, people and things are created to torment each other. But I noticed that he tolerated my irritability as if he had made up his mind to be kind to a sick person. Naturally, this annoyed me, but I suppose he wanted to imitate the prince in his Christian humility, which was already somewhat comical. He's a young, hot-headed boy and, of course, imitates everything, but sometimes it seemed to me that it was time for him to live his own life. I love him very much. I also tormented Suriakov, who lived above us and ran around from dawn till night on someone's errands; I constantly showed him that he was to blame for his poverty, and eventually he got scared and stopped coming to see me. This is a very humble man, the humblest creature (Note: They say that humility is a powerful force; I'll have to get some insight into this from the prince, it's his own expression); but when, in the month of March, I went up to him to look at how they 'frosted' the child, as he said, and unintentionally chuckled at the corpse of his infant, because I started explaining to Suriakov again that he was 'to blame', his lips suddenly quivered, and with one hand he grabbed me by the shoulder, with the other he pointed to the door and whispered to me, almost whispering, 'Leave!' I left, and it pleased me then, even in that very moment, as he was ushering me out; but his words had a strange, contemptuous pity on me which I would not have felt otherwise, when I remembered them later. Even in a moment of such offense (I do feel, after all, that I offended him, though I didn't intend to), even in that moment this man was unable to get angry! His lips merely quivered not with anger, I swear to it: he seized my hand and delivered his magnificent 'leave!' without a trace of irritation. He showed a lot of dignity, even too much, even too much for his face (so there was a lot of comedy in this, so to speak, and that's the truth), but there was no anger. Maybe he simply started to despise me. From that time on, two or three times when I met him on the stairs, he started removing his hat in front of me, which he never did before, but he no longer stood there like before, but quickly passed by, confused, just like before. If he did despise me, then he did so in his own peculiar way: he 'humbly despised'. Maybe he took off his hat just out of fear, like the son of my creditor, because he's always in debt to my mother and can never get out of it. And even this is the most likely explanation... I was about to talk to him, and I'm certain that in ten minutes he would have begged my pardon; but I decided that it was better not to bother him.

Just as they were drinking and celebrating, someone came to report: "Great King, there are two horned ghost kings outside who want to see the Great King." The Monkey King said, "Let them in." The ghost king rushed in, prostrating himself on the ground. The Monkey King asked him, "What business do you have with me?" The ghost king replied, "I have long heard that the Great King is recruiting the wise and the capable, and I have never had the chance to see him. Today I see the Great King granting the heavenly script, and I have achieved success and renown. I especially came to present this vermilion cloak to the Great King, to congratulate him on his good fortune. I, a lowly one, dare not be rejected; I would be grateful if you would accept me, and I would be willing to serve you like a dog or a horse."

The Monkey King was overjoyed and put on the vermilion cloak. All the others were delighted and lined up in order to pay their respects to the Monkey King. The Monkey King then appointed the ghost king as the commander-in-chief of the vanguard. The ghost king finished his thanks and said, "Great King, you have been in heaven for a long time, what position have you been given?" The Monkey King said, "The Jade Emperor favors the wise and has appointed me to be something called a 'Bamboo Warden'!" The ghost king heard this and then said, "Great King, you have such magical powers, why would you be responsible for taking care of horses? Why not just be a 'Pacifier of Heaven' and see no harm in it?" The Monkey King heard this and was extremely pleased, saying "Good! Good! Good!" and ordered his four mighty generals: "Quickly, set up a banner with the four characters 'Pacifier of Heaven' on it, and raise it up high. From now on, only refer to me as the Pacifier of Heaven, and do not call me Great King again. Also, inform all the other goblin kings in the various caves of this change."

As they were drinking and feasting together, someone came to report, "The Great King, there are two horned kings of ghosts at the door, asking to see the Great King." The Monkey King said, "Let them come in." The horned king came in, hurriedly removing his coat and bowing to the ground. The Monkey King asked him, "What brings you here to see me?" The horned king replied, "I have long heard that the Great King is recruiting talent and haven't had the chance to meet him. Today, having been granted the Heavenly Classic, I've returned in triumph and come to offer a piece of cinnabar-colored robes as a gift, to celebrate with the Great King. The Monkey King was overjoyed and repeatedly exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent! Excellent!" Miss offered incense at the Buddhist altar, and had the handmaiden bring a dish of offerings. When they arrived at the main hall, Miss then picked up some incense and worshiped. She instructed Elder Bhadanta to dismiss the other monks, and upon their departure, she quietly approached and knelt down beside him. Miss asked him to remove his sandals and socks, and upon looking at his left foot, she indeed found that he was missing a small toe. At that moment, the two of them clasped each other and wept, expressing gratitude for Elder Bhadanta's nurturing. Elder Bhadanta said, "Since you've seen your mother, the thief may learn of it, so you should hurry back and avoid any calamity." Miss replied, "My child, I'll give you a rosary. Travel north-west of the city of Hongzhou, approximately fifteen hundred li away. There's a Flower Shop there, and your paternal grandmother Zhang, who bore your father, is living there. I'll write a letter for you to take, and deliver it to your grandfather-in-law, the Prime Minister of You, who resides inside the imperial city, at the eastern side of the Golden Hall. You should hand the letter to your grandfather-in-law and have him present the matter to the King, commanding his generals to assemble the troops and capture the thief, thereby avenging your father. Only then can they rescue your mother. I dare not tarry any longer, lest the thief becomes suspicious of my delayed return." And with that, she stepped out of the temple and boarded a boat.

The Queen Mother heard the report and went to see the Jade Emperor to give an account of the matter. Her report had not finished when the group of people who made the wine arrived, accompanied by the officials of the heavens, to submit a report: "Some unknown person caused a disturbance at the 'Peach Festival' and drank the ambrosial elixir, as well as stole the eight treasures and the hundred flavors, all of which were also stolen." 

Just then, four heavenly sages arrived to submit a report: "The Great Lord of the Tao has arrived." The Jade Emperor went out to greet him together with the Queen Mother. When the Great Lord had completed his formal greeting, he said: "In the Lord of the Tao's palace, we had prepared some 'Nine-Turn Golden Elixir' in anticipation of a 'Great Elixir Meeting' for the Jade Emperor, but it was unexpectedly stolen by thieves. I especially report this to Your Majesty." The Jade Emperor heard the report and felt a sense of great alarm. Shortly afterwards, the official of the Heavenly Archives knelt down and said: "The Prime Saint of the Ten-Thousand Dynasties failed to keep his appointment. He has been absent since yesterday's outing and has not returned, and no one knows where he has gone." The Jade Emperor grew even more worried. Then that Big Red-Footed Immortal came forward, bending his knees to report: "I was summoned by the Queen Mother to attend the gathering yesterday. As I was on my way, I met the Prime Saint of the Ten-Thousand Dynasties, who told me that there was a decree from the Emperor that I should go with him and others to the Assembly Hall to perform the ceremony before attending the gathering. I followed his words and returned to the Assembly Hall outside, but I did not see the Imperial Dragon Carriage or the Imperial Chariot of the Phoenix. I rushed back here in anticipation of waiting." The Jade Emperor grew even more greatly startled and exclaimed: "This scoundrel pretended to have received an imperial decree to deceive the esteemed prime minister. Quickly summon the officials of the heavens to investigate the whereabouts of this villain!"

The Jade Mother heard the news and went to see the Jade Emperor to present her previous account. She had not yet finished speaking when the group of people who made the wine arrived, along with the heavenly officials, to submit a report: "We don't know who, but someone has caused a disturbance at the 'Pomegranate Assembly', and stolen the jade liquid and essence. And the eight treasures and hundred flavors, all have also been stolen." Then four Great Heavenly Masters came to submit a report: "The Supreme Way Ancestor has arrived." The Jade Emperor, together with the Jade Mother, went out to greet him. When the Old Master had completed his court etiquette, he said, "In the Old Master's palace, we have refined some 'Nine-Turn Golden Elixir' to prepare for the Emperor's 'Elixir Assembly'. It was not expected that thieves would steal it. I inform Your Majesty." The Jade Emperor, upon hearing the report, felt a sense of trepidation. A little later, there was a heavenly official from the Office of the Supreme Ascension who kowtowed and said, "Monkey King did not take his duties seriously, and since yesterday has been out playing, and up to now, we still do not know his whereabouts." The Jade Emperor became increasingly suspicious and anxious. Only then did the Fire-Clad Great Immortal come forward to submit a report, bowing on his forehead: "Your subjects were summoned by the Jade Mother's edict yesterday to attend the assembly. Just by chance, I met the Monkey King, who told me that the Jade Emperor had a decree, ordering him to invite us to perform a ritual at the Pavilion of Clarity before going to the assembly. What struck me as strange was that he came so late, but I'm not at all surprised by that. On the contrary, I hadn't expressed my thought clearly to him in the morning, but I know he understood it; this thought was of such a nature that I had thought we might discuss it again, at least if not at all early, then even quite late. I thought he had come for just that. We parted in the morning rather resentfully, and I even recall that he looked at me twice with a mocking glance. It was this very mockery that I see now in his look, and it's what annoyed me. That this was indeed Rogozhin, not a hallucination, not a fantasy, I didn't doubt in the least even for a moment. Not even a thought occurred to me.

Time flew swiftly. One day, Madam Liu's husband was away on official business, and Madam Liu was left in the office feeling homesick for her mother-in-law and husband. While sitting in the floral pavilion, she sighed and suddenly felt weary and a sharp pain in her abdomen, and fainted, unaware that she had given birth to a son. Someone nearby said to her: "Full Moon, listen to my warning. I am the Lord of the Southern Pole, acting on the command of Bodhisattva Guanyin, and I specially brought this child for you. In the future, his name will be famous, not comparable to ordinary people. If Liu the bandit returns, he will certainly harm this child. You must guard it carefully." When he finished speaking, he disappeared. Madam Liu came to, remembering each word, and held the child tightly. There was no way to cope. Just then Liu the bandit returned, saw the child, and was about to drown him. Madam Liu said, "It's late today, let's wait until tomorrow to throw him in the river." Fortunately, Liu the bandit had urgent official business that took him away, and Madam Liu thought to herself: "If the bandit returns, my life will be forfeit! I'd better throw him into the river early on and let fate decide. Perhaps Heaven will have mercy and someone will rescue him, and we will be reunited one day." However, she feared that no one would recognize him, so she bit her finger, wrote a blood-written note, listing her husband's and her family name, and the reason, in detail. She also bit off the small finger on the child's left foot to use as a token. Taking a piece of her inner garment, she wrapped the child, then carried him out of the office. Lucky enough, the official residence was not far from the river. When she reached the riverbank, she cried a sorrowful cry. Just as she was about to throw the child into the river, a piece of wood drifted out from the riverbank, and Madam Liu bowed to the heavens, placed the child on it, tied him down with a cord, and attached the blood-written note to his chest. She pushed the board into the river, and listened to the child's fate. Madam Liu, her tears unshed, returned to the office without a word.

Time passed quickly. One day, Master Liu went out on official business, and the young mistress was left alone at the yamen, longing for her mother and husband. Sitting in the pavilion, she sighed to herself, and suddenly felt weary in her body and a pain in her abdomen. She felt dazed and faint, and didn't even notice when she gave birth to a child. Suddenly someone spoke to her in her ear and said, "Little Beauty, listen to my instructions. I am the Star King from the South Pole, sent by the Bodhisattva Guanyin to give you this child. He will have a great reputation one day, unlike ordinary people. If Liu the bandit returns, he will definitely harm this child, so be careful to protect him. Your husband has already been saved by the Dragon King, and in the future, you and your husband will be reunited, and you will clear your family's wrongs and seek revenge one day. Remember my words, wake up quickly!" Having finished speaking, he disappeared.

The young mistress woke up and remembered every word. She held the child tightly, but didn't know what to do. Just then, Master Liu returned home, and upon seeing the child, he wanted to drown him. The young mistress said, "Today the sky is already late, let's wait until tomorrow to dispose of him in the river." Fortunately, the next day Master Liu suddenly had urgent official business to attend to and left, and the young mistress thought to herself, "If this bandit returns, my life will be in danger! It's better to abandon the child in the river early on and let fate decide. Maybe the heavens will have mercy on him, and someone will rescue him, and we'll meet again one day." But she was afraid that it might be difficult for someone to recognize him, so she bit her finger and wrote a blood letter on a piece of paper, detailing her parents' names, her own explanation of the circumstances, and every detail. She also bit off a small toe on the child's left foot, intending it as proof. Taking her undershirt, she wrapped the child in it and, on her own, slipped out of the yamen. Fortunately, the official yamen was not far from the river. The young mistress reached the riverbank and wept a great deal. Just as she was about to abandon the child, a wooden board floated by on the shore. The young mistress prayed to heaven and put the child on the board, binding it down and tying the blood letter to its chest. She then pushed the board into the river and let it go, listening to the current carry the child away. The young mistress returned to the yamen, tears streaming down her face.

The next day, Chekhov set out to dine and spend the evening with the police inspector, where from three o'clock in the afternoon they seated themselves at vist and played until two in the morning. There, by the way, he became acquainted with the nobleman Nezhdrev, a man of thirty, a broken-down little fellow, who, after three-four words, started saying "you" to him. With the police inspector and the prosecutor, Nezhdrev was on "you" terms and addressed them in a friendly manner; but when they sat down to play a high-stakes game, the police inspector and the prosecutor paid the utmost attention to his bets and closely watched every card he played. The next day, Chekhov spent the evening with the chairman of the court, who received his guests in his dressing gown, somewhat disheveled, and including two or so ladies. Then he was at a reception at the vice-governor's, at a large dinner at the tax collector's, at a small dinner at the prosecutor's, which, however, was expensive; at a snack after the dinner, given by the city head, which was also expensive. In short, he had no hour left to himself, and he arrived at the inn only to sleep. The traveler was able to make himself agreeable and showed himself to be an experienced man of society. Whatever the subject of conversation was, he always knew how to support it: if the conversation was about a horse-breeding business, he spoke about horse breeding; if the conversation was about good dogs, he shared very useful remarks; if the subject was the court's findings, he showed that he was well-versed in the judges' tricks; if the conversation was about billiards, he didn't miss a shot; if the conversation was about virtue, he spoke about virtue very well, even with tears in his eyes; if the conversation was about the preparation of hot wine, he knew his stuff; about customs inspectors and officials, he judged them as if he were himself a customs inspector or an official. But what was remarkable was that he was able to present it all with a certain level of dignity, was able to behave properly. He spoke neither too loudly nor too softly, but just as one should. In short, he was a very respectable man. All the officials were satisfied with the arrival of the new person. The governor expressed that he was a well-meaning man; the prosecutor said that he was a sensible man; the military police colonel said that he was an educated man; the chairman of the court said that he was a knowledgeable and respectable man; the police inspector said that he was a respectable and affable man; the police inspector's wife said that he was the most affable and courteous man. Even Sobakevich, who rarely spoke well of anyone, having come back fairly late from town and already quite undressed and lying next to his lean wife, said to her, "I, my dear, was at the governor's reception, and I dined at the police inspector's, and I became acquainted with Collegiate Councillor Pavel Ivanovich Chekhov: a pleasant man!" To which his wife responded, "Hmm!" and kicked him with her foot.

The next day Chevylov set out for dinner and the evening with the policeman, where from three o'clock after dinner they sat down to whist and played until two o'clock in the morning. It was there, incidentally, that he met a landowner named Nosov, a little beat-up man of thirty who, after three or four words, began to say "you." Nosov was on a first-name basis with the policeman and the prosecutor, and he addressed them in a friendly way; but when they sat down to play cards, the policeman and prosecutor paid him an extremely close attention to his bribes and watched almost every card he played. The next day Chevylov spent the evening at the president of the court's house, who received his guests in a slightly made-up gown, including two ladies of some sort. Then he was at a dinner at the vice-governor's, at a large dinner at the tax farmer's, at a small dinner at the prosecutor's, which, however, cost him a lot; at a snack after the dinner, given by the city head, which cost him the price of a dinner too. In short, he did not have a spare hour, and he would visit the inn only to sleep. A stranger such as he was managed to ingratiate himself somehow, and showed himself to be a refined man of society. Whatever the conversation was about, he always knew how to keep it going: if it was about a horse-breeding farm, he talked about the horse-breeding farm; if they were talking about good dogs, he shared very useful observations; if it was about the consequences produced by the official court, he showed that he was familiar with judicial shenanigans; if it was about billiards, he never made a mistake in billiards; if it was about virtue, he argued about virtue very well, even with tears in his eyes; about the making of hot wine, and hot wine, he knew his way around; about customs inspectors and officials, and about them, he judged as if he was an official and an inspector himself. But what is noteworthy is that he managed to wrap all this in some sort of dignity, managed to keep himself well. He spoke neither loudly nor quietly, but just as it should be. In short, he was a very respectable man. All the officials were pleased with the arrival of the new person. The governor explained to them that he was a well-intentioned man; the prosecutor said that he was a shrewd man; the garrison colonel said that he was a learned man; the president of the court said that he was knowledgeable and dignified; the policeman said that he was dignified and pleasant; the policeman's wife said that he was the most pleasant and courteous man. Even Sobakevich, who rarely said something nice about someone, having come fairly late from the city and already completely undressed and lying on the bed next to his slender wife, said to her: "I, dearie, was at the governor's dinner party and dined with the policeman, and met Collegiate Councilor Pavel Ivanovich Chevylov: a clever man!" To which his wife replied: "Hmm!" and kicked him with her foot.

The next day, Chichikov set off for dinner and evening with the police inspector, where they began to play vingt-et-un at three o'clock after dinner and continued until two in the morning. It was there that he became acquainted with the nobleman Nоздрев, a man in his thirties, a half-breed who, after a few words, started addressing him as "you" and speaking to him in a friendly manner; the police inspector and prosecutor, too, treated him with great familiarity, addressing him in a friendly way; but when they started to play a major game, the police inspector and the prosecutor kept a close eye on his stakes and watched him almost every card he played. The next day, Chichikov spent the evening at the chair's place, who received his guests in a dressing gown, a bit disheveled, and two ladies were also present. Then he was at the vice-governor's soiree, at a large dinner at the tax farmer's, at a small dinner at the prosecutor's - a dinner, by the way, that was quite expensive; at a snack after dinner, given by the city mayor, which also cost as much as a dinner. In short, he had not a single free hour and only came to the hotel to sleep. The arrival was somehow well-calculated, and he displayed himself to be an experienced man of society. No matter what was being talked about, he was able to keep the conversation going; if the conversation was about a horse breeding farm, he spoke about it; if they talked about good dogs, he offered very sensible observations; if it was about the conclusions drawn by the court, he showed that he was familiar with the judges' intrigues; if the topic was about billiards, he made no mistakes in his game; if they talked about virtue, he had good arguments and even shed tears; about hot wine, he knew its secrets; about customs inspectors and officials, and about them, he had opinions, as if he himself were an official and an inspector. What's remarkable is that he was able to invest all of this with a certain degree of dignity, was able to carry himself well. He spoke neither loudly nor softly, but in just the right tone. In short, he was a very respectable man. All the officials were satisfied with his arrival. The governor declared that he was a well-intentioned man; the prosecutor said he was a sensible man; the cavalry colonel called him an educated man; the chair of the court said that he was a knowledgeable and respectable man; the police inspector called him a respectable and amiable man; the police inspector's wife said he was the most amiable and courteous man. Even Sobakevich, who rarely praised anyone, coming home rather late from the town, completely undressed and lying down beside his skinny wife, said: "I, dearie, was at the governor's soiree and dined at the police inspector's, and I met Colonel Counsellor Pavel Ivanovich Chichikov: a very interesting man!" His wife replied with a "hm" and nudged him with her foot.

The next day, Chichikov set off to dine and spend the evening at the police inspector's, where, from three o'clock after dinner to two in the morning, they played whist. It was there that he became acquainted with the landowner Nozdrev, a man of about thirty, a rather broken-down little fellow, who, after exchanging three or four words with him, began to address him as "you" and speak in a friendly manner. However, with the police inspector and prosecutor, Nozdrev was also on familiar terms, addressing them with the same "you" and on friendly terms; but when they started playing a high-stakes game, the police inspector and prosecutor watched him extremely closely, scrutinizing every card he played.

The next day, Chichikov spent the evening at the chairperson of the town council's, who received his guests in a dressing gown, slightly worn, and included in this group were two of his lady friends. Then he was at a party at the vice-governor's, at a large dinner at the tax collector's, at a small dinner at the prosecutor's, which, however, cost a great deal; at the snack given by the head of the city, which also cost a dinner. In short, he had no free moment and arrived at the inn only to sleep. The traveler seemed to have an art for making himself known and showed himself to be an experienced man of society. About any subject they might discuss, he could always keep up the conversation: if they talked about a stud farm, he spoke about a stud farm; if they discussed good dogs, he shared some very useful remarks; if they interpreted the decision made by the government council, he showed himself to be familiar with the judges' tricks; if they talked about billiards, he made no mistakes in the game; if they discussed virtues, he talked about them very well, even with tears in his eyes; about the way to make hot wine, he knew his stuff; about customs inspectors and officials, and he judged them as if he himself were an official and an inspector. But what's remarkable is that he could wrap all this in a certain degree of formality, could keep himself well mannered. He spoke neither loudly nor softly, but just as he should. In short, wherever you turned, he was a very respectable man. All the officials were pleased with the arrival of the new guest. The governor expressed his opinion that he was a well-meaning man; the prosecutor said that he was a capable man; the jandarmerie colonel said that he was an educated man; the chairperson of the town council said that he was knowledgeable and respectable; the police inspector said that he was a respectable and courteous man; the police inspector's wife said that he was the most courteous and polite man. Even Sobakevich, who rarely said anything good about anyone, having arrived quite late from town and already undressed and lying on his bed beside his slender wife, said to her: "I, darling, was at the governor's party and dined at the police inspector's, and I made the acquaintance of Collegiate Councillor Pavel Ivanovich Chichikov: what a pleasant man!" To which his wife replied: "Hm!" and kicked him with her foot.

Li Tian Wang and Nezha kowtowed in thanks and bowed in farewell, then directly headed back to the imperial palace, gathered the troops, ordered the head of the army to lead the troops, instructing the Ling Tian to be the vanguard, the fish-belly brigades to press forward, and the Rakshasa to urge the soldiers. 

In no time, they emerged outside the southern gate of Heaven and made their way directly to the Flower Fruit Mountain. They chose a flat area to set up their camp, then ordered the Ling Tian to issue a challenge. Ling Tian received the order, arrayed himself with martial pride, took up the magnificent axe, and came to the outside of the Water Curtain Cave.

Looking outside the small cave entrance, they saw many demons, wolves, tigers, leopards, and other creatures, who were brandishing their spears and swords, engaging in a wild dance. Ling Tian spoke up: "What foul beasts! Quickly hurry and inform the Grand Marshal that I, a great marshal from heaven, have come on the Imperial edict to subdue them; instruct them to come out early to surrender, lest all of you suffer grievous injuries!"

The fiends, in a panic, rushed back and forth, reporting inside the cave: "Disaster! Disaster!" The Monkey King asked: "What disaster?" The demons replied: "Outside the gate, a heavenly general appeared, claiming to hold the rank of Great Sage, saying he has received the imperial decree to subdue us; instructing us to come out early to surrender, to spare our lives." The Monkey King heard the news and said: "Fetch my armor for me!" He then put on the purple-gold crown, strapped on the golden armor, climbed into the step-cloud shoes, and grasped the heavenly golden whip staff, and led the troops out the door, arraying them in battle formation. Ling Tian looked on and said to himself: "This Monkey King is indeed a fine one!"

The Heavenly King Li Tian Wang beat his head in gratitude and retreated, coming straight to the capital and summoning the army, commanding the head officials to assemble. Only then did he see the cave mouth outside filled with numerous demons, all sorts of wolves, wolves-beasts, tigers, and leopards, all wearing tattered and worn armor, brandishing guns and waving swords, dancing and leaping wildly. Those demons rushed and scurried about, reporting inside the cave, "Trouble has arrived! Trouble has arrived!" The Monkey King asked, "What trouble is this?" This visit to Rogninin was very tiring for me. To boot, I had not felt well since morning; by evening, I was extremely weak and lay in bed, experiencing at times a severe heat and occasionally becoming dazed for a few minutes. Kolya stayed with me until eleven o'clock. I remember, however, everything he said and we talked about. But as my eyelids would occasionally close, I would picture Ivan Fyodorovich getting millions of money. He didn't know what to do with them, he was grinding his head over them, trembling with fear that they would be stolen, and in the end he seemed to have decided to bury them in the ground. I finally advised him, instead of burying that heap of gold in the ground for nothing, to pour the entire pile into a golden coffin for the "frozen" child and dig a grave for that child. Surov took my jest as though with tears of gratitude and immediately set about carrying out the plan. I, as it were, spat and went away from him. Kolya assured me when I was completely awake that I had not been sleeping at all, and that we had been talking about Surov the whole time. For a few minutes I was in the utmost despondency and distress, so Kolya went off in distress. When I got up to lock the door behind him on the key, a picture suddenly came to mind that I had seen the day before at Rogninin's, in one of the darkest rooms in his house, in front of a door. He himself showed it to me in passing; I, I think, stood before it for about five minutes.

This visit to Rogozhin exhausted me. In addition, I had felt unwell since morning; by evening I was extremely weak and lay in bed, and I sometimes felt a strong fever and was delirious for moments. Kolia stayed with me until eleven o'clock. I remember, however, everything he said and what we talked about. But when my eyelids would momentarily shut, I would imagine Ivan Fomich receiving millions of money. He had no idea what to do with them, was tearing his hair over them, trembling with fear that they would be stolen, and in the end, as if he decided to bury them in the ground. I finally advised him, instead of burying such a pile of gold in the ground for free, to pour the whole stack into a golden coffin for the "frozen" child and dig a grave for that child. Surov took my jest as if with tears of gratitude, and immediately set about carrying out the plan. I supposedly spat and left him. Kolia assured me, when I had finally come to, that I had not slept at all, and that all this time he had been talking to him about Surov. I was in a state of the most extreme longing and perturbation for moments, so that Kolia went away in concern. When I myself got up to lock the door for him on the key, suddenly a picture that I had seen the day before at Rogozhin's came to mind, in one of the most dismal halls of his house, in front of the doors. He himself showed it to me in passing; I think I stood in front of it for about five minutes.

This visit to Rogozhin was utterly exhausting for me. Kolya assured me when I was fully awake that I was not asleep at all and that the whole time we had been talking about Surov. I was at times in the most extreme longing and disquietude that Kolya left in a state of worry. When I myself got up to lock the door after him on the key, suddenly a picture came back to mind that I had seen the day before at Rogozhin's, in one of the most dismal halls of his house, right next to the door. He himself showed it to me as he passed by; I think I stood before it for about five minutes.

The stranger seemed to avoid speaking a lot, but when he did, he spoke in general terms with considerable modesty, and his conversations took on a somewhat bookish tone. He claimed to be a man of no importance, not worthy of much attention, one who had experienced a great deal in his life, suffered for the truth in his service, and had many enemies who had even plotted against his life. Now, desiring peace, he was looking to settle in a place and, having arrived in this city, he considered it a matter of duty to pay his respects to its highest officials. That was all the city knew about the new face, which soon made a great impression at the governor's ball.

Preparations for the ball took up a bit over two hours, and in the guest's case, attention was paid to his toilette to a degree rarely seen elsewhere. After a brief post-dinner nap, he ordered a wash and spent a long time scrubbing his cheeks with a brush, then grasping a towel from the shoulder of the inn servant, he wiped his face clean from all sides, starting from behind his ears and having twice blown his nose into the face of the inn servant. He then put on a vest in front of a mirror, plucked out two hairpins from his nose, and immediately afterwards, he was found in a bluish-red coat with an epaulet. Thus dressed, he was taken away in his own carriage along the endlessly broad streets, illuminated by dim lighting from here and there flickering lanterns. However, the governor's house was lit up like for a ball; a carriage with lanterns, two gendarmes at the entrance, the cries of the coachmen in the distance – all was as it should be. Entering the hall, Chekhov had to close his eyes for a moment because of the dazzling light from the candelabras, lamps, and ladies' dresses. Everything was bathed in light. The black coats flitted and fluttered here and there, as the flies on a white sparkling plate in the hot summer when the old housekeeper is chopping and dividing it into sparkling crumbs in front of an open window; children gather around, looking with curiosity at the stiff hands that lift the hammer, and the air squadrons of flies, lifted by the light air, fly confidently, like full owners, and, taking advantage of the old woman's near-sightedness and the sun that bothers her eyes, they drop their choice morsels here and there in uneven, and in dense bunches. Sated with the rich summer and already offering sugary treats at every step, they flew not to eat, but only to show themselves, to fly back and forth on a sugar lump, to rub their hind or fore legs against each other, or to scratch them with their wings, or to extend their fore legs and rub them against their heads, to turn and fly away, and to fly back again with new annoying squadrons. Chekhov didn't have time to take in his surroundings when he was grabbed by the governor, who presented him to the governor's wife. The visiting guest did not let himself go; he said a very courteous remark, suitable for a man of average age, with a medium rank, and not too high. When the established pairs of dancers crowded everyone against the wall, he, putting his hands behind his back, looked at them for two minutes very intently. Many ladies were well-dressed and up-to-date, while others dressed in whatever God had sent to the governor's city. Men here, like everywhere else, were of two kinds: some were thin, and they all flocked around the ladies; some of them were of a kind that it was hard to distinguish them from St. Petersburg men; they had just as cleverly and tastefully styled mustaches or simply handsome, very smoothly shaved oval faces, just as carelessly sat next to the ladies, just as they spoke French and amused the ladies just as in St. Petersburg. The other kind of men were fat or just like Chekhov, that is, not very fat, but not thin either. These, on the contrary, avoided the ladies and looked around to see if the governor's servant had set up the green table for whist. They had full and round faces, with warts on some of them; some were bearded, their hair was short and well-groomed, and their facial features were more rounded and robust. These were the respected officials in the city. Alas! Fatties know better how to manage their affairs in this world than the thin ones. Thin men serve mostly on special assignments or just hang around and go back and forth; their existence is too light, airy, and utterly unreliable. The fat ones never occupy peripheral positions, and all direct ones, and if they sit down somewhere, they sit firmly and securely, so that the place creaks and bends under them, and they don't get up. They don't like outer display; their coats are not tailored as neatly as those of the thin men, but they have divine providence in their waistcoats. A thin man has no soul lent to the pawnshop by the third year; a fat man, meanwhile, quietly – and there's a house bought in the name of his wife somewhere in the city, then another house in the other end, then a village near the city, and then a village with all the land. Finally, the fat man, having served God and the state, having earned universal respect, leaves service, moves, and becomes a landowner, a renowned Russian nobleman, a grain hoarder, and lives well, and lives well. And then the thin descendants of his heirs follow, following the Russian custom, and leave all the good of their father on the courier. One cannot hide that Chekhov was engaged in such thoughts when he observed the society, and the result was that he eventually joined the fat men, where he met almost all the familiar faces: the prosecutor with very thick and dark eyebrows and a left eye that winked slightly, as if to say: "Come on, brother, to another room, I'll tell you something," – a man, however, who was serious and taciturn; the postmaster, a short man, but witty and a philosopher; the president of the court, a very reasonable and affable man – all of whom greeted him as an old acquaintance, to which Chekhov nodded slightly to the side, however, not without pleasure. There, he also became acquainted with the very courteous and courteous landowner Manilov and the somewhat clumsy Sobakevich, who stepped on his foot from the first time, saying, "Please excuse me." There, they pushed a card on whist into his hand, which he accepted with the same polite bow. They sat down at the green table and didn't get up until dinner. All the conversations completely ceased, as always happens when people finally engage in something worthwhile. Although the postmaster was very talkative, but as soon as he took the cards in his hands, he immediately displayed a thoughtful expression on his face, covered his upper lip with his lower one, and kept it in this position throughout the game. Leaving the game, he hit the table with his hand, saying, "Come on, old fool!" if a dame, or "Come on, Tambov man!" if a king; the president repeated: "And I on the ears! And I on the ears!" Sometimes, upon striking the cards on the table, the following expressions would be uttered: "Ah! was or wasn't, no point, it's a two of bubs!" or simply exclaim: "Flea! Fleas! Flea-bottom!" or "Pickenaise! Pickenschuk! Pickin!" and even just: "Pick!" – names by which they baptized the suits in their society. After the game, they argued, as is their wont, quite loudly. Our guest also argued, but in a very extraordinary manner, so that everyone saw that he argued, and yet he argued in a pleasant manner. He never said, "You go," but "You went, if you pleased," "I had the honor of covering your doublet," and the like. To agree on something more with his opponents, he offered them his silver snuffbox with inlays every time, on which two forget-me-nots were placed for the scent. And after him, his thin children, in accordance with Russian custom, take over their father's inheritance, all on couriers. You can't hide that Chekhov was pondering such thoughts when he observed the society, and the result was that he eventually joined the fat people, where he met almost all his acquaintances: the prosecutor with his very dark and thick eyebrows and his left eye slightly squinting, as if saying, 'Let's go, brother, to the next room, I'll tell you something there,' – a serious and taciturn man, in any case; the postmaster, a short man, but a witty and philosophical one; the chairman of the court, a very reasonable and affable man – who all greeted him warmly, as an old acquaintance, and Chekhov returned their greetings with a somewhat awkward nod, although not without a pleasant smile. He also met there a very courteous and polite landowner Mankin and a rather clumsy-looking Sobakevich, who, from the very start, tripped over his foot and said, 'Pardon me.' They also pushed a card on him for whist, which he took with a courteous bow. They sat down at the green table and didn't get up until dinner. All conversation ceased completely, just as it always does when people finally get down to something serious. Although the postmaster was very loquacious, but when he took the cards in his hands, he immediately showed a thinking face, covered his lower lip with his upper lip and maintained this position for the entire game. When he got out of the game, he slapped the table with his hand, saying, 'Off with you, old hag!' if a dame appeared, and 'Off with you, Tambov peasant!' if a king did. The chairman exclaimed, 'And I'll take you by the ears!' 'And I'll take you by the ears!' Occasionally, during the game, expressions like 'No, she wasn't, there's nothing, she has a spade!' or simply exclamation 'Bugs! Bug-ridden! Picnick!' or 'Picenderos! Pichurushka! Pichura!' or simply 'Pichuk!' – names they called suits in their little circle – would come out during the game. At the end of the game, they argued loudly, as is their wont. Our guest also argued, but in an extremely clever way, so that everyone saw that he was arguing, and he did it pleasantly. He never said, 'You go,' but rather, 'You decided to go,' 'I had the honor of covering your double,' and so on. In order to agree with his opponents on something even more, he always handed them his silver-tipped snuffbox, which had two forget-me-nots on the bottom, placed there for the scent. The attention of the guest was especially drawn to landowners Mankin and Sobakevich, about whom he had been told earlier. He immediately inquired about them, calling aside the chairman and postmaster. Several questions he asked them showed that in the guest not only showed curiosity but also a basis for inquiry; for he first asked how many peasants each of them had and what position their estates were in, and only then inquired after their names and patronymics. In a short time, he completely won them over. Landowner Mankin, still a fairly young man with sweet-looking eyes, like sugar, and squinting them whenever he laughed, was enchanted by him. He held his hand for a long time and begged him to make a favor of visiting him in his village, to which, according to his words, there were only fifteen versts from the city gates. To this, Chekhov responded with a very polite bow of the head and a sincere handshake, saying that he was not only willing to do so with great eagerness, but even considered it his sacred duty. Sobakevich also said it succinctly, 'And come to me, too,' – tapping his foot with his shoe, which was hardly likely to find a corresponding shoe, especially in these times, when even on Russia, giants are being bred.

In the doorway of the conference room stood a young man, he was small, had not quite straight legs, and was trying to give himself dignity by means of a short, thin, reddish beard, in which he constantly ran his fingers around. K. looked at him with interest; after all, he was the first student of unknown jurisprudence to whom he had, as it were, spoken as a human being, a man who would probably also rise to higher official positions. The student, however, did not appear to be interested in K. at all; he merely wiggled a finger he pulled out of his beard for a moment, to the woman and went to the window, the woman bent down to K. and whispered: "Don't be angry with me, I beg you, don't think poorly of me, I have to go to him now, to that detestable person, look at his crooked legs. But I'll be back soon, and then I'll go with you, if you take me, I'll go wherever you want, you can do with me as you please, I'll be happy if I can leave here for as long as possible, preferably forever." She stroked K.'s hand, jumped up, and ran to the window. K. involuntarily reached out for her hand, grasping at nothing. The woman was truly tempting him, and despite all his thinking, he found no solid reason not to give in to the temptation. He easily dismissed the fleeting objection that the woman would trap him for the court; he wouldn't be caught, not in any case, since he was always free to shatter the entire court, at least as far as it concerned him. (I've told them all!). Why, I'd buy him off for a hundred roubles, I'll give him a thousand, no, three, just to back out, and he flees on the eve of the wedding, leaving me the bride. Why, Ganya, scoundrel! Why didn't he take three thousand?! There you go, that's what they're after; he was traveling all the way to get you to sign such a bond; he said: 'I'll buy you' and he'll buy you!

— No? No!! — Rogozhin cried out, on the verge of frenzy with joy, — it's not true?! They told me so... Ah! Well! Nastasya Philippovna! They say you've spoken with Ganya! With him? Oh, can that be?
