The venerable Xuanzang was fated to be here at this moment. Like a Lo Han from the Blissful Realm, he surpassed the wonderful achievements of those in the Western Land of True Enlightenment. He carried a staff that resonated with nine cymbals and a monastic hat that glimmered with profuse adornments. Truly, this was a genuine transmission of the Buddha's teachings, surpassing even the flawless wisdom of Bodhi. At the time, all scholars and officials cheered, and Emperor Taizong was overjoyed. He then vested the venerable Xuanzang in a monk's robes and handed him a sacred staff. The emperor also gifted him two teams of attendants and assigned many officials to escort him out of the palace gates and instruct him to go to the temple. He walked on the main street as if he was a proud participant in a special examination, receiving prestigious titles. Xuanzang repeatedly bowed to express his gratitude. On the street, the enthusiastic cheers and applause shook the air. Everyone in Chang'an City, whether merchants, traders, sons of nobles, scholars, or literary figures, big men and small women alike, all vied to watch and praise him, saying in unison, "This is a wonderful master! He is indeed a living embodiment of a Lo Han descending to the world, a bodhisattva come among mortals." Xuanzang proceeded to the temple, where monks came to welcome him. When they saw him wearing his monk's robes and carrying his staff, they said, "The Guardian King of the Underworld has come!" They all gathered around him in reverence and service. Xuanzang ascended to the hall, burned incense to pay homage to the Buddha, and then expressed his gratitude to the emperor before the assembly, after which they all returned to their meditation seats. Unbeknownst to him, the sun had set, casting a reddish glow to the west. It was just the moment when the capital's drum and bell were just starting to ring out, marking the end of the day's business. The staff's gongs silenced the people's footsteps. Above, the temples were ablaze with candles, while the countryside lay deserted and quiet. The monks were engrossed in meditation, immersed in scriptures, and perfecting their inner nature.

The great monk Xuanzang was favored by fate, and now the time has come for him to take this opportunity. He looks just as if he were a virtuous monk from the Pure Land, even surpassing the sacred people of the Western world. His staff hits the ground with nine rings, and his Bhikṣu hat shines brightly, filled with blessings. Truly, the reputation of a Bodhisattva is not in vain, and is even more trustworthy than the attainment of enlightenment without any falsehood. At that time, people of letters and military prowess all rushed forward to express their admiration. Emperor Taizong was delighted beyond measure, and ordered the monk to put on the monastic robes and take up the sacred staff, and to have two teams of officials escort him out of the palace gate, and have many officials see him off as he walks down the main street towards the temple. He did so just like a provincial graduate, proudly walking down the street, full of dignity. This Xuanzang monk prostrated himself in gratitude, and on that main street, there was a great commotion and a great excitement, people looked at him and congratulated him, all saying: "What a wonderful monk! He is indeed a living embodiment of the virtuous ones descending to the human world, a living Bodhisattva manifesting in the human realm." Xuanzang walked all the way to the temple, where the monks came down from their seats to welcome him. Seeing him wearing these monastic robes and carrying this staff, they all thought that the King of the underworld had come, and they all paid their respects to him and followed him to the sides. Xuanzang went up to the hall, offered incense to the Buddha, and after finishing his expressions of gratitude to the sacred being, all the monks returned to their seats. Just then, the sun began to set, casting a red glow in the west, and the imperial drum in the capital started to beat, its three beats suddenly stopping the people in their tracks, and the front and back of the imperial court was quiet. In the upper courtyard, the lanterns shone brightly, while in the remote villages, there was a cold, quiet darkness. The monks entered a state of meditation, and were deeply engrossed in their scriptures.

The Great Master Xuanzang was most fortunate to have arrived at the right moment to accept this office. He looked just like a Bodhisattva from the Saha World, surpassing the blessed ones from the Western regions. His staff clinking with nine rings, his Bhikkhu hat reflecting numerous jade designs. This was truly a faithful transmission of the Buddha's lineage, surpassing even the unwavering wisdom of Bodhi. At that moment, the literati and martial classes all cheered in front of him, the Emperor himself was overjoyed beyond words, and thus bestowed upon the Master a monk's robes and a precious staff, and two teams of attendants to escort him out of the palace gates, instructing him to walk on the street and proceed to the temple. It was as if the valedictorian of the imperial examination was being honored in a grand procession.

The Great Master Xuanzang bowed in gratitude once more, and as he walked through the street, the road was filled with commotion and excitement, like the swaying and bustling of a festival. You see, in the Longan city, the merchants, business owners, nobles and sons of nobles, poets and scholars, the young and the old, all hurried to look and praise him, saying in unison: "This is a true and living Arhat come down to the mortal world, a living Bodhisattva descended to the human realm."

The Great Master Xuanzang walked to the temple, where monks came out to welcome him. As soon as they saw him wearing this monk's robes and carrying this staff, they exclaimed that the Heaven King of the Great Treasure had come, and all of them bowed in reverence, serving him left and right. The Great Master Xuanzang ascended the hall, incense burning, offering incense to the Buddha, and then addressed the assembly, expressing his gratitude to the sacred teachings. After finishing his words, they all returned to their meditation seats. Meanwhile, the sun was setting, with mist shrouding the grass and trees, and the Imperial City's drum struck its first beat, announcing nightfall. The sound of the three beats ceased, the palace was quiet, the front and rear courtyards were still. The temple lights were shining bright, a village in the distance was dark and quiet. The monks were immersed in meditation, while the scripture lessons continued.

The monk Xuanzang was incredibly fortunate, to be born with the karma to receive this honor. He shone like a saint in the realm of Bliss, surpassing the virtues of the Bodhisattva of the West. With his staff striking the ground with a resounding nine-hued sound, his Pusapata hat reflected the depths of his wisdom. This was truly the embodiment of the son of the Buddha, not a mere rumor or hearsay. The emperor himself was overjoyed, and ordered him to don the monastic robes and take the staff of the Dharma. He also assigned two teams of attendants to escort him, and many officials accompanied him as he walked out of the palace gates, instructing him to proceed to the temple as if he were the number one scholar holding high honors. 

Xuanzang bowed to express his gratitude, and in the midst of the bustling street, people shook and rustled with excitement. Look at the city of Chang'an, merchants and merchants, princes and nobles, scholars and men of letters, young and old, all rushed to catch a glimpse and praise him, saying in unison: "What a remarkable monk! He is indeed a living Arhat, descending to the mortal realm, a living Bodhisattva, incarnate in the world." 

Xuanzang continued on to the temple, where the monks came out to welcome him, greeting him as if the Lord of the Underworld himself had arrived. They were all overjoyed, venerating him from left and right. After ascending the temple steps, Xuanzang lit incense, bowed to the Buddha, and gave thanks to the benevolence of the emperor. Having finished his devotions, he returned to his seat. Suddenly, as dusk set in, with the smoke of the setting sun shrouding the grass and the imperial drums beginning to ring out, the three strokes of the temple gong stopped people in their tracks, bringing a stillness to the palace grounds. Up in the temple, the bright lights of the lanterns shone forth, but the distant village fell silent and dark. The monks were in a state of deep meditation, and were thoroughly devoted to the study and contemplation of the scriptures.

Master Xuanzang was extremely fortunate to be present at this opportune moment. He stood tall like a living Arhat from the Land of Bliss, rivalling the saints of the Western Regions. With his staff ringing with nine golden rings and his Bhiksus hood reflecting its luxurious colours, it was truly a genuine transmission from a Buddha, surpassing the enlightenment of Bodhi without deceit. When the time came for the civil and military officials to ascend to the stage to pay tribute, Emperor Taizong was overjoyed, donning the monastic robes for Master Xuanzang, bestowing upon him a staff of treasure, and granting him two accompanying guards, and also presenting him with multiple official positions, leading him out of the palace gates and instructing him to walk the streets and enter the temple, just like a top student proudly parading in the capital. Master Xuanzang bowed repeatedly to express his gratitude as he walked on that grand street, and a tumultuous din arose, with people swaying back and forth.

You see, in Chang'an City, merchants, traders, nobles and princes, scholars and literati, and men and women of all ages, all rushed to watch and praise him, saying in unison, "What a wonderful monk! He is indeed a living Arhat descended to earth, an incarnation of the Bodhisattva!" Master Xuanzang arrived at the temple, and the monks welcomed him by bringing out the bedding. Seeing him wearing this monastic robe and holding this staff of treasure, they all said, "The King of the Underworld has arrived!" and each and every one of them paid their respects and attended to his sides. Master Xuanzang ascended the altar, burned incense, paid homage to the Buddha, and after expressing his gratitude to the enlightened ones, he returned to his seat. Not a moment later, the red sun dipped below the horizon, shrouding the grass and trees in a haze, and the imperial bell tolled for the first time. The three successive beats of the bell stopped people in their tracks, and the front and rear of the imperial palace became quiet. The temple's radiant lamps shone brightly, and the village outside was eerily quiet. The monks entered their states of meditation, engrossed in scriptural study and self-cultivation.

But speaking of Tripitaka accompanying Monkey King on their westward journey, after travelling for several days, it was the cold season in the month of Lá (approximately January), the biting wind was howling, the snow was freezing, and they were traversing a rugged road amidst steep cliffs, perilous peaks, and rugged mountains. Tripitaka was sitting on his horse, and at a distance he heard the sound of rushing water resonating in his ears. He turned around and called, "Monkey, where's the sound of water coming from?" Monkey replied, "I remember this place is called Snake Ridge Mountain Eagles' Sorrow Gorge, and it's probably the sound of water coming from the gorge." No sooner had he said this than the horse arrived at the edge of the gorge. Tripitaka pulled on the reins to look, but all he saw was: the pulse of the water flowing like frost, the crystal clear waves reflecting the red sun. The sound of the night rain resonated in the secluded valley, the rainbow of dawn shone in the vast sky. The thousand-fathom high waves rose and splashed like jade, the waters tumbling and roaring made the wind clear. The currents flowed back into the smoke and misty waters, the egrets and herons forgot their forgotten fishing spots. Just as the master and disciple were gazing at the scene, a resounding noise came from the centre of the gorge, and a dragon suddenly emerged, stirring up the waves and crashing against the mountainside. It pounced at Tripitaka. Monkey was startled and lost his luggage, and hastily took his master down from the horse and turned to run back. The dragon gave chase, but couldn't catch up. It swallowed his white horse whole, and then hid underwater. Monkey brought his master to a high precipice and sat him down, then came back to retrieve his luggage, but only found one bundle of luggage left behind. He took the bundle of luggage and carried it to his master, saying, "Master, that wicked dragon has vanished into thin air, but it has scared off my horse." Tripitaka asked, "Disciple, how are you going to find your horse?" Monkey replied, "Don't worry, don't worry. Let me go and take a look."

But it was said that the Monkey King attended the Tang Monk as he journeyed west, and after travelling for a few days, it was the cold season of December, with a biting north wind howling and frost and snow falling. The terrain was rugged, with towering cliffs, precipitous peaks, and towering mountains. The Master was riding his horse when he heard in the distance the sound of rushing water, like a cacophony in his ear. He turned around and called out, "Monkey, where is the sound of water coming from?" The Monkey said, "I remember that this place is called Snake Coil Mountain Hawk's Chorus Brook, and I suppose the sound is coming from the brook below." He had hardly finished speaking when the horse reached the edge of the brook. The Master pulled on the reins to look, and when he did, he saw that the water was flowing rapidly, like a cold current cutting through the clouds, its clear ripples shining in the sunlight like a rosy dawn. The sound was like the distant patter of rain on a secluded valley, the morning clouds shining brightly in the sky. The waves were foaming and crashing against the rocks, as if they were a thousand cataracts breaking against jade. A wave had crashed over and was lost in the depths, its voice echoing like a thunderous cry in the wind. The water flowed back, disappearing into the vast expanse of misty waves, where herons and cormorants seemed to have lost sight of each other in their quest for fish. Just then, the Master and his disciple happened to be watching, when a mighty roar echoed through the brook, and a dragon burst out from the middle of it, stirring up the waves and crashing against the mountain peaks. It was chasing the Master, who panicked and dropped his luggage. He jumped off the horse and rushed to his side, and then the two of them hastily ran away. The dragon gave chase, but it could not catch up to them. In its haste, it swallowed the Master's white horse, including the saddle and reins, whole, and then disappeared into the water, leaving behind no trace. The Monkey led the Master to a high platform, where he sat down, and then went back to collect the luggage and the abandoned horse, except for one load, which was nowhere to be found. He carried the luggage to the Master and said, "Master, that calamitous dragon has vanished, but it has scared my horse away." The Master asked, "Disciple, how do you plan to find the horse?" The Monkey said, "Don't worry, don't worry, let me go take a look."

But speaking of Tripitaka accompanying Monkey King westward, they journeyed for several days, which happened to be in the depths of winter. The biting northerly winds howled fiercely, the frost bit, and the icy winds howled through the mountains. They were traveling on a road with overhanging cliffs, rugged ledges, precipitous mountain passes, and alternating ridges. On horseback, Tripitaka looked back and heard the rushing water's tumultuous sound. He called out, "Monkey, where is the water coming from?" Monkey replied, "I remember this place was called Snake Slithering Hill and Falcon's Lament Gully. It must be the water sound coming from the gully." Not a moment later, their horse arrived at the gully's edge, and Tripitaka pulled on the reins to stop and look, but saw only: a slender thread of icy water ran through the clouds, and a gentle wave reflected the crimson glow of dawn. The sounds of nocturnal raindrops echoed through the secluded valley; and the rippling colors of the morning sunrise dazzled the limitless sky. Waves rose a thousand fathoms and foamed and splashed against jade stones; one great wave crashed and boomed in the clear wind. The flowing water gradually returned, disappearing into the countless expanse of the haze, and the cormorants and herons forgot their fishing net. The two monks looked on in awe, just as a resounding noise came from within the gully. A dragon emerged, shooting out from the water, disturbing the waves, and shoving itself out of the cliff onto the mountain slope, and chased after the venerable elder. Monkey was so frightened that he dropped his luggage and picked up his master, getting him off the horse and turned around to run away. The dragon, in its haste, couldn't catch up, but devoured Monkey's white horse, saddle, and bridle whole, and then submerged itself in the water, disappearing without a trace. Monkey took the master and sat him on a high rock, then went back to fetch the luggage, only to find that it was abandoned, leaving none of the horse behind. He brought the luggage over to his master's presence and said, "Master, the evil dragon's whereabouts are nowhere to be seen; it just scared my horse away." Tripitaka asked, "Disciple, how will we find the horse?" Monkey replied, "Don't worry, don't worry, just wait and see."

As it happened, the Tang Monk was accompanied by the Monkey King westward, and they had journeyed for a few days. It was in the depths of the cold winter month, when the north wind howled fiercely and the frost was biting, and they had to traverse a mountain path which was steep and rugged, with craggy precipices and towering peaks. The Tang Monk was riding a horse, when he suddenly heard a loud rumbling sound in the distance and called out, "Monkey, where's the water roaring?" The Monkey replied, "I remember this place was called Snake Coil Mountain where the Song of the Pines resounds. It must be the sound of water flowing through the gully." He hadn't even finished speaking when the horse approached the edge of the gully, and the Tang Monk pulled on the reins to take a closer look. To his surprise, he saw a crystal clear brook that flowed through the clouds and reflected the red hues of the rising sun; the night rain-like sound of the water resonated through the secluded valley, where a riot of colors danced amidst the morning mist, filling the boundless expanse. The torrent surged and splashed, spewing out a thousand-foot-high waves that shattered into fragments like jade; one great wave crashed and roared, sending a gust of clear wind. The waters receded, returning to the countless acres of serene ripples on the horizon, and the cormorants and egrets forgot their fishing and merged into the backdrop of the scene. Just then, the two master and disciple stood transfixed, when suddenly a loud rumbling sound came from the gully, and a dragon shot out from its depths, causing the waters to churn and the waves to churn. The dragon leaped out of the precipice and down the mountain, straight towards the Tang Monk. In a state of panic, the Monkey discarded his luggage and dismounted to lift his master onto his feet, and then he turned to flee. The dragon gave chase, but failed to catch the Monkey, who then swallowed his white horse, saddle and bridle, all at once. The dragon vanished into the water, leaving no trace. The Monkey helped his master up to a high promontory and sat him down, then came back to pick up his luggage and the remaining load, but the horse was nowhere to be seen. He carried his master to the mountain's edge and presented himself before the Tang Monk, saying, "Master, that devilish dragon has vanished into thin air, and it's only taken my horse." The Tang Monk asked, "Disciple, how are you going to find the horse?" The Monkey replied, "Don't worry, don't worry, I'll go take a look."

While Tripitaka was accompanying Monkey on his westward journey, the days passed, and it was now the dead of winter, with a harsh north wind blowing fiercely and ice forming thickly. The road they were traveling was fraught with steep cliffs, rugged rocks, and treacherous mountains that made one's heart skip a beat. As Tripitaka rode his horse, he could hear a distant rushing sound of water growing louder by the second, and he turned around to ask, "Monkey, where is the sound of the water?" Monkey replied, "I remember that this place is called the Serpent-helix Mountain, where a river runs. I think the sound of the water must be coming from the river." No sooner had he spoken than the horse reached the riverbank, and Tripitaka reined in his horse to look down into the river. And there, beneath the clear sky, he saw the icy water flowing swiftly, its clear ripples reflecting the red glow of the rising sun. The water's roar was like a distant thunderstorm in a hidden valley; its foamy waves seemed to be dancing with colors that were as radiant as the dawn. A thousand fathoms high, the waves rose and crashed, sending shards of jade flying; the waters roared like a clear gale, echoing through the valleys. As the waters returned to the misty pools, the herons and egrets were oblivious to the fishing that lay scattered nearby. Tripitaka and his disciple stood there in awe, watching as a mighty roar burst forth from the depths of the river, and a dragon emerged from the water's edge, sending waves crashing and buffeting the mountainside. The dragon shot out, sprang at the old monk, and frightened Monkey. In the confusion, Monkey lost his pack, leapt down from his horse to grab Tripitaka, and then fled in haste. The dragon chased after them but was unable to catch up. As it vanished into the depths of the river, it swallowed Monkey's white horse whole, leaving behind only the empty saddle and harness. Monkey returned to the old monk, who sat on a high elevation, and carried his pack to him, leaving behind only a pack without any horse. Monkey presented the pack to Tripitaka and said, "Master, the evil dragon has vanished without a trace, but it has frightened my horse away." Tripitaka asked, "My son, how shall we find the horse?" Monkey replied, "Don't worry, don't worry. Let me go take a look."

Nоздрев was, in some respects, a historical figure. There was never a gathering he attended where something didn't happen. Some event was bound to take place: either the gendarmes would drag him out of the hall, or his friends would be forced to push him out. If that didn't happen, then something would occur that would never happen with anyone else: he'd either get served a serving so laughable at the buffet that only laughter would ensue, or he'd slyly act with such ferocity that, in the end, he'd even be ashamed of himself. And he'd lie, for no good reason: he'd suddenly tell you that he had a horse with a blue or pink coat, and similar nonsense, so that his listeners would eventually leave, saying, "Well, brother, you seem to be firing on all cylinders now." There are people with a passion to do mischief to others, sometimes with no reason whatsoever. One, for example, might be a man of rank, with a noble appearance, with a star on his chest, who would shake your hand, talk with you about profound matters that provoke thought, and then – right there in front of you – he'd urinate on you. And he'd urinate like a simple clerk, and not like a man of rank who talks about profound matters, so you'd just stand there in amazement, shrugging your shoulders, and do nothing more. He had the same peculiarity. The closer someone drew near to him, the more he'd deceive them: spinning out tales that were more absurd than could be invented, spoiling a wedding, disrupting a business deal, and not considering himself your enemy; on the contrary, if a chance encounter brought him together with you again, he'd behave in a friendly manner and even say, "You're such a scoundrel, you'll never be able to visit me." Nоздрев was a many-sided person in many respects, that is, a person of many talents. In the same moment, he'd offer you to go anywhere you liked, or get involved in any business you wanted, or exchange anything for anything. A gun, a dog, a horse – everything was subject to exchange, but not in order to win: this simply happened due to some impish quick-wittedness and sharp character. If he happened upon a simpleton at the fair and outsmarted him, he'd buy up a heap of all sorts of things that he'd previously seen in the shops: horseshoes, matchboxes, blankets for a nurse, a foal, raisins, a silver washbasin, Dutch cloth, wholemeal flour, tobacco, pistols, fish, pictures, a whetstone, pots, boots, china – as long as the money lasted. However, it rarely happened that this was brought home; almost the same day it would be sold to another lucky gambler, sometimes even with his own pipe, tobac case, and cigarette holder added, and another time with the entire set, including the perambulator and a coachman, so the owner himself would go out in a short jacket or a pair of epaulets to find a friend to use their carriage. This was Nоздрев! Maybe they'll call him a beaten character, say that there's no longer a Nоздрев. Alas, those who say so will be unfair. Nоздрев will be with us for a long time yet; he may be walking around in another caftan, but people are carelessly and unperceptive, and a man in another caftan seems to them like another man.

He'd tell outright lies for no reason at all: he'd suddenly tell you that he'd had a horse with blue or pink fleece, and other such nonsense, until the listeners would eventually get up and say, "Well, brother, it seems to you've started spouting nonsense." Nоздрев had the same sort of strange impulse. The closer you became with him, the more he would urinate on you: he'd spread ridiculous lies, more absurd than which it's hard to imagine, cause a row at a wedding, a trade deal, and didn't even consider himself your enemy; on the contrary, if he happened to run into you again, he'd be friendly once more, even saying, "You're such a scoundrel, you'll never avoid me." If he managed to catch some fool on a fairground and cheat him, he'd buy up a heap of everything he'd previously seen in shops: halters, candles for snuffing, nannies' shawls, a foal, raisins, a silver washbasin, Dutch calico, coarse flour, tobacco, pistols, salmon, paintings, whetstones, bowls, boots, chinaware – as long as the money would last. However, it rarely happened that this would be brought home; almost the very same day, it would be taken by another, luckier gambler, and sometimes even his own snuffbox with a plug and a mouthpiece would be added, and in another case, the whole four-wheeler with a nurse and a coachman, so the owner himself would go out in a short coat or an alpaca coat looking for some acquaintance to use their carriage. That's what Nоздрев was like! Perhaps he'll be called a character overused to exhaustion, and they'll say that now there's no Nоздрев left. Alas, those who will say that will be speaking unjustly. There are people who have a propensity to soil their neighbor, often entirely without any reason. Someone, for instance, a man of rank, with a noble bearing and a star on his chest, would shake your hand, talk to you about serious matters that make one think, and then, look, right there in front of you, he'd go and soil you. He'd soil you just like an ordinary collegiate registrar, and not like a man of rank talking about matters that make one think, so you'd only stand there and marvel, shrug your shoulders, and do nothing else. He had the same peculiarity. The closer he became with someone, the sooner he'd get on their nerves: spinning yarns, spinning a tale so absurd, it's hard to come up with a sillier one, ruining a wedding, a business deal – and he wouldn't consider himself your enemy. On the contrary, if circumstances brought him to meet you again, he'd be friendly once more and even say: "Why, you scoundrel, you'd never do anything to me." Nozdrhev was a versatile man in many respects – that is, a man of all talents. In an instant, he'd offer you to go anywhere you liked, to join any venture you pleased, to exchange everything you have for everything you like. A gun, a dog, a horse – all were up for grabs, not with the goal of winning, but simply from his irrepressible quickness and liveliness of character. If he was lucky enough to catch a simpleton at the fair and outwit him, he'd go and buy a whole bunch of things that he'd only seen in shops: halters, snuff boxes, baby blankets, a foal, raisins, a silver basin, Dutch cloth, coarse flour, tobacco, pistols, fish, paintings, a sharpening kit, jugs, boots, ceramics – as long as the money held out. However, it rarely happened that this made it home; almost immediately it would be resold to another, luckier player. Sometimes even his own pipe, handkerchief, and mouthpiece would be added, and in another case, even the whole carriage with the footman, so that the owner himself would go out in a short jacket or a leather tunic to find some friend whose carriage he could use. That's what Nozdrhev was like. Maybe he'll be called a character that's been beaten about the head, people will start saying that now there's no longer a Nozdrhev. Alas, those who will say this will be unjust. Nozdrhev will not be going out of the world soon. He's still here among us, and perhaps just walks around in another caftan; but people are gullible and lacking in perception, and a man in a different caftan appears to them as another man.

Nоздрев was a somewhat historical figure in every sense of the word. At no gathering where he was present did anything untoward fail to occur: either the gendarmes would suddenly come to drag him out by the arm, or his very acquaintances would have to push him out. If that didn't happen, something else was bound to happen that wouldn't happen to anyone else: he'd get talked to so sharply in the buffet that he'd have to laugh, or, conversely, behave with utmost scoundrelry to the point where even he'd feel ashamed of himself. And he'd lie completely without any provocation: he'd suddenly tell you that he had a horse of a certain blue or pink coat and the like nonsense, so that the listeners would finally rise up and say: "Well, brother, it seems you've started shooting blanks." There are people with a proclivity to defecate on someone's doorstep, even without any cause. One, for instance, a man of standing, with a noble appearance, a star on his chest, would shake your hand, chat with you about weighty matters that inspire thought, and then – just there, right before your very eyes – defecate on you. And defecate just like a plain collegiate registrar, not like a man with a star on his chest, talking about matters that inspire thought, so that you'd stand there just gaping and shrugging, and that's all.

Nоздрев had this very same peculiarity. The closer someone befriended him, the more he'd indulge in fabrications, even more preposterous than those he'd conjure up. He'd upset a wedding, a business deal, and wouldn't even think of himself as your enemy; quite the opposite – if he encountered you again, he'd treat you as a friend and even say: "You're such a scoundrel, you'll never come to visit me." Nоздрев was a many-faceted man in many respects, that is, a man for all occasions. In the same instant he'd invite you to go anywhere you pleased, even to the end of the world, to join any venture you chose, to swap everything you had for anything you wanted. A rifle, a dog, a horse – everything was a subject of barter, but not in order to win; it just happened due to some intractable lightheartedness and mischievousness of his character.

If he got lucky and caught a fool on the fair and outmaneuvered him, he'd go on a spree, buying up whatever he came across in the shops: horse halters, snuff-boxes, nurse's shawls, foals, dried grapes, a silver washbasin, Dutch cloth, coarsely ground flour, tobacco, pistols, pickled herring, paintings, sharpening tools, pots, boots, and ceramicware – as long as he had money. However, it rarely happened that it all got brought home; nearly the very same day it would all be off-loaded on some luckier gambler, sometimes even with his own pipe and pouch added, and in another case, the whole four-horse team with a nursemaid's chair and a coachman, so that the owner himself would set out in a short coat or a pelisse to find some acquaintance to use their carriage. That's Nоздрев for you! Maybe someone would call him a character with a battered image, and say that there's no longer a Nоздрев like that today. Oh, the injustice would be theirs who'd say so. Nоздрев is not done with the world yet; he's still among us, and maybe he just happens to be wearing a different caftan; but people are gullible and lack insight, and a person in a different caftan seems like a different person to them.

Nоздрев was, in some respects, a historical figure. No gathering, where he was present, passed without incident. Some kind of trouble was bound to happen: either he would be dragged out by the Cossacks, or his own friends would have to push him out. But if this didn't happen, something else would, something that wouldn't happen to anyone else: either he would get into a scrape in the buffet to the point of being laughed at, or he would cause such a commotion that he himself would finally feel embarrassed. And he would lie out of the blue without any reason: he would suddenly tell you that he had a horse with a blue or pink coat and other such nonsense, and those listening would finally leave, saying, "Well, brother, it seems you've started talking nonsense again." Nоздрев had this same strange passion. The closer he got to someone, the more he would scold them: he'd spin a yarn, a yarn even more foolish than he could ever have imagined, he'd ruin a wedding, a business deal, and not consider himself an enemy at all. On the contrary, if circumstances led him to meet you again, he'd behave just as friendly and even say, "After all, you're such a scoundrel, you'll never cheat me again." Nоздрев was, in many respects, a man of many talents, a man of many skills. At the same time, he'd offer you to go anywhere you pleased, to take on any business venture, to exchange everything you have for anything you want. A gun, a dog, a horse – all were up for exchange, but not in order to win: this simply came from some unmanageable quickness and liveliness of his character. If he happened upon a simpleton at the fair and managed to outsmart him, he'd go on a buying spree, purchasing a heap of everything he'd previously seen in the shops: horse collars, candlesticks, scarves for the nanny, a foal, raisins, a silver washbasin, Dutch cloth, coarse flour, tobacco, pistols, fish, paintings, whetstones, jugs, boots, porcelain – as long as the money held out. That's what Nоздрев was like! Maybe people will say his character was trite, that now there's no one like Nоздрев. Alas, those who will say so will be unfair. Nоздрев won't be leaving the world anytime soon. He's everywhere among us, and maybe he's just wearing a different kaftan; but people are careless and simple-minded, and a man in a different kaftan appears to them as a different man.

But was it confirmed? Was it justified? Why did he feel that shiver, that cold sweat, that darkness and spiritual chill again? Was it because he saw those eyes again? He was stubbornly determined to see those "old eyes" in order to finally be certain that he would definitely encounter them there, at that house. It was a feverish desire of his, and why was he now crushed and dismayed by the fact that he did see them now? He didn't expect it! Yes, those were the very same eyes (and there is no longer any doubt about that!) that sparkled at him in the morning crowd as he was leaving the St. Petersburg-Nikolayevsk Railway station; those very same (exactly those same!) that he caught later in the afternoon when he was sitting in the corner at Rogozhin's; Rogozhin himself had disavowed them earlier, asking with a crooked, numbing smile: "Whose eyes were they?" And it was unbearable to the prince, just a little while ago, at the Tsarskoye Selo railway station, when he was getting on the train to go to Aglaya, and suddenly saw those eyes again for the third time that day – he had wanted to approach Rogozhin and tell him, "Whose are those eyes!" But he ran out of the station and only came to, in front of the knife sharpener's counter, the very moment he stood there, evaluating one object for sixty kopecks with an elk's handle. A strange and terrifying demon had now firmly attached itself to him and wouldn't leave him alone any longer. This demon whispered to him in the Summer Garden when he was sitting, lost in thought, under the linden tree, that if Rogozhin needed to keep track of him from morning on and catch him every step of the way, it was because, upon learning that he wouldn't be going to Pavlovsk (which, of course, was already a fatal piece of information for Rogozhin), Rogozhin would certainly go to that house on Petersburg Street and would be certain to watch for him, the prince, who had given him a solemn promise in the morning that "he wouldn't see her" and that "he had come to St. Petersburg for no such reason." And so the prince is driven to that house with a burst of nervous energy, and what does he find there? He only encounters a wretched man with a gloomy but quite intelligible mental state. This wretched man was no longer hiding now; on the contrary, he was almost openly standing on the platform, even more openly than the prince himself. It was more likely the prince who was hiding, and not Rogozhin. And now, in front of the house, he was standing on the opposite side of the street, fifty paces to the side, on the opposite sidewalk, with his arms crossed, waiting. By now, he was completely visible, and it seemed that he intentionally wanted to be visible. He stood like an accuser and a judge, and not like... not like anyone else.

The emperor commanded the physicians to administer the medicine, without knowing how it would work. He instructed the consorts and concubines to beg the palace owner to let him into the palace. The palace owner was inside, wildly yelling, "What medicine is this I should be given? This is not my house. My house is a cool, tile-roofed one, not a diseased house like this one with fox demon-shaped shutters. Let me out. Let me out." Just as he was yelling, he saw four or five officials and three eunuchs supporting him, escorting him up to the dais. The crown prince asked, "Do you recognize your husband?" Yuanying replied, "How could I not recognize him? My husband and I have been married since we were young, and we have a son and a daughter together. Of course, I recognize him." The crown prince ordered the officials to escort him downstairs. The palace owner came down from the dais, and as he reached the white marble stairs, saw Liu Quan, and suddenly grabbed him, shouting, "Husband, where are you going without waiting for me? I fell down and was surrounded by those unreasonable people who scolded me. What kind of situation is this?" Liu Quan heard his words, saw the person, but did not recognize him. The crown prince said, "This is a case of a person seeing a seismic disaster, and capturing the living in place of the dead is impossible." A wise ruler like him, gave Liu Quan the imperial sister's dowry, her clothes, her jewelry, and all her belongings, and, as if it were a dowry, also granted him an edict to exempt him from corvée duty. He told him to lead the imperial sister back home. The husband and wife duo thanked the emperor at the stairs, and joyfully returned to their hometown. To confirm this, there is a poem:

A person's life and death are predetermined, each has a lifetime. Liu Quan returned to the world of the living, took the corpse back to bring life to Li Cui Lian. The couple bid farewell to the emperor and came directly to the city of Junzhou. Upon arrival, they found that their children and grandchildren were all well, and the couple proudly told of the good fortune they had experienced.

The emperor commanded the palace medical officer to bring him medicine, but he didn't know what to make of it.  Then he ordered the consorts and concubines to go into the palace to summon her. Inside the palace, the Empress was shouting wildly, "What medicine is this? This isn't my house! My house is a cool tile-roofed building, unlike this disease-ridden room with its tasselled silk awning!  Let me out! Let me out!"  Just as she was still shouting, a group of female attendants and three eunuchs came to escort her to the imperial dais.  The Crown Prince asked, "Do you recognize your husband?"  The empress retorted, "What nonsense! My husband and I have been together since childhood, and have had sons and daughters together; how could I not recognize him?"  The Crown Prince ordered the attendants to take her away. The empress went down from the palace, and, reaching the white jade steps, saw Liu Quan and grabbed hold of him, saying, "Husband, where are you going without waiting for me!  I tripped and fell, and those unreasonable people surrounded me, shouting. What's the meaning of this?"  Liu Quan, hearing her words as those of a wife, but seeing her face as that of a stranger, was afraid to recognize her. The Crown Prince said, "This is like a mountain collapsing and the earth splitting apart – even those who meet by fate will be hard to catch!"  A truly just king, he gave all of the empress's clothes, jewelry, and trousseau to Liu Quan, and rewarded him as if he was marrying him to her, also giving him an edict to forever exempt him from corvee labor.  He led the empress back to her village, where they thanked him and, overjoyed, returned home.  This is testified by the following poem:

Human life is predetermined, death is as well, with each person having a fixed lifespan. Liu Quan returned from death and reunited with the spirit of Li Ci-Lian. The two of them bid farewell to the king and went directly to the city of Jun, where they saw that their children and grandchildren were all well, and that they were touting the good fortune.

He dare not acknowledge her. The Emperor said, "It is indeed a case of earth shattering and rocks crumbling when people see each other, but it is hard to catch the living and substitute them for the dead!" A wise ruler indeed, the Emperor then bestowed on Liu Quan all the palace gifts of his concubine, including her clothes, jewelry, and cosmetics, and treated him as a matchmaker would, and issued an imperial decree, exempting him from corvee duty, allowing him to escort the palace concubine back home. The Tang King ordered the eunuchs to help her down. The palace mistress came down from the imperial dais and walked to the white marble steps, and when she saw Liu Quan, she grasped him tightly and exclaimed, "Husband, where are you off to, leaving me behind like this? I tripped and fell, and those unreasonable people surrounded me and yelled, what a terrible thing!" Liu Quan, upon hearing her words, saw her face, which was not that of his wife, and dared not recognize her. The Tang King said, "It's just as the saying goes, when a mountain collapses and the earth cracks, there are those who may see and also those who may not. What a wise king this is! The prince barely noticed that others were chatting and making pleasant conversation with Aglaya; at times, he even almost forgot that he himself was sitting next to her. He sometimes felt a desire to go somewhere, to completely disappear from here, and even the bleak, desolate place would be to his liking, as long as he was alone with his thoughts and no one knew where he was. Or at least be at home, on the veranda, but in such a way that there would be no one there – neither Lebedev nor the children; to collapse onto his divan, bury his face in the pillow, and lie there like that for a day, a night, another day. Fleeting moments saw him dreaming of mountains, and a familiar spot in the mountains that he loved to recall and visit whenever he lived there, and look down from there at the village, at the faint thread of the waterfall below, at the white clouds, at the abandoned old castle. Oh, how he wished to be there now, to think of just one thing – and for his whole life, nothing but that – and a thousand years would be enough! And let them forget him completely here. K. was interrupted by a scream from the back of the hall, he shaded his eyes to see what was happening, as the dim daylight made the fog look milky and blinding.  It was the laundress, whom he had immediately recognized as a major disturbance upon his entrance. Whether she was guilty or not was impossible to tell. K. only saw that a man had pulled her into a corner by the door and was holding her there. But it wasn't she who was screaming, it was the man, who had his mouth wide open and was staring at the ceiling. A small circle had formed around the pair, and the gallery viewers nearby seemed delighted that the seriousness K. had introduced to the gathering was being broken up in this way. K. wanted to run out immediately under the first impression, and he also thought that everyone would be interested in restoring order and at least expelling the couple from the hall, but the people in front of him remained frozen in place, no one budged, and none of them let K. pass. On the contrary, people obstructed him, old men held up their arms, and some hand – he hadn't had time to turn around – grabbed him from behind by the collar. K. was no longer thinking about the couple, it seemed to him as if his freedom was being restricted, as if the arrest was being taken seriously, and he jumped recklessly off the podium.

Now he stood face to face with the crowd. Had he misjudged the people? Had he given too much credence to his speech? Had they been pretending to be sincere as long as he was speaking, and were they now, as he reached the conclusions, satisfied with the deception? What faces surrounded him! Small, dark eyes darted back and forth, the cheeks drooped like those of drunks, the long beards stood stiff and sparse, and if one grasped them, it was as if one was grasping claws, not beards. But under the beards – and that was the real discovery K. made – medals glinted at the collar of their jackets in various sizes and colors. Everyone had these medals, as far as one could see. They all belonged to one another, the apparent factions on the right and left, and as he suddenly turned around, he saw the same medals on the collar of the examining magistrate, who was sitting calmly with his hands folded in his lap. "So," K. cried, throwing his arms up in the air, "you are all officials, as I see it, you are the corrupt clique I was talking about, you've pushed yourselves to the front as listeners and eavesdroppers, formed apparent factions, and one of them applauded to test me, you wanted to learn how to ensnare the innocent! Now, you haven't been useless here, I hope you've either discussed the fact that someone expects the defense of the innocent from you, or else – let me or I'll hit you," K. shouted at a trembling old man who had pushed himself particularly close to him – "or else you've actually learned something. And with that, I wish you good luck with your profession." He quickly grabbed his hat, which was lying at the edge of the table, and pushed his way through the general silence, which was absolute astonishment, towards the exit. The examining magistrate seemed, however, to have been quicker than K., because he was waiting for him at the door. "A moment," he said. K. stopped, but didn't look at the examining magistrate; instead, he looked at the door, whose handle he had already grasped. "I just wanted to draw your attention to the fact," the examining magistrate said, "that you've missed the benefit that an interrogation would have brought to you, a prisoner – it's probably not yet dawned on you –." K. laughed at the door. "You scoundrels," he cried, "I give you all interrogations," opened the door, and hurried down the stairs. Behind him, the noise of the reassembled gathering rose up, which probably began to discuss the events in the manner of students.

He was still free. "Allow," he said, and quickly walked between the guards into his room. "He seems reasonable," he heard someone say behind him. In his room, he immediately opened the desk drawers; everything was in perfect order, but in the commotion he couldn't find the identification papers he was looking for right away. As he returned to the adjacent room, the door opposite him just opened and Mrs. Grubach was about to enter. One could only see her for a moment because as soon as she recognized K., she seemed to feel embarrassed and apologized for it, disappeared, and closed the door very cautiously. "Come on in," K. had just managed to say. Bodhidharma recounted to Tripitaka his three sons' murmured words, and Tripitaka rejoiced. He had the morning meal provided in advance, and presented him with a string of silver to thank him. Tripitaka refused to accept any money. Bodhidharma's wife implored and implored, so Bodhidharma finally declined, saying, "The fact that you are willing to take pity on me and escort me a distance is enough to repay my deep gratitude."

Bodhidharma and his wife could not help but hastily prepared some coarse bread and dried food, ordered Bodhidharma to set off, and Tripitaka was overjoyed to accept them. The Master of the Scripture then received a mandate from Bodhidharma's mother, and called for two servants, each carrying hunting equipment, to accompany him on the main road. The scenery along the mountain was beyond count, with wild vistas and mountain grandeur stretching as far as the eye could see. After a half day of travel, a towering mountain came into view across from them, its peak reaching for the blue heavens, steep and precipitous. Before long, the Master of the Scripture arrived at the foot of the mountain.

The Master of the Scripture climbed this mountain as if he were walking on flat land. When he reached the middle of the mountain, Bodhidharma turned back, standing at the foot of the mountain, and said, "The Reverend, please proceed on your way, I must return." The Master of the Scripture heard his words and quickly dismounted his horse, saying, "Please, don't be troubled, Master Bodhidharma, escort me a bit further!" Bodhidharma said, "The Reverend does not know that this mountain is called the Two-Frontier Mountain. The eastern half belongs to our Great Tang, and the western half is the territory of the Turks. Over there, the wolves and tigers do not obey my summons, so I cannot cross the border. You should proceed on your way." Tripitaka was shocked, opened his hands, pulled up his sleeves, and sobbed uncontrollably.

Just as they were about to bid farewell, a loud cry echoed from the foot of the mountain: "My master has come! My master has come!" Tripitaka was dazed, and Bodhidharma shook him awake. They did not know who was shouting, and only proceeded on their way for now.

Buddha's disciple, Triangular, related to Tri-calm Buddha, the visions of his dream, and Tri-calm Buddha was pleased. He provided a vegetarian meal and gave Buddha one two-ounce piece of white silver in gratitude. Tri-calm Buddha did not accept the gift. The family once again implored and implored, and Tri-calm Buddha, ultimately, did not accept the gift, saying, "It is you who kindly showed compassion and took me on a journey; this has touched me deeply." 

Being left with no choice, Buddha's disciple and his mother and wife hastily prepared some coarse flour biscuits, ordered Buddha's disciple to bid farewell and escort Buddha, who was delighted to accept. Venerable Grand Guardian, on the order of the mother, called upon three house servants and each brought with them hunting equipment, accompanying the main road, observing an endless expanse of wild scenes and mountain vistas. They traveled for half a day, then came upon a large mountain, whose summit pierced the azure expanse and rose sheer and steep. Tri-calm Buddha soon arrived at the foot of the mountain. The Venerable Grand Guardian climbed the mountain as if on level ground. 

Just as they were in the middle of the mountain, Buddha's disciple turned back and stood on the road below, saying, "Elder, you continue on ahead, and I will return." Tri-calm Buddha heard the words and, dismounting, exclaimed, "Don't bother to send someone to escort me any further!" Buddha's disciple said, "Elder, you are unaware of this mountain's name. This mountain is called the Two-domain Mountain. The eastern half belongs to our great Tang, while the western half is part of the territory of the Turks. That side of the mountain is roamed by wolves and tigers that do not obey me, so I cannot pass through the border. You should go on alone." Tri-calm Buddha's heart was shocked; he opened his hand, grasped his robes, and couldn't help but cry. 

Just as they were taking their leave, with a sense of urgency, a loud cry from the foot of the mountain resounded like thunder, saying, "My master is coming! My master is coming!" The sound startled Tri-calm Buddha, who became dazed, while Buddha's disciple panicked. Ultimately, they didn't know who was shouting, and the story will be continued in the next chapter.

Master Sengchou retold to Master Tripitaka all about the dream in the presence of the three of them. Master Tripitaka was pleased. They then provided a vegetarian meal, and gave one and a half ounces of white silver as a gift. Master Tripitaka did not accept the money. Once again, Master Sengchou and his wife begged him, Master Tripitaka ultimately did not accept the money, but said, "It is enough for you to be willing to offer me a helping hand; this I shall regard as most loving." Master Sengchou and his wife could do nothing but, in a hurry, make some coarse steamed bread and dried food to send Master Tripitaka on his way. Master Tripitaka was delighted to accept them. The Protector, following his mother's orders, then called for two servants, and each of them took some hunting equipment, and, together with them, set off along the main road, watching the limitless scenery of the mountains, and the beautiful sights on the ridges. After half a day's travel, they came to a mountain opposite, a genuine great mountain, with its peak touching the heavens and its cliffs steep and rugged. Master Tripitaka took some time to arrive at the front of the mountain. The Protector climbed this mountain as if he were walking on flat ground. When they were in the middle of the mountain, Master Sengchou turned back and stood on the road below: "Master, you go on ahead, I'll return." Master Tripitaka heard this and dismounted his horse, saying, "I beg of you, Protector, please accompany me just a little further!" Master Sengchou said, "Master, you don't know that this mountain is called the Two-Jurisdiction Mountain. The eastern half belongs to the jurisdiction of our Great Tang, while the western half belongs to the territory of the Tanguts. Over there, there are wolves and tigers that do not submit to our rule, and I am also unable to cross into their territory; so you'd better go on your own." Master Tripitaka was alarmed, and waved his hand, pulling at his sleeves and weeping. At the moment they were bidding each other farewell, the sound of shouting like thunder could be heard from the foot of the mountain: "My master is coming! My master is coming!" Master Tripitaka was stunned, Master Sengchou was frightened, and he didn't know who was shouting, so he just listened and waited for the next chapter to continue.

Buddhist Master Buddha-lantern told Tang Sanzang his three-day dream, and also reported it to Tang Sanzang, who was delighted. Early, he provided a simple vegetarian meal, and then gave a white silver ounce as a thank-offering. Tang Sanzang refused to accept any payment. The mother and wife of Buddhilan, all the more begged to be excused, finally Tang Sanzang still did not accept any payment, saying, "If you're willing to show compassion and send me one step further, it would be a deep expression of your kindness." Buddhilan and his wife had no choice but to make some coarse bread, boil some coarse food, and order Buddhilan to send him off, and Tang Sanzang was happy to accept it.

Master Heavenly Guardian took the mother's instructions and again called for two house slaves to bring their hunting equipment, and went up the mountain road with him. They couldn't see the endless landscape of mountains and forests. After walking for half a day, they saw a great mountain, truly so high that it touched the sky, and so steep and rugged. After some time, they arrived at the front edge of the mountain. That Master Heavenly Guardian climbed the mountain as if he were walking on flat ground. As they walked to the middle of the mountain, Buddhilan turned back, standing at the foot of the mountain, saying, "Elder, you go ahead, I'll return." Tang Sanzang heard this and immediately dismounted his horse, saying, "Please don't trouble yourself, Master Heavenly Guardian, to go another step further!" Buddhilan said, "Elder, you don't know that this mountain is called the Two-boundary Mountain; the eastern half belongs to our Great Tang Dynasty, while the western half is part of the territory of the nomads. Over there, wolves and tigers do not obey our law, and I wouldn't be able to pass through either; you should just go ahead." Tang Sanzang was frightened, shook his hand open, and grabbed Buddhilan's sleeves and collar, his tears flowing uncontrollably. At the moment of their final farewell, a loud shout like thunder echoed at the foot of the mountain, saying, "My Master is coming! My Master is coming!" Startled, Tang Sanzang was numb, Buddhilan panicked. In the end, he did not know who was calling out; let's wait for the continuation of the next chapter to find out.

Monk Tripitaka recounted his dreams to Monk Sanzang, who was delighted. Early the next morning, he provided a vegetarian meal and a pair of white silver taels as a gift. Monk Tripitaka did not accept the gift. Monk Sanzang begged repeatedly, bowing deeply. Monk Tripitaka still refused to accept the gift, but said, "Your kindness in sending me on my way has greatly warmed my heart."

Monk Sanzang was at a loss, so he quickly made some coarse steamed buns and rice to take with him and bid farewell to Monk Tripitaka. Monk Tripita lay the blame on the Mother and ordered two attendants to each carry their hunting equipment. As they journeyed up the main road, the scenery in the mountains and on the ridges was beyond description. After walking for half a day, they saw a great mountain across from them, truly a lofty peak that touched the sky, with steep and rugged cliffs.

Monk Tripitaka soon arrived at the foot of the mountain, but Tai Bao, unlike before, climbed the mountain as if it were a flat ground. As he walked halfway up, Monk Sanzang turned back, standing at the foot of the mountain and said, "Venerable sir, please continue on. I'll return." Monk Tripitaka heard the words and quickly dismounted his horse, saying, "Monk Tripitaka, please do not trouble Tai Bao to send you any further!"

Monk Tripitaka said, "Monk Tripitaka does not know that this mountain is called two-domain mountain. The eastern half belongs to our Great Tang, while the western half is within the domain of the Tatars. In that quarter, there are wolves and tigers that do not submit to our authority. I also cannot cross into their domain, so please go on your way." Monk Tripitaka's heart was filled with shock, his hands shook as he grasped his robes, and tears streamed down his face. At the moment they were about to bid each other farewell, they heard a thunderous cry from the foot of the mountain, "My teacher has come! My teacher has come!"

This frightened Monk Tripitaka into a stupor, and Tai Bao was startled. Monk Tripitaka did not know who was shouting, and the story will be continued in the next chapter.

The poem says: The great Emperor of Tang has issued a decree, appointing Xuanzang to inquire about the Chan school. He firmly polishes and refines himself to seek the dragon's hole, making a determined effort to cultivate at Jade Summit. He has traveled to many countries beyond the frontier, crossing countless mountains and ranges. From now on, he is embarking on his journey to the West, carrying the teachings of the Buddha and seeking the understanding of the void.

It was said that Master Xuanzang, from the thirteenth year of Zhenguan, had in the ninth month, three days before the full moon, been accompanied by the Emperor and numerous officials as far as the suburbs of Chang'an. The next day and night, his horses did not stop, and by dawn, he arrived at the Fahua Temple. The temple master, Abbot Xiangfang, led a group of over five hundred monks, who stood on both sides, received him, and presented him with tea. After the tea, they had breakfast, and before they knew it, night fell. The moment was exactly that of the gentle movement of the stars in the river, the moon's brightness clearing the dust, the distant honking of wild geese, the echoes of the footboards in the west, the homing birds roosting on withered trees, and the monks delivering the teachings of the Sanskrit language.

Master Xuanzang sat on a single mats on the floor, and well into the night. The monks below the lamp discussed the fixed decree of the Buddhist teachings and the reasons for taking the scriptures to the West. Some said it was too far by water and high by land, some said it was too long, some said it was fraught with tigers and leopards, some said it was too steep and precipitous, and some said it was hard to conquer because of the poison demons and evil spirits. Xuanzang kept his mouth shut, but with his hand pointed to his heart, he nodded several times. The monks below were unable to fathom his intention, joined their hands, and asked, "The master points to his heart and nods, what is the meaning?" Xuanzang replied, "As long as the mind exists, various kinds of demons arise; as long as the mind ceases, various kinds of demons disappear. My disciples once swore the great vow to the Buddha at the Huayin Temple, and I could not help but do this with all my heart. From now on, I am certainly going to the West, to see the Buddha and request the scriptures, so that the wheel of the law may turn, and our great king's plan may be forever established." When the monks heard these words, everyone praised him, and all of them extolled his virtues, calling out in unison, "Great master, you are a paragon of loyalty and courage, incomparable to anyone else."

The Scripture says: When the Emperor of Tang bestowed an edict, an imperial emissary named Xuanzang went to inquire about the Chan sect. Jianxin stone-ground and polished to find the dragon's cave, and devotedly cultivated the meaning of the heavens on the top of the Eagle Peak. He traveled to distant lands and across mountains to visit countless kingdoms; before him, the clouds and mountains stretched as far as the eye could see. Today, I set aside my personal vehicle and embark on a journey west, carrying the teaching of emptiness. 

Let it be said that, from the thirteenth year of the Zhenyuan period of the Tang dynasty, nine months prior to the autumn equinox, I, a pilgrim, had the Emperor of Tang bestow an imperial decree upon me and dispatch many officials to escort me out of the Chang'an pass. One or two days passed and my horses did not rest, early arriving at the Fa Men Temple. 

The abbot of the temple, an elderly master residing in the upper chamber, led a group of five hundred monks or so, arranged on both sides to welcome and escort me inside. After bowing to each other and offering tea, we sat down to a meal. Not long after the meal, night had fallen. It was exactly that hour when: the shadow of the starry river danced, the moon was shining without a speck of dust; a distant wild goose called, and the tune of the mortise echoed from the west; birds returned to roost in the withered trees, and the monks lectured on the sound of the language of the Sanskrit. I sat on a large cushion of a magnum lump, sitting until it was almost midnight. 

The monks gathered below the light, discussed the decree of the Buddha and the origin of going to the West to acquire scriptures. Some said the water is far, the mountains are high; some said the road is long, tigers and leopards are numerous; some said the precipitous peaks and steep cliffs are difficult to cross; some said the demons and monsters are evil and treacherous, hard to subdue. I kept my mouth shut, and with my hand pointed to my heart, nodded several times. The monks below did not understand my intention, folded their hands and asked, "The Master pointed to his heart and nodded, what does it mean?" 

I replied, "Heart arises, countless demons arise; heart extinguishes, countless demons are extinguished. My disciple once made a vow at the birth temple of the Buddha, which is to eliminate the defilements of this heart without any hesitation. This time, I will certainly go to the West to see the Buddha and acquire scriptures, in order to make the dharma wheel turn and to fulfill the great aspiration of our holy king to preserve the imperial plan forever." 

When the monks heard these words, everyone admired and celebrated, each praising, all calling out in unison, "Our compassionate teacher is steadfast in his heart, with an unyielding loyalty as great as Mount Tai, unceasingly expounding the teachings of the law." Praising me beyond measure, they invited me to lie down on the couch and rest.

He traveled to many a country, beyond the frontier; tens of thousands of mountains and clouds blocked his view.

From now on, he's heading west to depart; with the teaching he will propagate and demonstrate emptiness. He sat on a simple mat, in the candlelight till nearly midnight. Some said the distance was far, the mountains high; others said the road was long, beset with tigers and leopards; some said the steep mountains and precipitous cliffs were treacherous to traverse; others said that demons and evil spirits made it difficult to overcome. Xuanzang replied, "When the heart exists, all kinds of demons arise; when the heart is extinguished, all kinds of demons cease to exist. As my disciple, I once took a vow at the Birth-Resurrection Temple to follow this path; it's not possible for me to abandon this resolve. This time I'm going to the West, to see the Buddha and seek scriptures, so that our law wheel may revolve and the sacred dynasty remain forever." When the monks heard this, they all extolled him, everyone praising him, calling out in unison, "You are a true and loyal master, completely devoted to the law!" They flattered him and spoke highly of him, unable to stop; they urged him to lie down on the mat and rest.

It is said that the Tang emperor's imperial edict bestowed upon me the title of Grand Master of Buddhism. Emperor Wu of the Tang sent Master Xuanzang to inquire about the teachings of Chan (Zen) Buddhism. With an unwavering determination, I spent years refining and polishing myself, searching for the source of the Dragon's Cave. My resolve was so strong that I devoted myself to cultivating the Way on the Peak of the Azure Bird. I traveled to many countries beyond the boundaries, crossing over countless mountains and rivers. From now on, I am embarking on a journey to the West, carrying the teachings of the Buddha to attain profound emptiness. 

It was in the thirteenth year of the Zhenguan era, on the twenty-seventh of September, three days before the twenty-eighth day, that I bade farewell to the officials of the capital and left Chang'an. Within a day or two, I arrived at the Fahua Temple, my horse not stopping once. In this temple, the Master of the temple, the venerable Abbot of the Upper Chamber, led five hundred and more monks in a procession to greet me, and they lined up on both sides to welcome me inside. After I had been served tea, I was led to the dining hall to take my meal. I finished my meal without even realizing that night had fallen. At that moment, the stars were twinkling like pearls in the sky, the moon was shining brightly without a single cloud, the geese were calling in the distance, the sound of the mortars came from the west, the birds were roosting on the dry trees, and the monks were lecturing on the Dharma. I sat on a mattress in a secluded corner of the temple, surrounded by the flickering light of the candles, until the night grew late. The monks below began to discuss the firm decision of the Buddha's teaching and the reason behind my journey to the West to fetch the sutras. Some said that the distance was too far and the mountains too high, some said that the road was fraught with tigers and leopards, some said that the rugged mountains and steep cliffs made it difficult to pass, and some said that the demons were evil and terrifying. I kept silent, my mouth closed, but pointed to my heart with my hand and nodded several times. The monks were puzzled and did not understand my intentions. They joined their hands together and asked me, "Master, what do you mean by pointing to your heart and nodding?" I replied, "When the mind is present, various demons arise; when the mind is extinguished, various demons are destroyed. My disciple once swore a great vow before the Buddha in the temple of the Reproducer of Life, that I would not rest until I had given my all to this cause. I am determined to go to the West, to see the Buddha and to fetch the sutras, so that the wheel of Dharma may revolve and the great purpose of our holy ruler may be achieved forever." The monks heard my words and were all impressed, and one after another, they praised me, calling me "Great Master with an unwavering heart and a loyal spirit," and they eulogized me, unable to express their admiration fully. They asked me to enter my bed, and I lay down to rest.

Chichikov became completely ill-tempered and flung his sabre onto the floor, which he had carried with him on the road to strike a commanding pose as needed. For about a quarter of an hour he fussed over the blacksmiths, because the blacksmiths, as they usually were, were outright scoundrels, and, grasping that the work needed to be done quickly, they had simply doubled their prices eightfold. As he grew hot, he called them scammers, robbers, highwaymen of travelers, even hinting at a dreadful judgment, but the blacksmiths remained steadfast - not only did they not back down on the price, but they even took more than double the time to do the work. In the meantime, he had the pleasure of experiencing the pleasant minutes known to any traveler when their trunks were packed and the room was strewn with mere scraps and odds and ends; when a man felt disconnected from the road and the place he was sitting, gazed out the window at people passing by, tugging at their horse manes, and looked at him with a foolish curiosity, and, catching his eye, continued on their way, which further irritated the poor traveling man's ill temper. All he saw, everything he looked at - the little booth opposite his windows, the head of the old woman living in the house opposite, approaching the window with short curtains - was detestable to him, yet he did not step away from the window. He stood there, now forgetting, now fixing a dull gaze on everything moving and unmoving, and chafed with annoyance at some mosquito buzzing and flitting against his finger. But everything has its end, and the moment he had been longing for arrived: everything was ready, the sledge had been properly hitched up, the wheel had been re-timbered with new thongs, the horses had been watered, and the thieving blacksmiths had left, counting their hard cash and wishing the traveler well. Finally, the sledge was loaded, and two freshly bought warm buns were placed inside, and Selifan had stuck something for himself into the coachman's pocket, and the hero, finally, with a wave of his felt hat, now standing in the same demiktonovoy coat, now standing among the tatterdemalion waiters and lackeys who had gathered to gawk, as if a strange master was departing, and with various other circumstances accompanying departure, got into the sledge. And the sledge, in which single men rode, which had stayed so long in the city and had probably become a bore to the reader, finally emerged from the hotel gates. 'Thanks to God,' thought Chichikov, and he crossed himself. Selifan cracked his whip; to him first climbed the coachman, Petrushka, who had hung around for a while on the footboard, and our hero, settling in better on the Georgian cushion, placed a leather cushion behind his back, pressed the two warm buns against his back, and the sledge began to swing and dance again, thanks to the cobblestones, which, as it's known, have a jolting power. He looked at the houses, walls, fence, and streets with some indefinite feeling, as if they too were somehow springing up and receding slowly, and who knows, may God judge, whether he would ever see them again in his life. When turning onto one of the streets, the sledge had to stop because a never-ending funeral procession was passing the length of it. Chichikov poked his head out and ordered Petrushka to ask who was being buried, and learned that they were burying a prosecutor. Filled with unpleasant feelings, he quickly hid in a corner, covered himself with a deerskin, and pulled down the leather hangings. At that time, when the sledge was stopped in this way, Selifan and Petrushka, piously doffing their caps, were counting the number of people walking and riding, including the number of the single and the mounted, while the master, ordering them not to acknowledge or bow to any acquaintances among the waiters, took a peek cautiously through the leather window hangings, where there were little glass panes, and saw that, hatless, all the officials were walking behind the coffin. He started to be afraid they might recognize the sledge, but they had no time for that. They did not start discussing mundane topics, such as those that usually pass between those accompanying the deceased, but all their thoughts were occupied with themselves: they were thinking about the new governor-general, how he would take up the job, and how he would treat them. Behind the officials walking on foot, followed a number of carriages, from which ladies in mourning caps were looking out. From their facial expressions and hand movements it was clear they were engaged in a lively conversation; perhaps they too were discussing the governor-general's arrival and making speculations about the favors he would bestow, and preoccupying themselves with their eternal ribbons and broideries. Finally, behind the carriages followed a few empty drozhki, stretched out in a crooked line, and nothing was left, and our hero could finally continue his journey. He opened the leather window hangings and let out a sigh, exclaiming from the heart: 'There you have it, prosecutor! He lived, he lived, and then he died! And now they will print in the newspapers that a respected citizen, a rare father, a model husband, has passed away, to the sorrow of his subordinates and all humanity, and they will write a lot of other nonsense; perhaps they will add that he was mourned by his widows and orphans; and yet, if one examines the matter carefully, you were no more than a man with thick eyebrows.' He ordered Selifan to hurry up and meanwhile thought to himself: 'However, it's good that the funeral procession passed by; they say that it's a good omen if you meet a corpse.'
