During this time, he had the pleasure of experiencing the pleasant moments familiar to every traveler, when everything is packed into a trunk and only the threads, papers, and various rubbish are scattered about in the room, when a person doesn't belong either to the road or to the seat, sees people passing by through the window, nudging their ribs and with some foolish curiosity looking up to glance at him, and then continuing on their way, which further irritates the ill-humored traveler's disposition. Everything, everything he sees: the little shop opposite his windows, the old woman's head living in the opposite house, approaching the window with little curtains, all seems vile to him; yet, he doesn't move away from the window. Standing, he occasionally forgets, occasionally gives a distracted glance at all that is moving and not moving before him, and is tormented by a certain annoyance, which a fly buzzing and bumping against his finger in that very moment seems to be suffocating him. But everything has its end, and the desired moment has arrived: everything was ready, the brougham had been properly assembled, the wheel had been greased with a new thong, the horses had been fed and watered, and the blacksmiths, the scoundrels, had departed, counting out the roubles they had received and wishing the traveler well. Finally, the brougham was loaded, and two hot just-bought cakes had been placed inside, and Selifan had put something for himself into the little pouch of the coachman's cossack, and the hero, finally, as he waved his fur cap, standing in the same shabby suit, accompanied by the tavern and foreign servants and coachmen who had gathered to gawk as a traveler departed, also got into the carriage. And the brougham, in which the bachelors were riding, which had been stuck in the city for so long and, perhaps, had grown tiresome to the reader, finally left the hotel gates. "Thanks be to God," thought Chichikov and made the sign of the cross. Selifan cracked his whip, and Petrushka, who had been sitting for a bit on the step, sat down next to him, and our hero, getting more comfortably seated on the Georgian carpet, put a leather cushion behind his back, pressed two hot cakes against it, and the brougham began to sway and dance along the pavement, which, as is known, had a lively swing to it. He gazed at the houses, walls, fence, and streets, which also seemed to be backing away from him, as if springing up, and he wondered, God knows, if he would ever see them again in his life. When the brougham turned into one of the streets, it had to stop because a long funeral procession was going along its entire length. Chichikov, poking his head out, ordered Petrushka to ask who was being buried, and he learned that a prosecutor was being buried. Feeling unpleasant emotions, he instantly hid in the corner, covered himself with his coat, and pulled down the leather curtains. At the moment when the brougham had been stopped in this manner, Selifan and Petrushka, devoutly doffing their caps, were observing who was riding, how, in what, and on what, counting up the total number of those who were walking and those who were riding, while the master, having ordered them not to notice and not to bow to any of the acquaintances, was also peeking timidly through the peephole in the leather curtains: behind the coffin were walking all the officials, removing their hats. He began to be afraid that they might recognize the brougham, but they didn't have time for that. They weren't even engaging in the usual everyday conversations that travelers engaged in when accompanying a deceased person. All their thoughts were occupied with themselves in that moment: they were thinking about who the new governor-general would be, how he would take up the job, and how he would treat them. Behind the officials, who were walking on foot, followed carriages from which ladies in mourning caps were visible. By their movements and gestures, it was clear that they were engaged in a lively conversation; perhaps they too were discussing the arrival of the new governor-general and making speculations about the favors he would bestow, and worrying about their eternal lace trimmings and embroidery. Finally, behind the carriages, a few empty drozhki stretched out in a row, and then there was nothing left, and our hero could continue on his way. Having opened the leather curtains, he sighed deeply, exclaiming with all his heart: "Ah, the prosecutor! He lived, he lived, and then he died! And they will write in the newspapers that he passed away, to the sorrow of his subordinates and all humanity, a respectable citizen, a rare father, a exemplary husband, and a lot of unnecessary nonsense will be written; perhaps they'll even add that he was accompanied by the lamentations of widows and orphans; but if you examine the matter carefully, you'll find that all he really had was thick eyebrows." Then he ordered Selifan to drive faster, and he thought to himself: "It's a good thing that we met the funeral; they say that it's lucky to meet a deceased person."

Here was my path: from a part to a whole; the part - R-13, the magnificent whole - our Institute of State Poets and Writers. I thought: how could it have been that the ancients did not notice the sheer absurdity of their literature and poetry. The enormous, magnificent power of the artistic word - was squandered completely in vain. It's simply ridiculous: everyone wrote - about whatever came into their minds. Just as ridiculous and absurd as it is that the sea in ancient times slammed bluntly against the shore around the clock, and kilogrammometers locked up in waves - went only to warming the feelings of the lovers. We extracted electricity from the lovers' whispering waves, and from the beast hissing foam - we made a domesticated pet; and just like that, we have tamed and domesticated once wild poetry. Now poetry is no longer a boundless nightingale's song: poetry is state service, poetry is utility.

That was my path: from the part to the whole; the part – R-13, the majestic whole – our Institute of State Poets and Writers. I thought: how was it that the ancients didn't notice the absurdity of their literature and poetry at all. The tremendous, magnificent power of artistic speech was squandered entirely. It's simply ridiculous: everyone wrote about whatever came to mind. Just as ridiculous and absurd as the way the sea of the ancients round the clock pounded flatly against the shore, and the metric tons sealed in the waves – only served to fuel the emotions of lovers. We took the whispers of waves from lovers and got electricity, we took the snorting beast spewing foamy mane and made a household pet: and exactly the same way we have domesticated and saddled the once savage storm of poetry. Now poetry is no longer the free-birdsong thrum: poetry is a state service, poetry is utility.

— He got upset, maybe it was justified, — Rogozhin said, — but what hurt me more than anything was my brother. As for Mother, I don't have much to say, she's an old woman, she reads the Chet'i-Minei, sits with old women, and whatever my brother settles, that's what it will be. But he wouldn't give me any answers back then, do you understand? I was out of my mind, it's true. They say there was a telegram sent. But the telegram was sent to my sister-in-law after all. And she's been living alone for thirty years, sitting with lunatics from morning till night. She's not a nun, but even more so. She was too afraid to open the telegram, so she had it sent back, and that's where it's been stuck ever since. Only Konev, Vasiliy Vasilevich, got involved, and he set everything straight. He cut off the parochial linings from my father's coffin, in the dead of night, with gold brushes: 'They cost an awful lot, supposedly.' But he can go to Siberia for that alone, if I want, because that's sacrilege. Hey, you, you pea-filled fright! — he turned to the official. — How is that according to the law: sacrilege?

— He got angry, he got angry, maybe that was it, but, above all, the brother got the better of him, — replied Rogozhin. — As for mother, there's nothing to say, the old woman reads the Chet'i-Minei, sits with old women, and what brother Sergy would decide, that's what would happen. And he didn't give me a say at the time, you understand? It's true, I was out of my mind then. They say, a telegram was sent, but the telegram arrived to the aunt anyway. And she's been a widow for thirty years and spends the whole day and night sitting with the crazy women. She's no nun, not even that. She got scared of the telegram and, not opening it, handed it over to the authorities, and she's been laid up ever since. Only Konov, Vasilyevich, bailed me out, everything got explained. At night, with a violet pall on the coffin, he snipped the gilt cuffs: 'They're worth, apparently, any amount of money.' But he's capable of going to Siberia for that alone if I want him to, it's sacrilege. Hey, you, little hop-o'-my-thumb! — he turned to the official. — According to the law: is that sacrilege?

They say the ancients conducted elections in secret, sneaking about like thieves; some of our historians even claim that they took part in what were carefully disguised election festivities (I imagine this fantastical and somber spectacle: night, square, figures creeping along the walls in dark cloaks; a reddish-orange flame of torches flickering in the wind...). Why the whole mystery was needed still hasn't been clarified; most likely the elections were connected with some kind of mystical, superstitious, or perhaps even criminal rites. But we have nothing to hide or be ashamed of: we celebrate our elections openly, honestly, by day. I see everyone voting for the Benefactor; everyone sees me voting for the Benefactor - and can it be otherwise, when "everyone" and "I" are one "We"? How much more uplifting, sincere, and noble than the ancient "secret" of the cowardly thieves. And then, how much more practical. For if even the impossible were possible – some discord in the usual monophony – still, the unseen Guardians are here, within our ranks: they can instantly identify those misled and save them from further false steps, and the Unified State from them themselves. And, finally, one more...

A saddle adorned with fine carvings, shining bright with inlaid silver, with a golden seat and bright silk trim.  A pair of velvet covers, each layer neatly folded, with three braided purple straps. The bits were of polished iron, and the reins had water-stained feathers attached to the ends.

Tripitaka's heart was filled with joy as he put the saddle and bridle on his horse, feeling as if he had made the purchase himself.  He bowed in gratitude to the old man, who hurriedly helped him onto his horse. "Please, please, don't thank me!"  The old man did not linger, but instead asked Tripitaka to mount his horse.  The elder, now mounted, followed by the pilgrim carrying his luggage, approached the old man.  The old man drew out a whip from his sleeve, its handle made of fragrant varnishwood, wrapped with tiger-fiber rope, and presented it to Tripitaka, saying, "Holy monk, I still have a parting gift, a riding crop, for you to take along."

Tripitaka accepted the gift in gratitude, and, inquiring about the old man, only to find that he had vanished.  On looking back, he saw only a blank space.  Just then, he heard a voice from the air: "Holy monk, do not tarry.  I am the mountain god of the Mount Lu, sent by the bodhisattva to give you the saddle and bridle.  You should press on westward, without delay."

Tripitaka hastily dismounted and bowed in the air, saying, "Your disciple is but a mortal with an ignorant eye, not knowing how to recognize a noble deity.  I humbly request your pardon.  Please convey my gratitude to the bodhisattva, who has bestowed such blessings upon me."

Just as Tripitaka continued to bow and pray, a laughing Monkey King and a jubilant Sun Wukong suddenly appeared, having been watching him from the side of the road.  Monkey King pulled Tripitaka to his feet and said, "Master, get up!  The old man is gone, and you cannot be heard praying, nor seen bowing.  Why do you continue to pray?"

The news of the event reached the church with extraordinary speed. As Keller was walking up to the prince, a large number of people, completely unknown to him, ran up to him with questions. A loud conversation was taking place, with people shaking their heads and laughing; no one left the church, everyone waited for the news to be confirmed. He had paled, but received the news quietly, almost inaudibly saying, "I was afraid; but I didn't think it would be... like this." – and then, after a brief pause, he added: "However... considering her condition... it's only to be expected." Keller himself later referred to this reaction as "incomparable philosophy."

The prince left the church, seemingly calm and cheerful; at least, many noticed this and later recounted it. It seemed as though he was very keen to get home and stay alone as soon as possible, but that was not to be. Some of the guests entered the room, among them Pticyn, Gavril Ardalionovich, and the doctor, who also showed no inclination to leave. Moreover, the entire house was literally besieged by idle onlookers. Even from the balcony, the prince could hear Keller and Lebedev engaging in a heated dispute with several unknown but respectable-looking individuals who were determined to get onto the balcony at all costs. The prince went over to the disputants, inquired about the matter, and, politely excusing Lebedev and Keller, gently addressed the already gray-haired and stout gentleman standing at the top of the steps, flanked by several others, and invited him to do him the honor of visiting him. The gentleman was taken aback, but nonetheless went in; so did another, and another.

From the crowd, about seven or eight visitors were selected, who made their way in, trying to do so as inconspicuously as possible; but there were no more eager beavers, and soon, within the crowd, people began to criticize the latecomers. The invited guests were seated, the conversation began, tea was served – all was extremely polite and dignified, to the surprise of the newcomers. There were, of course, a few attempts to sidetrack the conversation and steer it towards the "correct" topic; a few impertinent questions were asked, and some "lively" remarks were made. The prince answered everyone simply and hospitably, yet with such dignity and trust in the integrity of his guests, that the impertinent questions subsided on their own. Gradually, the conversation became almost serious.

One gentleman, attached to his words, suddenly swore in great indignation that he would not sell his estate, no matter what happened, that he would wait and see, and that "enterprises are better than money"; "well, your excellence, that is my economic system, you can learn about it." Since he was addressing the prince, the prince warmly praised him, despite Lebedev whispering in his ear that this gentleman had neither a farthing nor a patch of land, and never had any estate. Almost an hour passed, tea was drunk, and eventually the guests began to feel ashamed to stay any longer. The doctor and the gray-haired gentleman warmly bid farewell to the prince; and all the others bid farewell with equal warmth and commotion. Lebedev, who was quite "ready," sighed and said, "I concealed my wisdom from the wise and intelligent, and revealed it to children; I said this about him before, but now I add that God has saved him from the abyss, and all the saints have saved him!"

The prince left the church, seeming calm and cheerful; at least, many people noticed and later told about it. It appeared that he wanted to hurry home and be left alone as soon as possible, but this was not allowed to him. Some of the invited guests entered the room, including Pitygin, Gavril Ardalionovich, and the doctor, who did not seem disposed to leave. Besides, the whole house was literally besieged by idle crowds. From the balcony, the prince still heard Kuznetsov and Leshin engaged in a fierce argument with several completely unknown, though on the face of it respectable, people who were extremely eager to enter the balcony. The prince approached the disputants, inquired as to what the matter was, and, politely extricating Leshin and Kuznetsov, delicately turned to a rather old and stout gentleman, standing at the head of several other hopefuls on the porch, and invited him to do him the honor of visiting him. The gentleman blushed, but still went; another, the third followed. From the crowd, a handful of guests – seven or eight – were found, and they entered, trying to do so as unobtrusively as possible; but more enthusiasts were not to be found, and soon the crowd began to censure those who were pushing to the front. The newcomers were seated, conversation began, tea was served, all of which was extremely dignified, restrained, and, surprisingly, somewhat astonishing to the guests. There were, of course, several attempts to provoke a conversation and steer it onto "the appropriate" topic; several impertinent questions were uttered, and several "witty" remarks were made. The prince answered everyone so simply and kindly, yet with such dignity and such trust in the decency of his guests, that the impertinent questions subsided of their own accord. Gradually, the conversation began to become almost serious. One gentleman, clinging to a word, suddenly swore, with extreme indignation, that he would not sell the estate, no matter what happened; on the contrary, he would wait and see, and that "enterprise is better than money"; "there – that, Your Highness, is my economic system – you can see –". As he was addressing the prince, the prince warmly praised him, despite Leshin whispering in his ear that this gentleman had neither estate nor land and never had any. Almost an hour passed, the tea was finished, and after the tea, the guests finally felt ashamed to stay any longer. The doctor and the old gentleman said farewell to the prince with fervor; and everyone else bid farewell with fervor and noise. There were expressions of good wishes and opinions, such as "there's no need to grieve and that, perhaps, it's all for the best," and so on. There were, indeed, attempts to ask for champagne, but the elder guests stopped the younger ones. When all had left, Kuznetsov leaned over to Leshin and told him: "We would have started a row, fought, embarrassed ourselves, called the police; and he, on the other hand, has won new friends for himself, and such friends! I know them!" Leshin, who was quite "on the ready," sighed and said: "He kept the wise and the sensible hidden, and revealed himself to the foolish; I have been saying this about him even before, but now I add that even the very child was saved from the abyss, preserved by God, and all his saints!"

His appearance on the ball produced an extraordinary effect. Everything converged on him, whoever had cards in their hands, whoever was at the most interesting point of conversation, would exclaim: "The lower zemstvo authority responds to this..." but as for what the zemstvo authority responds, he tossed that aside and hurried to greet our hero. "Pavel Ivanovich! Ah, Lord above, Pavel Ivanovich! Dear Pavel Ivanovich! The most honorable Pavel Ivanovich! My soul, Pavel Ivanovich! There you are, Pavel Ivanovich! There he is, our Pavel Ivanovich! Allow me to shake your hand, Pavel Ivanovich! Come on, I'll kiss him more firmly, my dear Pavel Ivanovich!" Chichikov felt himself embraced by a dozen men in one instant. He had hardly extricated himself from the grip of the chairman, when he was already being hugged by the police master; the police master handed him over to the inspector of the health administration; the inspector of the health administration - to the tax collector; the tax collector - to the architect... The governor, who was standing near the ladies and held in one hand a fancy ticket and in the other a bolonka, saw him and flung ticket and bolonka to the floor; the little dog howled; in short, he spread an extraordinary joy and revelry. Not a single face showed a lack of pleasure, or at least reflected the general delight. This is how the faces of officials look during an inspection by the arriving chief of their administration: after the first fright had passed, they saw that he liked many things and he himself had finally started to joke, that is, to say a few pleasant words with a pleasant smile. The officials surrounding him laughed at this, laughed twice as much; those who had not quite caught the words he said laughed from the heart; and finally, a policeman standing far away near the exit, who had never laughed in his whole life and had just shown the crowd his fist, and who, by the laws of reflection, expressed on his face some kind of a smile, although this smile looked as if someone was about to sneeze after a strong cigar. Our hero responded to everyone and everything and felt an extraordinary agility: he bowed to the right and left as usual, slightly to the side, but completely freely, and so he captivated everyone. The ladies surrounded him with a dazzling garland and brought with them whole clouds of all sorts of fragrances: one breathed roses, another smelled of spring and violets, the third was suffused with the scent of iris; Chichikov raised his nose and sniffed. Their outfits were in great taste: muslins, silks, and gauzes were of such pale fashionable colors that even their names could not be mentioned (the taste had gone so far). Lacing and flower bouquets fluttered here and there on their dresses in a picturesque disorder, although a lot of decent people worked to achieve this disorder. A light hat was perched on their heads, and it seemed to say: "I'll fly away, what a pity that I don't take the beauty with me!" Waists were cinched and had the most robust and pleasant forms (it's worth noting that all the ladies of the city of N were somewhat plump, but they were cinched so skillfully and had such pleasant manners that it was impossible to notice their plumpness). Everything about them had been thought out and provided with extraordinary caution; the necks and shoulders were bared just as much as needed, and no more; each one revealed their assets up to the point where they believed they could kill a person with them; the rest was hidden with exquisite taste: either a lightweight ribbon tie, or a scarf as light as a pastry called "kiss", ethereally embracing the neck, or the little toothed frames from a thin batiste, known as "modesty", were released from under the dresses. These "modesties" hid in front and behind what was already unable to kill a person, but at the same time they made one suspect that it was precisely what lay hidden. Long gloves were not worn all the way up the sleeves, but were thoughtfully left with the erogenous parts of the hands visible above the elbow, which were full of seductive plumpness at many; some even burst through the cuffs, pushed on by the need to move further - in short, it seemed as if everywhere it was written: no, this is not a province, this is a capital, this is Paris! Only here and there a familiar peasant cap or even a barely seen peacock feather would occasionally stick out in defiance of all fashions, according to personal taste. But it's impossible without this, it's the peculiarity of a provincial town: it will always break out somewhere. Chichikov stood before them, thinking: "Which writer of this letter is that?" - and he was just about to stick out his nose, when a whole row of elbows, cuffs, sleeves, ends of ribbons, scented kerchiefs, and dresses jerked him by the nose. But our hero was already middle-aged, with the kind of cautious and tranquil temperament that sometimes comes with experience. He, too, thought, but his thoughts were not without a positive side, nor were they as shallow and chaotic as those of a certain someone. 'What a lovely girl!' he said, opening his snuffbox and inhaling the scent of snuff. 'But what's really good about her? It's that she's just been released from some boarding school or institute, so she hasn't yet developed that womanly way of being, which is precisely the most unpleasant thing about them. She's still like a child, everything is simple in her, she'll say whatever comes to her mind, laugh whenever she feels like it, and where she wants to laugh. You can make her into a miracle or a disaster, and she may well turn out to be a disaster! Now let the mother-in-laws and aunts take hold of her! In a year, they'll fill her to the brim with all that womanish nonsense, so that her own father won't recognize her. Where will she get that air of self-importance, that stiffness, that squirming about on the path laid out for her, that preoccupation with trying to figure out what to say, to whom, how often, and to whom to look? She'll be constantly afraid of saying too much, get herself all tangled up, and in the end she'll end up lying her whole life through, and she'll turn out to be God knows what!' He paused for a moment and then added: 'It's intriguing to wonder whose she is. What kind of father does she have? Is he a wealthy landowner with a respectable demeanor, or a sober-minded man with a capital earned through service? If we were to, say, give this girl a dowry of two hundred thousand roubles, she might turn out to be a very tasty morsel indeed. That would be a happy circumstance for an ordinary man.' The two hundred thousand roubles had by now become so tantalizing in his head that he began to scold himself inwardly for not inquiring about the occupants of the carriages as he was fussing about the equipage, and soon the village of Sobakovich distracted him and made him turn back to his usual preoccupation.

The traveler dragged a tiger along the way and said to the Master: "Father, let you sit for a while, and I will take off his clothes and put them on and then walk." The monk said: "Where does he have any clothes?" The traveler said: "Don't bother about that, I will take care of it myself." The Monkey King pulled out a single hair from his body, blew a puff of divine breath, and shouted "Transform!" and transformed it into a sharp goat-horned knife that he used to open the tiger's abdomen, peel off its skin, chop off its claws, and sever its head, then cut out a square piece of skin from the tiger's body and picked it up and measured it saying: "It's a bit wide, it could be made into two pieces." He took up the knife and cut it into two pieces. He put one piece away and wrapped the other piece around his waist, then plucked a strand of vine from the side of the road and tightly bound it around him to cover his lower body and said: "Father, go ahead! Go ahead! When we get to the village, we can borrow some needles and thread and sew it on later." He then took the iron club, rolled it between his palms and it looked just like a needle again, and put it away in his ear. He picked up his luggage, put it on his back, and invited the Master to mount his horse.

Yesterday morning there was the prince at my place. By the way, he convinced me to move to his dacha. I knew he would insist on it, and I was sure he would come out and say straight out that it would be "easier to die among people and trees" as he puts it. But today he didn't say "die," but rather "it will be easier to live," which, however, is almost the same for me in my situation. I asked him what he means by his constant "trees" and why he keeps pushing them on me, and was surprised to learn from him that I had supposedly said the other night that I had come to Pavlovsk for the last time to look at the trees. When I noticed him that it's all the same to die under the trees or staring at my bricks out the window, and that I don't need to fuss over it for two weeks, he instantly agreed; but in his opinion, the greenery and fresh air will undoubtedly bring about some physical change in me, and my anxiety and dreams will change and possibly become easier. I remarked to him with a smile that he's speaking like a materialist. He replied with his smile that he's always been a materialist. Since he never lies, these words must mean something. His smile is nice; I looked at it more closely now. I don't know if I love or hate him now; I don't have the time to fuss over it now. My five-month-old hatred for him has been slowly dying down over the last month. Who knows, maybe I came to Pavlovsk, mainly to see him. But... why did I leave my room? A man condemned to death shouldn't leave his corner, and if I hadn't made up my mind and had instead decided to wait until the last minute, I would certainly not have left my room for anything and wouldn't have accepted the offer to move to his dacha "to die" in Pavlovsk.

When the Monkey King heard this, his heart was filled with joy, and he said, "I shall leave you all and descend the mountain tomorrow, and journey to the farthest seas and distant lands, to search for these three beings and learn from them how to live forever young and avoid the troubles of the Lord of Hell." Tomorrow we'll climb over the mountain, search for some fruits, set up a grand feast to send off the Great King."

Eternity had already cast a dark wing over him. We would often spend hours in silence at night – occasionally, the dozing Mameluke Roustam would snore in the next room; the man was an incredibly heavy sleeper. "But he is loyal to me and the dynasty," Napoleon would say about him. Once I felt excruciating pain, and then he noticed the tears in my eyes; he looked at me with pity: "You pity me! – he cried out – you, a child, and perhaps another child, my son, the King of Rome, will pity me too; all the others hate me, and my brothers will betray me in my misfortune!" I wept and flung myself at him; and he could no longer hold back; we clasped each other, and our tears mingled. "Write a letter to Empress Josephine!" I sobbed at him. Napoleon shuddered, thought for a moment, and then said to me: "You reminded me of the third heart that loves me; thank you, my friend!" He sat down immediately and wrote that letter to Josephine, which was dispatched to Constantine the very next day.

Eternity already shrouded him in its dark wing. Sometimes at night we would spend hours in silence – Roustam, the mameluke, would snore in the adjacent room, he slept so soundly. "At least he is loyal to me and the dynasty," Napoleon would say about him. One time it pained me deeply, and suddenly he noticed the tears in my eyes; he looked at me with pity: "You're sorry for me!" he shouted, "You, a child, and maybe another child, my son, le roi de Rome, will pity me too! All the others hate me, and my brothers would sell me into misfortune first!" I burst into tears and flung myself at him; then he didn't hold back either; we hugged each other, and our tears mixed. "Write, write a letter to Empress Josephine!" I sobbed to him. Napoleon twitched, thought, and said to me, "You reminded me of the third heart that loves me; thank you, my friend!" Then he sat down and wrote that letter to Josephine, which was sent off to Constant the very next day.

Eternity itself was already casting a dark shadow over him. Sometimes, at night, we would spend hours in silence; Roustam the Mameluke would be snoring in the neighboring room – that man slept incredibly soundly. "At least he is loyal to me and the dynasty," Napoleon would say about him. One time, it hurt me terribly, and suddenly he noticed the tears in my eyes; he looked at me with compassion: "You feel sorry for me!" he cried out, "You, a child, and maybe, perhaps, another child, my son, the King of Rome [27]; they all hate me, and my brothers will be the first to betray me in misfortune!" I sobbed and threw myself at him; then he couldn't hold it in; we hugged each other, and our tears mixed together. "Write, write a letter to Empress Josephine!" I sobbed at him. Napoleon shuddered, thought for a moment, and said to me: "You reminded me of the third heart that loves me; thank you, my friend!" And at once he sat down and wrote that letter to Josephine, which was sent off the very next day to Constant.

Eternity was already spreading its dark wings over him. Sometimes, at night, we would spend hours in silence, alone – my mother, Roustam, would snore away in the next room; he slept incredibly soundly. "But he is loyal to me and to the dynasty," Napoleon would say about him. I was once acutely hurt, and suddenly he noticed the tears in my eyes; he looked at me with compassion: "You pity me! – he shouted – you, child, and perhaps even another child, my son, the king of Rome; [27] the rest all hate me, and my brothers would sell me out for misfortune!" I burst into tears and threw myself at him; then he could not hold back; we hugged each other, and our tears mingled. "Write, write a letter to Empress Joséphine!" I sobbed at him. Napoleon shuddered, thought, and said to me: "You reminded me of the third heart that loves me; thank you, my friend!" He then sat down and wrote that letter to Joséphine, which was sent to Constant the very next day.

Eternity was already casting its dark shadow over him. Sometimes, late at night, we would spend hours in silence; Mameluk Rustan would snore in the neighboring room, the man slept soundly, really. 'At least he is loyal to me and the dynasty,' Napoleon would say of him. Once, it pained me terribly, and suddenly he noticed tears in my eyes; he looked at me with compassion: 'You pity me!' he exclaimed, 'You, a child, and perhaps another child, my son, le roi de Rome[27], will pity me too; all the others hate me, and my brothers will betray me in misfortune!' I wept and flung myself at him; then he gave in; we hugged each other, and our tears mingled. 'Write, write a letter to Empress Joséphine!' I sobbed at him. Napoleon shuddered, thought, and said to me: 'You reminded me of a third heart that loves me; thank you, my friend!' Then he sat down and wrote that letter to Joséphine, with which Constantine was sent the next day.

Thousands of imperial officers stood in order, their halberds arrayed before and behind, their long banners aligned to the sides. Golden halberds and war axes stood in pairs, and bright silk candles and incense burners stood in pairs. The dragon and phoenix danced in the air, and the mandarin ducks and eagles fluttered about. The sage and virtuous Son of Heaven sat upright, surrounded by loyal and righteous ministers. The prosperity of the thousand-year dynasty surpassed that of Shun and Yu, and the peace of the ten-thousand-year reign excelled that of Yao and Tang.

There, a majestic parasol, a dragon-robe, and radiant lights shone; a jade circlet, a colorful fan, and auspicious clouds fluttered. A crown of jewels, a belt of jade, and a purple cord adorned with golden characters. A thousand squadrons of guards escorted the carriage, and the attendants formed two rows on either side. The Emperor bathed in piety and reverence, devoutly worshiping the Buddha, surrendering to the blessings of merit and rejoicing in the scent of incense. The Tang King's imperial carriage arrived early at the temple, instructing the musicians to sound their instruments, and alighting from the carriage, he led many officials into the temple. They paid homage to the Buddha and took up incense.

After three circumambulations, he looked up and saw that it was a grand assembly of Buddhist practitioners, and behold: the parasols and banners danced in the air, and the precious parasol's radiant light shone bright. The parasols and banners danced in the air, casting a kaleidoscope of colors, and the precious parasol's light shone bright, reflecting the sun's rays in a burst of red lightning. The Buddha's golden body appeared majestic and serene, and the Bodhisattvas' jade complexion was awe-inspiring. The bottles held lotus flowers, and the incense burners burned sandalwood. The bottles held lotus flowers, and the intricately embroidered trees shone with jewels, filling the entire sanctuary; the incense burners burned sandalwood, filling the air with a fragrant mist that ascended to the heavens.

Fresh fruits were arrayed on a red plate, and rare pastries piled high on a colorful table. The high-ranking monks recited the true scriptures, praying that the lonely spirits might be freed from suffering. The Supreme Emperor Taizong and his Wuwen both took up incense and bowed to the Buddha's golden body, and then bowed to the Bodhisattvas. Then he saw the Grand Master Xuanzang, who led the monks to pay homage to the Tang King. After the rituals, they divided into ranks and took their seats for meditation. The Master presented a scroll of scriptures to the Supreme Emperor, which read: "The virtue is profound and boundless, and the Chan school is extinct. The pure and luminous reality pervades the three realms. The myriad transformations and changes are unified and controlled by the yin and yang. The substance and function are always true and unchanged, and have no limits. Observing the lonely spirits, one should feel deep compassion. In accordance with the Supreme Emperor's sacred command, I hereby select and gather the monks to study Chan and propagate the teachings. I widely open the gate of expedience and operate the ship of mercy, rescuing the multitudes of living beings from the sea of suffering, freeing them from the hells of the six paths. I invite them to return to the true path, and enable them to exercise their own free will. With this good cause, I invite the blessings of the Celestial Vairocana; with this great success, I will escape the hells and the mundane world. I shall ascend to the blissful realm and roam freely, going and coming as I please. The poem says: 'One lamp of eternal incense fragrance, several volumes of transcendental decree. There are no bounds to the wonderful Dharma, and no limits to the blessings of heaven. The karmic debts are all eradicated, and the lonely spirits are all freed from prison. May I protect my people and bring peace to my kingdom, and may we have prosperity for ten thousand years.'"

The Supreme Emperor looked at the scroll with a heart full of joy and said to the monks: "You uphold the true principle, and do not be remiss in your respect for the Buddha. Wait until the work is completed and perfected, and you will all attain your own destinies. I will reward you generously, and will not waste your efforts." The thousand two hundred monks all bowed their heads in gratitude.

Thousand officials in ceremonial attire march in procession, in front and behind, five imperial guards with their banners held to the left and right, double and pair by pair. They bear golden halberds and wields axes, while red silken lanterns and ritual incense smoke wafts, a majestic sight. Dragons dance and phoenixes flutter, falcons rise and eagles soar. The sage and enlightened emperor ascends to his throne, accompanied by loyal and righteous ministers, worthy of emulating the benevolent Shun and Yu of the past, and surpassing Yao and Tang in their achievement of an enduring peace. Then behold, a magnificent parasol with a winding rope, the dragon's robes aglow, radiant light beams forth. A jade belt and a phoenix fan, with auspicious mist floating, and a bejeweled sash and a gold seal. A thousand attendants in formation, two rows to escort the carriage.

The emperor, devoted and pious, bathes in the revered and venerated presence of the Buddha, takes refuge in the wholesome blessings and delight in grasping incense. The great emperor's carriage, led by the emperor himself, arrives at the temple early, and orders the music to be stopped, dismounts, and enters, accompanied by many officials. Bowing to the Buddha and grasping incense. After three circuits, he raises his head and surveys the scene, and, indeed, the site is magnificent, with parasols and banners swaying in the air, the precious umbrella glowing with radiance. Parasols and banners swaying in the air, producing a kaleidoscope of colored mist, the precious umbrella radiating splendor, shining brightly with reflected light. The Buddha's golden form, like a vision of great beauty, appears in all its glory, the arhats with their jade countenances resplendent with vigor and sternness. An ewer containing fragrant flowers of the gods, an incense burner with sandalwood smoke wafting. The ewer containing fragrant flowers of the gods, with ornate trees shining brightly on the sacred grounds, the incense burner with sandalwood smoke wafting, permeating the clear expanse with fragrance. Fresh fruits of the season arranged on a vermilion platter, a colorful assortment of sweets piled on a dish. High-ranking monks chant the true sutras, praying that the lone souls be liberated from suffering and woe. The emperor and empress, skilled in both martial and literary arts, together take incense and bow before the Buddha's golden body, pay homage to the arhats. Then behold, the Venerable Xuanzang, the patriarch of the bodhisattvas, leads the assembly of monks in paying homage to the Tang emperor. The ceremony concluded, they return to their meditation seats, and the patriarch presents to the emperor a report on the salvational mission, which reads: "In the boundless expanse of mercy, the dharma is obscure, the mystic mantra is lost. Purity and clarity are manifest, pervading the three realms. A thousand changes, a million transformations, all phenomena are subsumed within the unity of yin and yang. This true and constant reality is beyond all limits. Looking upon that lone soul, it is deeply worthy of pity. By the imperial edict of the sage emperor: 'Gather the monks, and instruct them in the dharma, open the gate of mercy, and ferry the masses across the sea of suffering. Free them from the torments of the six paths, and lead them back to the path of truth. Bring them joy and liberation, and have them wander at will in the world beyond the veil of ignorance.' It is written in verse: 'One bowl of eternal incense, a few volumes of the sutras for rebirth. No bounds to the subtle dharma, no limits to the blessings of heaven. The accumulated karmic debt is erased, and all the lone souls are freed from prison. I pray that our country will be preserved, peaceful and prosperous for a thousand years.' The emperor read the report with joy in his heart, and to the assembly of monks, he said: 'You have grasped the essence, and diligently attend to the Buddha's teachings. Wait until your mission is accomplished and your work is complete, and you will all return to your former homes, and I will reward you generously, without leaving any empty-handed.'" The one thousand two hundred and forty monks, bowed their heads in unison in gratitude.

The imperial processions, numbering in the thousands, approached from the front and rear, their pennants and banners arrayed on either side. Carrying halberds and war axes, two by two, they stood steadfast; while crimson silk lanterns, emitting fragrant incense from their porcelain lamps, cast an eerie glow. Dragons danced in the air, while phoenixes spread their wings, their plumes fluttering in the breeze. Beneath the majestic attire of the emperor, embroidered with auspicious signs, were numerous vassals; his soldiers, numbering in the thousands, formed a cordon to protect him. The emperor, after bathing with sincere devotion and reverence for the Buddha, had converted to the path of good fortune, delighted in holding the fragrant incense. 

The King of Tang, with his grand procession, arrived early at the temple, instructing the musicians to sound their instruments and dismounting from his carriage, with many officials attending him. He paid homage to the Buddha, incense in hand. Upon finishing three circuits, he lifted his head to gaze, and lo, the temple was indeed an ideal site for spiritual practice; the banners and streamers danced in the air, their colorful silk flags fluttering in the wind; the ornate umbrellas shone with a resplendent glow, casting a brilliant sheen as they mirrored the sun. The Venerable One's golden countenance shone radiantly; the wise and virtuous bodhisattvas displayed their jade-like faces, their faces aglow with a fierce intensity. Incense sticks were inserted into vases, while fragrant incense burnt in the censer, filling the air with aromatic wisps; the incense sticks in the vases emitted an ethereal glow, their fragrance wafting up through the clear heavens; and the plates stacked with fresh fruits, colored sugar-coated pastries, and other delicacies on the altar, formed a majestic sight. The high-ranking monks stood in line to recite the true scriptures, praying for the liberation of the lost souls and their deliverance from suffering. The Emperor of Zhou and the King of Wu, each holding incense sticks, paid homage to the Buddha, then approached the bodhisattvas. And behold, the Grand Expositor, Master Xuanzang, led the monks in paying homage to the King of Tang. Having finished their obeisance, the monks took their seats in ranks, and the Master presented to the Emperor a scroll with the terms of the imperial edict, which read: "The utmost virtue is limitless and vast; the Chan school lies in stillness and quietude; the realm of spirit is pure and unobstructed, flowing through the three realms. All phenomena and transformations are unified, with the underlying principle ever-present and without bounds. Beholding those lost souls, it is deeply lamentable to see their sufferings. I hereby command the assembly: to gather monks and instruct them in Chan teachings, to open the gate of expedients, to ferry the myriad creatures in their wisdom, and to rescue those lost in the sea of suffering, releasing them from the cycle of birth and death. Lead them back to the true path, and let them explore the boundless mysteries; to have no action and no movement, and to become unadulterated and refined. Resting on this auspicious cause, I shall bestow benevolence from the Clear Capital's red gate; riding the currents of this auspicious moment, I shall have the blessings of the heavens. May I ascend to the Blissful Land, roam at will in the West, and enjoy the happiness without bounds." The Emperor of Zhou composed a poem in praise, saying: "One cauldron of long-lasting incense, and a few scrolls that bring birth to the living; limitless wondrous Dharma is proclaimed, endless blessings shower from the heavens. The crimes are all expunged, and all lost souls are freed from prison." The Emperor, having read the edict with great satisfaction, turned to the monks and said, "You, monks, stand firm in your convictions, and do not take things lightly in your reverence for the Buddha. When the task is accomplished and completed, each of you will have your own return; and I shall reward you accordingly, and not let your efforts go unrewarded." All one thousand two hundred monks bowed their heads in gratitude, offering thanks.

A thousand officials in ranked order, their badges of office arranged in order of precedence, the five escorts with their ensigns standing on either side. They carried golden gourds and axes, paired in perfect harmony; the crimson silk lanterns and the smoke of the incense burner swayed in the air. Dragons danced and phoenixes fluttered, peacocks spread their tails and eagles spread their wings. The majestic and wise emperor, with his virtuous and loyal ministers, were worthy of emulating the great reigns of Shun and Yu, rivaling the glorious era of Yao and Tang. Then I see that vermilion parasol, the dragon's majestic gown, radiating resplendent light. The jade ring and the phoenix fan fluttered and wafted, like lotus flowers blooming in paradise. The crown of pearls, the sash of jade, the golden seal. The escort troops numbering a thousand, the bearers of the palanquin in two rows.

This emperor, devoutly and respectfully bathing, took refuge in the Buddha, devoutly picking up the incense stick. The Tang king's magnificent carriage arrived early at the temple, and he ordered the music to strike up and the drums to roll; he descended from the carriage, and led a procession of numerous officials, paid respects to the Buddha, and picked up the incense stick. After three circuits, he lifted his head to behold the scene, and behold: the parasols and banners fluttered and danced, the golden umbrellas radiated brilliant light. The parasols and banners fluttered and danced, the colorful rainbows swaying in mid-air, the golden umbrellas radiating brilliant light, illuminating the red lights in the bright sunlight. The Lord Buddha's majestic form was perfectly clear, the image of the arhats' jade complexion was dignified and awe-inspiring. The vase inserted heavenly flowers, the censer emitted fragrant sandalwood smoke. The vase inserted heavenly flowers, the jade trees shining brightly across the precious mountain; the censer emitted fragrant sandalwood smoke, the incense wafting through the clear heavens. The newly prepared offerings were placed in a vermilion dish, various types of sugar-coated pastries piled high on the colorful tray. The high-ranking monks recited the true scripture, wishing to liberate the lonely spirits from suffering. Emperor Taizong and his generals, both holding the incense sticks, paid respects to the Buddha's golden body, and visited the arhats. I also saw the Great Master Xuanzang, leading the assembly of monks in paying respects to the Tang king. After the ceremony, the monks took their seats in their respective positions, and the Master presented to Taizong a scroll of merit, inscribed with the following words: "The Venerable's virtue is vast and far-reaching; the Chan tradition is extinguished in stillness. The pure and divine intellect pervades the three realms; all transformations and changes are unified and comprehended by the unity of yin and yang. The true and constant is without bounds and extremes. Beholding this lonely spirit, one is deeply moved by compassion. In obedience to the Imperial Edict, I select the monks and have them study Chan and preach the law. Open the gates of Expediency, spread the boat of compassion, rescue the suffering masses, and deliver them from the suffering of the six paths. Lead them back to the path of truth, and have them enjoy the pleasures of the western paradise. Let all stop their activities, and let their minds be in stillness. Relying on this good deed, we will invite blessings from the clear and purple capital; seize the opportunity of our victory, and escape the hell of mundane suffering. Let us ascend to the heavenly abode, and wander at will in the western paradise. The poem says: 'The ever-lasting incense of the furnace, a few scrolls that transcend the mundane scriptures. No bounds to the wondrous laws, no limits to the blessings from heaven.' All karmic debts are cleared, and the lonely spirits are released from prison. May we protect our nation, and bring peace and blessings to our ancestors for ten thousand years.'"

Taizong gazed upon the scroll with joy, and said to the assembly of monks, "You have fulfilled your duties with sincerity, and should not be remiss in your duties to the Buddha. Wait until the task is accomplished and completed, and each of you will have a place to return to; I will then reward you generously, and will not have labored in vain." One thousand and two hundred monks, with their heads bowed, expressed their gratitude.

Thousand officials arranged their official seals in front and behind, and the Five Guards arrayed their flags on the sides. Gold hooks and axes were held in pairs, with crimson silk lanterns and fragrance from the censor, veiling the altar in a misty splendor. Dragons danced in the air, and phoenixes fluttered about. The celestial emperor, resplendent and just, sat at the head; his virtuous and loyal officials stood around him, illuminating the court like Shun and Yu, casting a glory that surpassed Yao and Tang.

He beheld the imperial parasol, the dragon robes, and the radiant light that shot forth; the jade pendants, the fans with phoenix feathers, and the auspicious mist that wafted about. The jade crowns, the jasper sashes, and the golden insignia adorned him; the guards numbered a thousand and surrounded him; the bearers of the imperial litter walked by his side.

The emperor, with a devout and respectful attitude, bathed himself in reverence before the Buddha, and in homage, he lit incense. The Tang king arrived in his majesty, arriving at the temple in good time, ordering the music to begin and the drums to beat; he dismounted from his carriage and had the officials follow him. He bowed before the Buddha, taking incense in hand.

Three circuits around the Buddha finished, he lifted his head to behold, and indeed, the consecrated site was a wondrous sight; and he saw that banners and pennants fluttered and danced in the air, and that the gemstone parasols radiated a brilliant light. Banners and pennants fluttered and danced, casting a kaleidoscope of colors across the void; gemstone parasols radiated a brilliant light, reflecting the sun's vibrant colors.

The World Honored One's divine form was resplendent, his jade-like complexion fierce and profound; the Buddha's robes were arrayed with lotus flowers, the censor's incense was fragrant and perfumed. The lotus flowers inserted into the vases cast a colorful glow across the realm of enlightenment; the incense wafting from the censor transversed the clear heavens. Fresh fruits were arranged in an order of elegance on the vermilion plates, while various types of sugar paste were heaped upon the colorful table.

The high monks recited the sacred scriptures, making the wish for the liberation of the solitary soul from suffering; the Emperor Taizong, with his martial and civil virtues, all taking incense in hand, bowed before the Buddha's body, and offered obeisance to the Buddhas; they participated in the lecture on the Buddhist doctrine. He saw the great translator Xuanzang, the master, standing before the throne, leading the assembly of monks in bowing to the Tang king. After the rites were completed, the monks divided into ranks and took their seats in meditation. The master presented to the Emperor Taizong a scroll with an edict for his benevolence, which read: "The virtue of compassion is boundless, the Buddhist teaching is obscured. Spiritual purity and insight penetrate the three realms. The myriad forms and transformations are all under His control. His essence is eternal and unchanging, limitless in extent. He sees this solitary soul, and it is deeply pitiful; I, by the Emperor's sacred decree, shall gather the monks and teach the doctrine. I shall open the gate of compassion and cast a vast net of loving-kindness to save the masses from suffering. I shall rescue all those trapped in the cycle of birth and death, free them from the hellis, and bring them to the ultimate path. I shall invite them to join the ranks of the celestial beings, and I shall ascend to the Heavenly Palace. I shall ascend to the highest heaven and go as I please. The poem says: One incense burns for eternal life, a few scrolls bear the symbols of transcending mortality. No bounds of the sublime teaching are reached, no limits of heaven's blessings are bound. All grievances are wiped away, and all solitary souls are freed. May I protect my kingdom and bring peace and blessings for ten thousand years."

Emperor Taizong, with a happy heart, looked upon the monks and said, "You, who stand by my side, uphold the essence of our faith; do not be remiss in your duties towards the Buddha. Wait until the task is completed and perfected, and then you shall each return to your proper realm, and I shall reward you, not in vain." The one thousand two hundred monks, as one, bowed their heads in gratitude.

Are you, Russia, like that swift, unbeatable trio that's sweeping by? The road is shrouded in smoke beneath you, the bridges thunder, and everything that's lagging behind stays far behind. The awestruck onlooker has stopped, frozen in wonder: is that a lightning bolt that's been cast down from heaven? What does this terrifying movement signify? What unseen force lies hidden in these unknown steeds bathed in light? Oh, horses, horses, what horses are you? Whirlwinds do they hold in their manes? Does every fibre of your skin tingle with an acute ear? You caught the familiar melody from on high, instantly tensed your bronze chests and, barely touching the ground with your hooves, turned into a line of stretched figures flying through the air, and all inspired by god, you're speeding along! Russia, where are you racing to? She doesn't give an answer. A wondrous peal echoes through the bell; the air, torn apart by the wind, is shattering into pieces; everything on earth is flying by, and, glancing sideways, other nations and states are dodging out of her way, giving her the road.

Are you not, Russia, a swift and uncatchable trio tearing along? The road fumes beneath you, the bridges thunder, all lag behind and fall far behind. A stricken beholder stopped in wonder at the divine marvel: is this not lightning cast from the heavens? What does this awe-inspiring movement mean? And what unseen force is contained within these incomprehensible light steeds? Oh, horses, horses, what horses! Whirlwinds sit in your manes, does a sensitive ear throb in every vein of yours? You caught the familiar tune from far away, harmoniously and at once tensed your copper chests and, almost not touching the earth with your hooves, turned into stretched lines flying through the air, and the god-inspired whole races on! Russia, where are you rushing to? Give an answer. Gives none. A heavenly clang resounds from the bell; the air is torn apart by the wind and shatters into pieces; everything that exists on earth flies by, and the other nations and states glance, make way for it and give it a path.

Are you not, Russia, the swift, unbeatable troika dashing on? The road smokes beneath you, the bridges resound, all lag behind and remain behind. The wonder-struck observer halted: is it a lightning bolt flung from the heavens? What does this terrifying motion mean? What unknown force is contained in these unknown horses imbued with light? Ah, horses, horses, what horses are these! Are whirlwinds lodged in your manes? Does a sensitive ear burn in every strand of your hair? You caught the familiar tune from afar, all synchronized and tensed your bronze chests and, almost touching the ground with your hooves, transformed into stretched lines flying through the air, and the inspired-by-God procession rushes on... Russia, where are you speeding to? Give an answer. The wonder-struck one does not give an answer. A miraculous chime echoes, the air is shattered into shreds by a gust of wind; everything on the earth flies by, and, catching sight of you, other peoples and states glance and give you the road.

Are you not, Russia, a swift, untamed trio racing on? The road smokes beneath you, bridges resound, all lag behind and remain in the distance. The awestruck beholder has halted, wondering: is it lightning from the heavens? What does this dreadful movement signify? What unknown force is contained within these enigmatic horses? Oh, horses, horses, what horses are you! Are whirlwinds lodged in your manes? Does a sensitive ear burn in every strand of your hair? You caught the familiar song from afar, drew taut your metal breasts, and, barely touching the earth with your hooves, transformed into stretched lines, flying through the air, and sped along, inspired by the divine... Russia, where are you hurrying to? She gives no answer. A magical ringing peals through the bell; the air is shattered, torn into pieces by the wind; all that is on earth flies past, and, gazing on, other nations and states glance aside and give her passage.

Are you not, Russia, the speedy, uncatchable triad rushing on? The road is veiled in smoke beneath you, bridges rumble, and all falls behind, left in the dust. A dumbfounded beholder, struck by the divine wonder, stops: is it a lightning bolt cast down from heaven? what does this spellbinding movement portend? and what invisible force is contained within those unknown horses whose coats shine with an unknown light? Ah, horses, horses, what horses! Are whirlwinds nesting in your manes? Does your every nerve quiver with a sensitive ear? You have caught wind of a familiar melody from the heights, drawn together in unison, and stiffened your copper chests; without so much as touching the earth with your hooves, you have transformed into extended lines flying through the air, and a god-breathed whirlwind sweeps Russia along! Russia, where are you rushing to? Do not respond. The bell peals out with a divine clang; the air is rent asunder, splits into pieces, and rumbles with the wind; everything on earth is left flying by, and, gazing askance, other nations and lands part and give way.

— Come, let's go, it's a lovely evening! — shouted Evgeny Pavlovich. — But to prove to you that I'm speaking quite seriously this time, and mainly to prove it to the prince (you, prince, are particularly interesting to me, and I swear to you that I'm not such a completely empty person as I must necessarily seem to be — though I am an empty person in reality!), and... if you'll permit it, gentlemen, I'll pose the prince one last question, out of curiosity, and we'll put an end to it. This question came to me, as if on purpose, two hours ago (you see, prince, I sometimes ponder serious things too); I thought it over, but let's see what the prince has to say. Now they were talking about 'a private case'. This word is quite characteristic of us, one often hears it. Not long ago everyone was talking and writing about this awful murder of six people by that young man, and about the strange speech of the defense, in which it was said that it was natural for the poor defendant to have come up with killing those six people in his circumstances. This isn't literal, but the meaning seems to be either that or close to it. But in my personal opinion, the defense, declaring such a strange idea, was completely convinced that he was saying the most liberal, most humane, and most progressive thing one could say at the time. Well, so, in your opinion, is it an exaggeration of concepts and convictions, this possibility of such a twisted and remarkable view of the matter, is it a private case or a general one?

The charge is still leveled against the author by so-called patriots who sit quietly in the corners and engage in completely unrelated activities, amassing fortunes by manipulating the fate of others. But as soon as something happens that they consider to be an insult to the fatherland, some book appears where the bitter truth is occasionally mentioned. They come rushing out from all corners like spiders seeing a fly caught in their web and cry out: "Is it a good idea to bring this to light, to make it public? Is it good that all this is described here? Is it all our fault? And what will the foreigners think? Won't it be embarrassing to hear a bad opinion about oneself? Do they think it's not painful? Do they think they're patriots?" Such profound remarks, especially about foreign opinion, I confess, cannot be refuted. But why not this: two inhabitants lived in a remote corner of Russia. One was the family man, Kifa Mokiych, a man of a gentle disposition, who spent his life carelessly. He did not concern himself with his family; his existence was directed more towards the speculative side and occupied with the question he called "philosophical": "Look, for example, an animal is born unclothed," he would say as he walked around the room. "Why is it unclothed? Why not like a bird, why doesn't it hatch from an egg? How, I ask you, do you understand its nature the more you delve into it?" Such were the thoughts of the inhabitant Kifa Mokiych. But that is not the main thing. The other inhabitant was Mokiych Kifoich, his own son. He was what is known on Russia as a giant, and while his father was concerned with the birth of the animal, his twenty-year-old robust nature longed to break free. He was incapable of doing anything gently: either someone's hand would get scratched or a pustule would pop up on someone's nose. The entire household and neighborhood, from the kitchen maid to the kitchen dog, fled from him; even his bed in the bedroom was broken into pieces by him. Such was Mokiych Kifoich, but he had a good heart. But that is not the main thing. The main thing is that "Pity, master Kifa Mokiych, please," said the family and household help, both the master's and the neighbor's, "what are you doing with Mokiych Kifoich? Nobody finds peace with him; what a nuisance he is!" "Yes, he's a scamp, a scamp," replied his father usually. "But what's to be done? It's too late to scold him, and I'll be blamed for being cruel. He's a man of ambition, and if you rebuke him in front of someone else, he'll calm down. But the publicity is the trouble; if the town finds out, they'll call him a dog. What's the point, really? Do they think it hurts me? Do I not love my child? I'm too busy with philosophy and don't have time, so I'm not a father, I'm a father, by God, I'm a father! I have Mokiych Kifoich right here in my heart." Then Kifa Mokiych would hit himself hard on the chest with his fist and get all worked up. "If he turns out to be a dog, let it not be from me that he's exposed, let it not be me who brings it up." Having shown such a paternal feeling, he would let Mokiych Kifoich continue with his giant feats, and he would turn back to his favorite subject, posing himself some similar question: "Well, if an elephant were born from an egg, the shell would certainly be very thick, you wouldn't be able to knock it open with a bullet; you'd need to invent some new kind of gun." Thus lived the two inhabitants of the peaceful corner, who unexpectedly, like a window opening, burst out at the end of our poem to respond modestly to the accusations from some passionate patriots who, until now, have been quietly engaged in philosophy or accumulating funds for their beloved homeland, thinking not about not doing evil, but about not speaking about doing evil. But no, it is not patriotism or the first feeling that is the reason for the accusations; something else lies beneath. Who, if not the author, should tell the holy truth? You fear a deep, intent look, you are afraid to direct a deep look at anything, you like to slide over everything with indifferent eyes. You will even laugh at your heart at Chichikov, perhaps you'll even praise the author, saying: "However, he did manage to note something, he must be a cheerful person!" And after such words, with doubled pride, you'll turn to yourself, a self-satisfied smile will appear on your face, and you'll add: "And one has to agree, there are quite strange and comical people in some provinces, and scoundrels, no small ones at that!" But who among you, full of Christian humility, in the silence, alone, in moments of solitary conversation with yourself, will delve into your own soul this heavy question: "Is there perhaps a bit of Chichikov in me?" Ah, how not? Meanwhile, pass by during this time one of his acquaintances, a person of neither too high nor too low rank, he will immediately push his neighbor's arm and say to him, almost chuckling with laughter: "Look, look, there's Chichikov, Chichikov is walking!" And then, like a child, forgetting all decency, due to his station and age, will run after him, taunting him from behind and saying: "Chichikov! Chichikov! Chichikov!"

Emperor Taizong was startled and worried, and he nodded in secret, muttering to himself in sadness. Following the judges and the military marshal, he soon crossed the Nai River's cruel water and the realm of blood-filled cauldrons. We then arrived at the City of Wrongful Death, where we heard the hubbub of people shouting. It was clear that they said, "Li Shimin has come! Li Shimin has come!" He saw a group of ghosts with shoulders dragging and heads cut off, coming up to block his way, and calling out, "Give back our lives! Give back our lives!" The judge then instructed, "Take this gold and silver and divide it equally among yourselves, so you can let the Great Tang emperor pass, and he still has a long life ahead of him. Don't cause any more trouble." The ghosts heard this and, having received the gold and silver, all retreated in unison. The judge ordered the military marshal to shake the spirits' soul banners, leading the emperor out of the City of Wrongful Death and up the level road of Pingyang. They floated and drifted away, but it's still unknown which road they took to leave, and we will continue in the next chapter.

It was around that time, roughly when Surikov 'froze' the child, around mid-March, that I suddenly began to feel a great deal easier, and so it continued for two weeks. I started going out more frequently, mostly at dusk. I loved the March evenings when it started to freeze and the gaslights were lit; I'd often walk quite far. One day, in Six-Lavochkina Street, I was overtaken in the darkness by some "noble" person, whom I failed to recognize clearly; he was carrying something wrapped in paper and was dressed in a worn-out, out-of-season coat - it was quite easy to spot him. When he drew level with the lamp post, about ten steps ahead of me, I noticed something had slipped from his pocket. I hastened to pick it up - and I was in time, as another man in a long kaftan had already quickened his pace, but upon seeing what I was holding in my hands, he didn't bother to argue, glanced briefly at my hands and slipped past me. This thing was a large, worn, old-fashioned, tightly-packed notebook; yet, somehow, on the first glance, I guessed it could contain anything but money. The person who had lost it was walking about forty paces ahead of me and soon vanished from view in the crowd. I chased after him and started shouting; but since I had nothing to shout except 'Hey!', he didn't turn around. Suddenly he dodged to the left, into the gate of one house. When I ran into the gate, which was very dark, he was nowhere to be found. The house was enormous, one of those behemoths built by scammers for small flats; in some such houses there are sometimes as many as a hundred door numbers. As I ran through the gate, it seemed to me that someone was walking in the right, back corner of the enormous courtyard, although in the darkness I could barely distinguish anything. Reaching the corner, I saw the entrance to the staircase; the staircase was narrow, incredibly dirty and completely unlit; however, I could hear the sound of footsteps climbing the stairs and I rushed up the stairs, counting on catching up to him somewhere along the way. And I did. The stairs were endless, the number of them was countless, and I was extremely short of breath; the door was opened and closed again on the fifth floor, which I guessed even three flights below. Until I ran up, catching my breath on the landing, while looking for the bell, a few minutes had passed. A woman finally opened the door to me, who was blowing on a samovar in a tiny kitchen; she listened silently to my questions, understood nothing, of course, and silently let me into the next room, also small and dreadfully low-ceilinged, with wretched necessary furniture and a wide, enormous bed under the bedclothes, on which lay 'Terentyich', as the woman called him, who seemed to me tipsy. A glowing ember was burning in an iron nightlight on the table and a nearly empty half-bottle stood there. Terentyich muttered something while lying down and gestured towards the next door, and the woman left, so I had no choice but to open this door. I did so and entered the next room.
