He lived in prison and awaited execution for at least another week; he somehow relied on routine bureaucracy, that the papers still had to go somewhere, and would only come out a week later. But then the case was suddenly cut short. It was at five o'clock in the morning; it was cold and dark at that hour in late October. The jailer entered quietly, with a guard, and cautiously touched him on the shoulder; he sat up, leaned on his elbow, – he saw the light: 'What's this?' 'At ten o'clock, execution by death.' He didn't believe it from his sleep, began to argue that the papers would come out in a week, but when he was fully awake, stopped arguing and fell silent – that's what they said – then said, 'It's really difficult all of a sudden...', and fell silent again, and wanted to say nothing more. Then three or four hours pass on well-known things: on the priest, on the breakfast to which they give him wine, coffee, and beef (but is it not mockery? As if it's such a cruel thing, and on the other hand, those innocent people from the heart do it and are convinced it's kindness), then the toilet (you know what a prisoner's toilet is?), and finally, they take him around the city to the scaffold... I think it seems like there's still an eternity to live as long as they're taking me. I think he probably thought to himself: 'There are still three streets to live; I'll pass this one, and then there's still another one to pass, and then there's another one where the baker is to the right... we'll get to the baker sometime!' The crowd surrounds him, there's shouting and noise, ten thousand faces, ten thousand eyes – all this must be endured, and most importantly, the thought: 'There are ten thousand of them, and they won't be executed, but I'll be executed!' Well, that's everything that came before. The ladder leads to the scaffold; at the foot of the ladder he suddenly began to cry, and that was a strong and courageous man, a big villain, they say he was. He was always accompanied by a priest, and the priest was with him in the cart, and he was talking to him all the time – it's unlikely that the latter heard anything, began to listen, and from the third word could no longer understand. So it must have been. Finally, he began to ascend the ladder; at that point his legs were tied up, and he moved in small steps. The priest, probably a clever man, stopped talking and was only giving him a cross to kiss. At the bottom of the ladder he was very pale, and when he got up and stood on the scaffold, he suddenly turned white as paper, completely like white paper. I think his legs weakened and trembled, and nausea was there, as if something was pressing on his throat, and from this one could feel it, – have you ever felt this in fright or during very frightening moments when the mind is still, but has no power? I think that if, for example, certain and inevitable death is looming over you, and your house is falling on you, then suddenly you'll want to sit down and close your eyes and wait for whatever may be – just let it be! That's when this weakness began, the priest quickly, with a swift gesture and silently, held out a small silver cross to him with four arms, which he frequently and for a minute, at times, presented to his lips – as soon as the cross touched his lips, he opened his eyes, and for a few seconds seemed to come to life again, and his legs moved. He kissed the cross with greed, hurried to kiss it, as if he was hurrying not to forget to grab something for a reserve, for a precaution, but it's unlikely he was aware of anything religious in that moment. And so it was right up until the plank... It's strange that one rarely faints in those very last seconds. On the contrary, the head lives and works terribly, it must be working strongly, strongly, strongly, like a machine in motion; I imagine it's going 'click-click-click' with various thoughts, all unfinished and perhaps even silly, extraneous thoughts: 'This one is looking – he has a wart on his forehead, and the executioner has a rusty lower button...' – and at the same time you know and remember everything; there is one such point which you cannot forget, and you cannot faint from it, and everything around it, around this point, is moving and revolving. And to think that it's just like that up to the very last quarter of a second, when the head is already lying on the plank, and it's waiting, and... knows, and suddenly it hears above itself how the iron slid! You will necessarily hear it! I would, if I were lying, I would deliberately listen and hear it! It may be just a single-tenth of a moment, but you will necessarily hear it! And imagine, they still argue that perhaps the head might even know that it has already flown away, that perhaps it knows it's been flying for a second, maybe even five seconds! – what a notion! And what if I were to draw the scaffold so that only the very last step is visible; the prisoner stepped on it: the head, a face pale as paper, the priest holding out the cross, the prisoner stretching out his blue lips with greed, and looking, and – he knows everything. The cross and the head – that's the picture; the face of the priest, the executioner, his two attendants, and a few heads and eyes below – all this can be drawn on the background, in the fog, as an accessory... That's what the picture looks like.

Indeed, there's nothing more unfortunate than being, for example, rich, from a respectable family, of a decent appearance, well-educated, not dim-witted, even kind, and at the same time not having any talent, no peculiarities, no quirky qualities, no own ideas, being utterly 'just like everyone else'. The wealth is there, but not of the Rothschild kind; the family is decent, but has never distinguished itself; the appearance is decent, but expresses little; the education is respectable, but one has no idea what to use it for; there is intelligence, but it has no ideas; there is a heart, but no generosity, and so on and so forth in all respects. People of this sort are abundant in the world and even far more numerous than it seems; they're divided, just like all people, into two main categories: those who are limited and those who are 'far more intelligent'. The latter are happier. For the ordinary limited person, there's nothing easier than to imagine himself as an extraordinary and original person and to indulge in such fancies without any hesitation. Just think, some of our young ladies would cut their hair, put on blue glasses, and call themselves nihilists, and immediately they'd be convinced that by wearing glasses, they've instantly acquired their own 'beliefs'. 

It's the same with another, who just felt in his heart something of any kind of ordinary human and good feeling, and immediately he'd be convinced that he's the only one to feel this way, that he's a pioneer in general development. It's the same with one who, upon uttering a single word, adopted some idea or read a page of something endless, and immediately believed that these are his own thoughts that have germinated in his own brain. The audacity of naivety is almost unbelievable in such cases. This audacity of naivety, this unshakeable conviction of a fool in himself and his talents, is wonderfully portrayed by Gogol in the amazing type of Lieutenant Pirogov. Pirogov doesn't even doubt that he's a genius, a genius above all geniuses; he doubts it so little that he doesn't even ask himself this question; in fact, there are no questions for him. The great writer was forced to dispatch him to satisfy his outraged moral sense, but seeing that the great man just shook off the affront and to bolster his spirits ate a layered pastry, looked around in amazement, and then left his readers bewildered. I've always regretted that Gogol took Pirogov in such a minor rank, because Pirogov is so self-satisfied that it's not hard for him to imagine himself, as the years go by and the lines of his epaulets swell, to be a commander-in-chief, for example, an extraordinary commander; he doesn't even imagine it, he just doesn't doubt it: he was promoted to general, why not a commander-in-chief? And how many of them make disastrous fiascos on the battlefield afterwards? And how many Pirogovs have there been among our literati, scholars, propagandists? I say 'have been', but there are certainly some still...

The news utterly bewildered Elizabeth Prokofyevna. What was it supposed to be? But that was it, the mood had been reached. Her anxiety was raised to an extraordinary degree, and in fact - what about the beehive? What was the arrangement here? What was implied? What sign was this? What telegram? Moreover, the poor Ivan Fyodorovich, who happened to be present during the interrogation, completely ruined everything with his answer. According to him, there was no telegram at all, and what was a beehive - just a beehive, nothing more, or, indeed, does it signify, apart from friendship, forgiving past grievances, and reconciliation, in a word, this is all just a trifle, but at any rate harmless and forgivable.

The news was absolutely shocking to Liza Prokofyevna. What could this possibly mean? But it seems it's come to that, then. Her anxiety was in a state of extreme agitation, and the main thing – the owl, what does the owl signify? What's implied here? What does this symbolize? What kind of telegram is this? Moreover, the poor Ivan Fyodorovich, who happened to be present during the questioning, completely ruined the whole matter with his response. In his opinion, there was no telegram whatsoever, and as for the owl, "it's just an owl, and nothing but – does it mean, in addition to that, friendship, forgiveness of offenses, reconciliation, in a word, it's all nonsense, but at least harmless and forgivable."

Such news completely astounded Elizabeth Prokofievna. What's this? But it seems that's exactly what it is. Her anxiety was in an extreme state, and the question was - what does that even mean? According to him, there was no telegram at all, and as for the word 'bees', it's just a word for 'bees,' and that's it – unless, of course, by 'bees' one means, in addition to that, friendship, forgiveness for past wrongs, and reconciliation – in short, all this is a lighthearted and forgivable jest.

Then find the person who has come a thousand li away to respond to you; if his words are not good, then find the person who has come a thousand li away to suit you.' 'You have this thought, wait until I arrive at the East Land of the Great Tang Country to find a person to go on a pilgrimage, instruct him to save you. You can follow him as a disciple, hold the scriptures and enter my Buddhist sect. Then cultivate the fruition, how would it be?' The Great Sage spoke in a voice: 'I am willing to go! I am willing to go!' The Bodhisattva said, 'Since you have a good fruition, I will give you a dharma name.' The Great Sage said, 'I already have a name, it's called Sun Wukong.' The Bodhisattva was overjoyed and said, 'There have been two people who submitted to me before, and their names also contain the character "悟" ('wù', 'enlightenment'). You too have the character "悟" in your name, it's very good, very good. I won't need to caution you, I'll go.' Seeing that the Great Sage had a clear nature and returned to the teachings of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva was so delighted that he couldn't help but reminisce about the mythical realm.

Then when a person with good intentions from afar comes, he should be accepted; if one with ill intentions comes from afar, he should be dealt with accordingly.'If you have such intentions, I shall wait until I return to the Great Tang Country in the East, and then have a person go to rescue you. You may learn from him, take the precepts, and become a disciple in the Buddha's teaching. And thus cultivate the True Fruit, how would that be?' The Great Sage eagerly exclaimed, 'I am willing to go! I am willing to go!' The Bodhisattva said, 'Since you have the good intention, I will give you a monastic name.' The Great Sage replied, 'I already have a name, it is called Sun Wukong.' The Bodhisattva further said, 'I had two previous ones coming back to surrender, their names both start with the 'Wu' character, so yours is also 'Wu', which is very harmonious, very good. I need not worry, I will be off.' The Great Sage, now enlightened, returns to his nature, and has returned to the Buddha's teaching, but the Bodhisattva is emotionally moved and takes pity on him.

Then accept me a thousand li away; if his words are not good, accept me a thousand li away as well. 'Since you have this mind, wait until I arrive in the Great Tang Nation in the east, where I will find someone to go on a pilgrimage with, and have him save you. You can become his disciple, take on the precepts, and enter the Buddha's door. Then you will bring forth your good deeds.' The Great Sage spoke with eagerness: 'I'm willing to go! I'm willing to go!' The Bodhisattva said, 'Since you have a good heart, I'll give you a Buddhist name.' The Great Sage said, 'I already have a name – Monkey King.' The Bodhisattva was overjoyed and said, 'The two of them who have come to repent ahead of me also have names starting with the character "Wu" – how wonderful that you also have the character "Wu" and match them perfectly. This way, there's no need for me to advise you. I'll be off now.' Seeing that the Great Sage's nature was pure and his heart was wise, and he was returning to the Buddha's teaching, this Bodhisattva was deeply moved.

Then it's even better to respond from afar; if its words are not good, then respond accordingly from afar.'You have such a mind, then wait for me to arrive in the Eastern Land of Great Tang and find someone who comes to seek scriptures, teach him to save you. You can be his disciple, bear the teachings, and enter my Buddhist order. Then you can cultivate to perfection, how would that be?" The Great Sage shouted: "I'll go! I'll go!" The Bodhisattva said: "Since you have good roots, I will give you a Buddhist name." The Great Sage said: "I already have a name, it's called Sun Wukong." The Bodhisattva was pleased and said: "There were two of them in front of me who repented and returned, their names all started with the character 'wù', you too have the character 'wù' in your name, that's good, that's good. I won't have to caution you, I'm leaving." That Great Sage, seeing the saintly nature in the heart, returned to the Buddhist teaching, and the Bodhisattva cherished a sense of affection towards him.

"If the person from afar responds to your plea, I'll even go ten thousand li to provide an answer; if he doesn't speak well, I'll go ten thousand li to help him out. Since you have such thoughts, just wait for me to find someone who is going on a pilgrimage to the eastern land of the Great Tang to save you. You can be his disciple and carry on the teachings, entering the Buddhist path. Only then will you attain true fruition." The Great Sage responded loudly, "I'm willing to go! I'm willing to go!" The Bodhisattva said, "Since you're going to cultivate virtue, I'll give you a Buddhist name." The Great Sage said, "I already have a name – Sun Wukong." The Bodhisattva smiled and said, "Not only are there two people who surrendered to me before, they too have the 'Wu' character in their names. Now you also have the 'Wu' character, it's a very good combination. This is no need for further urging, I'll be off." Seeing the Great Sage's devout heart and enlightenment, the Bodhisattva cherished a feeling of fondness towards him.

When the Great Sage heard this, he chuckled to himself and said, "Good heavens! I, the Old Sun, can leap a distance of eighty thousand li with one somersault. How could I possibly be confined by such a small hand?" Suddenly he blurted out, "If you say so, may I take the lead?" The Buddha replied, "I agree! I agree!" He stretched out his right hand, and it expanded to the size of a large lotus leaf. The Great Sage put away his Ruyi staff, puffed out his divine might, and sprang upwards, landing on the Buddha's palm. He said, "I'm off!" He vanished into the clouds without a trace. The Buddha, with his keen eyes, watched as the Monkey King was like a whirlwind, continuously moving forward.

As he traveled, he suddenly spotted five crimson pillars, supporting a blue aura. He said, "This marks the boundary. When I return, the Buddha can bear witness that I have visited this place, and the Halls of the Jade Ceiling will be where I sit." After a moment's thought, he said, "Wait a minute! I'll leave some evidence behind so that I can argue with the Buddha later." He plucked a single hair, breathed a gust of divine energy, and said, "Transform!" It turned into a thick, dark ink brush, which he used to write a row of large characters on the middle pillar: "The Great Sage Equal to Heaven, passing by on a whim." Having finished writing, he retrieved the hair. Not content, he then urinated on the base of the first pillar and turned a somersault, returning to his original position in front of the Buddha. "I'm back," he said. "Now it's your turn, Buddha. Teach the Jade Emperor to send the Heavenly Palace to fetch me."

That great saint heard the words, smiled knowingly in the darkness, and said, "This Great Buddha is truly quite dense! I, Old Sun, can leap ten million eight thousand li with a single somersault. How could he, with a palm no more than a circle of less than a foot, possibly not jump out?" He suddenly shouted, "If it's like this, can you make the decision?" The Buddha said, "I can! I can!" Spreading out his right hand, it looked like a large lotus leaf. The great saint retrieved the Heaven-Sent Staff, shook off his divine might, and with a bound, stood on the Buddha's palm, saying, "I'll go out too!" You see him go one stretch of cloud light, with no shape or form, gone. The Buddha looked on with his wise eyes and saw the Monkey King moving like a wheel of wind, not stopping for a moment, just going forward. When the Monkey King was traveling, he suddenly saw five red pillars of flesh, supporting a green gas. He said, "This is the end of the road. On the way back, the Buddha can serve as witness; the Hall of the Spirit Heaven will be my throne seat." Again, he thought and said, "Wait! Let me leave some marks behind, so I can talk to the Buddha later." He plucked out a single strand of hair and blew a mouthful of divine breath, calling out, "Change!" and it turned into a thick black brush with two fine hairs, writing a line of large characters on the middle pillar: "The Great Sage Equal to Heaven, a journey to this place." After writing, he retrieved the hair. Without going back to his original state, he urinated a bubble of monkey urine under the base of the first pillar. He flipped a somersault of cloud and returned directly to the original place, standing on the Buddha's palm, saying, "I've gone, I've come. Teach the Jade Emperor to let the Heavenly Palace entrust me with the heavens."

Upon hearing this, the Great Sage sneered and said, "Your Maitreya is quite ridiculous! I, Old Monkey, can leap an incalculable distance with a single somersault. The Buddha held out his right hand, which was as wide as a lotus leaf. The Great Sage retrieved his divine rod, puffed out his divine might, sprang high into the air, and stood on the Buddha's palm. "I'm leaving too!" he declared. As he soared through the air, he vanished into the clouds without a trace. The Buddha watched closely with his wise eyes and saw that the Monkey King resembled a whirlwind, continually moving forward. As the Great Sage traveled, he suddenly saw five red pillars holding up a column of blue air. He said, "This is the end of the path. If I go back, the Buddha will bear witness, and the Hall of Numinous Emptiness will be my throne from now on." He thought for a moment and said, "Wait! I'll leave some signs to talk to the Buddha later." He plucked out a single hair, blew some divine breath, and said, "Change!" Instantly, a pair of thick ink pens as thick as two hairs appeared in his hand and he wrote a line of large characters on the middle pillar that read: "The Great Sage Equal to Heaven has come here to take a stroll." Chichikov bowed gratefully. Learning that he was on his way to conclude a deed, Mihailov expressed a willingness to accompany him. The friends took each other's arm and set off together. At every small elevation or rise, Mihailov supported Chichikov and almost lifted him by the hand, adding with a pleasant smile that he would not let Pavel Ivanovich break his legs. Chichikov felt embarrassed not knowing how to thank him, feeling somewhat fatigued. They came to the plaza by mutual assistance, where official establishments were located: a large three-story stone building, entirely white, like chalk, probably to illustrate the purity of the souls housed within it; other buildings on the plaza did not match the grandeur of the stone house. These were: a sentry box, where a soldier stood with a rifle, two or three hack driver's boards, and, finally, long fences with known fence signs and drawings scratched with charcoal and chalk; nothing else was to be found on this secluded, or as we say, beautiful plaza. Heads from the windows of the second and third stories of the stone house protruded and then immediately hid again: likely, at that moment, the chief had entered the room. The friends did not climb but ran up the stairs because Chichikov, trying to avoid being supported by Mihailov's hand, hastened his pace, while Mihailov also flew forward, trying not to let Chichikov tire, and therefore both became very out of breath when they entered the dark corridor. Neither in the corridors nor in the rooms was their gaze struck by the cleanliness. It was not yet a concern at that time, and what was dirty remained dirty, without taking on an attractive appearance. Justice was received by her guests simply, as she is, in a négligé and a dressing gown. One should describe the office rooms they passed through, but the author feels a strong timidity towards all official establishments. If he ever happened to pass through them even in a brilliant and nicely decorated state, with lacquered floors and tables, he tried to rush as quickly as possible, humbly lowering and veiling his eyes in the ground, and therefore does not know at all how things are flourishing and thriving there. Our heroes saw much paper, both rough and white, bent heads, wide foreheads, gubernatorial-style frock coats and waistcoats, and even a light gray coat that stood out very sharply, which, having turned its head to the side and laid it almost on the paper, quickly and hastily wrote out some protocol about the withdrawal of land or an incorrect land description, taken by some peaceful landowner, quietly living out his days under judgment, having children and grandchildren under his protection, and snippets of short expressions, spoken in a hoarse voice were heard: "Lend me, Fedosey Fedoseyevich, item 368!" - "You're always dragging a plug from the official inkwell somewhere!" Sometimes a voice more majestic, undoubtedly from one of the chiefs, was heard authoritatively: "Write that over! Or else they'll remove your shoes and you'll sit there for six days without eating." The noise from the quills was loud and resembled as if several carts with brushwood were passing through a forest, half-filled with withered leaves.

General Sokolovich (though I haven't been to see him in a long time, I never did see Anna Fedorovna)... you know, dear Prince, when you don't take yourself, you somehow involuntarily stop doing it for others either. And yet... hm... you seem not to believe... But why not introduce me to my best friend's son and childhood companion in this charming family home? General Ivolgin and Prince Myshkin! You'll see an extraordinary girl, not one, two, even three – a decoration of the city and society: beauty, education, views – the whole gamut of feminine and intellectual talents – all this has come together in a happy and diverse mix, not to mention at least eighty thousand rubles in dowry, spot cash, which never hurts, at any feminine or social occasion... in short, I must and am obliged to introduce you. General Ivolgin and Prince Myshkin!

"Who brought you here?" Tartar asked. Zu Da said, "The Tang Monk's horse fell in the slippery pit of the Eagle-ested gorge. That Sun Wukong was at a loss as to whether to advance or retreat.  He asked the local gods here, who said that the Buddha had sent the serpent-dragon that swallowed it, that Sun Wukong came here to beg the Buddha to send the serpent-dragon away, and return the horse to the Master. "The Buddha heard this and said, "This one was the son of Ouyang Zhi, the magician of the Western Sea. He set fire to the precious jewels in the hall, offended his father, and committed the crime of heaven. I myself presented a petition to the Jade Emperor and brought him down to let him be a footman for the Tang Monk. How did he end up eating the Master's horse? I will go to see to this." 

The Buddha descended from the lotus platform and, accompanied by Zu Da, departed in a divine carriage, leaving the Fairy Cave behind. They crossed the South Sea and arrived. There is a poem to attest this, which says: "The Buddha spoke the sutra of Maitreya, and the Bodhisattva spread kindness along the Great Wall. The Great Sacred Words traverse the heavens and the earth, the true words of Prajna save the spirits. This caused the cicada to break out of its shell again, and let Master Xuanzang resume his practice. It was only because of the obstruction of the Eagle-ested Gorge, and the dragon's son changed into a horse. 

The Bodhisattva and Zu Da did not take long to arrive at the Snake-Winding Mountain. They stayed in mid-air with a miraculous cloud, gazing down. They saw Sun Wukong at the edge of the gorge cursing and shouting. The Bodhisattva called out to him with Zu Da. Zu Da descended the cloudhead, bypassing the Tang Monk, and arrived at the edge of the gorge. He said to Wukong, "The Bodhisattva has come." 

Wukong heard this and jumped from the cloud, flying into the air and shouting at the Bodhisattva, "You, my revered teacher, the seven Buddhas' teacher, the compassionate Lord! How could you devise such a wicked scheme to harm me?" The Bodhisattva said, "I, the great Bodhisattva, shall ask you, you wily monkey! I have repeatedly expended my virtue to save the life of a scripture collector, and taught him to save your life. Why didn't you come to thank me for saving your life, and instead you scold me?" Wukong said, "You've treated me well! You let me go and now you're letting me frolic freely. However, on the day before yesterday, you met me on the ocean and insulted me. You said I had to devote all my energy to serving the Master, but instead you sent me a red hat to wear and caused me to suffer. You had me wear this noose on my head, and forced me to recite the spell of the noose, and the Master recited it repeatedly, causing me to feel more pain each time. Is this not your doing?" 

The Bodhisattva laughed and said, "You, monkey! You didn't follow my instructions and didn't achieve the proper enlightenment. If I didn't tie you up, you would deceive and cheat the heavens. You would only bring calamity upon yourself. This would be like the time when you stumbled into trouble before. Who would take responsibility for that? You need this magical dragon to serve as a gatekeeper so that you will enter the gate of my yoga." 

Wukong said, "This is my nemesis that you have created for me. Why did you send the serpent-dragon with the crime of eating the Master's horse? This is letting a wicked creature wreak havoc, and it's not good." The Bodhisattva said, "That serpent-dragon was brought by me from the heavens, specifically to serve as a mount for the scripture collector. How could an ordinary horse from the Eastern Region possibly reach the Western Heavens and the sacred mountain of the Buddha? Only by getting this dragon horse could he have gone." Wukong said, "If he's afraid of me and hides in the depths, how can he get out?" The Bodhisattva told Zu Da, "Go to the edge of the gorge and call out to the serpent-dragon, saying, 'Ouyang Zhi, Dragon King's third son, you come out, for the South Sea Bodhisattva is here.'" 

Zu Da went to the edge of the gorge and called out twice. The little dragon burst out of the water, transformed into a human form, stood on the cloud, and bowed to the Bodhisattva, saying, "I have been saved by the Bodhisattva from a life of death. I have been waiting here for a long time, but I have heard no news of the scripture collector." The Bodhisattva pointed at Wukong and said, "Isn't this the scripture collector's disciple?" The little dragon saw Wukong and said, "This is my sworn enemy. Yesterday I was famished, and I indeed ate his horse. He relied on his power to fight me and I was terrified and retreated, and he cursed me so that I dare not come out. He didn't mention the scripture collector even once." 

Wukong said:

"You're here for something?" (Sun Wukong) asked. The Bodhisattva replied, "The Tang Monk lost his horse at the Snares Mountain, where Eagle-Scowling Gorge is located. This Sun Wukong was at a loss for what to do. When asked the local gods, they said that a Bodhisattva had sent a evil dragon to swallow it, and now Wukong was at the Bodhisattva's place asking him to save the dragon and return his horse." The Bodhisattva heard this and said, "This creature is the son of the Patriarch of the Western Ocean. He set fire to the precious gem on the temple altar, incurring his father's wrath and the death sentence from Heaven. I personally pleaded with the Jade Emperor to have him brought down, and taught him to serve the Tang Monk as a steed. How did he dare devour the Tang Monk's horse? I'll go take care of this." The Bodhisattva descended a lotus platform, departed the grotto, and rode a cloudy carriage. With the Monkey King (Sun Wukong) accompanying him, they passed the Southern Ocean and arrived. A poem serves as evidence: 

The Buddha taught the Lotus Sutra, a scripture that fills the Eastern Wall. The Bodhisattva praises good deeds, liberating all creatures. His supreme words permeate heaven and earth, and the true word of Prajnaparamita saves the spirits of the dead. Thus the cicada regained its shell, and the Tang Monk continued his journey. Only because the path was blocked by Eagle-Scowling Gorge did the Dragon's son transform into a horse. The Bodhisattva and the Monkey King arrived at the Snares Mountain in no time. In mid-air, they let out a cloudy formation, and the Bodhisattva gazed downward. He saw the Monkey King at the edge of the gorge cursing. The Bodhisattva called out to the Monkey King, and he climbed down the cloudy formation and landed next to the gorge, facing the Monkey King. The Monkey King said, "The Bodhisattva has arrived." 

The Monkey King heard this and jumped up to the clouds, hurrying to where the Bodhisattva was, and cried out, "You, the seven Buddhas' master and a compassionate teacher, how could you create such means to harm me?" The Bodhisattva replied, "You this big evil demon, you foolish devil! I have used my all efforts to save a practitioner, instructing him to rescue your life. Why haven't you come to thank me for saving your life, but instead come to disturb me?" The Monkey King said, "You've done well for me! If you've let me go, I'll roam freely and happily. Yesterday, in the ocean, you spoke sharply to me, ordering me to serve the Tang Monk with all my heart. But you gave me a crown, deceiving me into wearing it and suffering. And then you made an iron ring appear on my head, ordering the old monk to recite a certain incantation. The old monk recited it over and over, and I felt pain in my head again and again. This isn't what you did to harm me?" 

The Bodhisattva laughed and said, "You, this monkey! You don't follow my instructions and don't attain the ultimate goal. If I didn't have you bound by this spell, you would have deceived heaven and know not good from evil. And then, who would take responsibility for your mistakes? It is only with this demon's head that you will enter my Yogacara path." The Monkey King said, "This matter is, after all, a demon I created myself. Why did you send the guilty evil dragon here, letting it transform into a horse and devour my master's horse? This is not good at all!" The Bodhisattva said, "That dragon was brought here by me, personally, to serve the practitioner as a steed. How could an ordinary horse from the East Country travel the ten thousand rivers and mountains and reach the Western Heavens?" The Monkey King said, "If I had to fear you like that and hide out, what would I do?" The Bodhisattva ordered the Heavenly Agent to call out: "Ao Li Dragon King, Jade Dragon, third son of Ao Li. Come out, the Bodhisattva from the Southern Sea is here." The Heavenly Agent called out the phrase twice, and the young dragon jumped out of the water, transformed into a man, stepped onto the cloudy formation, and came to the Bodhisattva, bowing down and saying, "I'm deeply grateful to the Bodhisattva for saving my life. I've been waiting here for a long time, but have heard no news of the practitioner." The Bodhisattva pointed at the Monkey King and said, "Isn't this the Tang Monk's chief disciple?" The young dragon saw the Monkey King and said, "Bodhisattva, this is my archenemy. Yesterday, my hunger was extreme, and I did eat his horse. He used his strength to fight me, forcing me to retreat in fear. He even cursed me, making me lock myself in and not dare come out. He didn't even mention the word 'practitioner'." The Monkey King said,

You've come here for what? The heavenly fairy said, "The Tang monk lost his horse on Snake Coils Mountain, and the Great Sage Sun was in a bind, not knowing what to do. He asked the local spirit here, who said it was a bodhisattva who had sent a sinful dragon to eat the horse. The Great Sage Sun came to beg the bodhisattva to send away the sinful dragon and retrieve his horse." The bodhisattva heard this and said, "This fellow is the son of Ao Qin, the monarch of the Western Sea. He set fire to the pearl on the palace, defied his father, and was sentenced to death by the heavenly court. I, the bodhisattva, personally interceded with the Jade Emperor to bring him down and use him as a servant for the Tang monk. How did he end up eating the Tang monk's horse? Let me go and see."

The bodhisattva descended to the lotus platform and, leaving the fairy cave, rode off with the heavenly fairies on a cloud, crossing the Southern Sea to arrive. There is a poem to prove this: "The Buddha spoke the Milanta scriptures, and the bodhisattva sang of kindness throughout the Long Wall. The Mahayana sutras were preached, and the true word of the Prajnaparamita saved spirits and ghosts. This made the cicada break free from its shell, and it was because of this that the Ven. Xuanzang embarked on his journey. Because the path was blocked by Eagle-Sharp Gorge, the dragon's son changed into a horse form to return to his true state."

The bodhisattva and the heavenly fairy soon arrived at Snake Coils Mountain, where they hovered in mid-air, observing. The Tang monk, Sun Wukong, was at the edge of the gorge, cursing. The bodhisattva called out to him with the heavenly fairy. The fairy descended from the cloud and, without passing by the Tang monk, went directly to the edge of the gorge, where he said to Sun Wukong, "The bodhisattva has come." 

Sun Wukong heard this and, with a cloud, leaped into the air, and shouted at the bodhisattva: "You, the greatest teacher of the seven Buddhas, the compassionate master of the Dharma! Why do you create a means to harm me!" The bodhisattva said, "I went to great lengths to save you, a foolish monkey, and led you to rescue the scriptures. Why don't you come and thank me for sparing your life? Instead, you're causing a commotion."

Sun Wukong said, "You've treated me well! If you've set me free, let me just roam freely and indulge myself, then that will do. Yesterday, on the sea, you met me and scolded me several times, instructing me to serve the Tang monk with all my strength. Then you sent him a flower hat, tricking me into wearing it and suffering. You put a tight leather cord on my head and told him to recite a close-up tight-neck curse, and the old monk recited it repeatedly, causing me to suffer time and again. Isn't this you tormenting me?"

The bodhisattva laughed and said, "You, you monkey! You refuse to follow instructions and achieve the correct cause-and-effect. If I didn't bind you in this way, you would have fooled Heaven and deceived others. Who would take care of the calamity that would arise? You must rely on this evil dragon; only then will you be willing to enter the path of my Vajrayana."

Sun Wukong said, "This matter is that you have made this evil dragon the instrument of my downfall. You've let a wicked being roam free and do evil deeds. This is truly not a good act."

The bodhisattva said, "That dragon is someone I personally petitioned the Jade Emperor to bring down to serve as the Tang monk's steed. Do you think a normal horse from the Eastern Land could traverse the ten thousand rivers and a hundred mountains, and reach the divine mountain where the Buddha resides? It had to rely on this dragon horse to accomplish this journey."

Sun Wukong said, "How can I hide from him? If I'm afraid of you, how can I escape?"

The bodhisattva called out to the heavenly fairy, "Go to the edge of the gorge and call out: 'Ao Qin's Dragon King, Jade Dragon Third Prince, come out! The South Sea bodhisattva is here.'"

The fairy went to the edge of the gorge and called out twice. The little dragon jumped out of the water, changing into a human form, stepped onto the cloud, and came before the bodhisattva, bowing and saying, "I am deeply indebted to the bodhisattva for rescuing me from death, and I've been waiting here for a long time. But I've yet to hear the sound of the scriptures being retrieved."

The bodhisattva pointed at Sun Wukong and said, "Is this not the great disciple of the one who retrieved the scriptures?" The little dragon saw this and said, "The bodhisattva, this is my arch-nemesis. Yesterday, I was famished in my stomach, and I indeed ate his horse. He, with some strength, beat me back and defeated me. He cursed me, and I was too afraid to come out. He didn't even mention the word 'scriptures.'"

Sun Wukong said:

"Why have you come?" said Hotei, "the Tang Monk was in the Deer Cave Mountain, his horse was devoured by the demonic dragon, and I, the great Monkey King, was at a loss for what to do. I asked the local deity here, he said that a Bodhisattva had sent the demonic dragon to eat the horse. I, the Monkey King, came here to ask the Bodhisattva to send the demonic dragon away, and return the horse to the Tang Monk."

The Bodhisattva replied, "That monster is the son of Ao Mazi, a fiend from the Western Sea. He had started a fire that burned the jewel on the altar, and his father had scolded him for being rebellious. He was sentenced to death in the heavenly court, but I, myself, intervened and requested the Jade Emperor to bring him down, to make him a servant to the Tang Monk. How could he possibly devour the Tang Monk's horse? Now, let me go and see."

The Bodhisattva descended on a lotus flower and parted the clouds, and with Hotei leading the way, they arrived at the Deer Cave Mountain. They hovered in mid-air, surrounded by auspicious clouds, and looked down to see the Monkey King scolding at the edge of the torrent.

The Bodhisattva instructed Hotei to call the Monkey King over. Hotei descended the cloud and went straight to the edge of the torrent. "The Bodhisattva has come," he said to the Monkey King.

The Monkey King heard the news and hastily leaped into the air, and scolded the Bodhisattva. "You, the venerable teacher of the seven Buddhas, the compassionate patriarch of the teaching! Why have you found me and sent me to suffer?"

The Bodhisattva said, "I have gone to great lengths to save you, the Monkey King, by rescuing you from danger. I have instructed you in the teachings, and yet you do not repay my kindness. You scold me instead!"

The Monkey King said, "You have treated me well! Since you have set me free, why don't you just let me roam and have fun? Yesterday, in the Southern Sea, you scolded me and ordered me to exert my utmost effort to serve the Tang Monk. But you presented me with a golden crown, and told me to wear it and suffer. You tied a halter around my head, and instructed the old monk to recite the scripture of the 'Tie-down curse', which made my head ache. This is not your kindness, but your cruelty!"

The Bodhisattva laughed and said, "You, a monkey! You don't follow my instructions, and don't cultivate the proper conduct. If I didn't tie you up, you would deceive heaven and defy the law. It is only by subjugating you that I can bring you onto the path of the yogic practices."

The Monkey King said, "This business, was it not my fate to be your enemy? And yet, you took that criminal demonic dragon, and brought it here, making it a demon, and it devoured the Tang Monk's horse. This is not showing compassion, but being overly merciful!"

The Bodhisattva said, "That demonic dragon was sentenced to death in the heavenly court, and I, myself, petitioned the Jade Emperor to bring it down. It was to be used as a servant for the Tang Monk. How could it possibly devour the Tang Monk's horse? The horses from the Eastern Land, how could they possibly cross the ten thousand rivers and a hundred mountains? How could they possibly reach the sacred mountain of the Buddha? It is only by having this dragon horse that they can accomplish their goal."

The Monkey King said, "Since you fear me so much, it cannot hide from me. What can it do?"

The Bodhisattva ordered Hotei to call out, "Ao Mazi Dragon King, third son of the Jade Dragon, come out! The South Sea Bodhisattva is here."

Hotei went to the edge of the torrent and called out twice. The small dragon leapt out of the water, transformed into a human form, stepped on the clouds, and bowed to the Bodhisattva in mid-air. "I, the son of Ao Mazi, had begged for mercy from the Bodhisattva, and have been waiting here for a long time, but have heard no news of the Tang Monk. Suddenly, I was brought here and devoured the Tang Monk's horse. This was indeed a wicked deed."

The Bodhisattva pointed to the Monkey King and said, "Is this not the great disciple of the Tang Monk?"

The small dragon looked and said, "This is my enemy. Yesterday, I was hungry, and indeed, I devoured his horse. He challenged me, and used his strength to drive me back, scolding me and making me fearful. I shut myself in and did not come out, and he never mentioned the Tang Monk's name. He just scolded me constantly."

The Monkey King said:

That Bodhisattva, up to this day still taking advantage of the situation,
His heart not intent on doing good,
Promoting the Buddhist scriptures, proclaiming a merciful nature,
Just pretending to help me escape danger, and subjugating me.

That Bodhisattva, in the end is just an old fox,
Pretending to use my foolishness to beguile me,
Leaving the rest for you all to decide,
Only having his own interests in mind.

He said, "What brings you here?" Reveille replied, "The Tang Monk's horse has gone astray in Eagle Shallows Gorge, and the Monkey King is at his wit's end. I asked the local gods here, and they said that the Bodhisattva sent a calamitous dragon to devour the horse. The Monkey King came here to implore the Bodhisattva to descend and save the dragon and retrieve the horse." The Bodhisattva replied, "This creature is a son of the Eastern Sea's Ao-Jun. He set fire to the tower's jewel and disobeyed his father, resulting in a death sentence from the heavenly court. I personally petitioned the Jade Emperor and brought him down to have him serve as the Tang Monk's mount. How could he repay this kindness by devouring the Tang Monk's horse? Let me go and see." The Bodhisattva descended from the lotus platform and flew off towards the fairy grotto with Reveille, riding the cloud, and passed over the Southern Sea. A poem serves as evidence:

The Buddha expounded the Maitreya Sutra, the Bodhisattva displayed benevolence throughout the Great Wall. His majestic speech reached the heavens and the earth, and his true words saved the spirits. It allowed the cicada to break free from its shell and enabled Xuanzang to continue his pilgrimage. Only because the path was blocked by Eagle Shallows Gorge, the dragon son returned to his original form, becoming a horse. The Bodhisattva and Reveille soon arrived at Snake Coiled Mountain. He hovered in mid-air, and a low cloud stayed under him, looking down. Xuanzang was standing at the edge of the gorge, calling out and cursing. The Bodhisattva told Reveille to call out to him. Reveille took a seat on the cloud and descended directly to the edge of the gorge, saying to Xuanzang, "The Bodhisattva has come." Xuanzang heard and immediately leaped from the cloud into the air, shouting at the Bodhisattva, "You, the master of the Seven Buddhas, the compassionate teacher! How did you come up with this wily scheme to harm me?" The Bodhisattva replied, "You, the rash and foolish one, you've been cursed by me. I went to great lengths to guide this pilgrim and taught him to save his life. How could you not repay my kindness by showing gratitude and instead come here to cause a commotion?" Xuanzang said, "You've had your fun with me! You'd let me roam freely and have my way if you hadn't put that binding on my head. Yesterday, you publicly shamed me in front of me, ordering me to serve the Tang Monk with all my might. You even put a spellbinding headgear on me, making me endure the pain and suffering. This isn't your doing, is it?" The Bodhisattva laughed and said, "You, this mischievous monkey! You don't follow my instructions and don't reap the benefits. If you're not tied down like this, you'd cheat and deceive the heavens. If you don't follow this path, you'll just bring disaster upon yourself again. Only with this devilish creature can you be taught the path of the Mahayana." Xuanzang said, "This matter, I did indeed make myself a devil. But why did you send the calamitous dragon, who had committed wrongdoing, to this place to become a demon and eat my master's horse? This is an even greater evil." The Bodhisattva replied, "The dragon was brought here by me, at the Jade Emperor's behest, to serve as the pilgrim's mount. You think that an ordinary horse from the mortal realm could cross over the myriad rivers and mountains and reach the Buddhist paradise? Only with this dragon horse can he do so." Xuanzang said, "If he's so afraid of me, how can he possibly escape?" The Bodhisattva ordered Reveille to call out, "Ao-Jun dragon king, Pearl-dragon, the Third Prince, come out! The Southern Sea Bodhisattva is here." Reveille went to the edge of the gorge and called out twice. The little dragon jumped out of the water, transformed into a human form, stepped onto the cloud, and came to the Bodhisattva, bowing down, saying, "I'm deeply grateful for the Bodhisattva's mercy in saving my life. I've been waiting here for a long time, but I've yet to hear any news from the pilgrim." The Bodhisattva pointed at Xuanzang and said, "Isn't this the great disciple of the pilgrim?" The little dragon saw him and said, "Bodhisattva, this is my arch-nemesis. Yesterday, I was starving, and I indeed ate his horse. He was far stronger than me, and he fought me to the point of exhaustion, cursing me to the point where I wouldn't dare come out. He didn't even mention anything about the pilgrim's quest." Xuanzang said, "You dog, you ought to atone for your past wrongdoings. In this case, you should have let me off with a warning, rather than putting me through this ordeal. You put that spellbinding headgear on me, ordering me to serve the Tang Monk with all my might, and when I got tired and screamed with pain, you still didn't intervene. Why are you now calling me your nemesis?"

—I was passionately in love with your mother even when she was still a bride, the bride of my friend. The prince noticed and was taken aback. He comes to me in the morning, at seven o'clock, wakes me. I get dressed in astonishment; silence from both sides; I understand everything. He pulls out two pistols from his pocket. Through a handkerchief. Without witnesses. What witnesses, when in five minutes we're sending each other off to eternity? He loaded them, stretched the handkerchief, stood, pressed the pistols against each other's hearts and looked each other in the face. Suddenly tears shower from both our eyes, our hands tremble. Both of us, both of us, at the same time! Well, here, naturally, there were hugs and a joint struggle of generosity. The prince cries out, 'yours,' I cry out, 'yours!' In a word... in a word... come to us... to live?

— I was passionately in love with your mother even when she was still a fiancée, the fiancée of my friend. The prince noticed and was taken aback. He comes to me in the morning, at seven, wakes me up. I dress with astonishment; silence from both sides; I understood everything. He takes out two pistols from his pocket. Through a handkerchief. They were loaded, stretched the handkerchief, stood, applied the pistols mutually to each other's hearts and looked each other in the face. Suddenly, tears burst forth from both eyes, their hands trembled. Both of us, both of us, at once! Well, then, genuine hugs and a battle of magnanimity ensued. The prince cries out: yours, I cry out: yours! In one word... one word... you two, to us... to live?

If anyone were to tell him at this moment that he was in love, in love with passionate love, he would reject the idea with astonishment and, perhaps, even with indignation. And if someone were to add that Aglaya's note is a love note, an appointment for a romantic tryst, he would burn with shame for that man and, perhaps, challenge him to a duel. All this was quite sincere, and he never once doubted or even allowed himself to entertain the slightest "double" thought about the possibility of his love for her or even of her love for him. The possibility of his love for her, for a man like himself, he considered a monstrous thing. He had the notion that it was simply a caprice on her part, if indeed there was anything to it; but he was too indifferent to the caprice itself and found it too much of a trifle; himself, he was preoccupied and busy with something entirely different. As for the words that slipped out of the agitated general yesterday about how she laughs at everyone, and him, the prince, in particular, he fully believed them. He felt no slight offense at this; in his opinion, it should have been so. For him, everything was mainly that tomorrow he would see her again, early in the morning, sit next to her on the green bench, listen to the guns being loaded, and look at her. That was all he needed. The question of what she meant to say and what important matter it was that directly concerned him did flicker through his mind twice or three times. Furthermore, in the actual existence of this "important matter," for which he was called, he never doubted for a single moment, but he thought very little about it now, to the point that he didn't even feel the slightest inclination to think about it.

If someone were to tell him in that instant that he was in love, that he was passionately in love, he would have disavowed the idea in surprise, perhaps even with indignation. If someone added that Aglaya's note was a love letter, a note setting a rendezvous, he would have burned with shame for the man and, perhaps, challenged him to a duel. Everything was utterly genuine, and he never doubted, let alone entertained the slightest doubt, about the possibility of love for him or the possibility of his love for her. The possibility of love for him, "a man like him," he would have considered a monstrous thing. Pondering, Selivan finally retreated to the most remote of abstractions. If Chichikov had been paying attention, he would have learned many details that pertained to him personally; but his thoughts were so engrossed in the matter at hand that a powerful clap of thunder was required to rouse him from his reverie and make him glance about. The entire sky was completely shrouded in clouds, and the dusty post road was bespattered with raindrops. A clap of thunder struck again, this time louder and closer, and the rain suddenly came pouring down like water from a jug. At first, it struck the kibitka obliquely, beating against one side, then the other; then, changing its line of attack and becoming completely direct, it drummed right into the top of the kibitka's roof; and finally, droplets began to splatter into his face. This caused him to draw himself in behind the leather curtains with two round peepholes designed for viewing the road, and he ordered Selivan to drive on more quickly. Selivan, who was interrupted in mid-sentence just like his master, realized that he shouldn't be dawdling, snatched something out from under the ox, something made of gray felt, slipped it into his sleeves, seized the reins in his hands, and shouted to his three-wheeled cart, which was barely taking its time, feeling a pleasant relaxation from the instructive speech. But Selivan was in no position to recall whether he had traveled two or three turns; guessing and trying to remember the road, he surmised that there were many turns he had missed. As a Russian person is wont to do in decisive moments, he didn't take the time to ponder, but instead, after turning right onto the first crossroads, shouted, "Hey, esteemed fellow travelers!" and took off at a gallop, hardly thinking about where the road he had chosen would lead.

They had hardly reached the top when the painter tore the door open completely and, with a deep bow, invited K to enter. He refused, however, to let the girls in, no matter how much they pleaded and pleaded, and even though they attempted to force their way in against his will. Only the hunchback managed to slip through under his outstretched arm, but the painter chased after her, grabbed her by the skirts, whirled her around once and then set her down again before the door with the other girls, who had not dared to cross the threshold while the painter left his post, but who had it anyway. K had no idea how to judge the whole situation, as it seemed as if everything was happening in a friendly, mutually agreeable manner. The girls at the door stretched their necks one after the other, called out various playful, jocular words to the painter, which K couldn't understand, and the painter laughed while the hunchback almost flew out of his hand. Then he closed the door, bowed again to K, offered him his hand and introduced himself: "Kunstmaler Titorelli." K pointed to the door behind which the girls were whispering, and said, "It seems that you're very popular in the house." "Those faces!" the painter said, and attempted in vain to fasten his nightshirt at his throat. He was barefoot and clad only in a wide, yellowish linen shirt tied with a belt whose long end swung to and fro. "These faces are a real nuisance," he continued, leaving the nightshirt, whose last button had just come undone, alone, and fetching a chair to force K to sit down. "I once painted one of them – she's not here today, anyway – and since then, they've all been after me. When I'm here, they only come in if I let them, but as soon as I'm gone, at least one of them is here. They've had a key to my door made and lend it to one another. One can hardly imagine how bothersome this is. For instance, I come home with a lady I'm painting, and I open the door with my key and find the hunchback at the little table, painting her lips red with a brush, while her little siblings, whom she's supposed to supervise, are running around and making the room untidy. Or, as happened to me yesterday evening – forgive me, with regard to my state and the mess in the room – I come home late at night and want to go to bed, and something tickles my leg, I look under the bed and pull out one of them. I don't know why they keep pressing in on me, since I'm not trying to lure them in, I'm sure you've noticed that. This is also disrupting my work. If this studio hadn't been provided to me for free, I would have moved out long ago." Just as he said that, a small voice called out from behind the door, "Titorelli, may we come in now?" "No," the painter replied. "And not me either?" it asked again. "No," said the painter, and went to the door to lock it.

"I don't want to achieve success as a speaker," said K, reasoning this out, "for it is probably unattainable for me anyway. The Chief Investigator speaks much better; it is part of his profession. What I want is only the public discussion of a public issue. Listen: I was arrested about ten days ago, and I laugh at the fact of the arrest itself, but that doesn't belong here now. I was broken into early in the morning, perhaps one had – it is by no means excluded according to what the Chief Investigator said – the order to arrest any housepainter, who is just as innocent as I am, but one chose me. The next room was occupied by two rough guards. If I were a dangerous burglar, one could not have made better arrangements. These guards were moreover demoralized riffraff, they chattered my ears full, they wanted to be bribed, they wanted to lure me out of my clothes and underwear with false promises, they wanted money, supposedly to bring me breakfast, after they had shamelessly eaten my own breakfast right before my eyes. That wasn't enough. I was led into a third room in front of the supervisor. It was the room of a lady I hold in high esteem, and I had to see how my room, not through any fault of mine, was so to speak defiled by the presence of the guards and the supervisor. It was not easy to remain calm. I succeeded, though, and I asked the supervisor completely calmly – if he were here, he could confirm it – why I was arrested. What did this supervisor, whom I see still sitting before me on the chair of the aforementioned lady as a representation of the most obtuse arrogance, answer? Gentlemen, he essentially answered nothing, perhaps he really didn't know, he had arrested me and was satisfied with that. He even did one more thing and brought three low-ranking employees of my bank into the lady's room, who busied themselves with touching and disarranging photographs that belonged to the lady. The presence of these employees, of course, had another purpose, just like that of my landlord and her maid, who were to spread the news of my arrest, damage my public reputation, and especially shake my position in the bank. Now none of that has come to pass, not the slightest bit of it. Not even my landlord, a completely simple person – I will mention her name in a dignified sense, she is called Frau Grubach – not even Frau Grubach was naive enough to see in this arrest anything more than a prank that had not been properly supervised by the young rascals on the street. I repeat, it has caused me only difficulties and temporary trouble, but it could have had more serious consequences?"

— Gentlemen, and like everyone else, I've made some less-than-elegant moves in my life, began the general, — but the most peculiar thing is that I consider a short anecdote I'm about to tell you the most disreputable in my entire life. Although it's been almost 35 years, I never managed to shake off a certain nagging, prickling feeling at the memory. It's a rather foolish matter: I was just a junior lieutenant at the time and was tasked with carrying a load. You know, a junior lieutenant: blood is boiling, and one's livelihood is on a shoestring. At that time, I had a valet, Niki for, who took pains to take care of my household, saved up, mended, scoured, and even snatched whatever he could to increase our household stores; he was an exemplary and honest man. I, of course, was strict but fair. It just so happened that we found ourselves stationed in a town. I was assigned a quarter in the suburbs by a retired sergeant-major and a widow, also. An elderly lady, nearly 80, or at least that's what I'd estimate, lived alone in a wretched, ramshackle wooden house and was too poor to have a maid. However, what distinguished her most was that she used to have a large family and relatives, but some had died over the course of her life, others had moved away, and a third group had forgotten about her, and she'd buried her husband 45 years prior. She lived with a niece, a hunchbacked, wicked, and, they say, witch-like woman who even bit her finger once but the old woman eventually passed away; the old lady was all alone for three years. I found it dull and pointless living with her; she was so vacuous, nothing could be salvaged from her. Eventually, she stole my chicken. This case remains a mystery, but there was no one else who could have done it. We quarreled over the chicken, and quite heatedly, and it just so happened that I requested to be moved to a different quarter immediately after. I was transferred, along with Niki for, to the opposite side of the suburbs to the family of a merchant with a large beard; it was a large family, I remember now. We left the old woman in disgust and moved in with joy. It took three days for me to notice that we had left our bowl behind at the old woman's house when I returned from my studies; Niki for reported to me, 'Your Excellency, we left our bowl with our former landlady, and we have nothing to serve soup with.' I was taken aback: 'How did our bowl end up with our former landlady?' Niki for was amazed, 'She didn't give it back to me because you broke her own bowl, and she's holding onto our bowl as compensation.' She's claiming that I myself suggested this arrangement. Such baseness on her part, of course, drove me to the extreme; my blood boiled over, I flew into a rage, and I rushed to her place. I stormed in, almost beside myself, and looked at her sitting in the corner, her face pale, her eyes bulging, and not a word in response; she just looked at me with an odd expression, as if she were swaying. I eventually calmed down, took a closer look, and asked her questions, but she remained silent. I stood there in confusion, the flies buzzed, the sun was setting, and the silence was oppressive; in a state of complete bewilderment, I left her place. I hadn't even made it home when I was summoned by the major, and I had to visit the barracks; I returned home very late at night. Niki for told me, 'You see, Your Excellency, our landlady passed away today, about an hour and a half ago.' This, of course, was the exact moment when I scolded her; she passed away while I was shouting at her. I was shocked, I'll be honest with you, and I couldn't think straight for a while. It even kept me awake at night. As I reflect on the matter now, I think it's this: an elderly woman, a human being, in these times, would call her a decent, kind creature, lived for a long time, grew old, and eventually breathed her last. She had children, a husband, a family, relatives – all of these, you see, used to buzz around her; and then – a complete disaster, everything went up in smoke, and she was left alone, like some fly carrying a curse on its back. And in that very instant, with the sun setting, on a quiet summer evening, my elderly woman takes off – and of course, there's a moral lesson there; and instead of a sympathetic tear, a young, desperate lieutenant, indignant and flustered, sends off a deceased woman into eternity with a barrage of coarse, Russian obscenities over the lost bowl. No doubt I'm to blame, and although I now look back on my actions with detachment, both in terms of the time elapsed and my own character, I still feel guilty; I continue to regret my actions even today. So I repeat, it's strange to me, all the more so since if I am to blame, it wasn't entirely my fault – after all, why did she choose to die at that exact moment? Of course, there's one explanation: the act had some psychological undertones, but I couldn't shake off the feeling of guilt; it wasn't until 15 years ago that I provided for two elderly women, bedridden and infirm, at my own expense, at a home for the elderly, with the intention of making their final days more comfortable; I even thought of leaving a legacy to make it an eternal foundation. Well, that's it – I repeat that, perhaps I've been guilty in many respects in my life, but this particular incident remains the most repugnant in my memory.

— Gentlemen, just as it has happened to everyone, I have committed some not exactly elegant actions in my life, — the general began. — But what's most peculiar is that I consider a brief anecdote that I'll share with you to be the most shameful of my life. It's been almost thirty-five years since it happened, but I've never been able to shake off a certain, so to say, gnawing impression. It's a rather absurd incident, by the way: I was still a young lieutenant and I was a private in the army, living on a tight budget. I had a soubrette, Niki-for, and he took care of my household with incredible zeal, saving, sewing, scrubbing, and cleaning, and even stealing everything he could lay his hands on to increase the household's assets. He was the most honest and conscientious man you could ask for. As for me, I was strict but fair. 

We were stationed in a small town for a while, and I was assigned a flat in the suburbs with a retired junior officer and a widow, who was over eighty years old, or at least around that age. Her tiny house was old, run-down, and made of wood, and she was too poor to afford a maid. What's more, she was once the mother of a large family and had many relatives, but over the years, they had either died or moved away, and some had simply forgotten about her. She had been a widow for forty-five years and had been living alone for a few years before that. Her niece, who was hunchbacked and wicked, they say she was as wicked as a witch, had even bitten her on the finger once, but had since passed away. So the old woman had been living alone for about three years.

I was terribly bored living with her, and it was also quite a bleak existence, as there was nothing to be gained from it. In the end, she even stole my chicken. The circumstances of the theft are still unclear to this day, but since there was no one else to blame, I suspected her. We quarreled over the chicken, and our disagreement was quite intense, and just then, they suddenly transferred me to a new flat on the opposite side of the suburbs, into the household of a merchant with a large family. I left Niki-for and the old woman with some relief. It's been three days since I moved, and I was out learning something, when Niki-for told me, 'It's a shame, sir, we left our bowl with our former landlady, and we have no soup to eat.' I was taken aback: 'How did our bowl end up with our former landlady?' Niki-for continued to report that the landlady, when we were leaving, had refused to return our bowl because I had broken her own cauldron, and that she was keeping our bowl as a way of compensation for her own. It seemed to her that I had suggested it myself in some way. Such meanness from her side completely threw me off balance; I was furious, I rose to my feet, and I flew into a rage. I went to see the old woman, who was sitting in the corner, looking like she'd been struck by lightning, holding her cheek in her hand. I immediately unleashed a torrent of abuse upon her, saying, 'You, you fiend!' and so on. But as I looked at her, something strange caught my attention: she sat there, her face fixed on me, her eyes wide open, and she said nothing in response. It was a strange, strange look, like she was swaying.

I finally calmed down, looked closer, asked her a question, but she remained silent. I stood there, unsure of what to do, the flies buzzed around me, the sun was setting, and the silence was oppressive. I was completely flustered and eventually left. I didn't even make it back home, as I was summoned to the major's office, and then had to go to my company, so I got home late in the evening. Niki-for's first words were: 'You know, sir, our landlady passed away.' 'When?' 'About an hour and a half ago, tonight.' It turns out that it was exactly at the time when I was yelling at her that she died. This took me aback, I must tell you, and I was barely able to collect myself. It even occurred to me in my dreams that night. Of course, I'm not a man given to superstitions, but on the third day, I went to church for her funeral. To put it simply, the more time passes, the more one thinks about it, and sometimes one starts to imagine things that aren't quite right. The main thing is that, as I finally realized, this woman, who was a human being, a being that's called humane in our times, lived for a long time, and finally died. She had children, a husband, a family, relatives – everything was swarming around her, so to say, full of laughter, and suddenly – nothing, everything went up in smoke, and she was left alone, like some sort of a fly, bearing the curse of the ages. And it was God who finally put an end to it. At sunset, in the quiet summer evening, she took her leave, and of course, there's a moral lesson in this. And it was exactly at this moment, instead of a comforting tear, the young, desperate lieutenant, fuming and spluttering, bid her farewell from the surface of the earth with a string of rude curses about the lost bowl. Undoubtedly, I am to blame, and even though I've looked back on my actions a long time ago, from a distance, and from a change of heart, as someone else's, I still feel a pang of regret. So, I repeat, this incident remains the most shameful act of my life, even if I was not completely at fault: why did she have to die exactly at that moment? One excuse, of course, is that it's a kind of psychological event, but still, I couldn't calm down until, fifteen years ago, I provided for two old women, who were in constant pain, in a charity home, out of my own pocket, so as to ease their final days on earth with a decent living. I think of bequeathing the capital for their benefit, to make it eternal. Well, that's all. I repeat that I may have erred in many things in life, but this incident, in my conscience, remains the most shameful act of my life.
