I sometimes imagine that I might have been just as guilty, and it can be unpleasant. The main thing is that I finally came to a conclusion: this old woman was a human being, a creature that is now called 'human' and 'humane' in our time, who lived for a long time, eventually settled down. She had children, a husband, family, and relatives around her, and everything was in full swing, like a never-ending laughter, and then, suddenly, it all came crashing down, leaving her alone, like some insignificant fly carrying a centuries-old curse. And so, in the end, fate brought it to an end. With the sunset, in a quiet summer evening, my old woman went, and, of course, it's not without a moral lesson. But at that very moment, instead of the expected sympathy, a young, desperate lieutenant, ranting and raving, sends her off into the afterlife with a barrage of coarse Russian curses for a lost pot. No doubt, I was at fault, and, despite looking at my actions now, after a long time and change of character, as if they were someone else's, I still feel sorry for it. So, I repeat that perhaps I was guilty of many things in life, but this incident remains, by my conscience, the most despicable act of my life."

— Gentlemen, it so happens to me, as to anyone, that I have made some not-so-refined decisions in my life, began the general. However, the strangest thing of all is that I consider the short anecdote I'm about to tell you the most base anecdote of my life. And that's been about thirty-five years now, but I could never shake off a certain, as it were, nagging impression when I remembered it. The matter, after all, is quite foolish: at the time, I was still only a lieutenant and I was hauling my pack in the army. You know, a lieutenant: the blood's boiling with fervor, but the household's a mere copper's wage; I had a valet, Nikiyor, and he was absolutely devoted to my household affairs, saving, mending, cleaning, and even pilfering here and there to increase the household's funds, a veritable paragon of virtue and honesty. I, naturally, was strict, but fair. For some time, we were stationed in a small town. They assigned me a quarters in the suburb in a widow's house, a spinster and an old woman, to boot, over eighty years old or thereabouts. Her little house was old, dilapidated, wooden, and she didn't even have a maid due to her poverty. But the main thing that set her apart was that she had once had a large family and relatives; some had died over the course of her life, others had moved away, a third group had forgotten about her, and she had been widowed forty-five years prior. She had lived with her niece for a little while before this, a hunchbacked and wicked woman, as wicked as a witch, who even bit the old woman on the finger, and she too died, so the old woman had been living alone for three years now. I was miserable in her house, and it was so empty, there was nothing to get out of it. Finally, she stole my hen. This affair remains unclear to this day, but besides that, there was no one else to blame. We fell out over the hen, and quite seriously, and at just that moment, I got moved to a different quarters, on my own request, to the other suburb, to the household of a wealthy merchant with a big beard, a family so numerous that I hardly remember them now. I was leaving Nikiyor and the old woman with relief; I was returning home after a few days, from my studies, when Nikiyor tells me, "Your Excellency, we left our pot at the old woman's place, and we don't have any soup to eat." I'm naturally shocked: "How on earth did our pot end up at the old woman's?" Nikiyor continues, "The old woman, when we left, didn't give it back to me because, as you had smashed her own pot, she's holding onto our pot as compensation, and it's said that you yourself proposed this arrangement." Such baseness on her part, naturally, drove me to the edge; my blood boiled, I jumped up, I flew into a rage. I go to the old woman, in other words, already beside myself; I look, and she's sitting in the corner, alone, as if she's been struck by the sun, her hand resting on her cheek. I at once, you see, unleash a veritable storm of abuse at her, "You're a wicked woman, a scoundrel!" and, you know, in the Russian manner. But look, something strange presents itself: she sits there, fixes me with a stern look, her eyes bulge out, and not a word in response; she looks at me with an unnatural air, as if she's swaying. I calm down, take a closer look, ask her a question, and she remains silent. I stand there, uncertain; the flies buzz, the sun sets, the silence is oppressive; I finally leave, in a state of utmost confusion. I hadn't even made it home yet when I was summoned by the major, and I had to go to the platoon, so I got home in the evening. Nikiyor's first words: "You see, Your Excellency, our old woman has passed away." "When?" "An hour and a half ago, this evening." This, in other words, was exactly the moment when I was abusing her. I was completely taken aback, I must tell you, and it even haunted me at night. I'm not a man given to superstitions, but on the third day, I went to church for her funeral. In short, the more time passes, the more I think about it; I begin to imagine, you see, that it's not quite right. The main thing, however, is that I finally figured out what the point was: a woman, a human being, they call it humane in our time, lived, lived for a long time, and finally passed on. She had children, a husband, a family, relatives – all these, as it were, smiles surrounding her, and suddenly – it's all gone, everything's flown up the drainpipe, and she's left alone, like some moth bearing a curse from time immemorial. And finally, God put an end to it. As the sun set, in a quiet summer evening, my old woman went, of course, with a moral lesson; and in this very instant, instead of a consoling, as it were, tear, a young, desperate lieutenant, raving and muttering, accompanies her from the surface of the earth with a stream of vile Russian curses for the deceased pot! There's no doubt I'm to blame, and although I look back on my deed now, distant in time and changed in nature, as if it were someone else's, I still feel sorry for it. So I repeat, I find it strange, the more so since, if I am to blame, I'm not entirely blameless: why did she happen to die just then? Naturally, one excuse: the deed had a certain psychological component, but still, I couldn't put my mind at ease until I, fifteen years ago, supported two permanently ill old women, at my own expense, in a hospital, in order to soften their final days on earth. I planned to make it eternal by leaving a capital to them. Well, that's all, I repeat; perhaps I've sinned in many ways in life, but I consider this incident the most base act of my life.

— Gentlemen, I, like everyone else, have made some clumsy acts in my life, began the general, — but the strangest thing is that I consider the short anecdote I am going to tell you the most scandalous one in my whole life, though it happened almost thirty-five years ago. However, I have never been able to shake off a certain, let's say, gnawing feeling of discomfort when I think about it. The matter, after all, is very silly: I was then just a junior lieutenant, and in the army, I was tugging at the leather straps. Of course, a junior lieutenant: blood is boiling water, and one's means are meager. I had then hired a servant, Nikiphor, and he took great care of my household, saving, sewing, scrubbing, and even everywhere pilfered whatever he could to increase our means; he was a most reliable and honest person. I, naturally, was strict, but fair. 

At some point, we found ourselves stationed in a small town. I was assigned a room in the outskirt of the town in the quarters of a retired junior lieutenant and, to boot, a widow. She was over eighty, or at least nearly so. Her little hut was old, dilapidated, and made of wood, and she didn't even have a maid because she was poor. But what struck me the most was that she had once had a large family and many relatives; some had died of old age, others had moved away, while others had forgotten about her; she had buried her husband forty-five years ago. She had lived with her niece, a hunchbacked and wicked woman, who, they say, was as wicked as a witch, and even bit her on the finger, but she died, leaving the old woman to live alone for three years. It was dull for me there, and she was so poor that it was impossible to get anything from her. In the end, she stole my hen. The matter is still murky, but, apart from her, there was no one else. 

We quarreled over the hen, and quite seriously, and just then an opportunity arose for me to be transferred to another room, on the opposite side of the town, into a large family of a merchant with a considerable beard, as I remember it now. I moved out with Nikiphor with joy, while leaving the old woman with indignation. Three days passed, and I came back from training, and Nikiphor reported, "Your Excellency, we left our bowl at the old woman's place, and we don't have any soup to serve." I, naturally, was shocked: "How could our bowl end up at the old woman's place?" Nikiphor was surprised, continuing to report that the old woman, when we were leaving, did not return our bowl on the grounds that, since I had broken her own chamber pot, she was holding onto our bowl in exchange for it, and that I had supposedly suggested this exchange myself. 

Such meanness on her part, naturally, infuriated me to the limit; my blood boiled, and I flew into a rage. I rushed to the old woman's place, in a fury; I looked at her sitting in a corner, in a shaded area, her hand pressed against her cheek as if she had been hit by the sun. I immediately, you see, let loose a loud shout at her, "So, you're the one who's so evil!" and, you see, in the Russian manner. I only just noticed something strange: she sat there, stared at me with her face twisted, her eyes popped out, and not a word in response; she looked at me in a strange, strange way, as if she was swaying. 

I eventually calmed down, took a closer look, asked her a question, but she remained silent. I stood there uncertain for a while; flies buzzed, the sun was setting, it was quiet; in complete perplexity, I eventually left. I didn't even make it back home before I was summoned to see the major, then I had to go visit the company, and I returned home late in the evening. The first thing Nikiphor said to me, "You know, Your Excellency, our old woman passed away." 

"When?" I asked. 

"About an hour and a half ago, in the evening," he replied. This, it means, was at exactly the time when I was scolding her that she passed away. I was flabbergasted, I must say. It even occurred to me to think about it even at night, and I even had a nightmare about it. I, of course, without any superstition, but on the third day, I went to the church for her funeral. In short, as time passes, the more I think about it, the more it bothers me. I wouldn't say it's that I'm bothered, but sometimes you might imagine something and it would make you feel uncomfortable. The main thing is that, in the end, I finally thought it through. First of all, the old woman, a human being, as they call it in our time, a humane creature, lived for a long time, and finally passed away. She used to have children, a husband, family, relatives, everything was whirling around her, let's say, and suddenly – the whole thing fell apart, and she was left alone, like some fly with a curse on it for centuries. And then, finally, God brought her life to an end – at sunset, on a quiet summer evening – and I, a young and desperate junior lieutenant, in a frenzy, in a state of frenzy, was escorting her from the face of the earth with a string of Russian curses for the lost plate! There is no doubt that I am to blame, and although I look at my actions now as quite far in the past and changed in nature, as someone else's, I still feel sorry for her nonetheless. So, I repeat, it is quite strange to me, and even more so because if I am guilty, I am not entirely guiltless: why did she happen to die at that very moment? 

Of course, there's one justification: the act was somehow psychological, but still, I couldn't calm down until, fifteen years ago, I started sending two regular old ladies to a nursing home, at my own expense, with the goal of alleviating their final days on earth. I thought of leaving a capital in perpetuity. Well, that's it. I repeat that, perhaps, I am guilty of many things in life, but I consider this episode the most scandalous act in my whole life.

You never asked me my name, how can I say anything? The little dragon said: "I never asked you where you came from, a monster from who-knows-where. You simply shouted: 'What's it to me where you came from, just give me back my horse!' You never mentioned a single word about the Tang dynasty!" The Bodhisattva said: "That monkey is so full of himself, never willing to acknowledge others' virtues. Now that we are about to go ahead, there is still a chance for him to be submissive. If you ask him about it, just mention the word 'fetching scriptures,' and he will naturally submit." The monkey was overjoyed to receive this lesson. 

The Bodhisattva went forward and plucked out the pearl from the little dragon's neck, dipped a branch of willow into the ambrosia and wiped it gently over the little dragon's body. He blew a breath of divine air, shouted: "Change!" and the dragon instantly transformed into his original horse-hair form. Then he instructed the little dragon: "You must seriously eradicate your evil karma, and when you have accomplished your mission, you will transcend the ranks of mortals and return to your true golden body." The little dragon, his mouth shut and his spirit willing, nodded his head in agreement. The Bodhisattva instructed the Monkey King to take him to see Tripitaka, "I'll return to the sea." The Monkey King pulled the Bodhisattva and wouldn't let go, saying: "I won't go! I won't go! The road to the West is so treacherous, how will I protect this ordinary monk? With so many hardships and perils, even I, the Monkey King, may not live to the end. How will I accomplish any achievement? I won't go! I won't go!" The Bodhisattva said: "When you were still a child, you were willing to be devoted to the path; now that you have escaped the tribulations of the heavens, how can you turn lazy and complacent? In our order, one must cultivate a heart of true faith and true virtues.

"You have never asked me my surname or name, so how can I say it?" the Weasel-dragon asked. "I never asked you where you came from, a monster," the Old Monk said. "You shouted, 'Give me my horse, why do you care where it comes from?' You never once mentioned the word 'Tang.' The Weasel-dragon said, "That beast, relying on his own strength, won't give praise to others; this time, when I go ahead, there will still be people surrendering. If you ask, you just need to mention the words of taking scriptures, then naturally they will kneel down." The Wanderer was delighted to follow the instruction. The Old Monk walked forward, plucked out the pearl from the Weasel-dragon's neck, and with a branch of willow, scooped up the ambrosial dew and brushed it on him. He blew his breath and said, "Transform!" The Weasel-dragon immediately transformed back into the original horse's fur. The Old Monk then instructed the Wanderer to take the Weasel-dragon away to see the Tripitaka, saying, "I will go back to the sea." The Wanderer grabbed the Old Monk's arm and would not let go, saying, "I won't go! I won't go! The road to the West is so treacherous, how can I, a layman, ever reach it? Having endured so much hardship and obstruction, the old monkey's life is hard to keep whole, how can I achieve any accomplishment? I won't go! I won't go!" The Old Monk said, "You were once unenlightened, and at that time you were willing to sincerely cultivate and be enlightened. Now you have escaped the calamity of heaven, why have you become lazy? In my sect, we attain enlightenment by renouncing worldly attachments, and it is only those with sincere faith that can achieve true fruit."

"You don't ask me my surname or name, how can I tell you?" the little dragon said. "I didn't ask you where you came from, a demon. You shouted, 'What has it got to do with where I came from? Give me back my horse!' You never said a single word of gratitude!"

The Bodhisattva said, "That monkey head, relying solely on his own strength, wouldn't admit the merits of others. Now that we are returning, there's still a chance for him to surrender. If you ask him, just remind him of the mission of retrieving scriptures, and he'll naturally submit without needing any effort."

The Monkey King was pleased to accept the task. The Bodhisattva approached the little dragon and removed the precious pearl from around his neck. He dipped a willow branch in ambrosia and sprinkled it on the little dragon's body, then blew a puff of divine breath at him. With a loud shout of "Transform!" the little dragon instantly turned back into his original form, a horse with a mangy coat. The Bodhisattva instructed the Monkey King, "You must focus on overcoming your karma, and after completing the task, you will surpass the mundane dragons and regain your true and pure body."

The little dragon, still holding a halter, bowed his head in agreement. The Bodhisattva told the Monkey King to take him to see the Tang Priest, "I'm going back to the ocean." The Monkey King held the Bodhisattva back, saying, "I won't go! I won't go! The Western Road is treacherous and arduous, how could I possibly protect this ordinary monk? I've already had so many hardships and setbacks, my old body is worn out, how can I possibly achieve any merit or fruit? I won't go! I won't go!"

The Bodhisattva said, "You were once not yet awakened to the Way, yet you were willing to put your heart and mind into cultivation; now that you've escaped calamity, how can you be idle and lazy? In our order, one cultivates to attain extinction and true being, and it is only through faith and genuine intentions."

"You never once asked me my surname or name, so how can I say it?" The Dragon Boy said, "I did not ask you where you came from, that fiend. You shout: 'What is it to me where you come from, just give me back my horse!' You've never mentioned the word 'Tang' even once!" The Bodhisattva said, "That ape, relying on his own strength, won't acknowledge anyone else's merits. This time, going ahead, there's still a chance to repent and be obedient. When asked, I'll just bring up the word 'Tang,' and naturally he'll kowtow." The Monkey King was delighted at this. The Dragon immediately transformed back into his original horse-like appearance. The Bodhisattva gave him an order, "You must use your heart to eradicate your karma, and once your work is done, you'll be able to transcend the mundane world and be returned a golden-bodied true result." The Dragon Boy, with a twisted bone in his mouth, acknowledged in his heart, accepting the order. The Bodhisattva instructed the Monkey King to lead him to meet the Monk Tang, saying, "I'll return to the sea." The Monkey King grasped the Bodhisattva and wouldn't let go, saying, "I won't go! I won't go! The Western Heaven's path is treacherous and rocky, how can I protect this ordinary monk? All these many hardships and twists will be hard on an old monkey's life, how can I achieve any results? I won't go! I won't go!" The Bodhisattva said, "When you were still unenlightened, you were willing to put your heart into cultivating the Way; now that you've escaped the disasters of heaven, why have you become lazy and complacent? We in our order achieve enlightenment through extinction, and we need a clear and correct faith."

"You've never asked me what my surname is or what my name is, so how could I tell you?" the little dragon said. "I never asked you where you came from, so how could you shout 'hand over the horse!'? You never mentioned the word 'Tang' at all!" The Bodhisattva said, "That monkey's mind is set on his own power, and he's unwilling to acknowledge anyone else. Now that he's turned against us again, there are still some left who'll surrender. If asked in the future, it's only natural that he'll fall on his knees. I've been instructing him." The Monkey King was overjoyed to learn of this.

Once the task is accomplished, you'll transcend the mundane world and attain a golden body." The little dragon bit the crossbeam, nodding its head in agreement.

The Bodhisattva instructed the Monkey King to lead the little dragon to see the Great Sage. "I'm going back to the sea," the Monkey King said. The Bodhisattva restrained him, saying, "Let go! I won't go! The western road is so perilous, how can a mortal like me possibly reach the end of it? With so many ordeals and hardships, my old body will hardly make it; how can I possibly attain any merit or benefit? I won't go! I won't go!" The Bodhisattva said, "You were once an ignorant being, yet you were willing to devote yourself to the way. Now that you've been freed from the cycle of birth and death, why have you become idle and careless? My disciples cultivate to attain extinction and realize their true nature, and it's only with unshakeable faith that we can achieve our goals."

One day, the four heavenly generals arranged a grand feast at the cave, inviting the Six Kings to dine, slaughtering oxen and horses to offer to heaven and earth, and letting all the monsters dance and sing. Everyone drank to excess and became completely drunk. When the Six Kings were sent away, the heavenly generals rewarded the grand and minor commanders, and had them lean against the iron bridge in the shade of the pines. In a moment, they all fell asleep. The four heavenly generals led the crowd to protect them, not daring to make any noise. As they watched, the Monkey King, still asleep, saw two people approaching with a scroll. On the scroll were three characters, "Sun Wukong," and the Monkey King rushed over, not giving them a chance to say anything, and tied them up. The Monkey King then dragged their spirits to a nearby city. The Monkey King gradually began to sober up and suddenly looked up to see an iron sign on the city gate with three big characters, "Yǔméng jiè" (The Underworld Realm). The Monkey King was suddenly enlightened, saying, "The Underworld Realm is the residence of the King of Hell, why am I here?" The two demons said, "Your time has come to an end on the outside, and we have a mandate from the King of Hell to bring you here." The Monkey King said, "I have transcended the Three Realms and am no longer subject to the laws of the Five Elements. Why are you here to harass me again?" The two demons just kept tugging and pulling, determined to drag him inside. The Monkey King grew angry and had a fit of temper. He produced a miraculous object from his ears and with a flick of his wrist, turned it into a massive and sturdy whip. He swung his hand and struck the two demons to pulp. He untied himself from the ropes and threw them aside, then grabbed a club and charged into the city. He terrified the ox-headed ghosts who ran in all directions, and the horse-faced ghosts ran north and south. The ghosts fled up to the Heavenly Lords' hall, crying out, "Great King! Trouble! Trouble! A creature with a monkey face has come to attack!"

One day, the four heavenly generals arranged a grand banquet and invited the six kings to attend. They slaughtered oxen and horses, offered sacrifices to heaven and earth, and the various demons danced and sang with joy. They all drank to the point of intoxication and passed out. As they sent the six kings away, they again rewarded the heads of the smaller demons, and the four heavenly generals leaned against an iron-plank bridge under the shade of the pines. In a moment, they fell asleep. The heavenly generals surrounded them, afraid to make a sound. Just then, the Monkey King, who was drunk, saw two figures approaching with a warrant in their hands, bearing the characters "Sun Wukong" on it. The Monkey King got no chance to say a word; they bound him with ropes and took him away, dragging him to the edge of a city. The Monkey King gradually came to his senses, and, looking up, saw a large iron plaque on the wall with the three characters "Jiāo Míng Jiè" – the Underworld Realm. The Monkey King was immediately enlightened and said, "The Underworld Realm is where King Yama resides; how did I end up here?" The two ghost-hunters said, "Your time of death had come, and we were the ones who came to take you." The Monkey King listened, then said, "I have transcended the three realms and am no longer bound by the five elements; how could I possibly be brought back under their control?" The two ghost-hunters kept tugging and pulling, trying to drag him inside. The Monkey King got angry and pulled out a precious treasure from his ear, snapped it open, and out came a rod. With a wave of his hand, he struck the two ghost-hunters to a pulp. He freed himself from the ropes, threw away the chains, and, wielding the rod, stormed into the city. The ghosts and spirits were terrified, scattering left and right; the Cow Head Demon and Horse Face Demon ran in all directions, and the various officers rushed to report to the Heavenly Emperor, "Oh no, oh no! A hairy-faced Ghost King has come out to wreak havoc!"

One day, in the Cave of Bliss, the Four Heavenly Kings prepared a grand feast and invited the Six Kings to come and drink. Cattle and horses were slaughtered, and sacrifices were made to heaven and earth. In attendance were a multitude of strange creatures who danced and sang in joy, all becoming intoxicated and drunk. Upon sending off the Six Kings, the Four Heavenly Kings rewarded their attendants, a great and small heads of the crowds, and leaned against an iron bridge under the shade of the willows, falling into a brief sleep. The Four Heavenly Kings led their entourage to surround them, too afraid to make a loud noise. Just then, the Monkey King, who was fast asleep, saw two people approaching with a scroll in hand, inscribed with the characters "Sun Wukong". The Monkey King got up without hesitation, and the two men quickly bound him with ropes. They dragged him away, stumbling and staggering, straight to a castle at the edge of a city. The Monkey King gradually sobered up, and suddenly lifted his head to look around. Above the city was an iron sign, bearing the three characters "Underworld Realm". The Monkey King suddenly realized, "The Underworld Realm is where the King of Hell resides; how did I end up here?" The two men said, "Your lifespan is at an end, and we have a warrant to bring you here." The Monkey King listened, saying, "I, the Great Sage Equal to Heaven, have gone beyond the three realms and am not within the Five Elements. I am no longer subject to their jurisdiction, so why would I be brought here?" Those two executioners simply wouldn't let him go, determined to drag him inside. The Monkey King got angry and pulled out a treasure from his ear, a stone that emitted a sharp whistling sound, a long tube that seemed to bite and chew. With a swipe of his hand, he knocked the two executioners into a pulp. He untied the ropes, discarded them, took up a stick, and charged into the city. The Oxhead Ghost and the Horseface Ghost fled east and west, while the multitude of ghosts and demons fled to the Forest of Justice, reporting, "Great King! Disaster! Disaster! A ferocious beast with a hairy face has burst in!"

One day, the Four Heavenly Kings hosted a banquet, inviting the Six Kings to come and drink. They slaughtered a bull and a horse, offered sacrifices to heaven and earth, and had the crowd of demons dance and sing, drinking to the point of drunkenness. After sending the Six Kings away, they rewarded the senior and junior leaders by leaning against an iron-plank bridge in the shade, where they suddenly fell asleep. The Four Heavenly Kings led the crowd in surrounding and guarding them, not daring to make a loud noise. They saw the Monkey King sleeping, whereupon two of them took out a written summons bearing the three characters "Monkey King," came near, without a word, bound the Monkey King's soul with a rope, and led him away, staggering and stumbling, straight to a city. The Monkey King gradually regained his senses, and suddenly lifted his head to look, seeing a sign on top of the city with three big characters reading "Domain of the Afterlife." The Monkey King was suddenly enlightened, saying, "The Domain of the Afterlife is the place of residence of King Yama, why did I come here?" Those two death-deceiving demons said, "You have reached the end of your appointed lifespan, we took the summons and came to fetch you." The Monkey King said, "I have transcended the three realms and am no longer within the five elements; I am no longer under the jurisdiction of others. Why do I still get summoned here?" Those two demons just kept tugging and pulling, determined to drag him in. The Monkey King grew enraged and brandished his precious item from his ear, flapped his hand, and made it transform into a rope as thick as a bowl; with a flick of his hand, he turned the two demons into minced meat. He released the rope, threw away his hands, and grabbed his rod, entering the city. The ox-headed ghosts and horse-faced ghosts scurried to hide, the demon officers ran up to the heavenly office, reporting, "Great King, disaster, disaster! Outside, a hairy-faced Lei Gong has come in!"

One day, the four heavenly knights prepared a grand banquet at the pit, inviting the six kings to drink and feast. They slaughtered oxen and horses, made offerings to the heavens and the earth, and had all the demons dance and sing in joy. They drank until they were drunk and exhausted. As they were sending the six kings away, they again rewarded their large and small officers by leaning on the iron board bridge under the shade of the willows, and soon they all fell asleep. The four heavenly knights and their retinue surrounded them, not daring to make a loud noise. At this time, Monkey King was caught sight of inside his dream. He saw two people carrying a scroll with the characters "Monkey King" written on it, and they came close to him without giving him a chance to resist. They quickly bound him with a rope, and pulled his spirit away, stumbling and staggering straight to the edge of a city. The Monkey King gradually regained his senses and suddenly raised his head to look around. He saw that above the city gate was a big iron plaque with three big characters, "The Realm of the Dead." The Monkey King suddenly came to his senses and said, "The Realm of the Dead is where the King of Hell resides. Why have I been brought here?" The two men said, "You are due to come to the end of your life, and we two have received orders to bring you here." The Monkey King heard this and said, "I, the Old Sun, have long since transcended the three realms and am no longer under their jurisdiction. Why then are they daring to come and fetch me again?" The two men, the reapers of the dead, just kept tugging and dragging him, determined to pull him in. The Monkey King's temper flared up, and he pulled out a handful of magical pills from his ears. A whirlwind formed, and the wind blew so strong that the man's bodies were reduced to pulp. He broke free from the rope, threw off his hands, took up a stick, and marched into the city. The ghostly ox and horse in terror fled east and west, and the ghostly guards ran up to the Heavenly Supreme Court to report, saying, "The King! Trouble! Trouble! Outside is a god with a hairy face, and he's coming to cause trouble!"

I woke up to a moderate, grayish light; the glass walls, glass armchairs, table sparkled. That calmed me down, and my heart stopped racing. Juice, Buddha... what an absurdity? Clear as day: I'm sick. I never used to see dreams before. They say it was the most ordinary and normal thing for the ancients to see dreams. Yeah, well, their lives were just as wretched a merry-go-round: green – orange – Buddha – juice. But we know that dreams are a serious mental illness. And I know that until now my mind was a chronometrically precise, sparkling, spotless mechanism, and now... Yes, now it's exactly like this: I feel a foreign body in there, in my head – like a single eyelash in the eye: you're aware of everything about yourself, but that eye with the eyelash is never out of your mind for a second.

But tell of the Heaven King Li and the Third Prince leading their troops, straight to the Heavenly Palace Hall. The Imperial Secretary presented the imperial edict: "Your servants have been sent out to conquer the underheaven world, capture the demonic monkey, Sun Wukong, but unexpectedly he has mighty powers, unable to be defeated, and now humbly request the Heavenly Emperor to add troops to eliminate him." The Heavenly Emperor replied, "I suppose this demonic monkey has some virtue, how can he still need more troops?" The Third Prince stepped forward and presented a petition: "I implore Your Majesty to pardon my death sentence! That demonic monkey wields a single iron rod, and previously defeated the divine spirit, and now struck my arm. A pole flag was erected outside the entrance, with the four characters 'Zǐtiān Dà Shèng' written on it, claiming that it's the title of his official position, and even if it is not, I would have no choice but to attack the Heavenly Palace Hall." The Heavenly Emperor heard these words and was amazed, saying, "This demonic monkey dares to be so arrogant! Order the troops to kill him at once." Just then, inside the imperial council chamber, a bright star, Tai Bai Jīn Xīng, flashed in and presented a petition: "That demonic monkey only knows how to speak, not how to discern his own size. If he is to be defeated by force, it will not be achieved in one battle, and we will only be exhausting the troops. It would be better, Your Majesty, to grant mercy and issue a decree of peace, and appoint him as the Zǐtiān Dà Shèng, but only a honorary title, with no power or emoluments, and let him live in the realm between heaven and earth, thus suppressing his evil thoughts, and preventing him from being arrogant, so that the world may be at peace and the universe clear and tranquil." The Heavenly Emperor heard his words and said, "I agree with your proposal." He immediately issued an edict, and ordered Tai Bai Jīn Xīng to take it back.

Now, the Li Tian Wang and the Third Prince led the multitude of generals straight to the Palace of Elysium. They kowtowed, saying: "We, your servants, were commissioned by your majesty's decree to venture into the mortal world, apprehend the wicked monk Sun Wukong, but he unexpectedly possesses an extraordinary range of magical abilities, and hence our defeat, so we pray that Your Majesty order additional troops to eradicate him." The Jade Emperor said: "Assuming this wicked monkey is as cunning as you say, how dare he ask for more troops?" The prince approached further and kowtowed, saying: "I humbly implore your majesty to pardon my transgression! That wicked monkey wields a rod of iron and routed the Celestial General, and then struck my arm. Outside the cave stands a flag on a pole, emblazoned with the four characters 'Great Sage of Heaven'. It is proclaimed that he is thus appointed an official position, and thus we should disengage and let him surrender; were he not appointed, we would attack the Jade Palace above." The Jade Emperor heard his words and exclaimed in surprise: "This wicked monkey dares to be so arrogant! I order you generals to kill him immediately." Just as he spoke, Grand Marshal Tai Bai Jin Xing emerged from among the attendants and kowtowed, saying: "The wicked monkey only boasts in words, unaware of his own limitations. If we add to the troops to engage in battle with him, it will be impossible to apprehend him in the near future and would only result in a greater strain on the troops. It would be more advisable, Your Majesty, to grant him an amnesty and issue a decree commanding him to submit. Have him do the role of Great Sage of Heaven, but give him a mere title without material benefits, and instead keep him in a secluded place to absorb his wicked heart, lest he develop further arrogance and render the world peaceful and the universe tranquil." The Jade Emperor heard his words and said: "How shall one call it 'a mere title without material benefits'?" Tai Bai Jin Xing replied: "It is called 'Great Sage of Heaven', but without powers to govern, without salary and stipend. Moreover, we will keep him in a secluded place between the earth and heaven, to absorb his wicked nature, so that he will not again develop arrogance, thus bringing tranquility to the world and purity to the universe." The Jade Emperor approved, saying: "I will do as you advise." He immediately ordered the decree to be drawn up, and appointed Tai Bai Jin Xing to take it to him.

The Imperial Commander Li and the Third Prince led the army to the Hall of Elysium. The Imperial Commander Li presented the imperial edict: "Your servant has been ordered by the Holy Emperor to lead the army out of the underworld, capture the rebellious Immortal Monkey Sun Wukong, and only unexpectedly, he was too powerful, and we couldn't defeat him. We now ask the Holy Emperor to mobilize more troops to eradicate him." The Jade Emperor replied, "I understand that he is a rebellious monkey with great prowess, and yet you still want to mobilize more troops?" The Third Prince stepped forward again and pleaded, "I humbly beg the Holy Emperor to pardon my transgression! The rebellious monkey used a iron rod to defeat the Great Spirit Guardian and injured my arm. Outside the Heavenly Gate, a flag was erected, bearing the four characters 'Great Sage Equal to Heaven'. It is his official title, and even if we stop fighting, he will come back to surrender; if not, he will besiege the Celestial Treasure Hall itself." The Jade Emperor was shocked and exclaimed, "That rebellious monkey dares to be so arrogant! Order the army to kill him immediately!" 

Just as the Jade Emperor was speaking, a junior official in the ranks of the celestial bureaucracy suddenly stepped forward, the Star of White Light Venus, and said, "That rebellious monkey only knows how to talk big, but not how to measure his own strength. If we decide to mobilize the army to fight him, it would be difficult to subdue him at once, and would only waste the troops' strength. It would be more merciful if the Holy Emperor would grant amnesty and issue a decree of amnesty, making him the Great Sage Equal to Heaven. Only bestow upon him a honorary title without any real power or benefits, and let him live a humble life in the wilderness, suppressing his evil tendencies and preventing him from being arrogant, so that the universe may be peaceful and serene." The Jade Emperor heard this and said, "As you recommend." He then ordered a decree to be issued, and entrusted White Light Venus to deliver it.

It was then said that Emperor Li and the Third Prince, accompanied by the countless officials, proceeded straight to the Palace of Divine Enlightenment. He presented the imperial edict: "We have been tasked by the divine decree to lead the troops out of the heavens, to subjugate the supernatural being Sun Wukong, but unexpectedly, he possesses boundless supernatural powers and cannot be defeated, so we beg the eternal emperor to dispatch additional troops to exterminate him." The Jade Emperor replied, "Assuming this mischievous monkey has as many skills as he claims, do we still need to dispatch more troops?" The Third Prince stepped forward and spoke: "I implore the eternal emperor to pardon me for my past transgressions. That mischievous monkey wields an iron rod, having defeated the divine spirit, and wounded my arm. Outside the Heavenly Gate stands a flagpole bearing the inscription 'The Great Saint of Heaven', which is an edict bestowing upon him this official position. Even if he does not hold this position, he still wants to attack the Heavenly Treasure Palace." The Jade Emperor heard his words and was startled: "This mischievous monkey dares to act so rashly! Order the generals to immediately strike him down at once." Just as he spoke, a Minister of the Board of Astronomy, the Star of White Iron, appeared suddenly and said: "That mischievous monkey only knows how to boast but is unaware of his own size. If we want to deploy troops to fight him, it will be difficult to subdue him immediately, and the army will be wearied. It would be more merciful of the eternal emperor to issue a decree of amnesty, and let him take on the title of the Great Saint of Heaven, with a ceremonial title but no salary, and let him live out his life in a remote place, so as to pacify his depraved mind and prevent him from acting rashly, in order to ensure the peace and harmony of heaven and earth, and the serenity of the universe." The Jade Emperor heard his words and said: "In accordance with your proposal." He immediately ordered a decree to be issued and told the Star of White Iron to take it along.

Speaking of Li Tianwang and the Third Prince leading the generals to the Palace of the Gods, the officials in attendance reported: "We were dispatched by the Imperial Decree to descend into the mortal realm and capture the demonic Monkey, but to our surprise, he was powerful beyond measure, and thus we were unable to overcome him. We humbly request that the Emperor augment our troops in order to eradicate him." The Jade Emperor replied, "How could a demonic monkey possibly have such great abilities? Do we need to augment our troops?" The Prince stepped forward and reported, "I humbly beg for forgiveness for my transgressions! That demonic monkey wields a magical iron rod, and first defeated the Great Spirit, and then injured my arm. A banner stands outside the entrance with the four characters 'Zǐ Tiān Dà Shèng,' saying that he has been conferred this title, and that we should stop our troops and let him surrender; if not, we will batter down the Palace of the Heavenly Treasure." 

The Jade Emperor was shocked and said, "This demonic monkey dares to be so audacious! Order the generals to immediately put him to death." Just then, Tai Bai Jin Xing, from the ranks, suddenly appeared and reported, "The demonic monkey only knows how to boast, but does not comprehend the situation. To deploy troops to fight him would only lead to an unremitting struggle, and our forces would not be able to subdue him in the short term. It would be wise for the Emperor to show mercy and benevolence, and to issue a decree summoning him to submit. Let us just confer on him the title 'Zǐ Tiān Dà Shèng,' but strip him of his authority and let him live without any official salary. This way, he will not be able to harbor wild ambitions, and the realm will be at peace." 

The Jade Emperor agreed with Tai Bai's suggestion and issued an edict accordingly, instructing him to lead it to the demonic monkey.

It has been more than a week since the guest, a gentleman, arrived in the town, attending parties and dinners and thus passing a most pleasant time. He finally decided to visit the Mnilovs and Sobakovichs, to whom he had promised to do so. Perhaps there was another, a more important reason, a matter closer to his heart... But the reader will learn about this gradually and in due time, if only they have the patience to read the lengthy story that lies ahead, one that will expand and unfold in scope as it reaches its conclusion, which will put everything to rest. 

Kuzma, the coachman, was given instructions to harness the horses to a certain carriage early in the morning; Petrushka was ordered to stay at home, to keep an eye on the room and the trunk. The reader will do well to get acquainted with these two serfs of our hero. Though they are not notable people, and those secondary or even tertiary characters, though the main plot and the springs of the poem do not rest on them and barely touch on them, the author is excessively meticulous in all things and, despite being a Russian, wants to be precise, like a German. This will not take much time or space because not much needs to be added to what the reader already knows, that is, that Petrushka went about in a wide, brown frock coat with a baronial shoulder and had a large nose and lips. He had a character that was more inclined to silence than to talk; he even had a noble desire for enlightenment, that is, to read books, of which he was not put off by the content; it was all the same to him, whether it was a book about a lovesick hero, a primer, or a prayer book, he read everything with equal attention; if they had offered him chemistry, he would not have refused it either. What pleased him was not what he was reading, but the act of reading itself, or rather the process of reading, where somehow out of the letters a word would emerge, sometimes God knows what it means. This reading took place mostly in a lying position in the front room, on the bed and on a small cushion that had become flat and thin, like a pancake. Besides his passion for reading, he had two other habits that were his distinguishing features: he never undressed to sleep, but slept in the same frock coat, and he always carried with him a certain special air, of his own peculiar smell, which reminded one of the quiet of a deserted room, so that if he just placed his bed somewhere, even in an uninhabited room, and dragged his greatcoat and belongings there, it seemed that people had lived in that room for ten years. 

Chichikov, being a very sensitive man, and even fastidious in some cases, upon catching the air on his fresh nose in the morning, would wrinkle his face and shake his head, saying, "You, brother, God knows, are you sweating, perhaps? Why not go to the bathhouse?" To which Petrushka would say nothing and would try to busy himself with something else; or he would approach the hanging barin's frock with his whip or simply tidy up something. What he thought when he was silent, perhaps he said to himself, "And you, after all, are fine, haven't you gotten tired of repeating the same thing forty times?" – God knows, it is hard to know what a low-ranking serf thinks at the time when his master is giving him instructions. 

And so, here is what can be said about Petrushka for the first time. Kuzma, the coachman, was a completely different person... But the author is very embarrassed to spend so much time on low-class people, knowing from experience how reluctantly they get to know about lower classes. Such is the Russian person: a strong passion to be proud of those who are one rank higher than him, and a brief acquaintance with a count or a prince is better than any close friendship. The author even fears for his hero, who is only a collegiate councilor. The privy councilors may get to know him, but those who have already reached the rank of general may, God knows, not even condescend to glance at him with a scornful glance, or, what's worse, may pass by with deadly indifference for the author. But whether it's sad or not, it's necessary to return to the hero. So, after giving orders the evening before, after waking up very early in the morning, washing, wiping himself with a wet towel from head to toe, which was done only on Sundays – and this day happened to be Sunday – after shaving himself, dressing in a billy-blue frock coat with a braid and then the greatcoat with large bearskins, he descended the stairs, supported on one side and then the other by the tavern servant, and sat down in the carriage. 

The carriage rolled out with a crash from under the hotel gate onto the street. A priest doffed his hat, several young boys in stained shirts held out their hands, saying, "Baryshka, give us alms for the orphans!" The coachman, noticing that one of them was particularly fond of sprawling, thrashed him with the whip, and the carriage started bouncing over the cobblestones. There was no little joy in seeing the striped gate in the distance, which signaled that the town street, like any other street, would soon be over; and having bumped his head several times against the carriage box, Chichikov finally rode off onto the soft earth. 

Just as the town disappeared from view, the stuff the people like to talk about, both on the left and on the right of the road, began to appear: mounds, a pine grove, low, scrawny young fir bushes, burned trunks of old trees, wild gorse and the like rubbish. Occasionally, stretched along a rope, were villages, built in a way that looked like old piles of firewood, covered with gray roofs with carved wooden decorations in the form of hanging, embroidered wall hangings. Several men, as usual, sat on benches in front of their fur-lined sheepskin coats. The women with thick faces and breastbanding peered out from the upper windows; a calf peered out of the lower window, or a blind sow stuck its snout out. In a word, familiar views. Having traveled fifteen versts, he remembered that here, according to Mnilov's words, his village was located, but the sixteenth verst passed by, and the villages were nowhere to be seen, and if not two men who met on the way, he would hardly have caught sight of them in the fog.

For over a week, the gentleman guest had been living in the city, attending parties and dinners and spending, as they say, a very pleasant time. Finally, he decided to venture out of the city and visit the landowners Milyov and Sobakevich, to whom he had promised to do so. Perhaps another, more substantial reason, a matter much closer to his heart, motivated him to do so. But the reader will learn about this in due time, provided he is patient enough to read the offered novel, which is very long and becomes wider and more spacious as it approaches its conclusion, which brings the story to an end.

The coachman, Selifan, was given the order to put the horses into a certain carriage very early in the morning. Petrushka was ordered to stay at home, keep an eye on the room and the trunk. It may be useful for the reader to get to know these two servants of our hero, although they are not so notable figures, and are often referred to as secondary or even tertiary characters, whose main plot threads and springs do not depend on them, and only occasionally concern them and catch their attention. This will not take much time or space, as the reader already knows very little, that is, that Petrushka wore a wide brown tailcoat with a noble shoulder, and had a prominent nose and lips, according to his social status. He was more inclined to be quiet than talkative; he even had a noble aspiration towards education, i.e., reading books, the content of which did not puzzle him: whether it was a romance, a primer, or a prayer book, he read everything with equal attention; if someone presented him with chemistry, he would not have refused it either. He liked not what he read, but the process of reading itself, or rather, the emergence of some word from letters, which, as it were, can be extracted from the book, the meaning of which is sometimes unknown. This reading took place in a reclining position on a bed in the front room, on a couch that had become flattened and thin, like a pancake, due to this circumstance. Besides his passion for reading, he had two other habits, which were the other distinguishing features of his character: he used to sleep without undressing, in the same tailcoat, and always carried with him a certain special air, his own personal scent, which had a slightly stale quality, so that it was enough for him to arrange his bed somewhere, even in an uninhabited room, to move the cloak and his belongings there, and already it seemed as if people had lived there for ten years. When Chichikov, being a rather fastidious man and even somewhat finicky in certain cases, was attracted to the fresh air on a clear morning by rubbing his nose, he would wrinkle his face and shake his head, saying, "You, brother, you must be sweating, or something. So, that is what can be said about Petrushka for the first time. Selifan, the coachman, was a completely different person...

The author feels quite ashamed to spend so much time with readers on low-class characters, knowing from experience that they are not eager to acquaint themselves with lowly social ranks. This is the nature of the Russian man: he has a strong passion for boasting about the fact that he outranks someone by one degree, and a familiar acquaintance with a count or a prince is more valuable to him than close friendly relations. The author even fears for his hero, who is only a collegiate councilor. Procurators, perhaps, will make his acquaintance, but those who have already reached general ranks, may, God only knows, even cast a contemptuous glance on him, as one would on everything that crawls at their feet, or, worse still, they may overlook him with a deadly indifference for the author. Though it may be unfortunate, yet it is necessary to return to the hero. After giving the necessary orders the previous evening, he woke up very early in the morning, washed, wiped himself with a wet sponge from head to toe, which was only done on Sundays, and then shaved himself so smoothly that his cheeks became a real atlas in terms of smoothness and sheen. He put on a brown fur coat with a fringe and then a cloak on large fur-trimmed shoulders, and went down the stairs, supported by the innkeeper's waiter on one side or the other. He got into the carriage with a rumble, and it drove out of the inn gate onto the street. A passing priest doffed his hat, and several ragged boys stretched out their hands, saying, "Give the orphan some alms, sir!" The heavenly edict arrived, and the Jade Emperor took it outside the Southern Heavenly Gate, and pressed down on the auspicious cloud, all the way to the Water Curtain Cave on Flower Fruit Mountain.  To the group of little monkeys, he said, "I am a heavenly messenger, with a heavenly edict in hand.  I have come to invite you, great king, to come out quickly!" The little monkeys passed the message layer by layer until it reached the deepest part of the cave, and said, "Great king, there is an old man outside with a document under his arm, saying that he is a heavenly messenger come from above, inviting you to come out as well." 

The Monkey King heard this and was greatly delighted, saying, "I was just thinking about going up to heaven a couple of days ago, and now there is a heavenly messenger here inviting me!" He called out, "Hurry and bring him in!" The Monkey King hastily put on his attire and greeted the guest. The Jade Star entered and stood still in the center, facing south, and said, "I am the star Venus of the Western He White, bearing a heavenly edict from the Jade Emperor, to summon you down below to come up to heaven to receive a certificate of immortality." The Monkey King laughed and said, "I'm delighted to see the great star descend."

He instructed, "Small ones, arrange a feast to entertain the guest." The Jade Star said, "The heavenly edict is in my possession; I shouldn't stay long; please come with me, and we'll talk about it afterwards when the honors and ranks have been bestowed." The Monkey King replied, "I thank you for your gracious visit, I will go first.  I will go first."  Immediately he summoned the Four Heavenly Kings and entrusted them with, "Be careful and teach my descendants; I'll go up to heaven to take a look at the road, and then I'll bring you all up to live with me."  The Four Heavenly Kings promised to do so.

The Monkey King and the Jade Star ascended together on a cloud, rising up into the empty space above.  This was the time when they reached the exalted position of the top heavenly grade, recorded in the Cloud Rank Treasure Roll.  As for what office or title they were granted, I'll tell you about it in the next chapter.

The heavenly decree was received, so the Monkey King went out through the Southern Heavenly Gate, pressed down on the auspicious cloud, and headed straight for the Jade Water Veil Cave on Flower Fruit Mountain. He said to the troop of monkeys, "I am a heavenly emissary, carrying a sacred mandate, please tell the Great King quickly!" The monkey outside the cave relayed the message, layer by layer, to the depths of the cave, saying, "The Great King, outside is an old man carrying an imperial decree, saying that he is a heavenly emissary come to summon you."

The Monkey King overjoyed upon hearing the news, saying, "I've been thinking of going to heaven for the past two days, and now there's a heavenly emissary here to summon me." He called out, "Come on in quickly!" The Monkey King hastily got dressed and came out to receive his guest. The Jade Star, entering in person, stood facing south, saying, "I am the West's Great White Star, bearing the decree of the Jade Emperor, come to invite you to heaven to accept the scrolls of immortality."

The Monkey King laughed and said, "Many thanks for your old self coming down to visit." He then said, "Everyone, make preparations for a banquet to receive our guest." The Jade Star said, "The mandate is in my possession, and I dare not linger; let us go to heaven together, and after the ceremony, we'll discuss the rest later." The Monkey King said, "Please accept my gratitude, I'll leave!" and immediately summoned his Four Valiant Generals, saying, "Be careful to instruct my descendants, and I'll go to heaven to take a look at the road, and bring all of you up to live with me."

The Monkey King and the Jade Star rose up on cloud heads, ascending to the sky, exactly in that moment:

They had attained a heavenly position of highest honor, listed in the Jade List among the heavenly troops. However, I do not know what office or rank they received, and I will have to continue the story next time.

The Jade Star received the edict, went out of the South Gate of Heaven, pushed down the auspicious cloud, and came straight to the Water Curtain Cave on Flower Fruit Mountain. The Monkey King laughed and said, "It's a great honor that the venerable star has descended." He ordered, " Servants, prepare a feast to welcome him!"

The four strong warriors replied, "We will comply."

Just then, he was appointed to the high position of the Heaven-Supreme, recorded in the Rolls of Cloud Banner Immortals.
