Feeling that it was fate to be saved from the jaws of wild beasts, even if I died of starvation, it would be better than feeding them. Bajian's mother heard this and said, "My child, don't bother talking to the venerable elder, I have simple provisions that I can use to entertain him." Bajian asked, "Where did you get these simple provisions?" His mother said, "Don't ask me about it, I have some." She had the maidservant take down the small pot, put firewood under it, and heated the oil until it was done and done and done again, then washed it and placed it back on the stove. She first boiled half a pot of water, then used it to make a tea broth with some wild elm leaves. Then she cooked some millet and rice, boiled some dried vegetables, and placed two bowls of them on the table. The old mother told the monk, "The venerable elder, this is what my child and his wife have prepared with their own hands – extremely clean and pure tea and rice." The monk came down to thank her and only then sat down. Bajian, however, prepared another place and arranged some wild boar meat, musk deer meat, snake meat, fox meat, rabbit meat, and shredded elk meat, full plates and full bowls of it, to accompany the monk in his vegetarian meal. Just as they were about to sit down, he saw the monk clasping his palms and reciting, and being startled, Bajian didn't dare move, leapt up, and stood beside him. The monk only recited a few lines before saying "Please refrain from eating." Bajian said, "You're an ordained person who recites short scriptures?" The monk replied, "This is not scripture, but a talisman for abstaining from food." Bajian said, "You monks are always so particular, even when eating, you continue to recite and recite."

As long as the world allows us to live, I'll be grateful; even if I'm to die of hunger, I'm still better off than being devoured by tigers and wolves. Baojin's mother heard about this and called out to him, "Son, don't talk nonsense with the venerable elder. I have my own ingredients to prepare food." Baojin asked, "Where have you gotten these ingredients?" His mother replied, "You don't need to ask me. I have them." The wife brought down a small cauldron, poured in oil, lit a fire to heat it, repeatedly scrubbed and washed it, and then placed it on the stove. First, she boiled some water in it without using it, then added some yew leaves from the mountains and steeped them in the water to make tea, afterward she cooked some millet and rice, and boiled some dried vegetables, then put two bowls of food on the table. The old mother said to the Buddhist Master of the Three Storehouses, "Venerable elder, this tea and food have been meticulously prepared by me and my daughter-in-law." The Master of the Three Storehouses came down to thank her and then sat down. Baojin set up another table with some old tiger meat, deer meat, python meat, fox meat, and rabbit meat, all without salt or sauce, as well as dried venison, a full plate and bowl, and sat down next to the Master of the Three Storehouses. As they sat down, he was about to speak when he saw the Master of the Three Storehouses joining his palms and reciting a scripture, which frightened Baojin into not daring to move. He quickly got up and stood by the side. The Master of the Three Storehouses recited a few lines, then said, "Please be seated." Baojin said, "You're an ascetic who is in the habit of reciting short scriptures?" The Master of the Three Storehouses replied, "This is not a scripture, but a talisman to purify the mind." Baojin said, "Monks like you are so particular; when eating, you still recite scriptures all the time."

Grateful for the Buddha's merciful protection, being saved from the tiger's den, it's better than being fed to the beast. Bapin's mother heard of this, called out and said, "My child, don't talk nonsense with the old master, I have some ingredients by myself, I'll manage." Bapin asked, "Where are the ingredients?" The mother said, "Don't ask me, I'll take care of it." She called her daughter-in-law to take down the small pot, lit a fire, put in oil and stoked it, scraped and washed it repeatedly, and still placed it on the stove. She first boiled half a pot of water without using it, then boiled some mountain ash leaves in the water to make tea soup, and then cooked some yellow rice and millet, and boiled some dried vegetables until they were done, and placed two bowls on the table. The old mother told the senior monk, "The venerable master, please take a fast, this is what my son and his wife and I have worked hard to prepare, extremely clean and pure tea and food." The senior monk came down to thank them, and then sat. Meanwhile, Bapin had prepared another place, arranged some old tiger meat, deer meat, python meat, fox meat, rabbit meat, and minced venison, full plate and full bowl, accompanying the senior monk in taking a fast. Just as they were about to sit down, one saw the senior monk clasping his hands and reciting scripture, scaring Bapin from moving, so he hastily stood up beside him. The senior monk didn't recite many sentences before he said "Please take a fast." Bapin said, "You are an ascetic who recites short scriptures?" The senior monk said, "This is not a scripture, but a scroll of a fast-breaking incantation." Bapin said, "You monks are peculiar, calculating everything, even when eating, you recite scripture, recite scripture."

My mother heard the news, then called out, "Son, don't keep company with the venerable elder, I have provisions of my own, I can manage." Bajin said, "Where did you get these provisions?" The mother said, "Don't bother asking me, I've got my own." She ordered the maid to take down the small cauldron, lit the oil, scrubbed and rinsed it, but still left it on the hearth. She first boiled half a cauldron of water without using it, then steeped some mountain ash leaves in water to make tea, and then cooked some millet and rice to make a meal. She boiled some dried greens to a tender state, and put them into two bowls, then brought them out and placed them on the table. The old mother said to Sanzang, "Venerable elder, this meal has been carefully prepared by my son and daughter-in-law." Sanzang came down to thank her, then sat back down. Bajin set another table, laying out some tiger meat, musk deer meat, snake meat, fox meat, and rabbit meat, along with some dried, chopped deer meat, a full dish and a full bowl, to accompany Sanzang in his fasting. Bajin couldn't help but tremble as he saw Sanzang clasp his hands in prayer and recite from a sutra. He hastily stood up to his feet, standing beside him. Sanzang had only recited a few sentences before he began to "invite the meal." Bajin said, "You're one of those monks who recite short suttas?" Sanzang replied, "This is not a sutra, but a spell of fasting." Bajin said, "You monks are often calculating and particular, even when eating, you're constantly reciting and reciting."

Upon taking refuge under the protection of heaven, being rescued from the wild beasts, even starving to death would be a blessing compared to being fed to them. Upon hearing this, Boren's mother called out, "My child, don't waste your time talking to the elder; I myself will prepare something for you." Boren asked, "What kind of thing?" His mother replied, "Don't bother asking me; I have my own things." She ordered the maid to take out a small pot, lit the fire and fried some oil until it was dripping, scrubbing it clean and washing it repeatedly, yet it remained on the hearth. She first boiled a half-pot of water but then cooked some mountain yew leaves in the water to make tea, afterwards boiled some glutinous rice and millet, and boiled some dried vegetables until they were done, serving them in two bowls and placing them on the table. The old mother said to the Tang monk, "The elder is invited to a vegetarian meal; these are a few exceptionally clean and pure dishes prepared by myself and my daughter-in-law." The monk descended and thanked her before taking a seat. Meanwhile, Boren prepared another place, laying out some raw tiger meat, deer meat, python meat, fox meat, rabbit meat, and dried, unseasoned venison, all filled to the brim in a bowl, accompanying the Tang monk in his vegetarian meal. As they sat down to eat, he wished to get up but just as he saw the monk join his hands in prayer and begin to chant, the fright left him frozen in place. He didn't dare move, but instead stood up beside him. After the monk had recited only a few lines, he then intoned the incantation for a vegetarian meal. Boren said, "You're an ordained monk with a stammering tongue?" The Tang monk replied, "This is no sutra, but an incantation for a vegetarian meal." Boren said, "Monks who have renounced the world are always so particular about things; even in eating, they continue to recite and recite."

"The assembly would convene as planned; only after my emissaries retrieve the Great Vehicle Sutra, shall I, in utmost sincerity, carry out a good deed." All the officials uniformly obeyed. At the time, within the temple, someone asked, "Who dares to carry out the emperor's intention and go up to the West to offer incense to the Buddha to seek the true scripture?" Before the question could be finished, a monk suddenly appeared beside them and, bowing to the emperor, said, "This humble monk is of no ability, and I wish to offer the service of a dog or a horse to Your Majesty, and pray that the Emperor's dynasty may be forever secure."

The Tang king was greatly pleased, rose from his seat to support the monk with his imperial hand, saying, "If the monk is able to exhibit such virtue and loyalty, I do not fear the long journey, traversing mountains and rivers; I wish to befriend you as my younger brother." Xuanzang bowed in gratitude for the benevolence.

The Tang king, indeed a person of utmost virtue, went with the monk in front of the Buddha and performed four bows. He called Xuanzang "Your Highness, Holy Monk." Xuanzang thanked him with boundless gratitude, saying, "Your Majesty, this humble monk, what virtues have I, what abilities do I possess, that I dare to be considered by Heaven and enjoyed such kindness and concern? When I go this time, I must definitely risk my life and exert my utmost efforts until I reach the West. If I do not reach the West, and fail to obtain the true scripture, I dare not return to the country; I shall forever fall into the abyss of hell." He took incense before the Buddha and vowed this.

The Tang king was greatly pleased and ordered him to return, awaiting the auspicious day and propitious hour, issued a decree to send him out, and thus the imperial escort set off, returning to their respective stations.

"The great assembly was convened, awaiting the arrival of the great sutra with the envoy. Then, following the imperial decree, all officials took it upon themselves to abide by it. Meanwhile, inside the temple, someone asked, 'Who is willing to execute the emperor's will, to ascend to the Western Heavens to seek the sutra?' Before the question could be completed, a monk rushed over and paid homage to the emperor, saying, 'I am but a humble monk, willing to take on the tasks of a dog or a horse, to accompany Your Majesty in seeking the true sutra, to pray for the perpetuation of the kingdom and the dynasty.' The king of Tang was greatly delighted and approached to take the emperor's hand, saying, 'Since you, the monk, are willing to fulfill this meritorious deed, you won't be afraid of the long journey, traversing mountains and rivers; I am willing to regard you as my brother.' Xuanzang bowed to express his gratitude. The king of Tang was truly a virtuous ruler; he then went to the temple, in front of the Buddha, and bowed four times, calling Xuanzang 'Your imperial brother, saintly monk.' Xuanzang expressed his boundless gratitude, saying, 'Your Majesty, what virtues or merits do I possess that I could be so favored by Heaven with such blessings? I will surely give my life my all and persevere until I reach the Western Heavens. If I fail to attain the true sutra, I dare not return to the country; I will forever fall into the hell of transmigration.' As he finished speaking, he took incense in his hand and vowed it before the Buddha. The king was extremely pleased and ordered Xuanzang to return to his quarters. He waited for a favorable day to depart and issued an edict, after which he sent him off."

"Gather your distinguished colleagues, wait for my messenger to obtain the sacred sutras from the West, and then carry out a thorough revision of the good deeds. All officials obey my instructions accordingly. At that time, when inquired by me in the temple, 'Who among you is willing to carry out my intentions and journey to the West to pray to the Buddha to obtain the sutras?' Nobody replied, when a monk suddenly appeared beside me, bowed to the emperor and said, 'A humble monk of no merit, I am willing to exert the diligence of a dog or a horse, and, at Your Majesty's service, seek the true sutras from the West. May it ensure the prosperity of our dynasty forever.' The Emperor was greatly delighted and went forward to take the imperial hand to help the monk rise, saying, 'The monk has indeed demonstrated his sincerity and loyalty, and I am not afraid that the journey is far, traversing mountains and rivers, I am willing to consider him as my brother.' Xuanzang bowed his head in gratitude. 

The Emperor indeed possessed great virtues and sincerely went to the temple in front of the Buddha with Xuanzang, and they performed four bows to each other. Xuanzang called him 'The Holy Monk, the Brother of the Emperor.' Xuanzang expressed his gratitude without end, saying, 'Your Majesty, the humble monk has no virtues and no abilities, yet the benevolent heavenly king has looked after him with favor. I, Xuanzang, when I set out on my journey, must certainly exhaust my life and efforts, and persevere until I reach the West. If I do not get the true sutras from the West, I will not dare to return to my country, and must fall into the pit of the hells.' Having received the sacred relics from the Buddha in his hands, he took an oath before the Buddha. The Emperor was very pleased and ordered them to return to the capital. Waiting for a suitable auspicious day, he issued a decree and sent them on their way, and then returned."

"The imperial decree says to bring the sacred scriptures here, and then I shall truly cultivate good deeds," all the officials were to carry out in accordance with it. At that time, in the temple, someone asked, "Who dares to fulfill my will, to go to the west to the Buddha to request the scriptures?" The question was not yet finished when a monk walked over from the side and bowed in front of the emperor, saying, "This humble monk is unrefined, I wish to exert the effort of a dog or a horse, and beg Your Majesty to seek the true scriptures with me, and pray for the permanent stability of the empire." The King of Tang was overjoyed, he went forward and held the emperor's hand to help him up, saying, "The venerable monk indeed truly acts with virtue, not afraid of the distant journey, to traverse mountains and rivers, I am willing to enlist you as my brother." Xuanzang bowed to express his gratitude. The King of Tang truly was very virtuous, so he went to the temple in front of the Buddha and bowed to him four times, calling him "Imperial younger brother, holy monk." Xuanzang expressed his boundless gratitude, saying, "Your Majesty, this humble monk has what virtue, what ability, dare to be favored by Heaven's benevolence, such as this? When I go, I must cast my body and life, persist until I reach the west. If I do not reach the west, and do not get the true scriptures, I dare not return to the country, forever to be submerged in the hells." He took incense in front of the Buddha, with this as his vow. The King of Tang was greatly pleased, and immediately ordered the imperial decree to be returned, waiting for a propitious day and time, to issue the imperial edict to dispatch him, and thus the imperial carriage returned, the guests dispersed.

"A great ceremony was held, and I shall await for my envoy to obtain the grand scripture. When the true intentions are obtained, I shall trust in the sincerity and deeply cultivate good deeds. All officials will definitely comply. At that time, I asked in the temple, 'Who is willing to follow my will and ascend to the west to seek the true scripture?' Before the question was finished, a monk walked by and, with a bow, said to the emperor, 'Your subject is poor and ignorant, but I am willing to expend my humble efforts and, together with the emperor, seek the true scripture and pray for the permanence of the imperial dynasty.' The Tang emperor was delighted and walked forward to take the monk by the hand, saying, 'The monk is truly virtuous. I will not be afraid of the long and difficult journey, traversing mountains and rivers. I am willing to make him a brother.' Xuanzang bowed in gratitude. The Tang emperor was indeed a wise and virtuous king. He went to the temple in front of the Buddha and bowed four times, addressing Xuanzang as 'Elder Brother Holy Monk.' Xuanzang thanked him without bounds, saying, 'Your Majesty, your subject has what virtues or abilities to deserve the imperial favor and benevolence? I am going to the west, and I will surely exhaust my life in effort until I reach the west. If I do not get the true scripture, I will not dare to return home and will forever be lost in the underworld.' He took incense in front of the Buddha and used it to make an oath. The Tang emperor was delighted and ordered him to return to the palace, to wait for a propitious day to depart. He then dispatched the imperial edict and all the courtiers dispersed."

— Why is it like that? From what source is this resentment towards me now? — the prince took up, both sorrowfully and with passion. — After all, you know now that everything you thought was untrue. And I, of course, thought that your resentment towards me had not yet passed, and you know why? Because you ventured against me, that's why your resentment hasn't passed. I'm telling you that I remember that same Parfen Rogozhin, with whom I argued with crosses that day; I wrote about it to you in yesterday's letter, so that you would stop thinking about all this nonsense and wouldn't bring it up with me. What are you being shy about with me? What are you hiding your hand from me? I'm telling you that I consider all of that, which was then, to be mere nonsense: I know you inside and out, as you were back then, just as I know myself. What you imagined didn't exist and couldn't have existed. So why should our resentment exist?

— Why is this? Why have you got such a grudge against me now? — the prince asked with a mix of sadness and passion. — After all, you know now that everything you thought was untrue. And yet, I, by the way, thought that your grudge against me had long since dissipated, and you know why? Because you yourself approached me, that's why your grudge hasn't faded. I'm telling you that I remember that very Parfen Rogozhin, with whom I got acquainted that day by exchanging crosses; I wrote about it to you in yesterday's letter, so you could forget about all this nonsense and not stir it up with me. What are you shy about with me? What hand are you hiding from me? I'm telling you, I consider everything that was then to be sheer nonsense: I know myself now as if I'd known myself back then all day long. What you imagined didn't exist and couldn't exist. So why should our grudge exist?

— Why? What has brought you to such anger towards me now? — the prince replied, his voice laced with sorrow and heat. — Don't you remember that you know now that everything you thought was untrue? And I must confess, I always believed that your anger towards me had not yet passed, and you know why? Because you made a claim against me, and that's why your anger hasn't faded. I'm telling you that I remember that Parfen Rogozhin, with whom I had a falling out that day; I wrote to you about it in yesterday's letter, so that you would forget about it all and wouldn't bring it up with me. What are you holding back from me? What hand are you hiding from me? I'm telling you that all that was back then is nothing but nonsense: I now remember myself from that whole day, word for word. What you imagined didn't exist and couldn't have existed. Why should our anger exist?

— Why? What's this grudge of yours now towards me? — Prince said, sorrowfully with ardor. — After all, you yourself know now that everything you thought was a lie. And I, too, thought that your anger towards me had long since passed, and you know why? Because you yourself have wronged me, and that's why your anger hasn't passed. I'm telling you, I remember that Parfen Rogozhin, whom I had a quarrel with that day over crosses; I wrote to you about this in yesterday's letter, so you'd forget all this nonsense and not start talking about it with me. What is it you're shying away from me for? What's making you hide your hand from me? I'm telling you, I consider all that was then to be just empty chatter: I know you now as you were that day, from start to finish. What you imagined didn't exist and couldn't have existed. So why should our anger still exist?

— Why? What's this animosity of yours towards me now? — the prince seized, both sorrowful and heated. — You yourself know now that all you thought was false. And as for me, I thought all along that this animosity towards me was still in you, and you know why? Because you pitted yourself against me, and that's why your animosity hasn't passed. I'm telling you that I remember that Parfen Rogozhin, with whom I exchanged crosses that day; I wrote about it to you in yesterday's letter, so you could forget about all this nonsense and not bring it up with me again. What are you hostile to me about? What are you hiding from me? I'm telling you, I think all that was then was just madness: I recall your whole behavior that day like the palm of my hand now. What you imagined didn't exist and couldn't have existed. Why should our animosity exist?

Saying that he and his two disciples rode up, they came to the entrance of the mountain and looked, and it was indeed a temple. And on looking at it closely, there were the layered halls and pavilions, the zigzag galleries and buildings, and outside the three mountains, a dense, infinite array of multicolored clouds obscured; in front of the Hall of the Five Blessings, a dense, radiant fog of a thousand threads swirled around. There were two rows of pines and cypresses, one row of them without year or season ever known to be, as ever clear and secluded; the other row of cypresses, with forms and colors, were impressive and dignified in their beauty. He also saw the towering clock tower and the stupa tower. The Zen monks sat in quiet repose, the songs of the trees were leisurely. It was a profound stillness, free from the dusty world; it was a pure and serene land, replete with the Tao. The saying goes: 'At the top of the mountain, the lush foliage is hidden within a secluded valley, inviting one to admire the splendid scenery, which rivals the hills and valleys.' It is true that the pure land is rare in the human world, but the renowned mountains of the world are occupied by monks. The venerable elder dismounted his horse, and the traveling monk set down his load, and was about to enter the gate, when he saw a group of monks emerging from the gate. What a sight! They were wearing a left earring cap, and a garment with no defilement; with copper rings hanging from the ears and silk cords girdling the waist; their grass sandals moving in a stable step, and a wooden fish box in hand. Their lips constantly recited words of enlightenment, and their hearts were firmly attached to the path of enlightenment. The three treasures saw them, and they stood on the side of the gate, greeted them, and asked for their names, whereupon the monk hastened to respond, smiled and bowed in respect, and asked, "Where have you come from? Please, enter the Abbot's quarters to offer tea." The three treasures said, "My disciple is an emissary from the East, and has come to the Thunder Sound Temple to pray to the Buddha and seek scriptures. It is almost dusk, and I wish to borrow a night's lodging." The monk said, "Please enter inside to rest, please enter inside to rest." The three treasures then called out for the traveling monk to lead his horse inside. The monk suddenly saw the traveling monk's appearance, and was terrified, and asked, "What is that thing leading the horse?" The three treasures whispered, "Hush! Hush! His temper is short, and if you call him a thing, he will become enraged. He is my disciple."

But to continue on with the story of the master and his disciple, they rode on horseback until they arrived at the gate of the mountain.  Indeed, it was a temple. Upon seeing the tier upon tier of halls and pavilions, and the lattice-style buildings, the three mountain gates were covered in majestic wavelike clouds; the veranda of the five blessings hall was surrounded by brilliant red fog.  To the east and west, two rows of cypress and pine trees stood. The cypress trees were without age or season, maintaining their fresh, cool, tranquil beauty. The pine trees had color and a majestic spirit, looking down upon their surroundings with haughty pride. Looking higher up, one could see a grand bell-and-drum tower, and a lofty pagoda.  The monks practiced the dharma with quiet dignity; the birds sang and sang, filling the air with peacefulness. The profound silence and tranquility were of a true, and the clear emptiness was filled with the truth. 

A poem says:

In the holy mountain the autumn moss is deep,
The great scenes are like a painted screen;
The earthly realm is rare in its purity,
But all over the world, the name of these famous mountains is monopolized by the monks.

The venerable master dismounted his horse, and the pilgrim lowered his pack, just as he was about to enter when, inside the gate, a group of monks walked out.  Have a look at their appearance: they wear a single peak hat on their heads, a spotless monk's robe on their bodies, copper rings hanging from their ears, a piece of silk wrapped around their waists.  Their feet were clad in grass sandals, their hands carrying a wooden fish.  They often recited scriptures with a deep murmur, and in their hearts, they were devoted to the Prajnaparamita Sutras. 

The Tripitaka saw them and stood there on the side, greeting them with a bow, and asked: "From where have you come?  May I ask your honor to enter the abbot's quarters and offer us some tea."  The monk hurriedly returned the bow, smiled and said: "You come from where? Please, enter the abbot's quarters to present tea."  The Tripitaka said: "My disciple is an envoy from the eastern world, come to Lingyun Temple to kowtow and ask for the scriptures. The day is about to end, so I'd like to spend the night here."  The monk said: "Please enter, please enter."

The Tripitaka then called for his disciple to lead the horse in.  The monk, upon seeing the disciple's appearance, was frightened and asked: "What kind of thing is that leading the horse?"  The Tripitaka whispered to him: "Quiet!  Quiet!  He has a bad temper. If he hears you call him by any name, he will be angry.  He is my disciple."

But it was said that the master and his two disciples arrived in haste, came and came until they reached the entrance to the mountain, and it indeed turned out to be a temple. As they gazed at the tiered halls and pagodas, the various roofs, the vermilion doors covered in an array of fine mist; and the five blessings hall with the vibrant red fog swirling around it. The two rows of pine and cypress trees, one stood untainted by time and years in quiet seclusion; the other stood out with its vibrant hues, rivaling the beauty of an elegant fairy. There was the high pagoda, the stupa standing tall and majestic. The monks sat in meditation, with the birds singing a carefree tune in the quiet trees. The stillness was as empty as the void, but still contained the essence of the empty; the clarity was as pure as a cloud, but still possessed the truth of the clear. There's a poem that says:

High and remote is the mountain, hidden in verdant foliage;
Inviting us to come and enjoy the spectacular view.

Indeed, the pure land is rarely seen in the human world,
The famous mountains of the world have many monks living here.

The elder got down from his horse, and the monk got off his pack,
Just as they were about to enter, they saw a group of monks coming out of the door. 

How would you describe their appearance? Their heads wore double-layered skullcaps, and their bodies were clad in spotless robes. Around their ears hung a pair of copper rings, their waists were tied with a sash of silk. Their walking sticks moved steadily as they came; in their hands they held wooden fish. Their mouths were always reciting sutras and uttering vows to the infinite universe. 

The three treasures (Buddhist master Tripitaka) saw them, stood beside the gate and greeted them with a bow, asking "How are you?" The monk immediately returned the bow, and smiled and bowed, and asked: "Where are you from? Come in and I'll bring you tea to the abbot." Tripitaka replied, "My disciple is a special envoy from the East, going to the Thunder Sound Temple to pay respects to the Buddha and seek the scriptures. The day is late, and I wish to rest here for the night." The monk said, "Please come in and sit, please come in and sit." Just as Tripitaka was calling for Monkey to bring in the horse, the monk suddenly saw Monkey's appearance and became frightened, and asked, "What is that creature that's leading the horse?" Tripitaka whispered to him, "Whisper, whisper! He's hot-headed, if you call him a creature, he'll get angry. He's my disciple."

Said he and his disciples, mounted and riding, came forward to the mountain gate to look; sure enough, it was a temple. Looking at the layer upon layer of halls and pavilions, and the interconnected corridors and halls, three mountain gates outside, were towering ten thousand streams of colorful clouds that shrouded it; five Happiness Halls in front, were fragrant a thousand threads of red mist that encircled it. Two rows of pines and cypresses, one line of pine and cypress trees, there were none to discern the passing of the seasons; there was color, there was hue, and was as proud as it was lovely. And there was that high stupa of the drum and bell tower, and the lofty Buddhist pagoda. The Venerable Monks sat in contemplation, the sweet songs of the crying trees swaying gently in the breeze. The silent and stillness was real, it was true silence, and the quietness and emptiness was filled with the Tao, and it was truly pure. The poem goes:

In the mountain monasteries, the Pruning Garden is hidden amidst the verdant verdure,
 Inviting the excellence in scenery to vie with the hundred beauties. 
As the land is so pure and the world is not so fertile with such gems, the monks at the world's famous mountains outnumber those at the earthly world. 

The elder dismounted his horse, and the pilgrim put down his load, and was just about to enter the gate when he saw a group of monks come out of the gate. Look at them how dignified and elegant: wearing a junzi hat on their heads, and wearing clean robes on their bodies. Copper rings hanging from their ears, silk belts binding their waists, grass-soled shoes were making their footsteps steady, and they held wooden fish in their hands.  Their mouths were reciting the name, repeatedly repeating the Mantra of Enlightenment. Trikaya saw them, and stood to one side, he bowed and asked for salutations. The monk was quick to bow in return, and with a smile said, "Where are you from? I invite you to the principal hall to offer tea." Trikaya said, "I am a disciple from the East, sent on a mission, came to the Lion's Roar Temple to pray to the Buddha and request scriptures. By the time I arrived, the day was drawing to a close, and I wish to stay here for a night." That monk said, "Please go in and rest, please go in and rest." Trikaya then called for his disciple to lead the horse in. That monk, however, upon seeing the pilgrim, was startled, and asked, "What in the world is that leading the horse?" Trikaya said in a low voice, "Hush, hush! His temper is hot. If he hears what you say, he will be enraged. He is my disciple."

It so happened that the master and his disciple came up, leading their horses, and rode forward until they reached the entrance to the mountain temple. Upon arrival, they saw indeed that it was a temple. Beholding the tiered pavilions, the layered halls, and the carefully arranged verandas, they also saw the majestic three great gates, on which thousands of fluttering clouds drifted by. Before the Five Fortune Hall, a vast expanse of crimson mist swirled about. Two groves of cedars stood on either side, their luxuriant branches in serene solitude for ages untold. The two groves of cedars had never seen the passage of time, nor the recording of annals; the single grove of cypresses had colors and hues and resplendent beauty. Furthermore, they saw the high Buddhist pagoda and the majestic, stately Buddhist bell tower. The devout monks had a tranquil mind, while birds with bird cries sang with ease. The complete stillness was a true stillness, the extreme quietness possessed a true essence. 

The poem says: "In the remote area of Upper Temple, the verdant shelter is ever so lovely, inviting the world to behold a wondrous sight. It truly is a place where heaven and earth have few people but many famous mountains. Many Taoist hermits reside here." The elder dismounted his horse, and the traveler rested his burden. Just as they were about to enter the gate, out came a group of monks from the gate. You look at him how he looks: his head is wearing a tufted hat, his body is dressed in a hair-shirt. He has copper rings dangling from his ears, and a silk belt binding his waist. He walks sturdily in his cloth shoes, and holds a wooden fish in his hands. He often murmurs a mantra in his mouth, always devoted to the practice of Pure Land. The Three Relics Master saw him, and stood by the side of the gate, and asked for a greeting. The monk quickly bowed down, smiling and looking delighted, and asked, "You come from where? Please enter the Buddhist hall to present tea." The Three Relics Master replied, "My disciple is a special envoy from the Eastern Country, and I come to the Heavenly Sound Temple to offer incense to the Buddha and request the scriptures. The sun is about to set, so I wish to spend the night at this temple." The monk said, "Please go in and rest, please go in and rest." The Three Relics Master then called out to have the traveler lead in his horse. But upon seeing the traveler's appearance, the monk looked somewhat frightened, and asked, "What is that thing you call your horse?" The Three Relics Master whispered, "Quietly! Quietly! It has a hasty nature. If you speak of it as something, it will be enraged. He is my disciple."

— Just so, but don't get carried away. Since only three out of all the Russian writers have so far managed to say something truly their own, their own property, unborrowed from anyone else, it is precisely these three who have at once become national. Whoever among the Russian people says, writes, or does something of their own, their inalienable and unborrowed thing, inevitably becomes national, although they may speak Russian poorly. That's an axiom for me. "Today is no interrogation," said the woman. "Why should there not be an interrogation?" he asked, and did not want to believe it. But the woman convinced him by opening the door to the next room. K. asked, not out of particular curiosity, but so as not to have been completely pointless here. "No," said the woman and closed the door again, "that is not allowed. The Great Sage emerged victorious, and took back his whiskers. Hurriedly turning around, he returned to his cave, and just as he arrived, he saw the Iron Bridge at the entrance, where the four capable generals, leading the troops, rushed out to meet him, choked and sobs broke out in three great cries, and then sobbed and laughed three times in succession. The Great Sage asked, "Why do you all cry and laugh at seeing me?" The four capable generals said, "This morning, we led the troops and battled with the Heavenly King, capturing the 72 evil demons and the Single Horned Devil King, and all were caught by the gods. We managed to escape with our lives, hence the crying. And seeing the Great Sage return victorious, without sustaining any damage, we therefore laugh." The Great Sage said, "Victory and defeat are a normal occurrence in warfare. The ancients said, 'For every thousand men killed, three thousand of one's own are injured.' Moreover, the leaders we've captured are tigers, leopards, wolves, hounds, badgers, rabbits, and foxes - my own kind who haven't been hurt, what need to be worried about? Although I've driven them off with a magical technique, they will still set up camp beneath our mountain. Let us tighten our defenses, enjoy a full meal, and rest, so we can concentrate on our spirits. Come morning, we'll use a mighty divine technique, capture these heavenly generals, and take revenge on them." The four generals and the troop of monkey warriors had a few bowls of coconut wine and, with tranquil hearts, fell asleep.

The Great Sage obtained victory, gathered his whiskers, and hurried back to the cave. Again, I saw the iron-board bridgehead, and four sturdy generals led the multitude to pay respects to the Great Sage, chokingly sobbing three times and heartily laughing three times. The Great Sage asked, "Why did you all see me and cry and laugh?" The four sturdy generals said, "This morning, our commander led the troops to battle with the Heavenly King, captured the seventy-two-demon king and the one-horned devil king, and all of them were caught by the heavenly army. We escaped with our lives, hence we should cry. Seeing the Great Sage returned victorious without being hurt, we should therefore laugh." The Great Sage said, "Victory and defeat are common in warfare. Ancient people said, 'Killing one thousand men results in three thousand losses.' And the ones we captured are merely the big cats, big tigers, wolves, badgers, hares, foxes, and leopards – not a single member of my own kind was harmed. Let us not worry about it. He may have been driven off by my splitting-body art, but he will still set up camp beneath our mountain. Let us closely guard, have a full meal, and rest soundly, cultivating our spirits. At daybreak, we'll use my divine power, take these heavenly generals and avenge ourselves." The four generals and the multitude of monkey soldiers ate a few bowls of coconut wine, and then rested soundly.

The Great Sage emerged victorious, collected the fluff from his scalp, and quickly turned back to his cave, only to see the iron bridge once more, where the four mighty warriors stood with the crowd, bowing and greeting the Great Sage, sobbing three times with hiccupping sobs, then bursting into three loud, chest-heaving laughs. The Great Sage asked, "Why are you all crying and laughing? Have you seen me?" The four warriors replied, "Today we led the troops into battle against the Heavenly King, and all the monarchs of the seventy-two hells and the solitary horned devil were captured by the gods, so we wept with joy that we ourselves were spared. Now we see the Great Sage has returned victorious and unscathed, and we can't help but laugh." The Great Sage said, "Victory and defeat are common in war. Ancient people said, 'For every thousand men you kill, three thousand of your own are injured.' Besides, the captured leaders we caught were tigers, panthers, wolves, badgers, and foxes, and I've not hurt a single one of my own kind. They may have been repelled by my magic, but they'll still be camped at the foot of my mountain. We'll just strengthen our defenses, have a hearty meal, and rest soundly, cultivating our spirits. Come dawn, we'll use a divine trick to capture these heavenly generals and avenge the crowd." The four warriors and the troop of monkey generals finished a few bowls of coconut wine and slept soundly.

When the Great Sage was victorious, he collected his hairs and hurried back to his cave. As he returned early, he saw the Iron Plateau Bridge, where the four generals were leading their troops in greeting him, bowing down on the ground. They sobbed loudly three times, and then burst into loud laughter three times. The Great Sage asked, "Why do you see me and cry and laugh alternatively?" The four generals replied, "This morning, the commander and we generals went to battle with the Heavenly King, and captured the 72 demonic kings of the Hidden Realm and the Single-Horned Ghost King. The gods took them prisoner. We barely escaped with our lives, hence the crying. Now that the Great Sage has returned victorious, without any injuries, hence the laughter." The Great Sage said, "Victory and defeat are common in war. It is said, 'For every thousand people killed, three thousand suffer injuries.' Furthermore, the chiefs we captured are all tigers, leopards, wolves, badgers, rabbits, and foxes. I, a member of the Monkey tribe, have not suffered a single loss. They may have been repelled by my Transfiguration magic, but they will still camp at my mountain's foot. We'll be on guard, eat a hearty meal, and rest. We'll keep our spirits up and wait until morning to use my divine abilities to catch those heavenly soldiers and exact revenge." The four generals and the Monkey troop drank a few bowls of fermented palm wine and fell fast asleep.

Great Sage prevailed, collected the strands of hair, and turned around to return to the cave. It was still early, and he saw the Iron Sand Bridge ahead, with four strong warriors leading the troops to welcome the Great Sage. They choked with sobs and wailed three times, and then let out three rounds of bursts of laughter. The Great Sage said, "You all see me, yet cry and laugh, what's the reason?" The four strong warriors said, "Today, we led the troops to battle with the Heavenly King and fought the 72 demon kings and the Unicorn King. All of them were captured by the gods, and we were lucky to escape. So I should cry. Seeing the Great Sage return victorious and unscathed, I should laugh." The Great Sage said, "Victory and defeat are the norm in the art of war. It is said, 'Kill a thousand men, and you suffer a loss of three hundred.' Moreover, the leaders we captured are tigers, leopards, wolves, civet cats, rabbits, and foxes, none of my kind were hurt. I used my art of transmigration to drive them off, but they'll still set up camp at the foot of my mountain. Let us tighten our defense, eat our fill, and rest well. We'll wait until morning to use my great spiritual power to capture those heavenly generals and take revenge on behalf of the people." The four generals and the monkey troops drank several bowls of rice wine and fell asleep, as for that matter.

Just as the hubbub was subsiding, the True Lord arrived, inquiring, "Brothers, where did they vanish?" The gods replied, "We were right here, surrounding them, and then they vanished." Erlang widened his eyes, took a look, and saw the Great Sage transformed into a sparrow, nailed to a tree. He collected his magical sword, discarded the divine dagger, unbent his bow, changed his form with a wave of his hand, transformed into a falcon, flapped his wings, and flew off to strike. The Great Sage saw him and, with a flutter of his wings, transformed into an old owl and took to the sky. Erlang saw him and hastily shook out his feathers, changed his form with a wave of his hand, and transformed into a great white crane, flying up to the clouds. The Great Sage, in turn, lowered his body, plunged into the ravine, and transformed into a fish. Erlang rushed to the edge of the ravine, but found no trace of him. He thought to himself, "This fellow must surely have dived into the water, and must have changed into a fish or shrimp of some sort. Let me change shape and catch him." True enough, he changed his form and became a fish-eagle, drifting about on the water's surface. After a moment, the Great Sage transformed into a fish, swimming smoothly along, when he spotted a bird, like a kestrel, with feathers that were not grey; like a heron, without a crest; like a kite, but its legs not red. "Must be that Erlang has changed shape and is waiting for me!" he thought...he hastily turned his head and flew off. Erlang saw him go, saying, "The fish with a flower on its head, like a carp, but its tail not red; like a mandarin fish, with no scales; like a black fish, but no star on its head; like a crucian carp, with no needle on its cheek. Why did he see me and fly away? It must be that the Monkey King has changed shape." He hastened to the spot and, with a flash, snapped his beak. The Great Sage leapt out of the water and changed, transforming into a water snake, swimming towards the shore and burrowing into the grass. Erlang, having failed to catch him, heard the sound of splashing water, saw a water snake slither out, recognized it as the Great Sage, and hastily turned around, changing into a red-plumed grey crane, its long beak resembling an iron tongs, and came to devour the water snake. The water snake sprang up, changed into a flower snipe, dull and plodding, standing on the papyrus patch. Erlang saw him change into something lowly and contemptible - a snipe, the lowest of birds, deemed the most lustful of all - so he did not pursue him, but instead transformed back into his original form, took his bow, drew back the string, and shot an arrow at him, striking him with a 'Foot of the Dragon'.

As they chattered, a True Ruler arrived, asking, "Brothers, where have you gone?" The gods replied, "We were just here surrounding, and now we don't see you." Erlang opened his eyes wide to look, and upon seeing the Great Sage transformed into a sparrow, nailed to a tree, he retrieved his supernatural talisman, sheathed his holy dagger, put down his bow, shook his body, and transformed into a bird of prey, flapping his wings to fly away to attack. The Great Sage saw him, raised his wing to take flight, and transformed into a big old goose, soaring to the heavens. Erlang saw him, shook his feathers, shook his body, and transformed into a big sea crane, soaring up into the clouds to catch him. The Great Sage pressed his body back down, plunged into the ravine, transformed into a fish, and submerged into the water. Erlang arrived at the ravine, but saw no sign of him. He thought to himself, "This little monkey must have gone into the water too. He will definitely transform into some fish, crab, or shellfish. I'll wait a bit and transform to catch him." He transformed into a fish-bird and hovered above the rippling waves. A while passed, and the Great Sage transformed into a fish, swimming smoothly, when he suddenly saw a bird with feathers not green like a sparrow, not long like a heron, and not red-legged like a stork: "It must be Erlang transforming into something to wait for me!" He turned his head and left in a flash. Erlang saw him, "The fish with the white tail, like a carp, but its tail isn't red; like a mandarin fish, but its scales don't shine; like a black fish, but its head doesn't have stars; like a catfish, but its cheeks don't have whiskers. Why did he see me and then leave? He must be that monkey transforming again." He chased after him, and, with a loud beak peck, the Great Sage splashed out of the water, transformed into a water snake, swam up to the shore, and burrowed into the grass. Erlang could not grasp him, and when he heard the splash, he saw a water snake splashing out, recognized it as the Great Sage, and rapidly transformed into a juan-red crested grey crane, stretching a long beak, similar to a pair of sharp-toothed iron tongs, and came to eat that water snake. The water snake jumped once, and transformed into a flower wood pigeon, standing listlessly on the lotus pond. Erlang seeing him degrade to being low and debased – the flower wood pigeon is the most base and lustful of all birds, not minding the dilly-bird, the phoenix, the eagle, or the crow, all of which associate with it – he did not pursue, but instead took his true form, walked away, drew his bow, and filled it with an arrow. He then shot it, hitting him with a might that kicked him to the ground.

Just then, the Patriarch arrived, asking, "Brothers, where did the fugitive disappear to?" The gods said, "We were all standing here surrounding him, and suddenly he was gone." Erlang's eyes widened in a circle as he looked around and saw the Great Sage transformed into a sparrow, nailed to a tree. He collected his spirit sword, sheathed his divine whiskers, removed his bow, shook his body, and transformed into a falcon, spreading his wings and flying off. The Great Sage saw him and raised a wing in flight, transforming into a big old swan, soaring into the heavens. Erlang saw him and quickly shook his feathers, transforming into a big sea crane, diving into the clouds to strike. The Great Sage again transformed, entering the ravine, changing into a fish. Erlang ran to the edge of the ravine and couldn't see any sign of him. He thought to himself, "This monkey must have dived into the water, and he must have transformed into a fish, shrimp, or something like that. I'll just wait a bit and transform again to catch him." After a while, the Great Sage transformed into a fish, swimming along the water, when suddenly he saw a bird flying above, which looked like a blue kite, but its feathers were not blue; it looked like a heron, but had no crest; it looked like an old crane, but its legs were not red: "I bet Erlang has transformed into a bird to wait for me!" The fish quickly turned its head and swam away in a splash. Erlang saw the splashing fish and said, "This fish looks like a carp, but its tail is not red; it looks like a mandarin fish, but it has no scales; it looks like a black fish, but it has no star on its head; it looks like a crucian carp, but it has no whisker; how did it see me and swim away so quickly? It must be that monkey transformed." Erlang chased after and struck the fish with a beak, but the fish swam out of the water, transforming into a snake and slithering into the grass. Erlang couldn't catch him, but then he saw the commotion in the water, and a snake was swimming out, which he recognized as the Great Sage, so he transformed into a crested grebe with a crimson crest on its head, extending a long beak, which resembled a pair of sharp iron scissors, and came to devour the snake. The snake jumped out of the water, transforming into a water hen, standing stolidly on the Caltrops above the lotus pad. Erlang saw that he had transformed into a low and despicable creature, a water hen being the most base and lustful among birds, which were often seen associating with all manner of creatures; therefore, he did not approach him, and instead assumed his true form, and walked away, took up his bow and drew it full, and shot an arrow at him, striking him with a solid thud.

Just then, True King arrived, inquired, "Brothers, where has he gone?" The gods replied, "He was just here, then he vanished." Erlang's phoenix eyes widened as he took a look, and saw the Great Sage transformed into a sparrow, nailed to a tree. He then put away his talisman, discarded his divine spear, took off his bow, and, with a single transformation, changed into a bird of prey. It spread its wings and flew off to strike. The Great Sage saw him and flapped his wings to fly up, transformed into a large old duck, and flew straight up into the sky. Erlang saw him and hastily ruffled his feathers, then transformed into a large sea crane, and flew up to him with its beak. The Great Sage then put himself down and transformed into a fish, and submerged himself in the water. Erlang arrived at the water's edge, but could see no sign of him. He thought to himself, "This ape must have certainly gone into the water. He must have transformed into something like fish or shrimp. Let me transform into something else and catch him." Indeed, he transformed into a fish eagle, drifting on the surface of the waves. After a moment, the Great Sage transformed into a fish, and was swimming steadily down the stream, when he suddenly saw a flying bird, with feathers that were not green like a falcon, nor crestlike on top like a heron, nor red legs like an old crane: "It must be that Erlang has transformed to wait for me...!" He hastily turned his head, and fled in confusion. Erlang said, "The fish I chased is like a carp, with no red tail; like a mandarin fish, with no scales; like a black fish, with no star on its head; like a carp, with no barb on its cheek. Why did it flee from me as soon as it saw me? It must have been the Monkey King!" He rushed forward, and in a flash of lightning, beaked him. The Great Sage then splashed out of the water, transformed, and became a water snake, swimming towards the shore, then burrowed into the grass. Erlang couldn't catch him, so he saw a snake splash out of the water, and recognized it as the Great Sage. He turned around hastily, and transformed into a vermilion-roofed grey crane, with a long beak, like an iron pincer, and came straight to eat the water snake. The water snake leaped out of the way, then transformed into a tree sparrow, looking disheveled, standing on a willow dike. Erlang saw that he had become base and depraved – the sparrow is the most contemptible and debased of birds, and the crane, eagle, crow, and other birds all avoid it – so he didn't go after it, and instead, he retransformed into his original form, and went his way, taking up his bow and pulling it taut, and shot a pellet that hit the Great Sage with the force of a thousand pounds.

Just as that was, the Young Lord arrived, asking, "Brothers, where have those fellows gone?" The gods said, "We were just standing around here, and then they vanished." Erlang opened wide his phoenix eyes to look, saw the Great Saint transformed into a sparrow, nailed to a tree, and thus took back his magic seal, discarded his divine sword, put down his crossbow, and with a shake of his body transformed into a sparrow hawk. He spread his wings and flew off to pounce. The Great Saint saw him, seized his wing in a swoop, and turned himself into a big old goose, flying up to the heavens. Erlang saw him, threw off his feathers in agitation, and with a shake of his body transformed into a big sea crane, soaring up to the clouds to grab him. The Great Saint then pressed his body down, plunged into the ravine, and transformed into a fish, plunging into the water.

Erlang rushed to the edge of the ravine, and didn't see a trace. He thought to himself in secret, "This monkey must certainly have gone down into the water, and must have transformed into some kind of fish or shrimp. I'll just transform again and catch him." So he transformed into a fish hawk, floating on the face of the whirlpool's wave. After a moment, the Great Saint had transformed into a fish, swimming along the water, when he suddenly saw a flying bird, with feathers not a bit green, like a goshawk, but no crest on the top; like a heron, but no plumes; like an old stork, but its legs were not red: "I suppose Erlang has transformed to wait for me!..." - He turned his head hastily and flew off with a whistling sound. Erlang said, "The whistling fish, looks like a carp, its tail is not red; looks like a loach, but it doesn't have scales; looks like a black fish, but it has no star on its head; looks like a silver carp, but it doesn't have a whisker on its cheek. How can it see me and fly off? It must be that the monkey has transformed." He chased up to it, and the Great Saint suddenly leapt out of the water, transforming into a water snake, swimming close to the shore, and slithering into the grass. Erlang missed him, and since he heard a commotion in the water, he saw a snake slithering out, and knew it was the Great Saint, and turned his body again, transforming into a scarlet-plumed grey crane with a long beak, like a pair of sharp-pointed iron pincers, coming to eat the water snake. The water snake jumped out of the water, and transformed into a duck-pheasant, standing dumbly on the lotus bank. Erlang seeing that he had become a lowly creature - the duck-pheasant is the lowest and most wanton of all birds, and even the qilin, phoenix, eagle, and crow wouldn't associate with it - he didn't go to catch it, and revealed his true form, walking away, took over his crossbow, drew the string tight, and shot a bolt at him, striking him right on the back of his heel.

The thought of the proceedings had long haunted him. He had often considered writing a defense statement and submitting it to the court. He wanted to include a brief description of his life and, for every significant event, explain the reasons behind his actions, whether they should be accepted or rejected in light of current circumstances, and the grounds he had for this or that. The benefits of a defense statement over the defense provided by the somewhat unreliable lawyer were undeniable. K. did not know what the lawyer was doing; it was probably little, as he had not summoned him for a month, and during previous meetings K. had the impression that this man could accomplish little for him. Moreover, he had not been questioned thoroughly. 

On the contrary, instead of asking questions, the lawyer told stories or sat silently opposite K., leaned forward, probably because of his poor hearing, and nodded over the desk, pulled on a tuft of his beard within his beard, and looked down at the carpet, perhaps exactly at the spot where K. had lain with Leni. Occasionally, he gave K. some empty warnings, the kind given to children. These were as useless as they were dull, and K. was determined to pay him nothing in the final reckoning. 

After the lawyer had sufficiently humiliated him, he would usually begin to cheer him up. He had, he said, won many similar cases, completely or partially, and, although these cases may not have been as difficult as this one in reality, they appeared hopeless to the outside world. He had a list of these cases in this drawer – he knocked on some shelf of the desk – but, unfortunately, he could not show the documents because they were classified as official secrets. Nonetheless, this extensive experience, which he had gained through all these cases, was an advantage for K. He had begun working on the case right away, and the first application was almost completed. It was important because the initial impression the defense made often determined the direction of the proceedings. Unfortunately, he had to warn K. that it sometimes happened that the initial applications were not even read by the court. They were simply added to the files and noted that, for the time being, the interrogation and observation of the accused were more important than anything written. When the petitioner became insistent, they added that, when all the material had been collected, the case would be reviewed in connection with all the files, including the first application. However, it usually did not happen that way; the first application was often misplaced or entirely lost, and even if it remained until the end, it was rarely read. 

This was a shame, but not entirely unjustifiable. K. should not forget that the proceedings were not public; if the court deemed it necessary, they could become public, but the law did not require it. As a result, the court's documents, particularly the indictment, were inaccessible to the accused and his defense. Consequently, one often did not know exactly what the first application should respond to; it could only contain something relevant to the case by chance. Only later, during the interrogations of the accused, would the individual charges and their grounds become clearer, and one could then produce genuine and relevant applications. Under these circumstances, the defense was in an unfavorable and difficult position. 

However, this was also intended. The defense was not allowed by the law, but only tolerated. Even the question of whether the law even allowed tolerance in this case was disputed. In reality, there were no officially recognized lawyers before this court; all those who appeared as lawyers were, in essence, just court-appointed lawyers. This naturally humiliated the profession as a whole, and if K. were to visit the courtrooms, he could, out of curiosity, look at the lawyers' office. He would probably be shocked by the society there. 

The narrow, low room indicated the contempt in which the court held these people. The room was only lit by a small window high up, making it necessary for anyone who wanted to look out to find a colleague who could stand behind him and support him, as the smoke from a nearby stove would blow into one's face and darken it. In the floor of this room – to cite another example of these conditions – there was a hole, not large enough for a person to fall through, but big enough to make one's leg sink in. The lawyers' office was on the second attic floor, so if someone were to fall, their leg would hang down into the first attic and precisely into the corridor where the parties were waiting. It would be no exaggeration to say that in lawyer circles such conditions were considered scandalous. Complaints to the administration were pointless, and it was strictly forbidden for lawyers to make any changes to the room at their own expense. However, this treatment of lawyers also had its justification. The aim was to eliminate the defense as far as possible, making everything depend on the accused himself. This was not a bad point in principle, but it would be a fatal mistake to conclude from it that lawyers were unnecessary before this court. On the contrary, they were more necessary here than anywhere else. 

The proceedings were not only secret from the public but also from the accused. This was possible to a great extent, as the accused did not have access to the court documents, and it was difficult to infer the underlying documents from the interrogations. This made the defense necessary. At interrogations, defense lawyers were usually not allowed to be present, so they had to question the accused after the interrogation, often in the doorway to the interrogation room, and try to extract from the often unclear reports what was relevant to the defense. However, this was not the most important thing. What mattered most was the personal connections of the lawyer. It was in these relationships that the value of the defense lay. K. had already learned from his own experiences that the court's lowest levels were not entirely efficient, that there were employees who were forgetful of their duties and corrupt. This meant that the court's strict isolation was not absolute. 

It was here that most lawyers tried to gain entry, where they were bribed and questioned, and in some cases, even court documents were stolen. It was not to be denied that, at least for the time being, some lawyers could achieve surprisingly favorable results for the accused, with which these small lawyers would proudly walk around and attract new clients. However, for the continued course of the proceedings, this meant nothing or nothing good. Only honest personal relationships, particularly with higher-ranking officials, were genuinely valuable. Only through these could the proceedings, at first only imperceptibly, but later more clearly, be influenced. Only a few lawyers could demonstrate such connections, and K.'s choice had been very fortunate. Perhaps only one or two lawyers could claim similar connections like Dr. Huld. They, however, were not concerned with the society in the lawyers' office and had no dealings with it. On the other hand, their connections with the court officials were much closer. It was not even necessary for Dr. Huld to appear in court; he would wait in the ante-chamber of the investigating judges, and depending on their mood, he would either achieve a seeming success or not achieve one at all. No, K. had seen for himself that the officials, including high-ranking ones, would come to him willingly, provide information, open or at least easily understandable, discuss the next steps in the case, and in individual cases, they could even be convinced and take on a foreign opinion. However, one should not rely too much on this in this regard, for even if they express a new, favorable intention for the defense, they might immediately go to their office the next day and issue a court ruling that directly contradicts this intention and is even harsher for the accused than their first intention, which they claimed to have abandoned. This, of course, cannot be objected to, for what they say between themselves is only said between themselves and does not allow for any public consequences. Besides, it is also correct that the officials are not only motivated by friendship or benevolent feelings when they deal with the defense, but also, in a certain sense, depend on it. The weakness of the court's organization is evident here, which sets the court as a secret institution from the start. The officials lack a connection to the public, and for ordinary, medium-sized cases, they are well-equipped; such a case runs almost on its own, requiring only occasional prompts. However, in simple cases and in particularly complex ones, they are often at a loss, as they are constantly bound to their law and lack a sense of human relationships, which they miss in such cases. Then they turn to the lawyer for advice, and a servant carries the files that are otherwise so secret.

This naturally cast a disparaging light on the entire profession, and when K. next visited the court offices, he could, to see it for himself, take a look at the lawyers' room. He would likely be shocked by the company present there. The small, low room spoke for itself, revealing the contempt in which the court held this class of people. The room only got any light through a small window high up, so that if one wanted to look out, the smoke from the chimney of a nearby furnace would blow into one's face and soot it, and one would have to ask a colleague to support one on the back. This is, of course, only possible to a very great extent; nevertheless, it is possible. It was here that most lawyers pressed their way in, here they were bribed and interrogated, and, at least in earlier times, there were even cases of theft of court documents. No, K. had seen it himself, high officials, among them quite high-ranking ones, would come to him, and give him information freely, openly or at least transparently, discuss the further course of the proceedings with him, and sometimes even allow themselves to be convinced and would accept foreign opinions gladly. However, one should not place too much trust in this, as they might, as soon as they had decided on a favorable intention for the defense, go back to their office and issue a court decision the very next day that was directly opposed to their earlier intention, and perhaps even stricter for the accused than their earlier intention.
